0.title: Give Us a King: The Book of 1 Samuel
0.overview:
First Samuel is a dramatic, psychologically rich and theologically deep book. It spans roughly a century, from the birth of Samuel under the corrupt priesthood of Eli's sons to the deterioration of Saul and the rise of David. At its center stands one epoch-making demand: Now appoint for us a king to judge us like all the nations (8:5). God's response, they have not rejected you, but they have rejected me from being king over them (8:7), frames everything that follows.

The book moves in three parts. Samuel (chapters 1–7): the last judge, who holds a collapsing nation together by intercession and integrity. Saul (chapters 8–15): the people's king, tall and impressive, who cannot obey and cannot repent. David (chapters 16–31): the man after God's own heart, hunted by Saul's hatred and sustained by covenant friendship and the Spirit of the Lord.

Who wrote Samuel? The book does not say. Samuel cannot have written it all, since his death is recorded (25:1); it probably draws on the records of Samuel, Nathan and Gad (1 Chr 29:29) and was completed after the kingdom divided (27:6). It was one book in the Hebrew Bible, divided in two by the Greek translators because of its length. Many scholars see it as part of a longer history running from Deuteronomy to Kings; how and when it was edited is debated. Its frank portraits of Saul’s failures and David’s sins are hard to explain as royal propaganda, and its places and customs fit the world of about 1000 BC. Its Hebrew text is sometimes uncertain; the Dead Sea Scrolls often side with the Greek translation (the Septuagint), and English versions note where they follow them (1:24; 13:1).

Christologically, 1 Samuel is a treasury. Hannah's prayer is the seed of the Magnificat, and her he will give strength to his king and exalt the horn of his anointed (2:10) is an early use of mashiach (anointed one, the word behind Messiah) that reaches beyond any king then living. Samuel, prophet, intercessor and judge, points to Jesus, in whom prophet, priest and king are one. The ark narratives (chs. 4–6) tell of the glory departing (4:21); that glory finally dwells among us in Christ (John 1:14). And in David, the shepherd-king on whom the Spirit rushes, who fights for his paralyzed people and will not seize the kingdom by force, the attentive reader sees the shape of One greater than David.

The book puts it in one sentence: man looks on the outward appearance, but the LORD looks on the heart (16:7). That inversion of human values, the youngest son anointed, the smooth stone over the giant's spear, is the grammar of grace, and it reaches its height when the carpenter's son from Nazareth is crowned on a cross.

1.title: The Barren Woman's Prayer
1.text: <sup>1</sup>There was a certain man of Ramathaim-zophim of the hill country of Ephraim whose name was Elkanah the son of Jeroham, son of Elihu, son of Tohu, son of Zuph, an Ephrathite.<sup>2</sup>He had two wives. The name of the one was Hannah, and the name of the other, Peninnah. And Peninnah had children, but Hannah had no children.<sup>3</sup>Now this man used to go up year by year from his city to worship and to sacrifice to the LORD of hosts at Shiloh, where the two sons of Eli, Hophni and Phinehas, were priests of the LORD.<sup>4</sup>On the day when Elkanah sacrificed, he would give portions to Peninnah his wife and to all her sons and daughters.<sup>5</sup>But to Hannah he gave a double portion, because he loved her, though the LORD had closed her womb.<sup>6</sup>And her rival used to provoke her grievously to irritate her, because the LORD had closed her womb.<sup>7</sup>So it went on year by year. As often as she went up to the house of the LORD, she used to provoke her. Therefore Hannah wept and would not eat.<sup>8</sup>And Elkanah, her husband, said to her, "Hannah, why do you weep? And why do you not eat? And why is your heart sad? Am I not more to you than ten sons?"<sup>9</sup>After they had eaten and drunk in Shiloh, Hannah rose. Now Eli the priest was sitting on the seat beside the doorpost of the temple of the LORD.<sup>10</sup>She was deeply distressed and prayed to the LORD and wept bitterly.<sup>11</sup>And she vowed a vow and said, "O LORD of hosts, if you will indeed look on the affliction of your servant and remember me and not forget your servant, but will give to your servant a son, then I will give him to the LORD all the days of his life, and no razor shall touch his head."<sup>12</sup>As she continued praying before the LORD, Eli observed her mouth.<sup>13</sup>Hannah was speaking in her heart; only her lips moved, and her voice was not heard. Therefore Eli took her to be a drunken woman.<sup>14</sup>And Eli said to her, "How long will you go on being drunk? Put your wine away from you."<sup>15</sup>But Hannah answered, "No, my lord, I am a woman troubled in spirit. I have drunk neither wine nor strong drink, but I have been pouring out my soul before the LORD.<sup>16</sup>Do not regard your servant as a worthless woman, for all along I have been speaking out of my great anxiety and vexation."<sup>17</sup>Then Eli answered, "Go in peace, and the God of Israel grant your petition that you have made to him."<sup>18</sup>And she said, "Let your servant find favor in your eyes." Then the woman went her way and ate, and her face was no longer sad.<sup>19</sup>They rose early in the morning and worshiped before the LORD; then they went back to their house at Ramah. And Elkanah knew Hannah his wife, and the LORD remembered her.<sup>20</sup>And in due time Hannah conceived and bore a son, and she called his name Samuel, for she said, "I have asked for him from the LORD."<sup>21</sup>The man Elkanah and all his house went up to offer to the LORD the yearly sacrifice and to pay his vow.<sup>22</sup>But Hannah did not go up, for she said to her husband, "As soon as the child is weaned, I will bring him, so that he may appear in the presence of the LORD and dwell there forever."<sup>23</sup>Elkanah her husband said to her, "Do what seems best to you; wait until you have weaned him; only, may the LORD establish his word." So the woman remained and nursed her son until she weaned him.<sup>24</sup>And when she had weaned him, she took him up with her, along with a three-year-old bull, an ephah of flour, and a skin of wine, and she brought him to the house of the LORD at Shiloh. And the child was young.<sup>25</sup>Then they slaughtered the bull, and they brought the child to Eli.<sup>26</sup>And she said, "Oh, my lord! As you live, my lord, I am the woman who was standing here in your presence, praying to the LORD.<sup>27</sup>For this child I prayed, and the LORD has granted me my petition that I made to him.<sup>28</sup>Therefore I have lent him to the LORD. As long as he lives, he is lent to the LORD." And he worshiped the LORD there.
1.overview:
The history of Israel's kings opens with a man nobody has heard of and a woman who cannot have a child. Elkanah of Ramah goes up every year to Shiloh. The sanctuary is run by Eli's two sons, named before we know anything about them.

Twice the narrator gives the reason for Hannah's barrenness, and it is not medical: the LORD had closed her womb. She is not appealing past her circumstances to a God who has not noticed them; she is appealing to the one who arranged them.

She prays silently, and the high priest watches the most genuine worship in the building and calls it drunkenness. Her reply gives Scripture one of its best definitions of prayer: I have been pouring out my soul before the LORD. And she asks for a son she promises, in the same breath, to give away for life.

Something changes in her before anything changes around her. The answer comes afterwards, and she carries it up the hill and hands it over.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — A House Divided, and a Womb Closed
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Elkanah of Ramah goes up year by year to worship at Shiloh, where Eli's two sons are priests (vv. 1-3). Peninnah has children; Hannah, whom he loves, has none, because the LORD had closed her womb (vv. 2, 4-6). Peninnah provokes her year after year on the way up to the house of the LORD, until Hannah weeps and will not eat (vv. 6-7). Elkanah's comfort is am I not more to you than ten sons? (v. 8).
verseByVerse.theology: Rivalry in a family can be sharpest at the very times meant for joy. Scripture does not hide that; it names it, and shows where Hannah took it.
verseByVerse.examples: Elkanah kept going up to worship, year after year, though the men in charge were ruining the place. Faithfulness in a compromised church is not compromise.

verseByVerse.quote: There was a certain man of Ramathaim-zophim of the hill country of Ephraim whose name was Elkanah the son of Jeroham, son of Elihu, son of Tohu, son of Zuph, an Ephrathite. He had two wives. The name of the one was Hannah, and the name of the other, Peninnah. And Peninnah had children, but Hannah had no children. Now this man used to go up year by year from his city to worship and to sacrifice to the LORD of hosts at Shiloh, where the two sons of Eli, Hophni and Phinehas, were priests of the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The book of the kings of Israel opens with no throne, no army, no prophet, no crisis: a certain man, from a town with a double-barrelled name, in the hill country, with four generations of ancestors listed so that we know he is somebody's son and not a symbol. Ramathaim-zophim is simply Ramah, Samuel's home town and his grave.

Chronicles lists Elkanah’s family among the Levites (1 Chr. 6:26-28, 33-34). That is no contradiction. Levites had no tribal territory of their own and lived among the other tribes, so a Levite could be called a man of the hill country of Ephraim by where he lived, as the Levites of Judges 17 and 19 were. It also helps explain why Samuel could serve at the sanctuary.

Two wives is already a household with a fault line through it. Sarah and Hagar, Leah and Rachel, and now Peninnah and Hannah: a fruitful wife and a loved one, and the misery that runs between them. Scripture shows that arrangement producing strife again and again. The narrator does not moralise about the polygamy; he states it and lets the next seven verses do the work.

Then the address: Shiloh. Judges named it once, to indict everybody: the Danites kept their stolen idol as long as the house of God was at Shiloh (Judg. 18:31). The real sanctuary, the ark, the appointed priesthood, all stood in the same hill country while a whole tribe walked past it to worship something they could carry. First Samuel opens with a man who goes every year.

And a title, here for the first time in the Bible: the LORD of hosts, Yahweh Sabaoth, the LORD of the armies of Israel, of the stars, of the angelic hosts, of every power that exists. It is the great name for God's total sovereign force, and prophets and psalmists will use it for a thousand years. Its first appearance is not on a battlefield, in a throne room or in a vision, but in a sentence about an ordinary man's annual walk to a country shrine. The God of all the armies there are is introduced by that name in connection with a household that cannot have a baby.

The last clause lands like a stone: Hophni and Phinehas, named at the first mention of the sanctuary. By chapter 2 we will know a great deal: that they took the meat by force, slept with the women serving at the entrance, and did not know the LORD. The place Elkanah walks to every year is being run by two men who are the reason it will shortly be destroyed. That is the world this book starts in. The worship is real, the God is the LORD of hosts, and the men in charge are ruining it.

Is polygamy approved here? The narrator records it without approving it, and shows its fruit: rivalry and grief (vv. 6–7). God’s design is one man and one woman (Gen 2:24).
verseByVerse.note: The book covers Israel’s move from judges to kings (about 1100–970 BC). Shiloh, where the tabernacle stood, lay about 20 miles north of Jerusalem.

verseByVerse.quote: On the day when Elkanah sacrificed, he would give portions to Peninnah his wife and to all her sons and daughters. But to Hannah he gave a double portion, because he loved her, though the LORD had closed her womb. And her rival used to provoke her grievously to irritate her, because the LORD had closed her womb. So it went on year by year. As often as she went up to the house of the LORD, she used to provoke her. Therefore Hannah wept and would not eat. And Elkanah, her husband, said to her, "Hannah, why do you weep? And why do you not eat? And why is your heart sad? Am I not more to you than ten sons?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The sacrifice at Shiloh was a shared meal, the portions handed round in front of everybody, once a year, for years. Peninnah receives a portion for herself and one for each son and daughter, and the pile grows while the family watches. Hannah receives a double portion, because her husband loves her, and it is a kindness that shines a light on exactly what she has not got.

Then the sentence the chapter turns on: the LORD had closed her womb. Not "she was unable to conceive". Not a medical note, not bad luck, and not a silence. Somebody closed it, and the narrator names him, and says it again in the next verse.

It is uncomfortable, and it is the foundation of everything Hannah does. She is appealing to the one who arranged her circumstances, and that is why there is any point in praying. A closed womb that God did not close is a fact to be endured. A closed womb that God closed can be opened.

That is not a promise that every closed womb will be opened. Many faithful couples pray as Hannah prayed and are never given a child, and their childlessness is no sign of God’s displeasure or of weak faith. What this chapter offers every one of them is what came to Hannah first, in verse 18: a God who hears, who takes the weight, and who has better things than sons and daughters to give, a name and a place in his house that will never be cut off (Isa. 56:4-5).

Note when the provoking happened: as often as she went up to the house of the LORD, at the feast, in the one season set aside for rejoicing before God. Peninnah timed her cruelty to the worship and aimed it at the one thing Hannah could do nothing about. There is a malice that does not invent a wound but finds the one already there and presses it. It is usually practised by somebody who has what the other person wants. Hannah weeps and will not eat, year by year; this is not a bad afternoon but years of dreading the same festival. Anyone who has found the church building the hardest place to be, because that is where the families are, and the babies, and the people whose lives worked out, is reading about themselves in verse 7.

Elkanah means it kindly, and he is trying, and the sentence is still about him. Three questions ask her to account for her grief, and a fourth offers himself as the solution. Am I not more to you than ten sons? Ten is the round number for completeness: let me be enough. It is affection, and it is not comfort; he has answered a specific sorrow by asking her to feel differently about it, which is what most of us do when someone we love is in pain we cannot fix. Hannah does not answer him. She gets up and goes somewhere else.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Hannah rises after the meal and prays where Eli sits by the doorpost (vv. 9-10). She asks God to look, remember and not forget, and promises the son back for life, with no razor on his head (v. 11). She prays silently, and Eli takes her for a drunk (vv. 12-14). Her answer is one of the great definitions of prayer: I have been pouring out my soul before the LORD (v. 15). Eli blesses her, and she goes and eats, and her face is no longer sad (vv. 17-18).
verseByVerse.theology: Prayer does not need to be tidy. What God hears in vv. 10-16 is bitterness, weeping and words nobody else can make out.
verseByVerse.examples: Leaders can misread grief. Hannah answered Eli's mistake gently, and he had the grace to bless her; both responses are worth learning.

verseByVerse.quote: After they had eaten and drunk in Shiloh, Hannah rose. Now Eli the priest was sitting on the seat beside the doorpost of the temple of the LORD. She was deeply distressed and prayed to the LORD and wept bitterly. And she vowed a vow and said, "O LORD of hosts, if you will indeed look on the affliction of your servant and remember me and not forget your servant, but will give to your servant a son, then I will give him to the LORD all the days of his life, and no razor shall touch his head."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hannah rose. Two words, and the whole chapter turns on them. She has wept and refused food year after year while her husband asks why and her rival watches. Now the meal ends and she gets up. Nobody sends her, nobody suggests it, and the narrator does not tell us she had decided anything in advance. She carries the grief no argument had touched into the presence of God.

The one detail we are given about Eli is his seat by the doorpost. Hold that picture: when the news arrives from the battle he falls backwards off his seat and dies (4:18). The narrative keeps finding him in a chair by a door.

Three verbs, and the middle one is the point: she was in bitterness of soul, and she prayed, and she wept. The praying is not a calmer activity that replaces the tears once she has composed herself; the distress and the crying are the material she brings.

She addresses him as LORD of hosts, the title that appeared at the top of the chapter in the narrator's description of the sanctuary. She is the first person in the Bible recorded praying by that title. A childless woman in a provincial shrine reaches past every smaller name for God and addresses the commander of every army in heaven and earth about her own body. She has understood verse 5 exactly: if the LORD closed it, the LORD of hosts is the right person to ask.

The requests climb. Look on the affliction: see it. Remember me: act. Do not forget your servant: the same thing said again, because she cannot stop saying it. And at last the thing itself: a son. She calls herself your servant three times, and never mentions Peninnah, asks for vindication, or points to her own faithfulness.

Then the vow, the astonishing half. She is not asking for a child to hold, to raise, to lean on in old age. She asks for a son in order to give him away, permanently, from infancy, and says so at the moment of asking. The one thing she wants is the one thing she promises not to keep.

The uncut hair is the mark of a Nazirite, the vow of Numbers 6, and the previous man in Scripture to carry it from the womb was Samson, announced by an angel to parents who were told what their son would be (Judg. 13:5). Nobody tells Hannah anything. There is no angel under a tree and no fire out of a rock. She works it out herself, in a sanctuary run by corrupt priests, and offers her unconceived child to God.
verseByVerse.note: Numbers 6 describes a Nazirite vow for a set time; Hannah’s, like Samson’s, is for life.

verseByVerse.quote: As she continued praying before the LORD, Eli observed her mouth. Hannah was speaking in her heart; only her lips moved, and her voice was not heard. Therefore Eli took her to be a drunken woman. And Eli said to her, "How long will you go on being drunk? Put your wine away from you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Her prayer is silent, which was unusual enough that the narrator explains it. Prayer in that world was spoken aloud. What Eli sees is a woman at the doorpost with her lips moving and no sound, going on and on, and he watches her mouth to work out what is happening. The narrator's phrase is speaking in her heart, lips moving and no sound. This is prayer with the volume turned off and God still hearing every syllable.

Take the failure at full weight. The high priest of Israel, the senior spiritual authority in the nation, sitting at the door of the house of God, looks at the most genuine act of worship in the building and concludes the woman has been drinking. His whole office is to stand between Israel and the LORD, and he cannot tell a broken woman pouring out her soul from a drunk. Nor is he gentle. He does not ask; he accuses, and how long will you go on being drunk assumes a habit. He has decided the kind of woman she is.

Here is what makes it worse rather than merely sad. This same Eli has two sons at this sanctuary taking the sacrificial meat by force and sleeping with the women who served at the entrance (2:13-17, 22), and he does not see that clearly enough to stop it. A man can be quick to detect sin in a stranger and slow about it at his own table, and Eli is the Bible's standing example.

verseByVerse.quote: But Hannah answered, "No, my lord, I am a woman troubled in spirit. I have drunk neither wine nor strong drink, but I have been pouring out my soul before the LORD. Do not regard your servant as a worthless woman, for all along I have been speaking out of my great anxiety and vexation." Then Eli answered, "Go in peace, and the God of Israel grant your petition that you have made to him." And she said, "Let your servant find favor in your eyes." Then the woman went her way and ate, and her face was no longer sad.
verseByVerse.commentary:
She corrects the high priest without a trace of temper. No, my lord: the denial is flat and the address respectful, and she does not tell him what she thinks of his discernment. She simply explains what he has been looking at.

Her explanation is one of the best definitions of prayer in Scripture: I have been pouring out my soul before the LORD. The image is a vessel being emptied. Not a request being submitted, not a form of words being performed, but the whole contents of a person tipped out in God's presence. That is what Eli mistook for drink, and a soul being poured out does not look composed.

She asks him not to take her for "a daughter of Belial", a worthless woman. The next chapter says the sons of Eli were worthless men. They did not know the LORD (2:12): sons of Belial. The same phrase. A childless woman is pleading with the high priest not to mistake her for what his own two sons demonstrably are, and neither of them knows it as she says it.

To his credit, he takes the correction without defensiveness and turns his accusation into a blessing. It is not a prophecy; he does not know what she asked. It is a priest doing the ordinary business of a priest: saying go in peace to somebody who came in pieces, and asking God to grant a petition whose contents he has not heard.

This is the turning point. She ate, and her face was no longer sad. She is not pregnant. She has no sign and no promise beyond an old man's blessing over a request he could not hear. What has changed is that it is no longer hers to carry. She brought the whole thing in and left it there, and she went and had dinner for the first time in the story. That is what casting your care on someone looks like when it works: not the arrival of what you asked for, but the departure of the weight, long before anything else moves. Peter puts it in one line, and the last clause is the whole reason it is possible: casting all your anxieties on him, because he cares for you (1 Pet. 5:7).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 19–28 — Asked For, and Given Back
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: They worship and go home, and the LORD remembered her (v. 19). Samuel is born, the son she asked for (v. 20). She stays home until he is weaned (vv. 21-23), then brings him to Shiloh with a bull, flour and wine (v. 24), and lends him to the LORD for as long as he lives (vv. 26-28).
verseByVerse.theology: The LORD who closed Hannah's womb is the LORD who remembers her (v. 19). The same sovereignty that made her prayer necessary made it worth praying.
verseByVerse.examples: Weaning took two or three years in that world. She had him that long, and then walked back down the hill without him. Everything in this book runs through a woman who got exactly what she asked for and gave it away.

verseByVerse.quote: They rose early in the morning and worshiped before the LORD; then they went back to their house at Ramah. And Elkanah knew Hannah his wife, and the LORD remembered her. And in due time Hannah conceived and bore a son, and she called his name Samuel, for she said, "I have asked for him from the LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
They worship first, then go home, and then God acts. The LORD remembered her, and zakar is not about memory; God does not mislay people. It is remembering that does something, attention that moves.

Scripture uses it at the hinges. God remembered Noah, and the waters went down (Gen. 8:1). God remembered Rachel, and opened her womb (Gen. 30:22). God heard their groaning, and God remembered his covenant, and the exodus began (Ex. 2:24). Hannah had asked him to remember her; the narrator uses her own word back.

Her explanation of the name is a play on sound rather than a dictionary meaning (the name itself probably means “name of God” or “heard by God”). The verb is sha'al, to ask, and it comes back in verses 27 and 28. The same root gives the name Saul. Seven chapters from now Israel will ask for a king, and the man they get will be called Asked-For, and the boy named here will anoint him and then tell him God has rejected him. The book is full of asking, and of what people get when they ask for the wrong thing.
verseByVerse.note: “Samuel” sounds like the Hebrew for “heard of God” (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: The man Elkanah and all his house went up to offer to the LORD the yearly sacrifice and to pay his vow. But Hannah did not go up, for she said to her husband, "As soon as the child is weaned, I will bring him, so that he may appear in the presence of the LORD and dwell there forever." Elkanah her husband said to her, "Do what seems best to you; wait until you have weaned him; only, may the LORD establish his word." So the woman remained and nursed her son until she weaned him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The household goes up as usual, Elkanah with a vow of his own to settle (the text does not say what it was), and Hannah stays home.

Weaning was commonly two years, sometimes three. She is asking for the whole of the time she will ever have him under her roof, in order to hand him over at the end of it, that he may appear in the presence of the LORD and dwell there forever. There is no wavering in it. She is not buying time in the hope that the vow will lapse; she names the surrender in the same breath as the delay.

Under the law a husband could annul his wife's vow (Num. 30:10-15). Elkanah could have cancelled this and kept the son of the wife he loves, born after years of waiting. He does not. Do what seems best to you, and a short prayer that the LORD would establish his word. He hands the decision to his wife and the outcome to God, and goes up to Shiloh without her.

verseByVerse.quote: And when she had weaned him, she took him up with her, along with a three-year-old bull, an ephah of flour, and a skin of wine, and she brought him to the house of the LORD at Shiloh. And the child was young. Then they slaughtered the bull, and they brought the child to Eli. And she said, "Oh, my lord! As you live, my lord, I am the woman who was standing here in your presence, praying to the LORD. For this child I prayed, and the LORD has granted me my petition that I made to him. Therefore I have lent him to the LORD. As long as he lives, he is lent to the LORD." And he worshiped the LORD there.
verseByVerse.commentary:
She keeps the vow, and not cheaply. The standard Hebrew text reads three bulls here (so the KJV); the Dead Sea Scrolls and the Greek read a three-year-old bull, which fits the bull of the next verse, and the ESV follows them. A three-year-old bull is a full-grown animal at the peak of its value, where the law required only a lamb for most occasions, and an ephah of flour is something over twenty pounds: a large sacrifice for a family from a hill village.

Then a clause the narrator did not have to write: and the child was young. He knows what he is describing: a woman walking up to a sanctuary with an animal, a sack of flour, a skin of wine and a toddler, to leave the toddler there. The bull is killed and the boy is handed over in the same sentence, and the writer does not pause between them.

She reintroduces herself, quietly magnificent. She does not say "I am the woman you accused of being drunk"; she says she is the woman who stood here praying, and leaves his mistake out of it entirely, though it would be fair to mention it. The prayer God heard was silent, and the answer is standing beside her holding her hand.

The astonishing word is therefore. Not "nevertheless", not "although he is all I have". Because the LORD granted the petition, the petition goes back; the gift is returned on the grounds that it was given, and the word lent is the same root again. A woman who wept through years of festivals for one thing got it, and handed it to the man who had called her a drunk, in a sanctuary whose priests God was about to judge.

She could not know that the boy would hear God's voice in the night, judge Israel for a lifetime, anoint two kings, or that the second would father a line that runs to a manger in Bethlehem. She knew only that she had asked, and been answered, and said what she would do.

The standard Hebrew text says he worshipped, probably Samuel or Elkanah; one Dead Sea Scroll appears to read she, meaning Hannah. Somebody in that room, having just given away a child, worshipped.

Take the chapter in one movement. God closed a womb (v. 5). A woman asked him to open it (v. 11). He remembered her (v. 19). She gave the answer back (v. 28). Everything in the two books of Samuel comes out of that exchange. She thought she was asking for a baby; she was being made the door the whole story walks through.
verseByVerse.note: “Petition” and “lent” in vv. 27–28 come from the same Hebrew root as “asked” in v. 20 (sha’al).

1.theology:
The LORD had closed her womb (vv. 5-6). Said twice, in case we took it for an aside. It is not a comfortable doctrine, and it is the reason prayer makes sense here: Hannah prays to the God who did this, and she is right to.

The LORD of hosts (vv. 3, 11). The title for the commander of every power in heaven and earth first appears in a chapter about a household that cannot have a baby.

Her face was no longer sad (v. 18). Before the pregnancy, before any promise, what lifted was not the circumstance but the weight (1 Pet. 5:7).

Therefore (v. 28). The gift is handed back precisely on the grounds that it was given. The whole ending is built on one root, sha'al, to ask, which is also the name Saul.

From Hannah to Mary. Hannah stands in a line of women whose closed wombs God opened when his promise seemed to hang on a child: Sarah, Rebekah, Rachel, Samson’s mother, and later Elizabeth. The line ends with a virgin who conceived with no human father at all, and Luke tells her story in Hannah’s colours. Mary’s song echoes Hannah’s (Luke 1:46-55; 1 Sam. 2:1-10); her child is presented to the Lord at the house of God (Luke 2:22); and he grows in favour with God and man as Samuel did (Luke 2:52; 1 Sam. 2:26). Hannah gave back to God the son God had given her. In the gospel the giving runs the other way: the Father gave his only Son for us (John 3:16), and that gift is the comfort offered to every believer, with a child or without.
1.examples:
Then: A woman dreaded one festival a year for years, because the pilgrimage was where her rival could reach her and where the families and children were all in one place. She went anyway, and one year she got up from the meal and took the whole thing to God.

Now: Three things. If the church building has ever been the hardest place to walk into, verse 7 is about you, and verse 9 is what to do about it: take it to the God who cares for you, who is not waiting for you to compose yourself first. If you are waiting on something God has not given, notice that Hannah's face changed at verse 18 and her son arrived at verse 20: the weight can be lifted before any answer comes, and God's care does not depend on the answer being yes. And if you have been given the thing you asked for, verse 28 is the harder half: she handed it over, and said therefore while she did it. We open our hands like that not by gritting our teeth but because the Father did not hold back his own Son from us, and his Spirit teaches our clenched hearts to trust him.

2.title: The Horn of His Anointed
2.text: <sup>1</sup>And Hannah prayed and said, "My heart exults in the LORD; my horn is exalted in the LORD. My mouth derides my enemies, because I rejoice in your salvation.<sup>2</sup>"There is none holy like the LORD: for there is none besides you; there is no rock like our God.<sup>3</sup>Talk no more so very proudly, let not arrogance come from your mouth; for the LORD is a God of knowledge, and by him actions are weighed.<sup>4</sup>The bows of the mighty are broken, but the feeble bind on strength.<sup>5</sup>Those who were full have hired themselves out for bread, but those who were hungry have ceased to hunger. The barren has borne seven, but she who has many children is forlorn.<sup>6</sup>The LORD kills and brings to life; he brings down to Sheol and raises up.<sup>7</sup>The LORD makes poor and makes rich; he brings low and he exalts.<sup>8</sup>He raises up the poor from the dust; he lifts the needy from the ash heap to make them sit with princes and inherit a seat of honor. For the pillars of the earth are the LORD's, and on them he has set the world.<sup>9</sup>"He will guard the feet of his faithful ones, but the wicked shall be cut off in darkness, for not by might shall a man prevail.<sup>10</sup>The adversaries of the LORD shall be broken to pieces; against them he will thunder in heaven. The LORD will judge the ends of the earth; he will give strength to his king and exalt the horn of his anointed."<sup>11</sup>Then Elkanah went home to Ramah. And the boy was ministering to the LORD in the presence of Eli the priest.<sup>12</sup>Now the sons of Eli were worthless men. They did not know the LORD.<sup>13</sup>The custom of the priests with the people was that when any man offered sacrifice, the priest's servant would come, while the meat was boiling, with a three-pronged fork in his hand,<sup>14</sup>and he would thrust it into the pan or kettle or cauldron or pot. All that the fork brought up the priest would take for himself. This is what they did at Shiloh to all the Israelites who came there.<sup>15</sup>Moreover, before the fat was burned, the priest's servant would come and say to the man who was sacrificing, "Give meat for the priest to roast, for he will not accept boiled meat from you but only raw."<sup>16</sup>And if the man said to him, "Let them burn the fat first, and then take as much as you wish," he would say, "No, you must give it now, and if not, I will take it by force."<sup>17</sup>Thus the sin of the young men was very great in the sight of the LORD, for the men treated the offering of the LORD with contempt.<sup>18</sup>Samuel was ministering before the LORD, a boy clothed with a linen ephod.<sup>19</sup>And his mother used to make for him a little robe and take it to him each year when she went up with her husband to offer the yearly sacrifice.<sup>20</sup>Then Eli would bless Elkanah and his wife, and say, "May the LORD give you children by this woman for the petition she asked of the LORD." So then they would return to their home.<sup>21</sup>Indeed the LORD visited Hannah, and she conceived and bore three sons and two daughters. And the boy Samuel grew in the presence of the LORD.<sup>22</sup>Now Eli was very old, and he kept hearing all that his sons were doing to all Israel, and how they lay with the women who were serving at the entrance to the tent of meeting.<sup>23</sup>And he said to them, "Why do you do such things? For I hear of your evil dealings from all these people.<sup>24</sup>No, my sons; it is no good report that I hear the people of the LORD spreading abroad.<sup>25</sup>If someone sins against a man, God will mediate for him, but if someone sins against the LORD, who can intercede for him?" But they would not listen to the voice of their father, for it was the will of the LORD to put them to death.<sup>26</sup>Now the boy Samuel continued to grow both in stature and in favor with the LORD and also with man.<sup>27</sup>And there came a man of God to Eli and said to him, "Thus says the LORD, 'Did I indeed reveal myself to the house of your father when they were in Egypt subject to the house of Pharaoh?<sup>28</sup>Did I choose him out of all the tribes of Israel to be my priest, to go up to my altar, to burn incense, to wear an ephod before me? I gave to the house of your father all my offerings by fire from the people of Israel.<sup>29</sup>Why then do you scorn my sacrifices and my offerings that I commanded for my dwelling, and honor your sons above me by fattening yourselves on the choicest parts of every offering of my people Israel?'<sup>30</sup>Therefore the LORD, the God of Israel, declares: 'I promised that your house and the house of your father should go in and out before me forever,' but now the LORD declares: 'Far be it from me, for those who honor me I will honor, and those who despise me shall be lightly esteemed.<sup>31</sup>Behold, the days are coming when I will cut off your strength and the strength of your father's house, so that there will not be an old man in your house.<sup>32</sup>Then in distress you will look with envious eye on all the prosperity that shall be bestowed on Israel, and there shall not be an old man in your house forever.<sup>33</sup>The only one of you whom I shall not cut off from my altar shall be spared to weep his eyes out to grieve his heart, and all the descendants of your house shall die by the sword of men.<sup>34</sup>And this that shall come upon your two sons, Hophni and Phinehas, shall be the sign to you: both of them shall die on the same day.<sup>35</sup>And I will raise up for myself a faithful priest, who shall do according to what is in my heart and in my mind. And I will build him a sure house, and he shall go in and out before my anointed forever.<sup>36</sup>And everyone who is left in your house shall come to implore him for a piece of silver or a loaf of bread and shall say, "Please put me in one of the priests' places, that I may eat a morsel of bread."'"
2.overview:
Hannah has just left her only child at a sanctuary run by two men God is about to destroy, and she prays, and what comes out is a psalm about God: the rock, the God of knowledge, and the God who reverses the fortunes of the mighty and the feeble. She has taken the most private thing that ever happened to her and stated it as a law of how God runs the world.

And the song ends somewhere nobody could have predicted: he will give strength to his king and exalt the horn of his anointed, his messiah, when Israel has no king and has not asked for one.

Then the camera turns to the altar. Eli's sons are worthless men who did not know the LORD. They stab a fork into the worshippers' pots and demand raw meat before the fat is burned to God, with violence if refused. Their father hears of it for years, speaks to them once, and leaves them in office.

So a man of God comes with the charge, aimed at Eli, not his sons: you honour your sons above me. And the sentence to carry out of the chapter: those who honour me I will honour, and those who despise me shall be lightly esteemed.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–10 — The Song of a Woman Who Gave Her Son Away
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Hannah prays, and what comes out is a psalm. Her horn is exalted in the LORD; there is none holy like him and no rock like him; he is a God of knowledge who weighs what people do (vv. 1-3). Then the reversals: the mighty broken and the feeble armed, the full hungry and the hungry filled, the barren bearing seven (vv. 4-5). The LORD kills and brings to life, and lifts the needy off the ash heap to seat them with princes (vv. 6-8). And the last line reaches somewhere nobody expects: his king, his anointed (v. 10).
verseByVerse.theology: Answered prayer turns Hannah to the Giver, not the gift. Her thanks are about who God is.
verseByVerse.examples: For worship. Hannah's song was taken up in Israel's psalms (Ps. 113:7-8) and on Mary's lips (Luke 1:46-55). A private mercy, sung aloud, becomes the church's song.

verseByVerse.quote: And Hannah prayed and said, "My heart exults in the LORD; my horn is exalted in the LORD. My mouth derides my enemies, because I rejoice in your salvation. "There is none holy like the LORD: for there is none besides you; there is no rock like our God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
There is no baby in any of these ten verses: not how long she waited, not what he looked like, not what it cost to leave him. She has just handed over the only thing she ever asked God for, and what comes out of her is a psalm about God.

Horn is the Hebrew Bible's picture of strength, the thing an animal fights with. Hers is exalted in the LORD, and the phrase will come back at the end of the song attached to somebody who does not exist yet.

Her enemies get one clause. Peninnah is not named, not described, and never mentioned again in the Bible. And the reason for the exulting is your salvation: not my son, not my vindication.

Of her three statements about God, the middle one grounds the other two. None holy like the LORD: holiness first, set apart, in a category by himself. Then there is none besides you: not the best of the gods but the only one, said flatly in the age of the judges, when half of Israel was hedging its bets with the Baals. Then no rock like our God, the oldest image Israel had for him, from Moses' song: the Rock, his work is perfect (Deut. 32:4). Something you stand on, shelter behind, and do not have to check.
verseByVerse.note: Hannah’s prayer is poetry, like the psalms: its lines come in pairs that echo each other.

verseByVerse.quote: Talk no more so very proudly, let not arrogance come from your mouth; for the LORD is a God of knowledge, and by him actions are weighed. The bows of the mighty are broken, but the feeble bind on strength. Those who were full have hired themselves out for bread, but those who were hungry have ceased to hunger. The barren has borne seven, but she who has many children is forlorn.
verseByVerse.commentary:
She turns on someone unnamed, Peninnah or everyone like her, and the warning is not that God punishes arrogance but that he is a God of knowledge, who weighs actions on a balance, knowing what each one actually weighs as opposed to what it looked like. Consider who is saying this: a woman whose case, publicly weighed, had looked for years like a verdict against her, barren, mocked, and accused of drunkenness by the high priest. She is telling the confident to be careful, because the scales are not the ones they can see.

The reversals come in pairs, all running the same direction. The strong lose what made them strong; the feeble are armed. The full hire out their labour for a loaf; the hungry stop being hungry. Not that the low are helped and the high left alone: both ends move, and they change places.

Then Hannah and Peninnah, in one line, with the names taken off. The astonishing move in this song is the generalising. She has stated the most private thing that ever happened to her as a general law: not "this happened to me" but "this is what happens". Seven is the number of fullness rather than a headcount (verse 21 will record five more children after Samuel, which makes six); she is not doing arithmetic. When God reverses a barrenness he does not do it by halves.

A childless reader may hear this line as a promise she has not been given. It is not a guarantee that every barren woman will bear children; many faithful women never did, and their childlessness was no verdict against them. It is a statement about the direction of God's dealings, which runs towards the lowly. Its final form is not a nursery in Ramah but the kingdom Mary's son brings, where those who mourn are comforted and no one's worth is measured by what she has borne (Isaiah 54:1; 56:3–5; Galatians 4:27).

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD kills and brings to life; he brings down to Sheol and raises up. The LORD makes poor and makes rich; he brings low and he exalts. He raises up the poor from the dust; he lifts the needy from the ash heap to make them sit with princes and inherit a seat of honor. For the pillars of the earth are the LORD's, and on them he has set the world.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is the furthest any Old Testament believer goes, and it repays taking at full strength. Not "the LORD gives life and permits death": both verbs are his, in the same grammar. He brings down to Sheol, the place of the dead, and raises up.

Hannah is not spelling out a doctrine of resurrection; she is saying that the whole range, from the grave to life, is under one hand. Yet her words reach further than she could see. The God who brings down to Sheol and raises up is the God who raised Jesus, loosing the pangs of death because it was not possible for him to be held by it (Acts 2:24), and that is the ground on which a bereaved Christian stands at a graveside. It is chapter 1's theology worked out to its end: the LORD closed her womb and opened it. A God who only ever did the pleasant half would be no use to her, because he would not have been in charge of the years she actually lived through.

The ash heap is where the destitute sat outside a village, where Job sat when he had lost everything, the lowest address there is. God does not merely move such a man indoors; he seats him with princes, from the tip to the top table. The psalms took this up almost word for word: he raises the poor from the dust and lifts the needy from the ash heap, to make them sit with princes (Ps. 113:7-8).

And the reason he can do it goes under everything: the pillars of the earth are his. The God who arranged what the earth stands on will not find a childless woman in Ramah beyond his reach.

verseByVerse.quote: "He will guard the feet of his faithful ones, but the wicked shall be cut off in darkness, for not by might shall a man prevail. The adversaries of the LORD shall be broken to pieces; against them he will thunder in heaven. The LORD will judge the ends of the earth; he will give strength to his king and exalt the horn of his anointed."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Not by might shall a man prevail is the argument of the whole book. Israel is about to demand a king to fight its battles, and will be given the tallest man in the country. Then a boy with a sling will kill a giant and say it in his own words, the LORD saves not with sword and spear (17:47). Hannah says it first, and she says it while nobody is listening.

The last line needs its setting. Israel has no king, no throne, no candidate; nobody has asked for one, and when they do it will be treated as a rejection of God. And anointed is mashiach, messiah. A countrywoman who has just left a weaned toddler at a corrupt sanctuary finishes by asking God to strengthen a king who does not exist. Her own horn was exalted in verse 1; his in verse 10. She has followed the thread from her answered prayer out to the ends of the earth and landed on an anointed king.

Eleven centuries later a young woman in another hill village, told she will bear a son by God's direct act, sings almost this song again. My soul magnifies the Lord, and my spirit rejoices in God my Savior, as Hannah exulted in the LORD's salvation; he has brought down the mighty from their thrones and exalted those of humble estate, as Hannah sang that he brings low and exalts; he has filled the hungry with good things, and the rich he has sent away empty (Luke 1:46-53). Mary knew this song. It is what a godly Israelite girl had in her head, and when the angel had gone and Elizabeth greeted her, it is what came out.

Here is the difference that makes the parallel worth having. Hannah reached forward to an anointed king who did not yet exist; Mary was carrying him. The king Hannah prayed for would be David first, and his line after him; but only one of that line was ever both lifted from the lowest place and given strength over the ends of the earth, and Mary's song is the New Testament's way of saying who he is.

A textual note: the Greek Old Testament (the Septuagint, the ancient translation used by the early church) adds a few lines to verse 10, close to Jeremiah 9:23–24, about not boasting in wisdom or strength but in knowing the LORD. Most English versions follow the Hebrew text, and the thought added is fully biblical either way.
verseByVerse.note: The first time the Bible speaks of the LORD’s “anointed” king: in Hebrew, his messiah.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–17 — Worthless Men at the Altar
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Elkanah goes home and the boy stays, ministering to the LORD (v. 11). The narrator's verdict on Eli's sons: worthless men. They did not know the LORD (v. 12). A servant's fork thrust into the pot took whatever came up (vv. 13-14); worse, they demanded raw meat before the fat was burned, by force if refused (vv. 15-16). The men treated the offering of the LORD with contempt (v. 17).
verseByVerse.theology: Corruption at the altar did not cancel the worship of the faithful. Hannah's gift and the people's sacrifices were real, though the priests were not.
verseByVerse.examples: There are two thefts here and the second is the grave one. The law gave the priest the breast and the right thigh, after the fat had been burned to God (Lev. 7:31-34). These men took what the fork found, and took it first, robbing the worshipper of his portion and God of his.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Elkanah went home to Ramah. And the boy was ministering to the LORD in the presence of Eli the priest. Now the sons of Eli were worthless men. They did not know the LORD. The custom of the priests with the people was that when any man offered sacrifice, the priest's servant would come, while the meat was boiling, with a three-pronged fork in his hand, and he would thrust it into the pan or kettle or cauldron or pot. All that the fork brought up the priest would take for himself. This is what they did at Shiloh to all the Israelites who came there.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The family goes home and one of them does not. What the boy was doing is given in a phrase the writer keeps returning to, here, at v. 18 and at 3:1: ministering to the LORD.

Then two short sentences for the two priests of Israel, both devastating. Worthless men is sons of Belial, the word for the scum of a community, and the exact phrase Hannah used at this same doorway when she begged Eli not to take her for "a daughter of Belial" (1:16). A woman prays in silence out of real grief and is accused of being worthless; two men rob the worshippers and sleep with the women at the door, and the high priest is their father. He got it exactly the wrong way round, in both directions, in his own house. The writer has put the two scenes together on purpose.

They did not know the LORD. These are priests, whose office is to teach the people who God is, and the narrator says, flatly, that they had no acquaintance with him. Judges said that of a whole generation (Judg. 2:10), the sentence the whole book turned on; now it is laid on the clergy.

The narrator describes the fraud with the patience of a man building a case. The law was not vague: the priest's portion was the breast and the right thigh, given him by name (Lev. 7:31-34). It was a provision, and it was enough. Instead a servant stabbed a three-pronged fork into the pot and kept whatever came up, theft by lottery; the four vessels listed say that no worshipper's dinner was safe whatever he cooked it in. And it was done to all the Israelites who came there: not occasionally, but as the custom of the house.

verseByVerse.quote: Moreover, before the fat was burned, the priest's servant would come and say to the man who was sacrificing, "Give meat for the priest to roast, for he will not accept boiled meat from you but only raw." And if the man said to him, "Let them burn the fat first, and then take as much as you wish," he would say, "No, you must give it now, and if not, I will take it by force." Thus the sin of the young men was very great in the sight of the LORD, for the men treated the offering of the LORD with contempt.
verseByVerse.commentary:
One phrase turns a racket into blasphemy: before the fat was burned. In every sacrifice the fat was God's, burned on the altar before anybody ate: all fat is the LORD's (Lev. 3:16). Eli's sons are not merely taking more than their share; they are putting themselves at the head of the queue in front of God. And the reason is appetite: they wanted it raw to roast it. The order of precedence at Israel's altar had been rearranged around what two men preferred for dinner.

The worshipper's answer is the most striking thing in the passage. He offers them everything, take as much as you wish, on one condition: let God have his part first. An ordinary Israelite up from the country has better theology than the priesthood, and he is overruled by threat: I will take it by force. A priest of the LORD standing over a worshipper at the sanctuary, promising violence if he does not get the meat before God does.

The narrator names the offence, and he does not name it as greed. They treated the offering of the LORD with contempt: the sin was what they thought of the thing they were handling. Every day, before people who had walked for miles to bring it, they showed that the sacrifice was food and nothing more. That is what makes it very great, and it is a warning aimed precisely at anybody who handles holy things for a living. Familiarity with the sacred is a dangerous place to stand, because contempt does not arrive as a decision. It arrives as a habit.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–21 — A Little Robe, Year by Year
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Samuel ministers before the LORD, a boy in a linen ephod (v. 18), and his mother brings him a little robe every year (v. 19). Eli blesses Elkanah and Hannah (v. 20), and the LORD visits Hannah, who bears three more sons and two daughters (v. 21).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 19 is quietly heartbreaking. She had a few days a year with him, and she spent the rest making him a coat, guessing at how much he had grown.
verseByVerse.examples: Parents who have had to let a child go, to a calling, to a distance or even to estrangement, may find in Hannah's yearly robe a picture of love that keeps giving without taking back.

verseByVerse.quote: Samuel was ministering before the LORD, a boy clothed with a linen ephod. And his mother used to make for him a little robe and take it to him each year when she went up with her husband to offer the yearly sacrifice. Then Eli would bless Elkanah and his wife, and say, "May the LORD give you children by this woman for the petition she asked of the LORD." So then they would return to their home. Indeed the LORD visited Hannah, and she conceived and bore three sons and two daughters. And the boy Samuel grew in the presence of the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The camera cuts from the fork in the pot to a small boy in priest's clothes. A linen ephod is what a priest wore to serve, and Samuel is not of Aaron's line; he is a Levite whose family lives in Ephraim (1 Chr. 6:26-28). The two men who are entitled to wear it are defiling the altar, and a child given by his mother is ministering properly.

Few sentences in the book are tenderer than the little robe. She sees him once a year. For the other three hundred and sixty-four days she is at home in Ramah with a piece of cloth and a needle, making a coat for a boy she cannot measure, guessing at how much he has grown since last year. The word is used elsewhere of a priest's garment and of Jonathan's cloak, the outer coat a man was known by. Every year a slightly bigger one, carried up the hill, and she goes home again. There is no complaint, and no attempt to take him back. She kept the vow, and she kept sewing.

Eli's blessing uses the chapter's key verb again, the petition she asked. He has understood what happened, even if he did not at the time.

She gave one child away, and God gave her five. It is not a transaction and the text does not offer it as one; there is no promise anywhere in Scripture that surrendering something to God results in more of it, and plenty of God's servants have given up what they never got back. The verse records what God did for this woman, and the writer wants us to feel it. Visited is the same movement as remembered in 1:19, attention that acts. And the last clause matters most: the boy grew in the presence of the LORD. The five at Ramah are the postscript; the one she left is the point.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 22–26 — Why Do You Do Such Things?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Eli is very old, and he kept hearing everything his sons were doing, including sleeping with the women who served at the entrance to the tent of meeting (v. 22). He speaks to them once (vv. 23-24), and asks a question with no answer in it: if someone sins against the LORD, who can intercede for him? (v. 25). They would not listen, for it was the will of the LORD to put them to death. Between the two halves of the family's ruin, Samuel keeps growing in favour with the LORD and with man (v. 26).
verseByVerse.theology: Eli's failure was not ignorance: he kept hearing (v. 22). Knowing and doing nothing is its own kind of sin.
verseByVerse.examples: Hold on to Eli's question in v. 25. He meant it hopelessly, and the rest of Scripture answers it.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Eli was very old, and he kept hearing all that his sons were doing to all Israel, and how they lay with the women who were serving at the entrance to the tent of meeting. And he said to them, "Why do you do such things? For I hear of your evil dealings from all these people. No, my sons; it is no good report that I hear the people of the LORD spreading abroad. If someone sins against a man, God will mediate for him, but if someone sins against the LORD, who can intercede for him?" But they would not listen to the voice of their father, for it was the will of the LORD to put them to death. Now the boy Samuel continued to grow both in stature and in favor with the LORD and also with man.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The verb is kept hearing, and it is doing a great deal of work. He did not fail to find out. Nobody hid it, he was not deceived, the reports were not doubtful. It came in steadily, over years, from all over the country, and he heard all of it.

A new offence appears: the women who served at the entrance to the tent of meeting were doing a recognised duty, and Eli's sons were sleeping with them. Many think the Canaanite shrines practised something like this as part of their worship, though scholars now debate how widespread it was; either way, Shiloh has begun to look like a pagan shrine.

A textual note: the clause about the women at the entrance is missing from the oldest Hebrew copy of Samuel among the Dead Sea Scrolls and from the main manuscripts of the Greek Old Testament. Some think it was added from Exodus 38:8; most English versions keep it, and the charge of contempt for the sanctuary stands on the rest of the chapter in any case.

Measure Eli's response against that. He asks why do you do such things?, reports his sources, and calls it no good report: what he objects to, in his own words, is what is being said about them. He could remove them from the altar that afternoon, and the law in his keeping warned that priests who profaned the holy things would die for it (Lev. 22:9). He does not remove them, does not discipline them, and does not stop them. He speaks to them once, and the next verse tells us how that went. And he calls them my sons in the middle of it, which is exactly the problem God will name in verse 29.

Then, in the middle of the feeblest rebuke in Scripture, the old man asks the deepest question in the book. Follow the logic, because it is exact. When a man wrongs his neighbour, God himself will arbitrate. But when the offence is against God, the party wronged and the judge, who is left to stand in the middle?

The Old Testament gives only glimpses of an answer: Moses standing in the breach for a guilty people, the Servant of Isaiah 53 who bore the sin of many and made intercession for the transgressors (Isa. 53:12). Job asks it in his own words when he says there is no arbiter between them who might lay his hand on both (Job 9:33), and it stays open for a thousand years.

For there is one God, and there is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus, who gave himself as a ransom for all (1 Tim. 2:5-6). Eli meant "nobody", and was right about his own day and wrong about the answer. He would be born in David's town, and be exactly what the question required: one who could lay a hand on both, because he was both.

Then both halves of verse 25b stand, and the writer makes no attempt to relieve the tension. They would not listen: that is their act, and they are answerable for it. It was the will of the LORD to put them to death: that is God's, stated as the reason. Scripture does this repeatedly and never apologises. God hardened Pharaoh's heart and Pharaoh hardened his own. Joseph's brothers meant evil and God meant good. Men crucified Christ by lawless hands, according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God (Acts 2:23).

And between the sentence of death and its execution the narrator drops in the boy, growing in stature and favour. It sounds familiar on purpose: And Jesus increased in wisdom and in stature and in favor with God and man (Luke 2:52). Luke, who has already given Mary Hannah's song, gives Jesus Samuel's childhood. He is telling us where to look.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 27–36 — Those Who Honour Me I Will Honour
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: An unnamed man of God arrives with a covenant lawsuit (a formal charge brought by God against those bound to him by covenant). First the recital of what God gave Eli's house (vv. 27-28); then the charge, aimed at Eli: you scorn my sacrifices... and honor your sons above me (v. 29); then the sentence, with both sons dead on one day as the sign (vv. 30-34). And a promise: a faithful priest who will do what is in God's heart (v. 35).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 30 is the chapter in one line. Eli's sin was not his sons' sin. It was that when forced to choose between them and God, he chose them, by doing nothing.
verseByVerse.examples: Watch for this word being kept: both sons die on one day (4:11), and a lone survivor escapes the massacre at Nob (22:20).

verseByVerse.quote: And there came a man of God to Eli and said to him, "Thus says the LORD, 'Did I indeed reveal myself to the house of your father when they were in Egypt subject to the house of Pharaoh? Did I choose him out of all the tribes of Israel to be my priest, to go up to my altar, to burn incense, to wear an ephod before me? I gave to the house of your father all my offerings by fire from the people of Israel. Why then do you scorn my sacrifices and my offerings that I commanded for my dwelling, and honor your sons above me by fattening yourselves on the choicest parts of every offering of my people Israel?' Therefore the LORD, the God of Israel, declares: 'I promised that your house and the house of your father should go in and out before me forever,' but now the LORD declares: 'Far be it from me, for those who honor me I will honor, and those who despise me shall be lightly esteemed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
An unnamed prophet arrives, and what he delivers is built like a legal case. He is never named and never appears again, exactly like the unnamed prophet God sent to Israel before Gideon (Judg. 6:8). God has a habit of sending a man with a message and no biography.

The recital comes first, as it always does, and it is a list of gifts: I revealed myself, I chose you, I gave you the altar, the incense, the ephod, and the offerings to live on. Every clause is something God did for this family, and the questions are rhetorical: none of it is in dispute. The offerings by fire come last for a reason. The very thing the sons were stealing was already theirs by gift; they were robbing a table God had set for them.

Read the charge carefully, because it would be easy to assume the prophet has come about Hophni and Phinehas. He has not. It is addressed to Eli, in the second person: you honour your sons above me. It is the indictment of a man who did nothing. He did not steal the meat or sleep with the women at the door. He heard about it for years, spoke once, kept them in office, and went on eating, fattening yourselves, which puts him at the same table. When it came to a choice between his sons and his God, he chose his sons by not choosing. That is how most such choices are made.

A promise is quoted and withdrawn, and that needs care. God does not break his word. The priesthood given to Aaron's line was a standing arrangement with obligations attached; a promise of office is not the same kind of thing as the covenant of grace. What is revoked is a family's tenure of a job, and the job continues, as verse 35 says.

Then the principle, which is exact justice and terrifyingly simple. Eli honoured his sons above God; God will esteem Eli lightly. The measure a man uses is measured back to him, and the currency is honour. It does not say "those who serve me": Eli had given his whole life to the sanctuary and was still at his post as an old man. The question is whether, when something else competes for the top place, God gets it.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, the days are coming when I will cut off your strength and the strength of your father's house, so that there will not be an old man in your house. Then in distress you will look with envious eye on all the prosperity that shall be bestowed on Israel, and there shall not be an old man in your house forever. The only one of you whom I shall not cut off from my altar shall be spared to weep his eyes out to grieve his heart, and all the descendants of your house shall die by the sword of men. And this that shall come upon your two sons, Hophni and Phinehas, shall be the sign to you: both of them shall die on the same day. And I will raise up for myself a faithful priest, who shall do according to what is in my heart and in my mind. And I will build him a sure house, and he shall go in and out before my anointed forever. And everyone who is left in your house shall come to implore him for a piece of silver or a loaf of bread and shall say, "Please put me in one of the priests' places, that I may eat a morsel of bread."'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The sentence is passed, and its cruellest feature is stated first: no old men. Eli is himself a very old man, which is why the punishment is worded this way; he will look round his family and find nobody who reached his age. Israel will prosper while it happens. The nation the family was appointed to serve will flourish under Samuel and David, and the house of Eli will watch from the outside.

One survivor is promised, and the promise is worse than the sentence. He is spared in order to watch, and the phrase is unbearable: to weep his eyes out to grieve his heart. It is fulfilled with terrible precision. Abiathar alone escapes when Saul massacres the priests at Nob (22:20), serves David for forty years, and is removed by Solomon, and the historian stops to say why: thus fulfilling the word of the LORD that he had spoken concerning the house of Eli in Shiloh (1 Kings 2:27). A sign is given so that Eli will know the rest is coming, and it arrives two chapters later: both sons die on a single day when the Philistines take the ark, and the man who brings the news adds it almost as an afterthought (4:11, 17).

Then, in the middle of a judgment oracle, a promise. A corrupt priesthood is not answered by abolishing the priesthood. God will raise up a faithful priest, and the qualification is not lineage or competence but that he will do according to what is in God's heart and mind: a priest who wants what God wants. The near fulfilment is Zadok, who replaces Abiathar under Solomon and whose line holds the office for centuries; Scripture makes the connection itself in the verse quoted above.

But the last clause does not stop there: he shall go in and out before my anointed forever. Anointed again, Hannah's mashiach, and forever, which no son of Zadok managed. Hebrews finishes it. There is a merciful and faithful high priest (Heb. 2:17), who came saying, I have come to do your will, O God (Heb. 10:7). He holds his priesthood permanently, because he continues forever (Heb. 7:24), and he needed no sacrifice for his own sins first (Heb. 7:27), which is precisely where every priest in Shiloh's line failed.

The chapter ends with a picture, and it is exact retribution. Two men who stood over worshippers demanding the best meat with a threat, I will take it by force, will have descendants begging another priest for a place at the bottom of the rota and a piece of bread. They took the choicest parts; their children will ask for a morsel.
verseByVerse.note: Zadok’s line held the high priesthood down to the exile (1 Chr. 6:8-15).

2.theology:
A song with no baby in it. The reversal at v. 5 is Hannah's own case with the names taken off: not "this happened to me" but "this is what happens".

The LORD kills and brings to life (v. 6). Both verbs are his, in one sentence. It is chapter 1's theology worked out to the end: he closed the womb and he opened it.

Not by might shall a man prevail (v. 9). The argument of the whole book, stated before anyone needs it (17:47).

His king, his anointed (v. 10). There is no king, and the word is mashiach. Mary sings the song again (Luke 1:46-53), and the difference is everything: Hannah reached forward to an anointed king who did not exist, and Mary was carrying him.

Contempt for the offering (v. 17). The sin is not named as greed; the offence is what they thought of what they handled. Familiarity with holy things is a dangerous place to stand.

Who can intercede? (v. 25) When the offence is against God, who is both the party wronged and the judge, who stands in the middle? The Old Testament glimpses an answer, and then it is given in full: there is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus (1 Tim. 2:5).

Both ends held (v. 25b). They would not listen, and it was the will of the LORD to put them to death. The writer makes no attempt to relieve it, as at Acts 2:23.

You honour your sons above me (v. 29). The charge is Eli's, not his sons'. He chose his sons by not choosing, and the answer is exact: those who honour me I will honour (v. 30). Not those who serve me; Eli served all his life. The question is whether God gets the top place when something else competes for it. None of us has always given it to him, and that is why the faithful priest of v. 35 matters: Christ did the whole will of God in our place, honoured the Father perfectly, and is counted ours.
2.examples:
Then: A woman walked home from leaving her only son with strangers and sang about the God who empties and fills, and finished by asking blessing on a king who would not exist for two generations. Meanwhile the two men she had left him with were stabbing forks into other people's dinners.

Now: Three things. Hannah's song is the model for what to do with an answered prayer: she generalised it, and the mercy shown to her became a statement about how God treats everybody, the opposite of hoarding a testimony as a private possession. Second, verse 17 is for anyone who handles holy things often, preaching, leading, serving, or simply having been in church a long time. Contempt creeps in unannounced. The remedy is not to handle holy things less but to remember whose they are: the sacrifice was the LORD's, and the one Sacrifice it pointed to was his own Son. And third, verse 29 is the searching one. It is possible to serve God for a lifetime and still, at the point of collision, honour something else above him, by declining to choose. If that is you, Eli's house is not the end of the story: confess it to the God who has already provided the faithful Priest who honoured him for us (1 John 1:9), and ask the Spirit he gives for the courage Eli never found, to put God first where it costs.

3.title: The Word of the LORD Was Rare
3.text: <sup>1</sup>Now the boy Samuel was ministering to the LORD in the presence of Eli. And the word of the LORD was rare in those days; there was no frequent vision.<sup>2</sup>At that time Eli, whose eyesight had begun to grow dim so that he could not see, was lying down in his own place.<sup>3</sup>The lamp of God had not yet gone out, and Samuel was lying down in the temple of the LORD, where the ark of God was.<sup>4</sup>Then the LORD called Samuel, and he said, "Here I am!"<sup>5</sup>and ran to Eli and said, "Here I am, for you called me." But he said, "I did not call; lie down again." So he went and lay down.<sup>6</sup>And the LORD called again, "Samuel!" and Samuel arose and went to Eli and said, "Here I am, for you called me." But he said, "I did not call, my son; lie down again."<sup>7</sup>Now Samuel did not yet know the LORD, and the word of the LORD had not yet been revealed to him.<sup>8</sup>And the LORD called Samuel again the third time. And he arose and went to Eli and said, "Here I am, for you called me." Then Eli perceived that the LORD was calling the boy.<sup>9</sup>Therefore Eli said to Samuel, "Go, lie down, and if he calls you, you shall say, 'Speak, LORD, for your servant hears.'" So Samuel went and lay down in his place.<sup>10</sup>And the LORD came and stood, calling as at other times, "Samuel! Samuel!" And Samuel said, "Speak, for your servant hears."<sup>11</sup>Then the LORD said to Samuel, "Behold, I am about to do a thing in Israel at which the two ears of everyone who hears it will tingle.<sup>12</sup>On that day I will fulfill against Eli all that I have spoken concerning his house, from beginning to end.<sup>13</sup>And I declare to him that I am about to punish his house forever, for the iniquity that he knew, because his sons were blaspheming God, and he did not restrain them.<sup>14</sup>Therefore I swear to the house of Eli that the iniquity of Eli's house shall not be atoned for by sacrifice or offering forever."<sup>15</sup>Samuel lay until morning; then he opened the doors of the house of the LORD. And Samuel was afraid to tell the vision to Eli.<sup>16</sup>But Eli called Samuel and said, "Samuel, my son." And he said, "Here I am."<sup>17</sup>And Eli said, "What was it that he told you? Do not hide it from me. May God do so to you and more also if you hide anything from me of all that he told you."<sup>18</sup>So Samuel told him everything and hid nothing from him. And he said, "It is the LORD. Let him do what seems good to him."<sup>19</sup>And Samuel grew, and the LORD was with him and let none of his words fall to the ground.<sup>20</sup>And all Israel from Dan to Beersheba knew that Samuel was established as a prophet of the LORD.<sup>21</sup>And the LORD appeared again at Shiloh, for the LORD revealed himself to Samuel at Shiloh by the word of the LORD.
3.overview:
The chapter opens on one of the bleakest sentences in the Old Testament: the word of the LORD was rare. Israel still had its sanctuary, its priests and its sacrifices; what it did not have was God speaking. Eli's eyes have failed, and the lamp of God has not yet gone out.

God calls the boy by name three times while he sleeps, and three times Samuel runs to the wrong person, because he did not yet know the LORD. Eli works out who is calling, teaches the boy how to answer, and sends him back alone to hear a word against Eli's own house.

Eli's reply sounds magnificent, and nothing changes. The chapter closes where it could not have begun: the LORD revealing himself again at Shiloh by the word of the LORD.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–3 — When the Word Was Rare
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The boy ministers before Eli in a dark time: the word of the LORD is rare, Eli's eyes are dim, and the lamp of God has not yet gone out (vv. 1-3).
verseByVerse.theology: A famine of the word is the worst thing that can happen to a people (Amos 8:11), and it can fall on a nation whose worship is in perfect working order.
verseByVerse.examples: A congregation can have a full calendar, a sound building and a long history and still be hungry, if the Bible is not being opened and heard. The remedy at Shiloh was not more activity but a word from God.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the boy Samuel was ministering to the LORD in the presence of Eli. And the word of the LORD was rare in those days; there was no frequent vision. At that time Eli, whose eyesight had begun to grow dim so that he could not see, was lying down in his own place. The lamp of God had not yet gone out, and Samuel was lying down in the temple of the LORD, where the ark of God was.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Rare, not absent. And no frequent vision says it a second time, because the writer wants us to feel it.

Israel still had everything else. The tabernacle stood at Shiloh with the ark inside it; there was a high priest, a rota of sacrifices, and pilgrims coming up year by year. The whole apparatus of the covenant was in working order. What was missing was God saying anything.

Amos gives that condition its name centuries later, and it is the worst judgment in his book: not a famine of bread, nor a thirst for water, but of hearing the words of the LORD (Amos 8:11). A nation can keep every outward form of religion running smoothly and be starving.

Eli's failing eyes are a plain fact, and in a book this carefully written they are also the third time we have watched him fail to see. He could not see that Hannah was praying. He could not see what his sons were doing at the altar, though he kept hearing about it. Now he cannot see at all.

The lamp is the menorah, which the law required to burn from evening until morning (Ex. 27:20-21), so it is still night, with morning not far off. The writer does not press it as a picture, but it is hard to miss. The light in the house of God has not gone out; it is very nearly out. Israel's priesthood is corrupt, its high priest is blind, its word from God is rare, and the lamp is still burning, just, in the hour before morning.

The temple is the sanctuary at Shiloh, by now a more settled building with doors and doorposts (1:9; 3:15). The ark is the throne of God on earth, the most dangerous object in Israel, the thing men die for touching, and a child is asleep on the floor near it, because that is where he lives.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 4–10 — Speak, for Your Servant Hears
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The LORD calls three times and three times Samuel runs to Eli (vv. 4-8), because he does not yet know the LORD (v. 7). Eli understands at last and tells him what to say, and when the LORD comes and stands and calls, the boy answers (vv. 8-10).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 7 is the hinge of the chapter. The boy who has served at the tabernacle since he was weaned does not yet know God, and that small word yet is what separates him from Eli's sons (2:12).
verseByVerse.examples: Eli cannot hear God himself, yet he points a child to the voice he cannot hear. A parent or teacher whose own faith feels dim can still do that much, and it may be the most useful thing they ever do.
