verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD called Samuel, and he said, "Here I am!" and ran to Eli and said, "Here I am, for you called me." But he said, "I did not call; lie down again." So he went and lay down. And the LORD called again, "Samuel!" and Samuel arose and went to Eli and said, "Here I am, for you called me." But he said, "I did not call, my son; lie down again." Now Samuel did not yet know the LORD, and the word of the LORD had not yet been revealed to him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God speaks, and the first word out of the boy is the right one. Here I am (hinneni) is the answer Abraham gave on the mountain, and Jacob at Beersheba, and Moses at the bush, and Isaiah in the temple: not information about his location but a man putting himself at somebody's disposal. Samuel says it correctly and runs to the wrong person.

He runs, and the detail is affectionate: when somebody calls him in the night he goes at once. Eli is patient too. My son, he says the second time, with no irritation at being woken twice before dawn.

Samuel did not yet know the LORD. The chapter turns on this verse, and it is easy to read past. This boy was given to God before he was conceived and has lived at the sanctuary since he was a toddler. He wears a linen ephod and ministers to the LORD daily; the narrator has said so three times. He sleeps in the room with the ark, his mother makes him a robe every year, and there is not a word of complaint about him anywhere in the book. He does not know God.

Set that beside 2:12, where Eli's sons did not know the LORD. Samuel did not yet know him; Eli's sons simply did not. One is a boy who has never been introduced; the other is two men who have had every opportunity and made up their minds. The distance between them is the direction they are facing.

Take this personally if you were raised in it. It is entirely possible to grow up inside the building, to know the services and the songs, to serve faithfully and be thought well of, and to have had no personal dealings with God at all. Samuel's case is the hopeful one: the yet was about to expire. And note who does the work. Samuel does not seek God; God calls Samuel, by name, three times, while the boy has no idea who is speaking. Nobody in this chapter comes looking for the LORD. He comes looking for a child in the dark.

Does God speak audibly today, as he did to Samuel? He spoke this way while he was giving his word through the prophets. Now in these last days he has spoken to us by his Son (Heb 1:1–2), and the Scriptures are complete and sufficient (2 Tim 3:16–17). Some Christians believe God still speaks by voices and impressions, and faithful believers differ here. This commentary holds that such revelation has ceased, because God's word in his Son is final and the Scriptures are complete; but it gladly owns as brothers those who see it otherwise, and all agree that every claimed voice must be tested by Scripture. The way to hear God today is to open the Bible: Speak, for your servant hears is the right prayer as we read.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD called Samuel again the third time. And he arose and went to Eli and said, "Here I am, for you called me." Then Eli perceived that the LORD was calling the boy. Therefore Eli said to Samuel, "Go, lie down, and if he calls you, you shall say, 'Speak, LORD, for your servant hears.'" So Samuel went and lay down in his place. And the LORD came and stood, calling as at other times, "Samuel! Samuel!" And Samuel said, "Speak, for your servant hears."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Third time, and the old man works it out. Give him this. He is blind, his family is under sentence, he has not heard from God himself in who knows how long, and it takes him three attempts, but he gets there: not that somebody is calling, but who.

Then one of the best things Eli does in this book. He does not tell the boy to fetch him so that he can hear it too. He teaches a child how to answer God and sends him back to bed alone. And the words are exactly right: not "listen, LORD, for your servant is speaking", which is what a great deal of prayer amounts to, but you talk, and I am here to receive it. He is sending the boy to hear a word he has every reason to think will be against himself, and he sends him anyway. Whatever else the man was, he did not try to keep God quiet.

The LORD came and stood. The earlier calls were a voice. This time God comes, and calls him by name twice over, the way a person is addressed when what follows matters: Abraham on the mountain, Moses at the bush, Saul on the Damascus road.

Readers have long noticed that Samuel leaves out the name Eli gave him: not speak, LORD but speak. The text does not tell us why, and it would be easy to make too much of it. It may be nerves, or a boy who has just realised who is standing in the room. What he says is the whole of the substance, and God answers it.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The message is about Eli. God will do a thing that makes ears tingle and fulfil all he has spoken against Eli's house (vv. 11-12), and the charge is that Eli knew and did not restrain his sons (v. 13). Then the oath that this iniquity will never be atoned for by sacrifice (v. 14).
verseByVerse.theology: Sins of omission are real sins. Eli did not approve, join in or get deceived; he had the information and the authority and used neither.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 14 is a sentence on one priestly family, not a general rule that sin can put a person past forgiveness. The note below says why, and what the verse does teach.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD said to Samuel, "Behold, I am about to do a thing in Israel at which the two ears of everyone who hears it will tingle. On that day I will fulfill against Eli all that I have spoken concerning his house, from beginning to end. And I declare to him that I am about to punish his house forever, for the iniquity that he knew, because his sons were blaspheming God, and he did not restrain them. Therefore I swear to the house of Eli that the iniquity of Eli's house shall not be atoned for by sacrifice or offering forever."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The first word of God to Samuel is a word of judgment on the household he lives in. A boy of perhaps twelve is given his first message from God, and it is the destruction of the man who taught him the words to receive it with.

The image is physical: ears that ring, the sensation after a very loud noise, and God uses it of what Israel will feel when the news comes. Scripture uses it twice more, both times of national catastrophe (2 Kings 21:12; Jer. 19:3).

Nothing new is being announced. This confirms the oracle the man of God brought in chapter 2: all that I have spoken. So Eli has already had this warning, in detail, from a prophet, and has had time to act on it. Between chapter 2 and chapter 3 the sons are still in office.

Now the charge, and it is sharper than chapter 2's. He knew: chapter 2 told us he kept hearing about it from everybody in the country, so there is no ignorance to plead. And he did not restrain them. He had the authority to stop it, as high priest and their father, and the law he administered warned that priests who profaned holy things would die (Lev. 22:9); he used it to have one conversation. God does not charge Eli with his sons' sin. He charges him with his own, a sin of omission committed with full information over years.

Verse 14 is the most frightening in the chapter and must be handled exactly. For this house, this iniquity, no sacrifice will remove it, and God swears to it. The cruelty for a priestly family is precise: they had made a living out of the offerings, and the offerings will do nothing for them.

Say what it does not mean, because a verse like this can do great damage to an anxious reader. It is not a general statement that a person's sin can put him beyond forgiveness. It is a judicial sentence on one household in one generation, spoken through a named prophet, and no comparable oracle stands over anybody reading this. A reader who lies awake afraid that he has sinned beyond forgiveness shows by that very fear that his heart has not turned to contempt; the door Christ opened is still open to him (John 6:37).

What it does establish is that sacrifice is not a machine. Eli's family assumed the system they administered would cover whatever they did. God tells them the altar is not a laundry, and that a man who despises the offering cannot then shelter behind it. Hebrews says the same to Christians in almost the same shape: if we go on sinning deliberately after receiving the knowledge of the truth, there no longer remains a sacrifice for sins (Heb. 10:26). The warning is not that Christ's blood is insufficient. It is that there is no other, and a man who treats it with contempt has nowhere else to go.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Samuel is afraid to tell Eli, who puts him under oath to hide nothing and then says, it is the LORD (vv. 15-18). Samuel grows, the LORD lets none of his words fail, all Israel knows him as a prophet, and the LORD appears again at Shiloh (vv. 19-21).
verseByVerse.theology: Eli's answer sounds like the finest submission in the book, and nothing follows it. The note on vv. 15-18 weighs the difference between resignation and repentance.
verseByVerse.examples: The chapter's two ends answer each other: it opened with the word of the LORD rare and closes with God revealing himself at Shiloh by the word.

verseByVerse.quote: Samuel lay until morning; then he opened the doors of the house of the LORD. And Samuel was afraid to tell the vision to Eli. But Eli called Samuel and said, "Samuel, my son." And he said, "Here I am." And Eli said, "What was it that he told you? Do not hide it from me. May God do so to you and more also if you hide anything from me of all that he told you." So Samuel told him everything and hid nothing from him. And he said, "It is the LORD. Let him do what seems good to him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
He has been awake since before dawn holding the worst news in Israel, and at first light he opens the doors of the house of the LORD, as he does every morning. The routine goes on while he works out how to say it. He is also afraid, and the narrator neither excuses nor criticises it: the message destroys the only family he has.

My son, again, and here I am, again, this time to the right person.

The old man puts him under oath, in the strongest form the language has, to conceal nothing. He knows what is coming, and he insists on hearing the whole of it from a frightened child. There is a kind of courage in that. Most of us, given the chance to avoid the specifics of a judgment we already suspect, would take it.

Eli's answer is, on the face of it, magnificent. No protest, no bargaining, no blaming the messenger or pleading his years of service. He acknowledges whose word it is and submits to it, as Job did when his children were gone, and Scripture says that in all this Job did not sin (Job 1:21-22).

Then nothing. The sons are not removed. There is no discipline, no repentance, no change of any kind. One chapter later Hophni and Phinehas carry the ark out of Shiloh into a battle, and their father lets them, and they die exactly as promised.

So weigh the sentence again. Let him do what seems good to him can be the voice of faith, and it can be the voice of a man who has decided nothing can be done and is therefore relieved of doing anything. From outside the two are indistinguishable; the difference shows afterwards, in whether anything changes. That is the whole tragedy of Eli, and a common enough shape: submission to God's sovereignty used as a reason to leave sin where it is. Resignation is not repentance. It is much easier, and it can be made to sound more spiritual.

verseByVerse.quote: And Samuel grew, and the LORD was with him and let none of his words fall to the ground. And all Israel from Dan to Beersheba knew that Samuel was established as a prophet of the LORD. And the LORD appeared again at Shiloh, for the LORD revealed himself to Samuel at Shiloh by the word of the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He grew, as the book keeps saying while the house of Eli shrinks. The LORD was with him, and this history can say nothing higher about anybody. And God let none of his words fall to the ground: no word of his lay in the dust having come to nothing. Every word he spoke as a prophet arrived.

That is the test Moses laid down for a true prophet: when a prophet speaks in the name of the LORD, if the word does not come to pass or come true, that is a word that the LORD has not spoken (Deut. 18:22). Samuel passes it from the first message, and the first message was against the man who raised him.

The same chapter of Deuteronomy promises a prophet like Moses, whose words the people must hear (Deut. 18:15). Peter, preaching in the temple, says that promise is fulfilled in Jesus, and adds that all the prophets from Samuel onward proclaimed these days (Acts 3:22–24). So the New Testament itself sets this boy at the head of the line of prophets that ends in Christ. Samuel's words did not fall to the ground; Christ's words, he said, will never pass away (Mark 13:31).

The northern end of from Dan to Beersheba is the town whose founding stands near the end of Judges, taken by six hundred armed men from an unsuspecting people and furnished with a stolen idol and a hired priest (Judg. 18:27-31). It has settled into the language as simply the top of the map. The country has a man again through whom God speaks.

Read the last verse against the first. Verse 1: the word of the LORD was rare. Verse 21: the LORD appeared again at Shiloh by the word of the LORD. The famine is over, and it ended because God called a sleeping child by name three times in the dark and the child eventually said speak, for your servant hears.

God did not break the silence by restoring the priesthood, which was beyond saving, or by a sign in the sky or an army. He raised up one person who would listen, and that was enough to end a famine in a whole nation. And he revealed himself by speaking, which is how he has always chosen to be known: not first by displays of power but by speech. That is why the New Testament opens its greatest argument here: Long ago, at many times and in many ways, God spoke to our fathers by the prophets, but in these last days he has spoken to us by his Son (Heb. 1:1-2). The rare word at Shiloh became frequent through Samuel and the prophets after him, and then God said everything he had to say in a person. That word now stands written, and the church that holds it need never be left as Israel was at Shiloh. The night ended.
verseByVerse.note: “From Dan to Beersheba” means the whole land, north to south.

3.theology:
A famine of the word (v. 1). The forms were all intact and God was not speaking. A church can keep every outward thing running smoothly and be starving.

Did not yet know the LORD (v. 7). It is possible to grow up inside the building, to serve faithfully and be well thought of, and still not know God. Samuel's is the hopeful case: the yet was about to expire, and it expired because God came looking for him, not he for God.

Knew, and did not restrain (v. 13). God charges Eli not with his sons' sin but with his own: an omission committed with full information, over years, by a man with the authority to stop it.

No sacrifice for this house (v. 14). This is a sentence on one household, not a general rule that sin can put a person past forgiveness. Its lesson is that a man who despises the offering cannot then shelter behind it; for Christians the warning is not that Christ's blood is insufficient but that there is no other.

Resignation is not repentance (v. 18). Eli spoke the words of faith and changed nothing. Submission and giving up can sound identical; the difference shows afterwards, in whether anything changes.

The famine ends (vv. 19-21). God broke the silence not by reforming the priesthood, which was beyond saving, but by raising up one person who would listen, and he did it by the word of the LORD. That is how he has always chosen to be known, and his word in the Son is final and stands written.
3.examples:
Then: A blind old priest, his family under sentence, taught a child the words to answer God with and sent him back alone to receive a message about Eli's own house.

Now: Two things, pulling in opposite directions. Verse 7 is for anyone who grew up in church: you can serve for years and not yet know the LORD, and the word to hold on to is yet, because God was the one doing the calling. And verse 18 is for anyone who has made peace with a sin in their family, their church or themselves and dressed the peace up as submission to God's will. Eli said exactly the right thing and removed nobody from office. Ask what actually changed after the last time you said let him do what seems good. Then take it where Eli never did: not to resignation but to confession, to the God who has not closed his altar to us, because Christ's one offering stands for every failure we bring to it, and his Spirit gives the courage to act on what we know.

4.title: Ichabod: The Glory Has Departed
4.text: <sup>1</sup>And the word of Samuel came to all Israel. Now Israel went out to battle against the Philistines. They encamped at Ebenezer, and the Philistines encamped at Aphek.<sup>2</sup>The Philistines drew up in line against Israel, and when the battle spread, Israel was defeated before the Philistines, who killed about four thousand men on the field of battle.<sup>3</sup>And when the people came to the camp, the elders of Israel said, "Why has the LORD defeated us today before the Philistines? Let us bring the ark of the covenant of the LORD here from Shiloh, that it may come among us and save us from the power of our enemies."<sup>4</sup>So the people sent to Shiloh and brought from there the ark of the covenant of the LORD of hosts, who is enthroned on the cherubim. And the two sons of Eli, Hophni and Phinehas, were there with the ark of the covenant of God.<sup>5</sup>As soon as the ark of the covenant of the LORD came into the camp, all Israel gave a mighty shout, so that the earth resounded.<sup>6</sup>And when the Philistines heard the noise of the shouting, they said, "What does this great shouting in the camp of the Hebrews mean?" And when they learned that the ark of the LORD had come to the camp,<sup>7</sup>the Philistines were afraid, for they said, "A god has come into the camp." And they said, "Woe to us! For nothing like this has happened before.<sup>8</sup>Woe to us! Who can deliver us from the power of these mighty gods? These are the gods who struck the Egyptians with every sort of plague in the wilderness.<sup>9</sup>Take courage, and be men, O Philistines, lest you become slaves to the Hebrews as they have been to you; be men and fight."<sup>10</sup>So the Philistines fought, and Israel was defeated, and they fled, every man to his home. And there was a very great slaughter, for thirty thousand foot soldiers of Israel fell.<sup>11</sup>And the ark of God was captured, and the two sons of Eli, Hophni and Phinehas, died.<sup>12</sup>A man of Benjamin ran from the battle line and came to Shiloh the same day, with his clothes torn and with dirt on his head.<sup>13</sup>When he arrived, Eli was sitting on his seat by the road watching, for his heart trembled for the ark of God. And when the man came into the city and told the news, all the city cried out.<sup>14</sup>When Eli heard the sound of the outcry, he said, "What is this uproar?" Then the man hurried and came and told Eli.<sup>15</sup>Now Eli was ninety-eight years old and his eyes were set so that he could not see.<sup>16</sup>And the man said to Eli, "I am he who has come from the battle; I fled from the battle today." And he said, "How did it go, my son?"<sup>17</sup>He who brought the news answered and said, "Israel has fled before the Philistines, and there has also been a great defeat among the people. Your two sons also, Hophni and Phinehas, are dead, and the ark of God has been captured."<sup>18</sup>As soon as he mentioned the ark of God, Eli fell over backward from his seat by the side of the gate, and his neck was broken and he died, for the man was old and heavy. He had judged Israel forty years.<sup>19</sup>Now his daughter-in-law, the wife of Phinehas, was pregnant, about to give birth. And when she heard the news that the ark of God was captured, and that her father-in-law and her husband were dead, she bowed and gave birth, for her pains came upon her.<sup>20</sup>And about the time of her death the women attending her said to her, "Do not be afraid, for you have borne a son." But she did not answer or pay attention.<sup>21</sup>And she named the child Ichabod, saying, "The glory has departed from Israel!" because the ark of God had been captured and because of her father-in-law and her husband.<sup>22</sup>And she said, "The glory has departed from Israel, for the ark of God has been captured."
4.overview:
Israel loses four thousand men, and the elders ask the right question, why has the LORD defeated us today? Then they answer it themselves and send to Shiloh for the ark. Nobody asks the prophet.

The ark arrives to a shout that shakes the ground and terrifies the Philistines. Israel loses thirty thousand, the ark of God is captured, and Eli's two sons die on the same day, as promised.

A runner reaches Shiloh, and it is the news of the ark, not of his sons, that topples Eli from his seat. His daughter-in-law, dying in childbirth, names her son Ichabod: the glory has departed.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Defeated at Ebenezer, the elders ask why the LORD has done it and then answer for themselves: fetch the ark from Shiloh (vv. 1-3). It comes, with Hophni and Phinehas (v. 4).
verseByVerse.theology: Naming God as the agent of their defeat was right; not waiting for his answer was the failure. Samuel had just been established in all Israel as a prophet of the LORD (3:20), and nobody sent for him. They had a word from God within reach and sent for furniture.
verseByVerse.examples: The elders' instinct is a familiar one: when things go wrong, reach for whatever seemed to work last time rather than ask God what he is saying. It feels like faith, and it can be the opposite.

verseByVerse.quote: And the word of Samuel came to all Israel. Now Israel went out to battle against the Philistines. They encamped at Ebenezer, and the Philistines encamped at Aphek. The Philistines drew up in line against Israel, and when the battle spread, Israel was defeated before the Philistines, who killed about four thousand men on the field of battle. And when the people came to the camp, the elders of Israel said, "Why has the LORD defeated us today before the Philistines? Let us bring the ark of the covenant of the LORD here from Shiloh, that it may come among us and save us from the power of our enemies." So the people sent to Shiloh and brought from there the ark of the covenant of the LORD of hosts, who is enthroned on the cherubim. And the two sons of Eli, Hophni and Phinehas, were there with the ark of the covenant of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The first clause and the second have nothing to do with each other, and that is the point. Chapter 3 ended with God speaking again and a prophet established from Dan to Beersheba; the word of Samuel came to all Israel. Then the nation goes out to fight with no sign that it consulted him.

Note the place name, because it will come back. Ebenezer, stone of help. Israel loses two battles on this ground, and three chapters later Samuel will set up a stone and give it that name for a reason (7:12).

Four thousand dead, and the day is lost. The elders' question is a good one. They do not blame the Philistines' strength or the ground or their equipment. They name God as the agent of their own defeat, which is better theology than much of the book of Judges. Then they do not wait for the answer.

The grammar shows the sin. In the ESV the subject of save is it (the footnote allows "he", but the scene shows where their trust lies). The subject is not the LORD but the ark. A wooden box overlaid with gold has been made the saviour of Israel by the elders of the nation.

And consider what they had instead. God had just broken a generation of silence. There was a prophet in the land, known to every tribe, at Shiloh, where they sent the messengers. They asked why has the LORD defeated us, and the man who could have told them was standing in the building they sent the cart to.

This is Micah's mistake with a national budget (Judg. 17:13): get the right object, install it properly, and the outcome follows. It is religion run as machinery. And the ark was not a fraud. It was the real thing, made to God's own specification, the place where he had said he would meet with them. That is what makes this so dangerous. Nobody here has abandoned the true religion; they have taken the genuine article and used it as a lever.

The narrator gives the ark its longest title yet, the LORD of hosts, who is enthroned on the cherubim. He is not being ceremonious. He is telling us what they thought they were carrying and what they were actually carrying, the throne of the God of every army there is, and then who was carrying it: Hophni and Phinehas, the two men whose deaths were promised in chapter 2, have their hands on it.
verseByVerse.note: Aphek lay on the edge of the coastal plain; Ebenezer was nearby.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Israel's shout at the ark terrifies the Philistines, who resolve to be men and fight (vv. 5-9). Israel is routed, thirty thousand fall, the ark is captured, and Hophni and Phinehas die (vv. 10-11).
verseByVerse.theology: Being near holy things is not the same as trusting God. Israel had the ark in the camp and no prayer on its lips.
verseByVerse.examples: God had warned both Eli and Israel (2:34; 3:11-14). What happens at Ebenezer is not bad luck but a word coming true, the kind that does not fall to the ground.

verseByVerse.quote: As soon as the ark of the covenant of the LORD came into the camp, all Israel gave a mighty shout, so that the earth resounded. And when the Philistines heard the noise of the shouting, they said, "What does this great shouting in the camp of the Hebrews mean?" And when they learned that the ark of the LORD had come to the camp, the Philistines were afraid, for they said, "A god has come into the camp." And they said, "Woe to us! For nothing like this has happened before. Woe to us! Who can deliver us from the power of these mighty gods? These are the gods who struck the Egyptians with every sort of plague in the wilderness. Take courage, and be men, O Philistines, lest you become slaves to the Hebrews as they have been to you; be men and fight."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The cheer is enormous and entirely misplaced. A beaten army is roaring, not because God has spoken or anybody has repented, but because a box has arrived. No prayer, no confession, no enquiry. Just noise.

Philistia's fear is more accurate than Israel's confidence. A god has come into the camp. They do not think a religious object has been delivered; they think a person has arrived, and they are right.

Their theology is a mess and their instinct is sound. They say gods, plural, because that is the only grammar they have. They put the plagues in the wilderness. They have the story second-hand and garbled, some two to four centuries old (the date of the exodus is debated), passed down among people who lost. But they have the essential thing right: this is the God who did Egypt, and there is no standing in front of him. The exodus is still, centuries later and in a foreign army, the thing everybody knows about the God of the Hebrews. It got out, and it stayed out.

Their response is honest. No idol is sent for. They do not fetch Dagon from Ashdod to even the odds, though the next chapter shows they had him. They judge the situation desperate and decide to be men and fight.

Put the two camps side by side, because the writer has. Israel: a shout, a box, and no prayer. Philistia: terror, an accurate assessment, and a decision to do the only thing they can. One of these armies is about to lose thirty thousand men.

verseByVerse.quote: So the Philistines fought, and Israel was defeated, and they fled, every man to his home. And there was a very great slaughter, for thirty thousand foot soldiers of Israel fell. And the ark of God was captured, and the two sons of Eli, Hophni and Phinehas, died.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Thirty thousand. (Some think the Hebrew word for thousand can also mean a military unit, which would make both figures smaller; either way the second slaughter dwarfs the first.) The first time they lost four thousand and thought the problem was that God was not with them; now they lose seven and a half times as many with the ark in the camp.

That is the answer to the elders' question, in the only language they were listening to. He defeats them again, worse, with his own throne standing in their lines, so that nobody can say the ark was absent.

The ark of God was captured. The chest that held the tablets of the covenant, with the mercy seat and the cherubim over it, the place from which God had said he would speak, is carried off by the Philistines. God allowed the sign of his own presence to be taken by pagans as a trophy rather than let his people go on using it as a charm. He would sooner be carried into the temple of Dagon than be treated as a lucky object by Israel.

That is sobering for anyone who assumes God is obliged to protect the institutions that bear his name. He is not. He has let a sanctuary fall, a priesthood end and the ark itself go into captivity, and the next chapter shows he was in no difficulty whatever while it happened.

Then, almost in passing, the sons die. The sign given to their father has arrived, both of them shall die on the same day (2:34), and the narrator does not stop to point it out.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A runner reaches Shiloh where blind old Eli sits by the road, trembling for the ark (vv. 12-15). He hears four items of news, and at the fourth, the ark, he falls backwards and dies (vv. 16-18).
verseByVerse.theology: A long life of faithful-sounding words and weak action ends in a single afternoon. The story is told without contempt, and it warns that putting off dealing with sin does not make the reckoning smaller.
verseByVerse.examples: The book has kept finding Eli in a chair by a door: sitting by the doorpost when Hannah prayed (1:9), lying in his own place when God called the boy (3:2), and now sitting by the gate. He dies in it. He had judged Israel forty years.

verseByVerse.quote: A man of Benjamin ran from the battle line and came to Shiloh the same day, with his clothes torn and with dirt on his head. When he arrived, Eli was sitting on his seat by the road watching, for his heart trembled for the ark of God. And when the man came into the city and told the news, all the city cried out. When Eli heard the sound of the outcry, he said, "What is this uproar?" Then the man hurried and came and told Eli.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He runs about twenty miles, and everybody who sees him knows before he speaks. Torn clothes and earth on the head are the signs of mourning; the messenger is wearing the news.

The narrator tells us what the old man at the roadside was thinking about. Not his sons. His heart trembled for the ark of God. He failed to restrain his boys for years, and God's charge was that he honoured them above the LORD. Yet on the last afternoon of his life, blind, at ninety-eight, sitting by the road because he cannot go and look, what he is afraid for is the ark. Whatever was wrong with the man, that was in him too.

The town hears first and the high priest hears the town. He cannot see the messenger arrive; the news reaches him as a noise from a street he cannot look down, and he has to ask what the shouting is.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Eli was ninety-eight years old and his eyes were set so that he could not see. And the man said to Eli, "I am he who has come from the battle; I fled from the battle today." And he said, "How did it go, my son?" He who brought the news answered and said, "Israel has fled before the Philistines, and there has also been a great defeat among the people. Your two sons also, Hophni and Phinehas, are dead, and the ark of God has been captured." As soon as he mentioned the ark of God, Eli fell over backward from his seat by the side of the gate, and his neck was broken and he died, for the man was old and heavy. He had judged Israel forty years.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In chapter 3 his eyes had begun to grow dim; now they are set, fixed, gone. And my son: he has called Samuel that, and his own boys, and now a stranger off the battlefield. It is the last thing he says.

The runner delivers four items in order of increasing weight: flight, defeat, your sons, the ark. Any one of the first three would flatten a man, and a messenger who is no trained diplomat has instinctively put them in the order a priest of Israel would feel them.

It is the last kind thing the Bible says about Eli. He heard the army was routed and stayed upright. He heard of the great slaughter and stayed upright. He heard that both his sons were dead, the two boys he had protected for a lifetime, whose deaths two prophets had foretold, and he stayed upright. As soon as he mentioned the ark of God, he went over backwards.

The man whose whole indictment was that he honoured his sons above God died of the other news. It does not undo the years of doing nothing, and God's sentence stood and was carried out. But the narrator wants us to know where the old priest's heart finally broke, and it was not at his own family.

Then a detail almost comic and without malice: old and heavy. The word for heavy is from the same root as kabod, glory, and the narrator probably wants us to remember why he had grown fat: he had been eating the choicest parts of Israel's offerings (2:29). The last physical fact recorded about him is the shape the sin left on his body.

An obituary of six words for four decades in the highest office in Israel. Forty years is a full generation, the span given to the best judges. He was not a wicked man; he was a weak one, and his epitaph records the length of his service and nothing he did with it. (The Greek Old Testament reads twenty years here; the Hebrew, followed by most English versions, has forty.)

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Phinehas's widow, giving birth, hears the news and is dying; told she has a son, she does not answer (vv. 19-20). She names him Ichabod and says it twice, the second time for the ark alone (vv. 21-22).
verseByVerse.theology: Set her beside Hannah. One woman wept for years for a son and sang when she had to give him away; the other is told she has a son and will not turn her head. Between them stands everything that has happened to Israel in four chapters.
verseByVerse.examples: Ichabod's name appears once more, in the pedigree of a later priest, his nephew Ahijah (14:3). The family went on, carrying the name of its worst day.

verseByVerse.quote: Now his daughter-in-law, the wife of Phinehas, was pregnant, about to give birth. And when she heard the news that the ark of God was captured, and that her father-in-law and her husband were dead, she bowed and gave birth, for her pains came upon her. And about the time of her death the women attending her said to her, "Do not be afraid, for you have borne a son." But she did not answer or pay attention. And she named the child Ichabod, saying, "The glory has departed from Israel!" because the ark of God had been captured and because of her father-in-law and her husband. And she said, "The glory has departed from Israel, for the ark of God has been captured."
verseByVerse.commentary:
In one day she loses her husband, her father-in-law and her nation's holiest possession, and goes into labour. The book never names her. She is the wife of one of the two worst men in Israel, and she is about to speak the chapter's title.

You have borne a son is the sentence Hannah wept through years of festivals to hear, the whole of what the first chapter was about, and it is spoken here to a woman who cannot be reached by it.

She names her son for a national catastrophe. Kabod is a word about weight, the substance and sheer significance of God among his people. She is saying the weight has gone out of Israel. Everyone who calls the boy will say aloud what happened on the day he was born.

She says it twice, and the second time she keeps only one of her three reasons: the ark. A woman dying in childbirth, who has just lost her husband and his father, states the disaster in its true order of magnitude on her way out. Her private grief is real and she does not put it first.

She is right that something has gone: Shiloh is finished, never again a working sanctuary in the Bible. The psalmist looks back on this day: he forsook his dwelling at Shiloh, the tent where he dwelt among mankind, and delivered his power to captivity, his glory to the hand of the foe (Ps. 78:60-61). And Jeremiah, in the temple gate, tells a congregation who thought their building made them safe to go and see what God did to Shiloh (Jer. 7:12).

Where she is wrong is the geography. She thinks the glory left Israel. In fact it went to Ashdod. It was not rescued by an Israelite army, or ransomed, or recovered by a raid. It went into a pagan temple as a trophy, and demolished the god it was set beside, and came home seven months later on a cart pulled by two cows, with nobody in Israel having lifted a finger. God did not need the ark defended. He had let it be taken precisely because his people had begun to think he did.

And the last word on Ichabod's name is not in this book. Centuries after a woman at Shiloh gasped out that the glory had departed, John writes the answer in one sentence: and the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we have seen his glory, glory as of the only Son from the Father, full of grace and truth (John 1:14). John's verb for dwelt means pitched his tent. The glory that left the tabernacle at Shiloh came back, and not in a box. And what the elders tried to do with the ark cannot be done with him. The lid of the ark, the mercy seat where the blood was sprinkled, is the word Paul uses when he says God put Christ forward as a propitiation by his blood, to be received by faith (Rom. 3:25). He is not a charm to be carried into battle; he is the Lord who gave himself, and is trusted, not operated.
verseByVerse.note: Ichabod means “no glory” or “where is the glory?”

4.theology:
The right question, unanswered (v. 3). The elders named God as the agent of their defeat and did not wait to hear why, though Samuel was at Shiloh when their messengers arrived.

Religion as machinery. That it may come among us and save us makes the ark the saviour. The danger is precisely that the ark was genuine: nobody here abandoned the true religion; they took the real thing and used it as a lever.

The enemy nearer the truth (vv. 7-9). The Philistines' memory of the exodus was garbled, yet they knew a person had arrived, and they did not send for Dagon. Israel shouts; Philistia fights.

God let it be taken (v. 11). He is not obliged to protect the institutions that bear his name, and he would rather lose the ark to pagans as a trophy than let his people go on using it as a charm.

Where Eli's heart broke (vv. 13, 18). He stayed upright through the news of his sons and fell at the news of the ark. It undoes nothing, and the sentence stood; but it is where the narrator chooses to leave him.

Ichabod, and where the glory went. She is right that the glory has gone from Shiloh, and wrong about where: it went to Ashdod and came home on a cart, with nobody in Israel lifting a finger. The last word on her son's name is John's: the Word dwelt among us, and we have seen his glory (John 1:14). The glory came back, and not in a box.
4.examples:
Then: A defeated army sent twenty miles for a gold-covered chest, cheered when it arrived, and lost seven and a half times as many men as in the first battle. The enemy, who had the story of the exodus garbled and second-hand, were the only people on the field who took the God of Israel seriously.

Now: Two things. The first is the elders' question, and it repays finishing as well as copying: they were right to ask why God had let it happen and wrong to stop asking before he answered. The second is harder. The ark was not a superstition; it was God's own arrangement. So the warning here is not about false religion but about the true one (the sound church, the right doctrine, the disciplines that have worked before) quietly reclassified as the thing that produces the outcome. God would rather let such a thing be taken from you than let you go on operating it. The cure is not a better technique but the Lord himself, who came near in his Son and gave himself for us: he is trusted, and he is not far from the one who turns back to him.

5.title: Dagon Falls Before the Ark
5.text: <sup>1</sup>When the Philistines captured the ark of God, they brought it from Ebenezer to Ashdod.<sup>2</sup>Then the Philistines took the ark of God and brought it into the house of Dagon and set it up beside Dagon.<sup>3</sup>And when the people of Ashdod rose early the next day, behold, Dagon had fallen face downward on the ground before the ark of the LORD. So they took Dagon and put him back in his place.<sup>4</sup>But when they rose early on the next morning, behold, Dagon had fallen face downward on the ground before the ark of the LORD, and the head of Dagon and both his hands were lying cut off on the threshold. Only the trunk of Dagon was left to him.<sup>5</sup>This is why the priests of Dagon and all who enter the house of Dagon do not tread on the threshold of Dagon in Ashdod to this day.<sup>6</sup>The hand of the LORD was heavy against the people of Ashdod, and he terrified and afflicted them with tumors, both Ashdod and its territory.<sup>7</sup>And when the men of Ashdod saw how things were, they said, "The ark of the God of Israel must not remain with us, for his hand is hard against us and against Dagon our god."<sup>8</sup>So they sent and gathered together all the lords of the Philistines and said, "What shall we do with the ark of the God of Israel?" They answered, "Let the ark of the God of Israel be brought around to Gath." So they brought the ark of the God of Israel there.<sup>9</sup>But after they had brought it around, the hand of the LORD was against the city, causing a very great panic, and he afflicted the men of the city, both young and old, so that tumors broke out on them.<sup>10</sup>So they sent the ark of God to Ekron. But as soon as the ark of God came to Ekron, the people of Ekron cried out, "They have brought around to us the ark of the God of Israel to kill us and our people."<sup>11</sup>They sent therefore and gathered together all the lords of the Philistines and said, "Send away the ark of the God of Israel, and let it return to its own place, that it may not kill us and our people." For there was a deathly panic throughout the whole city. The hand of God was very heavy there.<sup>12</sup>The men who did not die were struck with tumors, and the cry of the city went up to heaven.
5.overview:
The Philistines set their trophy beside Dagon in his temple at Ashdod. Two mornings running their god is found face down before the ark, the second time broken, and his priests respond with a rule about a doorstep.

Then come tumours, in Ashdod, Gath and Ekron. The five lords hold two emergency councils, and the whole of Philistine theology comes down to a decision about which town to move the box to. Not one person turns to the LORD.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — Face Down Before the Ark
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The ark is set beside Dagon in Ashdod (vv. 1-2). Two mornings running Dagon is found face down before it, the second time with head and hands broken off (vv. 3-4), and his priests still avoid the threshold to this day (v. 5).
verseByVerse.theology: The God who seemed beaten is the only one acting in the room. He needs no army and no priest to deal with a rival god in that god's own house.
verseByVerse.examples: Idols are not only statues. Anything we look to for the security only God can give, whether money, reputation or a person, has to be propped up by the one who trusts it, and sooner or later it falls on its face.

verseByVerse.quote: When the Philistines captured the ark of God, they brought it from Ebenezer to Ashdod. Then the Philistines took the ark of God and brought it into the house of Dagon and set it up beside Dagon. And when the people of Ashdod rose early the next day, behold, Dagon had fallen face downward on the ground before the ark of the LORD. So they took Dagon and put him back in his place. But when they rose early on the next morning, behold, Dagon had fallen face downward on the ground before the ark of the LORD, and the head of Dagon and both his hands were lying cut off on the threshold. Only the trunk of Dagon was left to him. This is why the priests of Dagon and all who enter the house of Dagon do not tread on the threshold of Dagon in Ashdod to this day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Putting the ark next to the statue is a statement. When one nation beat another, the victors took the loser's god home and set it before their own deity: our god defeated yours, and here is yours standing in his house as a servant. The ark is a trophy, and its position beside Dagon is the caption.

Dagon was the chief god of the Philistines, with temples at Ashdod and Gaza. He is the god in whose temple Samson brought down the roof, and in whose house Saul's head will hang (Judg. 16:23; 1 Chron. 10:10). Older books made him a fish-god, but his name is more probably linked to the Hebrew word for grain, and he was worshipped across the region long before the Philistines arrived.

They open the temple in the morning and their god is lying on his face in front of the prisoner. The posture is the point: face downward on the ground before the ark of the LORD. That is not how something falls over. That is how a man worships.

Their response comes close to comedy. Two or three men lift their god off the floor, brush him down, and stand him up again, because he cannot do it himself. This is the deity they had just credited with defeating the God of Israel, and he requires assistance to remain upright in his own building. Isaiah spent a whole chapter on precisely this: a man burns half a tree to cook his dinner, carves a god out of the other half, and bows to it, and never says is there not a lie in my right hand? (Isa. 44:14-20).

Morning two is not a repeat but an escalation, and the details are chosen. The head that knows and the hands that act are off, lying on the doorstep where everybody coming in has to step over them. Only the torso is left: the part that does nothing. Psalm 115 could be the caption for this room: They have mouths, but do not speak; eyes, but do not see, and then the line that turns it on the worshipper: those who make them become like them; so do all who trust in them (Ps. 115:5-8).

Note who is not present. No Israelite army, no priest, no prophet, no prayer. Israel does not know where the ark is. The whole thing is conducted overnight, in a locked pagan temple, by God, with nobody on his side for miles. Joash once said the only thing that needed saying about this kind of god: if he is a god, let him contend for himself (Judg. 6:31). Dagon has had two nights to contend, and he cannot stand up.

Their god has been decapitated in his own temple by a box, twice, and what the priesthood of Ashdod produces in response is a rule about where to put your feet. The custom outlives the incident and everybody knows why it exists. Nobody says the obvious thing, that if the LORD can do this to Dagon in Dagon's own house then Dagon is not worth the stone he is cut from. The evidence was total, and it was converted into a superstition about a doorstep.

That is what the human heart does with evidence it does not want. It does not deny it (these men remembered the event so exactly that they were still avoiding the spot generations later); it simply declines to draw the conclusion, and builds a small ritual around the place where the conclusion should have been.
verseByVerse.note: Ashdod was one of the five Philistine cities. Dagon was their chief god.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–12 — The Hand of the LORD Was Heavy
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Tumours strike Ashdod (v. 6), and the lords pass the ark to Gath, where the same happens (vv. 7-9). Ekron cries out the moment it arrives (v. 10), and a second council resolves to send it home while the cry of the city goes up to heaven (vv. 11-12).
verseByVerse.theology: The hand of the LORD was heavy (5:6) is the language of Egypt (Ex. 9:3), and so is the cry going up. The Philistines had told each other one chapter back that this was the God who did Egypt, and they were about to find out at first hand.
verseByVerse.examples: The citizens of Ekron turn on their own rulers before anything else (v. 10). Under pressure people usually argue about who brought the trouble in long before they ask what it means.

verseByVerse.quote: The hand of the LORD was heavy against the people of Ashdod, and he terrified and afflicted them with tumors, both Ashdod and its territory. And when the men of Ashdod saw how things were, they said, "The ark of the God of Israel must not remain with us, for his hand is hard against us and against Dagon our god." So they sent and gathered together all the lords of the Philistines and said, "What shall we do with the ark of the God of Israel?" They answered, "Let the ark of the God of Israel be brought around to Gath." So they brought the ark of the God of Israel there.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The god of Ashdod is dealt with, and then the city is. The hand of the LORD was heavy is a phrase with a history: Moses warned Pharaoh that the hand of the LORD will fall with a very severe plague upon your livestock (Ex. 9:3). The men at Aphek had said this was the God who struck the Egyptians. They were right, and the demonstration is now in their own towns. What the tumours were is not certain and little depends on it. The text is certain whose hand it was.

The men of Ashdod understand the situation exactly and draw the wrong conclusion. His hand is hard against us and against Dagon our god: they know who is doing this and that their own god has lost. They state the whole case correctly in one sentence, and decide that the ark must not remain with us.

A summit is convened, and its resolution is to move the problem to another city. Ashdod has a god it cannot fight and cannot get rid of, and the best five rulers can manage between them is to pass him along.

The “tumors” may have been boils, or the swellings of bubonic plague, since mice are part of the story (6:4–5); the old rendering “hemorrhoids” (the KJV’s “emerods”) is less likely. The Greek Old Testament adds at verse 6 that mice swarmed in the land, which fits the gold mice of the next chapter; the Hebrew mentions them only there.

verseByVerse.quote: But after they had brought it around, the hand of the LORD was against the city, causing a very great panic, and he afflicted the men of the city, both young and old, so that tumors broke out on them. So they sent the ark of God to Ekron. But as soon as the ark of God came to Ekron, the people of Ekron cried out, "They have brought around to us the ark of the God of Israel to kill us and our people." They sent therefore and gathered together all the lords of the Philistines and said, "Send away the ark of the God of Israel, and let it return to its own place, that it may not kill us and our people." For there was a deathly panic throughout the whole city. The hand of God was very heavy there. The men who did not die were struck with tumors, and the cry of the city went up to heaven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Gath gets what Ashdod got, with two words added: both young and old. Nobody is outside it.

By the third city the news has travelled ahead of the cart. Ekron is shouting before it is unloaded, and the complaint is not against the God of Israel but against their own leadership: they have brought around to us the ark... to kill us. The lords are now moving a weapon between their own towns and the citizens can see it.

The second summit reverses the first, and they put it this way: let it return to its own place. They are not releasing a prisoner or restoring stolen property; they are getting something out of the house.

The last verse is written in the language of Egypt again. The cry of the city goes up to heaven, as on the night of the firstborn there was a great cry in Egypt, for there was not a house where someone was not dead (Ex. 12:30).

Now stand back. Israel lost the ark because it treated the ark as a machine, and any onlooker would conclude that the God of Israel had been beaten and his box taken as a prize. Then, with no Israelite present, no army in the field, no prophet praying and nobody in the covenant nation even knowing where it was, God ran a campaign through three Philistine cities from inside a locked temple. He knocked down their god, dismembered him on his own doorstep, and made the rulers of Philistia hold two emergency summits about how to get rid of him. He did not need defending. That is the point of chapter 5, and it is the answer to Ichabod.

Christians have long seen here a pattern that reaches its height at the cross. There too the presence of God among men was handed over to the Gentiles, apparently beaten, and carried off by its enemies; and there, at the moment of seeming defeat, Christ disarmed the rulers and authorities and put them to open shame, triumphing over them (Col. 2:15). The Philistines carried the ark in as a trophy and carried it out as a terror. The powers that crucified the Lord of glory did not know what they were doing (1 Cor. 2:8), and the grave that received him could not hold him.

Yet not one Philistine turns to him. Three cities, seven months, a broken idol, a plague, and a nation that says out loud his hand is hard against us and against Dagon our god, and nobody worships. They want the God of Israel out of town.

A reader may ask why ordinary townspeople, young and old, suffered for what their lords and soldiers had done. The plague was judgment on a nation that had made war on God's people and paraded his throne as plunder, and it was also a summons. Rahab and the Gibeonites had shown that Canaanites who heard of this God's hand could turn to him and live (Josh. 2:9–11; 9:24). The door stood open, and Philistia spent seven months looking for a different one.

Hold that, because the next chapter shows Israel saying exactly the same thing.

5.theology:
God needs no defending. With no Israelite present and nobody praying, God ran a campaign through three Philistine cities from inside a locked pagan temple. That is the answer to Ichabod: the glory had not departed from God, only from Israel's keeping.

Let him contend for himself. Dagon had two nights to contend and had to be lifted back into position by his own worshippers, which is Isaiah's whole argument about idols in one image (Isa. 44:14-20).

The doorstep (v. 5). The heart does not deny evidence it does not want; it declines to draw the conclusion, and builds a small ritual where the conclusion should have been.

Right diagnosis, wrong conclusion (v. 7). They state the case correctly and decide the answer is to move it to Gath. Knowing exactly who God is and wanting him somewhere else is a position a person can hold indefinitely, and Israel takes it up at 6:20.
5.examples:
Then: A nation put the God of Israel in its temple as a prize, watched its own god fall before him, suffered seven months of plague, and produced as its entire response a rule about a doorstep.

Now: Two things. When the church looks beaten and its opponents look established, remember that God has been carried off as a trophy before, and the trophy demolished the building it was displayed in. He is never in the difficulty his people assume he is in. And the harder one: verse 5 is not really about Philistines. It asks what you have done with the evidence you already have, whether there is some fact about God you have quietly refused to draw the conclusion from, and built a small habit around instead. The door Philistia would not walk through is open to you: the God who disarmed the powers at the cross receives all who turn to him, and his Spirit gives the eyes to draw the conclusion and the will to follow it.

6.title: The Ark Returns

Tell us with what we shall send it to its place."<sup>3</sup>They said, "If you send away the ark of the God of Israel, do not send it empty, but by all means return him a guilt offering. Then you will be healed, and it will be known to you why his hand does not turn away from you."<sup>4</sup>And they said, "What is the guilt offering that we shall return to him?" They answered, "Five golden tumors and five golden mice, according to the number of the lords of the Philistines, for the same plague was on all of you and on your lords.<sup>5</sup>So you must make images of your tumors and images of your mice that ravage the land, and give glory to the God of Israel. Perhaps he will lighten his hand from off you and your gods and your land.<sup>6</sup>Why should you harden your hearts as the Egyptians and Pharaoh hardened their hearts? After he had dealt severely with them, did they not send the people away, and they departed?<sup>7</sup>Now then, take and prepare a new cart and two milk cows on which there has never come a yoke, and yoke the cows to the cart, but take their calves home, away from them.<sup>8</sup>And take the ark of the LORD and place it on the cart and put in a box at its side the figures of gold, which you are returning to him as a guilt offering. If it goes up on the way to its own land, to Beth-shemesh, then it is he who has done us this great harm, but if not, then we shall know that it is not his hand that struck us; it happened to us by coincidence."<sup>10</sup>The men did so, and took two milk cows and yoked them to the cart and shut up their calves at home.<sup>11</sup>And they put the ark of the LORD on the cart and the box with the golden mice and the images of their tumors.<sup>12</sup>And the cows went straight in the direction of Beth-shemesh along one highway, lowing as they went. They turned neither to the right nor to the left, and the lords of the Philistines went after them as far as the border of Beth-shemesh.<sup>13</sup>Now the people of Beth-shemesh were reaping their wheat harvest in the valley. And when they lifted up their eyes and saw the ark, they rejoiced to see it.<sup>14</sup>The cart came into the field of Joshua of Beth-shemesh and stopped there. A great stone was there. And they split up the wood of the cart and offered the cows as a burnt offering to the LORD.<sup>15</sup>And the Levites took down the ark of the LORD and the box that was beside it, in which were the golden figures, and set them upon the great stone. And the men of Beth-shemesh offered burnt offerings and sacrificed sacrifices on that day to the LORD.<sup>16</sup>And when the five lords of the Philistines saw it, they returned that day to Ekron.<sup>17</sup>These are the golden tumors that the Philistines returned as a guilt offering to the LORD: one for Ashdod, one for Gaza, one for Ashkelon, one for Gath, one for Ekron,<sup>18</sup>and the golden mice, according to the number of all the cities of the Philistines belonging to the five lords, both fortified cities and unwalled villages. He struck seventy men of them, and the people mourned because the LORD had struck the people with a great blow.<sup>20</sup>Then the men of Beth-shemesh said, "Who is able to stand before the LORD, this holy God? And to whom shall he go up away from us?"<sup>21</sup>So they sent messengers to the inhabitants of Kiriath-jearim, saying, "The Philistines have returned the ark of the LORD. Come down and take it up to you."
6.overview:
After seven months the Philistines ask their priests how to send the ark back. The advice is unexpectedly good: return it with a guilt offering, give glory to the God of Israel, and do not harden your hearts as Pharaoh did. Then they set a test designed to fail, and two nursing cows with no driver walk straight to Beth-shemesh.

Beth-shemesh rejoices and offers the cows on the wood of the cart. Then men die for looking into the ark, and the village asks two questions: who can stand before this holy God, and where can he be sent away from us?

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — A Guilt Offering, and a Test
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: After seven months the Philistines ask their priests and diviners what to do (vv. 1-2). Send it back with a guilt offering and give glory to the God of Israel, they say; do not harden your hearts like Pharaoh (vv. 3-6). And they set a test: an unyoked pair of nursing cows, a new cart, no driver (vv. 7-9).
verseByVerse.theology: Acknowledging God's power is not the same as turning to him. The diviners tell their nation to give glory to the God of Israel and keep their own gods in the same sentence (v. 5).
verseByVerse.examples: The diviners are a reminder that God can use even a muddled, second-hand knowledge of him to bring people to the edge of the truth. Whether they step over it is another matter.

verseByVerse.quote: The ark of the LORD was in the country of the Philistines seven months. And the Philistines called for the priests and the diviners and said, "What shall we do with the ark of the LORD? Tell us with what we shall send it to its place." They said, "If you send away the ark of the God of Israel, do not send it empty, but by all means return him a guilt offering. Then you will be healed, and it will be known to you why his hand does not turn away from you." And they said, "What is the guilt offering that we shall return to him?" They answered, "Five golden tumors and five golden mice, according to the number of the lords of the Philistines, for the same plague was on all of you and on your lords. So you must make images of your tumors and images of your mice that ravage the land, and give glory to the God of Israel. Perhaps he will lighten his hand from off you and your gods and your land. Why should you harden your hearts as the Egyptians and Pharaoh hardened their hearts? After he had dealt severely with them, did they not send the people away, and they departed?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Seven months, and by the end of it the question is not whether to send it back but how.

The diviners reach for a technical word, and they have it right. Guilt offering is asham, the sacrifice of Leviticus 5 and 6, brought when a person has wronged God or a neighbour and must make restitution with something added. They have taken something that was not theirs and there is a debt.

The same word appears in a place every Christian knows. The Servant of Isaiah 53, whom the New Testament identifies as Jesus, makes his soul an asham, an offering for guilt (Isa. 53:10). The Philistines tried to pay what they owed with gold modelled on their own wounds. The debt that sinners truly owe to God is paid in a different coin: by the wounds of the one who was pierced for our transgressions (Isa. 53:5; 1 Pet. 2:24).

Their instinct is sound in another way too. You do not dismiss the God of Israel from your territory with an apology and nothing in your hands.

Five and five, one set for each city, because the affliction was national. The images are of the thing that hurt them, cast in the most expensive material available: an admission of exactly what God did to them and that he did it. The mice have made many readers think of plague carried by rodents, a reasonable guess on which nothing in the passage turns.

Give glory to the God of Israel is the correct instruction, from a Philistine priest. But it is not "worship him" or "abandon Dagon". Their own gods are still in the sentence: from off you and your gods and your land. They intend to acknowledge his power, pay the debt, and keep their religion.

Then pagan diviners preach the exodus to their own nation, and the reasoning is good. Egypt hardened its heart against this God, the hardening did not work, and in the end they let the people go anyway after enormous loss. Learn from a nation that has already run the experiment. They have the story centuries old and second-hand, muddled in chapter 4, and they reason from it correctly to their own situation. Israel had the exodus in writing and used it to justify a superstition. Philistia had it as a rumour and drew the right conclusion.

verseByVerse.quote: Now then, take and prepare a new cart and two milk cows on which there has never come a yoke, and yoke the cows to the cart, but take their calves home, away from them. And take the ark of the LORD and place it on the cart and put in a box at its side the figures of gold, which you are returning to him as a guilt offering. Then send it off and let it go its way and watch. If it goes up on the way to its own land, to Beth-shemesh, then it is he who has done us this great harm, but if not, then we shall know that it is not his hand that struck us; it happened to us by coincidence."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the test, and every element is chosen to make the answer they want impossible. A new cart, never used for common work. Two milk cows, still nursing, with the strongest instinct an animal has running in them. Cows never yoked: untrained, animals that have never pulled anything and do not know how to walk straight under a beam. Then the cruel refinement: the calves are shut up behind them, in the byre, calling.

Let it go its way and watch. No driver, nobody leading them, nobody with a goad. The cart is pointed at nothing in particular and released.

The hypothesis is stated in advance, with both outcomes specified. They have not designed a test they can pass. Untrained cows will not pull straight; nursing cows will turn back to their calves within a hundred yards. The overwhelmingly likely result is a cart in a ditch and two animals trotting home, and the diviners say plainly that then the honest conclusion is coincidence. They have built an experiment that will exonerate chance unless God overrules the strongest instinct in the animal.

Compare Israel two chapters ago. The elders asked the right question, refused to wait for an answer, and reached for the object. These men ask a question, design a fair test, name what each outcome would prove, and watch.

None of this commends divination, which the law forbids (Deut. 18:10); God answered them in spite of their methods, not through them. But honest enquiry that is genuinely prepared to be told coincidence is a better thing than religious certainty that never tested anything, and God, as it happens, is not reluctant to answer it.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The cows go straight to Beth-shemesh, lowing, turning neither right nor left, with the five lords behind (vv. 10-12). The reapers rejoice; the cart stops at a great stone, becomes firewood, and the cows are offered while the Levites take down the ark (vv. 13-15). The lords go home (v. 16).
verseByVerse.theology: Every detail of the journey closes off an escape route: the destination, the single road, the cows that never turn aside. By the Philistines' own test, this was not chance.
verseByVerse.examples: The reapers' joy is right (v. 13). The ark coming home was good news and the day was rightly a festival; what went wrong afterwards was not the joy but the familiarity.

verseByVerse.quote: The men did so, and took two milk cows and yoked them to the cart and shut up their calves at home. And they put the ark of the LORD on the cart and the box with the golden mice and the images of their tumors. And the cows went straight in the direction of Beth-shemesh along one highway, lowing as they went. They turned neither to the right nor to the left, and the lords of the Philistines went after them as far as the border of Beth-shemesh.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They do it exactly as prescribed, and the calves are shut in.

Three details, and each closes off an escape route. Straight in the direction of Beth-shemesh: the town the test specified, the nearest Israelite settlement over the border and a Levitical city. Along one highway: they did not wander and find it. Neither to the right nor to the left: the law's phrase for perfect obedience, applied here to two cows.

And in the middle, the detail that makes the scene: lowing as they went. They are calling for their calves the entire way. Every instinct is screaming to turn round, and their voices are doing it, and their legs carry them steadily the other way down a road they have never walked, pulling a load they have never pulled, without a driver. The Philistines wanted to know whether this was God's hand or coincidence. They were given an answer that could not be misread, and the writer lets the animals' distress stand in the middle of it, because that is what it cost to make the answer unambiguous.

The five lords follow the cart to the edge of their own territory, watching, and then they stop and look.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the people of Beth-shemesh were reaping their wheat harvest in the valley. And when they lifted up their eyes and saw the ark, they rejoiced to see it. The cart came into the field of Joshua of Beth-shemesh and stopped there. A great stone was there. And they split up the wood of the cart and offered the cows as a burnt offering to the LORD. And the Levites took down the ark of the LORD and the box that was beside it, in which were the golden figures, and set them upon the great stone. And the men of Beth-shemesh offered burnt offerings and sacrificed sacrifices on that day to the LORD. And when the five lords of the Philistines saw it, they returned that day to Ekron.
verseByVerse.commentary:
It is harvest, the men are in the field with sickles, and they look up. Over the rise come two cows, lowing, pulling a new cart with no driver, and on it the ark of the covenant, which nobody in Israel has seen for seven months and everybody assumed was lost forever in a Philistine temple. Of course they rejoiced.

The cart stops of its own accord at a stone in a named man's field, and Beth-shemesh does the right thing with everything in front of it. The cart becomes the firewood and the cows the offering. Nothing is kept: not the new cart, nor two healthy milk cows, a small fortune to a farming village. Everything that touched this journey goes up in smoke.

The Levites handle the ark, which is correct: Beth-shemesh was a Levitical town, and lifting the ark was their work. So far everything is being done properly, and the day is a festival.

The lords watched the whole thing from the border and went home. Nothing is recorded of what they thought. They had their answer: it was the hand of the God of Israel, not coincidence. They had said so in advance. And they turned round and went back to Ekron, and Dagon went on being worshipped in Ashdod.
verseByVerse.note: Beth-shemesh was an Israelite town about 15 miles west of Jerusalem.

verseByVerse.quote: These are the golden tumors that the Philistines returned as a guilt offering to the LORD: one for Ashdod, one for Gaza, one for Ashkelon, one for Gath, one for Ekron, and the golden mice, according to the number of all the cities of the Philistines belonging to the five lords, both fortified cities and unwalled villages. The great stone beside which they set down the ark of the LORD is a witness to this day in the field of Joshua of Beth-shemesh.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The writer stops the story to list the contents of the box, city by city: five golden tumours for the five capitals, and golden mice for every settlement they governed, fortified towns and open villages alike. The plague had reached the whole country and the restitution is itemised to match. It is almost legal: a schedule of damages, drawn up by the debtor.

The stone is still there when the book is written. Israel had a habit of leaving stones about: twelve out of the Jordan at Gilgal, one under the terebinth at Shechem, and in the next chapter Samuel will set up another and name it. They are not monuments to human achievement. They are answers to a question a child might ask years later, and this one answers: the ark came back by itself, and it stopped here.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 19–21 — Who Is Able to Stand?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God strikes the men of Beth-shemesh who looked upon the ark (v. 19), and they ask two questions, the right one and Ashdod's (v. 20), and send the ark on to Kiriath-jearim (v. 21).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 19 shows that holiness is not dangerous only to Philistines; verse 20 shows that Israel's first instinct, faced with it, is the same as Philistia's.
verseByVerse.examples: Kiriath-jearim keeps the ark in a private house for twenty years (7:2). A God kept at a safe distance can be honoured and ignored at the same time.

verseByVerse.quote: And he struck some of the men of Beth-shemesh, because they looked upon the ark of the LORD. He struck seventy men of them, and the people mourned because the LORD had struck the people with a great blow. Then the men of Beth-shemesh said, "Who is able to stand before the LORD, this holy God? And to whom shall he go up away from us?" So they sent messengers to the inhabitants of Kiriath-jearim, saying, "The Philistines have returned the ark of the LORD. Come down and take it up to you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The festival ends in a funeral, and the reason given is that they looked.

The number is textually difficult (see the note below). Fifty thousand would be impossible for a village, and the ESV prints the seventy that the sense requires. Nothing depends on the figure.

The law was not vague. The ark travelled covered; Aaron and his sons put the veil over it before the Kohathites came near, and the warning was explicit: they must not touch or look at the holy things, lest they die (Num. 4:5, 15, 20). It was carried on poles that were never removed, precisely so that nobody would handle it. This is not God being touchy about a glance. It is a village that has spent a joyful day growing steadily more familiar with the most dangerous object in the world.

It is also deliberately placed. After chapter 5 a reader could think holiness is dangerous to Philistines. Verse 19 says it is dangerous full stop. The ark did not become safe when it crossed the border. Uzzah will discover the same on the journey's last stage, generations later, when he puts out his hand to steady it and dies (2 Sam. 6:6-7).

Two questions, and they could not be further apart. The first is the best sentence anybody speaks in these three chapters. It is the question the whole apparatus of the ark existed to raise, and the one the elders never asked when they sent for it as a battlefield charm. Isaiah asks it in the temple and thinks he is finished (Isa. 6:5). The answer, when it finally comes, is a person.

Then the second question undoes the first. Hear Ashdod again: the ark of the God of Israel must not remain with us (5:7). The same sentence: a pagan city and a Levitical town in Israel, both having seen exactly who this is, both asking for him to be taken somewhere else. That is the sting of the chapter, and it should not be softened. Israel's instinct on meeting the holiness of God is identical to Philistia's. In neither town does anybody say "teach us how to come near."

So the ark is passed on again, this time by Israelites. Shiloh, a battlefield, Ashdod, Gath, Ekron, Beth-shemesh, and now Kiriath-jearim, where it will sit in a private house on a hill for twenty years, and longer, until David goes to fetch it. Nobody wants it near them. That is the honest summary of three chapters, and it is why the question in verse 20 matters so much.

Who is able to stand before the LORD, this holy God? The men of Beth-shemesh meant it as a reason to send him away, and it is in fact the question the gospel exists to answer. Somebody was able to stand there, and did, on our behalf, and the whole point of him is that he came towards people rather than being sent up the road to somebody else. Jesus Christ, the holy one without sin, has entered the presence of God for us (Heb. 9:24), and by his blood he has opened a new and living way for sinners to draw near with confidence (Heb. 10:19–22). Beth-shemesh never asked how to come near. In him the question is answered before it is asked.
verseByVerse.note: Most Hebrew manuscripts read “seventy men, fifty thousand men” (ESV note).

6.theology:
Pagans reasoning better than Israel. The diviners reach for the right sacrificial category (v. 3), tell their nation not to repeat Pharaoh's mistake (v. 6), and design a fair test with both outcomes named in advance (v. 9). Honest enquiry genuinely prepared to be told coincidence is a better thing than religious certainty that never tested anything.

Acknowledgement is not conversion (v. 5). They give glory to the God of Israel and keep their own gods. The five lords watch the sacrifice from the border and go home to Ekron.

Lowing as they went (v. 12). The writer leaves the animals' distress in the middle of the miracle, because that is what it cost to make the answer unmistakable.

Holiness did not become safe at the border (v. 19). God is not dangerous only to Philistines. The law had told Israel not to look at the holy things lest they die (Num. 4:20), and Uzzah learns the same on the last stage of the same journey.

The two questions (v. 20). Who is able to stand before the LORD, this holy God? is the question the ark existed to raise, and Isaiah asks it in the temple and thinks he is finished (Isa. 6:5). And then the same men ask Ashdod's own question: to whom shall he go up away from us? (cf. 5:7). A pagan city and a Levitical town, both having seen who this is, both asking for him to be moved on. Nobody in either place says "teach us how to come near".
6.examples:
Then: Five pagan rulers followed an unmanned cart to their border to see whether the God who had wrecked their temple and their health was real, received an answer they themselves called decisive, and went home to their own gods.

Now: Verse 20 is the uncomfortable one. The right question and the wrong one come out of the same mouths in the same breath. It is entirely possible to grasp that God is holy, to be genuinely frightened of it, and to respond by wanting him at a manageable distance, and that instinct is not pagan. It was Israel's, on the day the ark came home. The answer is not to keep him further off but to come near the way he has opened, through Christ, who stood in his presence for us; and the Spirit he gives teaches us to call this holy God Father.

7.title: Return to the LORD
7.text: <sup>1</sup>And the men of Kiriath-jearim came and took up the ark of the LORD and brought it to the house of Abinadab on the hill.
