And they consecrated his son Eleazar to have charge of the ark of the LORD.<sup>2</sup>From the day that the ark was lodged at Kiriath-jearim, a long time passed, some twenty years, and all the house of Israel lamented after the LORD.<sup>3</sup>And Samuel said to all the house of Israel, "If you are returning to the LORD with all your heart, then put away the foreign gods and the Ashtaroth from among you and direct your heart to the LORD and serve him only, and he will deliver you out of the hand of the Philistines."<sup>4</sup>So the people of Israel put away the Baals and the Ashtaroth, and they served the LORD only.<sup>5</sup>Then Samuel said, "Gather all Israel at Mizpah, and I will pray to the LORD for you."<sup>6</sup>So they gathered at Mizpah and drew water and poured it out before the LORD and fasted on that day and said there, "We have sinned against the LORD." And Samuel judged the people of Israel at Mizpah.<sup>7</sup>Now when the Philistines heard that the people of Israel had gathered at Mizpah, the lords of the Philistines went up against Israel. And when the people of Israel heard of it, they were afraid of the Philistines.<sup>8</sup>And the people of Israel said to Samuel, "Do not cease to cry out to the LORD our God for us, that he may save us from the hand of the Philistines."<sup>9</sup>So Samuel took a nursing lamb and offered it as a whole burnt offering to the LORD. And Samuel cried out to the LORD for Israel, and the LORD answered him.<sup>10</sup>As Samuel was offering up the burnt offering, the Philistines drew near to attack Israel. But the LORD thundered with a mighty sound that day against the Philistines and threw them into confusion, and they were defeated before Israel.<sup>11</sup>And the men of Israel went out from Mizpah and pursued the Philistines and struck them, as far as below Beth-car.<sup>12</sup>Then Samuel took a stone and set it up between Mizpah and Shen and called its name Ebenezer; for he said, "Till now the LORD has helped us."<sup>13</sup>So the Philistines were subdued and did not again enter the territory of Israel. And the hand of the LORD was against the Philistines all the days of Samuel.<sup>14</sup>The cities that the Philistines had taken from Israel were restored to Israel, from Ekron to Gath, and Israel delivered their territory from the hand of the Philistines. There was peace also between Israel and the Amorites.<sup>15</sup>Samuel judged Israel all the days of his life.<sup>16</sup>And he went on a circuit year by year to Bethel, Gilgal, and Mizpah. And he judged Israel in all these places.<sup>17</sup>Then he would return to Ramah, for his home was there, and there also he judged Israel. And he built there an altar to the LORD.
7.overview:
The ark sits in a private house for twenty years while Israel laments after the LORD with its idols still on the shelf. Samuel tells them plainly what returning would mean, and they put the idols away.

At Mizpah they pour out water, fast, confess, and ask Samuel to keep crying out to the LORD for them. The Philistines attack while the lamb is still burning, God answers with thunder, and Samuel sets up a stone called Ebenezer: Till now the LORD has helped us. This time Israel asked for prayer, not equipment, and the chapter is written as the answer to chapter 4.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — Twenty Years of Longing, and One Instruction
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The ark rests twenty years at Kiriath-jearim while Israel laments after the LORD (vv. 1-2). Samuel tells them that returning means putting away the foreign gods and serving the LORD only, and they do (vv. 3-4).
verseByVerse.theology: Grief over distance from God is real, but it is not the same as coming back. Samuel's test is not a feeling but a removal.
verseByVerse.examples: A congregation that confesses its sins together, as Israel did at Mizpah, is not performing sorrow but clearing the house: doing in words what Israel did when it carried the Baals out.

verseByVerse.quote: And the men of Kiriath-jearim came and took up the ark of the LORD and brought it to the house of Abinadab on the hill. And they consecrated his son Eleazar to have charge of the ark of the LORD. From the day that the ark was lodged at Kiriath-jearim, a long time passed, some twenty years, and all the house of Israel lamented after the LORD. And Samuel said to all the house of Israel, "If you are returning to the LORD with all your heart, then put away the foreign gods and the Ashtaroth from among you and direct your heart to the LORD and serve him only, and he will deliver you out of the hand of the Philistines." So the people of Israel put away the Baals and the Ashtaroth, and they served the LORD only.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Its journey ends in a private house on a hill, in the care of one man. There is no sanctuary to take it to; Shiloh is finished. So a family takes it in, a son is set apart to look after it, and that is the arrangement for the next two decades and longer, because it is still there when David comes for it.

Twenty years, and one clause to describe them. The verb is a strong one: mourning, grieving, longing after him. This is not a nation that has forgotten God; it is a nation that misses him.

And the next verse tells us what was in their houses the whole time. That explains why the lamenting achieved nothing. A whole generation grieved after the LORD, knew that something enormous had gone out of the national life, and kept the Ashtaroth on the shelf.

Samuel separates the two with a hinge: if you are returning... then put away. He does not doubt the sincerity of their grief; he refuses to let it count as repentance on its own. To long is not to return. A person can be painfully aware of distance from God for years and never take one thing out of the house, and the ache itself can become a substitute for the removal, because it feels like devotion and costs nothing.

The order matters and is easy to get backwards. The idols go out because the heart has turned; they do not go out in order to turn it. Samuel is not prescribing a method for producing repentance. He is naming the thing that would show it had happened. And the call rests on a promise already given: he will deliver you. The God who is calling them back is the one who means to rescue them.

The two positive clauses are as important as the negative one. Direct your heart to the LORD: the word is about fixing, aiming, setting something firmly in one direction. And serve him only. Not chiefly. Not first among several. Only.

They did it. After twenty years of grief the thing that had stood in the way is carried out of the house, with no record of argument, delay or compromise. It is the first national repentance in this history, and it took one man saying plainly what was actually required.

The Baals and Ashtaroth were the gods and goddesses of Canaanite fertility worship: Baal, the storm god, and Ashtoreth, his consort.
verseByVerse.note: The ark stayed at Kiriath-jearim twenty years before this revival (v. 2), and longer still until David brought it to Jerusalem.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: At Mizpah Israel pours out water, fasts and confesses (vv. 5-6). The Philistines come up, and Israel asks Samuel not to cease crying out for them (vv. 7-8). As he offers a lamb, the LORD thunders and the Philistines are routed, and Samuel sets up Ebenezer (vv. 9-12).
verseByVerse.theology: The God who fights for Israel here is answering prayer, not responding to equipment. Samuel cries out, and the LORD answers (v. 9).
verseByVerse.examples: Israel's request in v. 8 is a good model for anyone who is frightened: not a plan or a show of strength, but asking someone to keep praying, and trusting the God who hears.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Samuel said, "Gather all Israel at Mizpah, and I will pray to the LORD for you." So they gathered at Mizpah and drew water and poured it out before the LORD and fasted on that day and said there, "We have sinned against the LORD." And Samuel judged the people of Israel at Mizpah. Now when the Philistines heard that the people of Israel had gathered at Mizpah, the lords of the Philistines went up against Israel. And when the people of Israel heard of it, they were afraid of the Philistines. And the people of Israel said to Samuel, "Do not cease to cry out to the LORD our God for us, that he may save us from the hand of the Philistines." So Samuel took a nursing lamb and offered it as a whole burnt offering to the LORD. And Samuel cried out to the LORD for Israel, and the LORD answered him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He calls a national assembly, and what he offers to do there is pray. Mizpah will be where Saul is presented as king in chapter 10.

The water poured out is unusual. Nothing in the law prescribes it, and it appears nowhere else in quite this form. The best sense of it is what David does with the water from Bethlehem's well: he refuses to drink it and pours it out to the LORD (2 Sam. 23:16). It is a gesture of total emptying: this is ours, we are giving it away, and it cannot be got back.

Then fasting, and the confession, six words long. We have sinned against the LORD. No explanation, no mitigation, no account of what the Philistines had done to them.

The moment the nation repents, the enemy attacks. From the Philistine side it is sensible: a large gathering of Israelites on a hill looks like a muster, and you break that up before it becomes an army. But name the timing. Israel has put away its idols, fasted, confessed and assembled to pray, and the immediate consequence is that the Philistines march. Anyone who has done business with God will recognise the pattern. The trouble frequently arrives immediately after the surrender, and it is not evidence that the surrender was a mistake.

Now set the request beside chapter 4 and the whole book turns on the difference. Then: let us bring the ark of the covenant of the LORD here from Shiloh, that it may come among us and save us from the power of our enemies (4:3). Now: do not cease to cry out to the LORD our God for us. The last half of each is nearly identical. Everything before it has changed. In chapter 4 the subject of save was a box; here it is he. Then they organised a transport; now they beg a man not to stop interceding.

A nursing lamb, still with its mother, offered whole: nothing kept back, nothing eaten. Then the two clauses that carry the chapter: Samuel cried out, and the LORD answered.

Scripture remembers Samuel above all as an intercessor, named beside Moses as one who called on the LORD and was answered (Ps. 99:6; Jer. 15:1). Here is the shape of the gospel in miniature: a lamb on the altar, a mediator crying out for a frightened people, and God himself fighting for them. Israel begged one man not to cease praying, and one day Samuel did cease, because he died. Christians have a mediator who never stops: the Lamb offered once for all, who always lives to make intercession for those who draw near to God through him (Heb. 7:25).

How could Samuel offer sacrifices here, and later at Ramah (v. 17), when the law limited sacrifice to one place (Deut 12)? The sanctuary at Shiloh had been destroyed and the ark was in exile at Kiriath-jearim (7:1–2). In that emergency God’s prophet led worship where he was, and God accepted it (v. 9).
verseByVerse.note: Mizpah lay about 8 miles north of Jerusalem.

verseByVerse.quote: As Samuel was offering up the burnt offering, the Philistines drew near to attack Israel. But the LORD thundered with a mighty sound that day against the Philistines and threw them into confusion, and they were defeated before Israel. And the men of Israel went out from Mizpah and pursued the Philistines and struck them, as far as below Beth-car. Then Samuel took a stone and set it up between Mizpah and Shen and called its name Ebenezer; for he said, "Till now the LORD has helped us."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The attack comes while the lamb is still burning, and God answers with weather. No angel, no plague, no Israelite tactics: a noise out of the sky at the moment of the assault, and an army that had beaten Israel twice in this book goes to pieces in front of it.

Hear where that verb came from. Years earlier a woman sang in this same story: the adversaries of the LORD shall be broken to pieces; against them he will thunder in heaven (2:10). She had no army, no standing and no reason to expect anything of the kind; she had just handed over a toddler at a corrupt shrine. Her son is standing at the altar when it happens, and the thing she sang about is going on over his head.

Israel does the pursuing, which is real work and theirs to do. God broke them; the men of Israel chased them.

The name of the stone is one the reader has met before. Chapter 4 opened with Israel encamped at Ebenezer, where they fetched the ark, gave the great shout, lost thirty thousand men and watched the covenant chest carried off. This stone stands near Mizpah, some miles from the battlefield by Aphek, and the writer probably called that earlier site by the name it would later bear. Either way he has bracketed the story with one name: the place where Israel trusted a box and lost, and the place where it trusted God and was helped.

The stone is more careful than the hymn that came from it. Till now: hitherto, up to this point. It is not a prediction. Samuel does not say the LORD will always help, or that the Philistines are finished, or that Israel has turned a corner it cannot turn back round. He marks the ground as far as they have come and says: this far, he has helped.

That is what a memorial stone is for, and why they were set up all over that country: twelve out of the Jordan, one under the terebinth at Shechem, one in a wheatfield at Beth-shemesh. They do not tell you what is coming. They stop you forgetting what happened, so that when the next trouble arrives you have something in the landscape to argue from. Anyone can raise this stone tonight. Not "God will fix it", which you do not know, but till now the LORD has helped us, which you do.
verseByVerse.note: “Ebenezer” means “stone of help” (ESV note).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–17 — All the Days of Samuel
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Philistines are subdued all the days of Samuel and the cities are restored (vv. 13-14). Samuel judges Israel on a yearly circuit and at his home in Ramah, where he builds an altar (vv. 15-17).
verseByVerse.theology: Peace that depends on one man's lifetime is real but fragile. The rest is genuine, and the chapter already looks ahead to the day Samuel grows old.
verseByVerse.examples: Samuel's ministry after the great day at Mizpah is mostly ordinary: a yearly circuit, disputes settled, an altar at home. Faithfulness after a high point usually looks like this.

verseByVerse.quote: So the Philistines were subdued and did not again enter the territory of Israel. And the hand of the LORD was against the Philistines all the days of Samuel. The cities that the Philistines had taken from Israel were restored to Israel, from Ekron to Gath, and Israel delivered their territory from the hand of the Philistines. There was peace also between Israel and the Amorites. Samuel judged Israel all the days of his life. And he went on a circuit year by year to Bethel, Gilgal, and Mizpah. And he judged Israel in all these places. Then he would return to Ramah, for his home was there, and there also he judged Israel. And he built there an altar to the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The phrase used against Israel's enemies in these chapters now holds for a lifetime. The hand of the LORD was heavy against Ashdod, Gath and Ekron; now it is against the Philistines not for a day but all the days of Samuel.

The qualification is deliberate. The peace is tied to a man, exactly as every rest in Judges was tied to a judge, and the reader who has just come through that book knows what that means. Samuel will grow old in chapter 8, and the first thing Israel will do about it is ask for a king.

The lost territory comes back, and the way it comes back is the point. No campaign of reconquest is described. The cities are restored after a single day in which a nation that had already thrown away its idols stood on a hill and asked a man to keep praying. There is peace with the Amorites as well, the Canaanite population Israel had never managed to drive out. Even that settles.

He works a circuit, and the three towns are chosen with care. Bethel, where Jacob saw the ladder. Gilgal, where the twelve stones came out of the Jordan. Mizpah, where the nation had just repented. Samuel rides between the places where God had met Israel, year after year, doing the ordinary work of settling disputes. And he does not attempt to rebuild Shiloh. The sanctuary he grew up in is gone, God has abandoned it, and he does not spend his life restoring the institution that formed him. He goes to the people instead.

Ramah is where his mother made him a little robe every year and could not keep him. He was given away from that house as a toddler. He comes back to it as a grown man and puts an altar in it.

Take the whole chapter beside chapter 4, because the book has set them side by side. Chapter 4: they asked the right question and did not wait for the answer, sent for the ark, shouted so that the earth resounded, and lost four thousand, then thirty thousand, and the ark, the priesthood, the sanctuary and the glory. Chapter 7: they put away the idols, poured out water, fasted, said six words about their own sin, and asked one man not to stop praying. And God thundered.

Nothing changed in the intervening twenty years except the direction of a nation's heart. Nobody had a better weapon, a larger army or a cleverer plan; they did not even have the ark, which stayed in a private house on a hill. They had God, because they had stopped trying to operate him.

The Philistines “did not again enter” Israel in force, yet they held garrisons later (10:5; 13:3). The verse means that their invasions stopped in Samuel’s days as judge; their grip returned under Saul.

7.theology:
Longing is not returning (vv. 2-3). The ache for God can become a substitute for removing what stands in the way, because it feels like devotion and costs nothing. The idols go out because the heart has turned, not in order to turn it, and the call is to serve him only.

Chapter 4 answered. Same enemy, same nation, same place name, Ebenezer (4:1; 7:12), and the opposite outcome, because this time Israel looked to God rather than to the ark.

Trouble after the surrender (v. 7). The Philistines march the moment Israel assembles to repent. Trouble that follows obedience is not evidence that the obedience was a mistake.

Till now (v. 12). A memorial stone does not tell you what is coming; it stops you forgetting what happened, so that the next time trouble arrives you have something in the landscape to argue from.

All the days of Samuel (v. 13). The peace is tied to a man, as every rest in Judges was tied to a judge. Samuel grows old in chapter 8, and the first thing Israel does about it is ask for a king.
7.examples:
Then: A nation that had grieved after God for twenty years without moving an idol moved them all when one man told it plainly what returning meant, and God broke an army with a noise in the sky.

Now: Two things. First, verse 2 describes a great many sincere Christians: genuinely aware of distance from God, genuinely grieved about it, and genuinely unwilling to carry one particular thing out of the house. Samuel's test is not how strongly you feel it but what has actually left the building. And the God who sent him to say so was not waiting to condemn them; the next thing he did was thunder on their behalf. We never serve him only as we should, but Christ did, wholeheartedly and in our place, and his obedience is counted as ours; so the way back is still the six words of Mizpah, and the Spirit he gives is the power to carry the idol out. Second, verse 12 is the discipline of memory, and it is deliberately modest. You do not know what God will do next; you do know what he has already done. Put the stone there and name it, because when the Philistines come back you will want something you can point at.

8.title: Give Us a King
8.text: <sup>1</sup>When Samuel became old, he made his sons judges over Israel.<sup>2</sup>The name of his firstborn son was Joel, and the name of his second, Abijah; they were judges in Beersheba.<sup>3</sup>Yet his sons did not walk in his ways but turned aside after gain. They took bribes and perverted justice.<sup>4</sup>Then all the elders of Israel gathered together and came to Samuel at Ramah<sup>5</sup>and said to him, "Behold, you are old and your sons do not walk in your ways. Now appoint for us a king to judge us like all the nations."<sup>6</sup>But the thing displeased Samuel when they said, "Give us a king to judge us." And Samuel prayed to the LORD.<sup>7</sup>And the LORD said to Samuel, "Obey the voice of the people in all that they say to you, for they have not rejected you, but they have rejected me from being king over them.<sup>8</sup>According to all the deeds that they have done, from the day I brought them up out of Egypt even to this day, forsaking me and serving other gods, so they are also doing to you.<sup>9</sup>Now then, obey their voice; only you shall solemnly warn them and show them the ways of the king who shall reign over them."<sup>10</sup>So Samuel told all the words of the LORD to the people who were asking for a king from him.<sup>11</sup>He said, "These will be the ways of the king who will reign over you: he will take your sons and appoint them to his chariots and to be his horsemen and to run before his chariots.<sup>12</sup>And he will appoint for himself commanders of thousands and commanders of fifties, and some to plow his ground and to reap his harvest, and to make his implements of war and the equipment of his chariots.<sup>13</sup>He will take your daughters to be perfumers and cooks and bakers.<sup>14</sup>He will take the best of your fields and vineyards and olive orchards and give them to his servants.<sup>15</sup>He will take the tenth of your grain and of your vineyards and give it to his officers and to his servants.<sup>16</sup>He will take your male servants and female servants and the best of your young men and your donkeys, and put them to his work.<sup>17</sup>He will take the tenth of your flocks, and you shall be his slaves.<sup>18</sup>And in that day you will cry out because of your king, whom you have chosen for yourselves, but the LORD will not answer you in that day."<sup>19</sup>But the people refused to obey the voice of Samuel. And they said, "No! But there shall be a king over us,<sup>20</sup>that we also may be like all the nations, and that our king may judge us and go out before us and fight our battles."<sup>21</sup>And when Samuel had heard all the words of the people, he repeated them in the ears of the LORD.<sup>22</sup>And the LORD said to Samuel, "Obey their voice and make them a king." Samuel then said to the men of Israel, "Go every man to his city."
8.overview:
Samuel grows old and makes his sons judges at Beersheba, and they take bribes. The elders come to Ramah and ask for a king to judge them like all the nations. A monarchy was never forbidden; the trouble is in that last phrase, and in what they want the king for.

Samuel is stung and prays. God tells him the people have rejected not Samuel but God himself, and then tells him to give them what they ask. Samuel warns them what a king will take, down to their freedom, and they hear it all and still say no: they want a king to fight their battles.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — Your Sons Do Not Walk in Your Ways
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Samuel makes his sons judges at Beersheba, and they take bribes (vv. 1-3). The elders come to Ramah: you are old, your sons do not walk in your ways, give us a king like all the nations (vv. 4-5).
verseByVerse.theology: Even the best of leaders can repeat the failure they once condemned, and Scripture does not hide it.
verseByVerse.examples: The elders' complaint is fair as far as it goes: Samuel is old and his sons are corrupt (v. 5). A true grievance can carry a wrong request, and the two need to be told apart.

verseByVerse.quote: When Samuel became old, he made his sons judges over Israel. The name of his firstborn son was Joel, and the name of his second, Abijah; they were judges in Beersheba. Yet his sons did not walk in his ways but turned aside after gain. They took bribes and perverted justice.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The weight of the verse lies in who is doing it. This is the boy woken three times in the dark and given his first message from God: that Eli's house would be destroyed for the iniquity that he knew, because his sons were blaspheming God, and he did not restrain them (3:13). He was afraid to say it and he said it all. He is now old, and he has made his own sons judges over Israel.

Note where he posted them. Beersheba is the southernmost town in the country, the far end of from Dan to Beersheba, and Samuel lives at Ramah on his circuit of Bethel, Gilgal and Mizpah (7:16-17). The text does not say why he placed them there, and it may have been simple need in the south; but the effect was that he could not see what they did.

Nor was the office ever hereditary. Not one judge in the previous book passed the work to a son, and when Israel offered Gideon a dynasty he refused it plainly: I will not rule over you, and my son will not rule over you; the LORD will rule over you (Judg. 8:23). Samuel installs one without being asked.

They are a new version of Eli's sons. The charge is judicial. Gain is unjust profit, money got by bending something. They took bribes. And they perverted justice, which for a judge is not a sin alongside the job; it is the destruction of the job itself. The writer has built forty years of narrative so that we would set the two households side by side. Eli's sons stole the offerings and God said their father honoured them above him. Samuel's sons sold verdicts, and Samuel appointed them.

The narrator says nothing: no oracle, no man of God, no sentence on the house of Samuel. That silence is more damning than a comment would be, and it is honest about something most histories will not admit. The best man in Israel, whose words never fell to the ground, made, so far as we are told, much the same mistake he had been sent as a child to condemn. The book does not say whether he rebuked them; it says only that he appointed them and that they were not removed.

A grieving parent should not read too much into this. Scripture does not say Samuel's sons went wrong because of him, and godly fathers and mothers have often watched children turn aside despite everything they taught; what Samuel is answerable for is giving them public office. Be careful, too, how the failure is applied. It is not the reason Israel asks for a king (verse 20 gives that reason and it is something else). But it is the occasion, and the elders will use it, and they will be right about the facts.

verseByVerse.quote: Then all the elders of Israel gathered together and came to Samuel at Ramah and said to him, "Behold, you are old and your sons do not walk in your ways. Now appoint for us a king to judge us like all the nations."
verseByVerse.commentary:
They come to his house and open with two statements that are simply true, and Samuel cannot contradict a word of either. Both are his responsibility: he got old, which is nobody's fault, and he appointed the sons, which is entirely his.

The request has three parts. Appoint for us a king: the institution. To judge us: the function, and a fair one, since judging is precisely what has broken down at Beersheba. And like all the nations. Everything turns on the third clause; the first two are not the problem.

God had legislated for a king. Deuteronomy anticipated this request, in these words, generations before it was made: when you come to the land... and then say, I will set a king over me, like all the nations that are around me, you may indeed set a king over you whom the LORD your God will choose (Deut. 17:14-15). A job description follows: he must not multiply horses or wives or silver, and he must write out a copy of the law and read it every day of his life.

So a monarchy was never forbidden. Israel's ultimate hope is a king; Hannah sang about one in chapter 2 before anybody had thought of asking, and Jacob had promised the sceptre to Judah before that. The problem is the phrase like all the nations, and what it means comes out plainly in verse 20 when they say it again and add what they want him for.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Samuel, displeased, prays (v. 6). God tells him the people have rejected not him but God, as they have since Egypt (vv. 7-8), and bids him obey their voice and warn them solemnly (v. 9).
verseByVerse.theology: Samuel's first move when he is hurt is to pray (v. 6). It is easy to read past, and it is the right order for anyone who has been criticised or passed over.
verseByVerse.examples: Being given exactly what you asked for is not always a sign of God's approval. Sometimes it is the opposite, as the note on vv. 6-9 explains.

verseByVerse.quote: But the thing displeased Samuel when they said, "Give us a king to judge us." And Samuel prayed to the LORD. And the LORD said to Samuel, "Obey the voice of the people in all that they say to you, for they have not rejected you, but they have rejected me from being king over them. According to all the deeds that they have done, from the day I brought them up out of Egypt even to this day, forsaking me and serving other gods, so they are also doing to you. Now then, obey their voice; only you shall solemnly warn them and show them the ways of the king who shall reign over them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
He is stung, and the narrator tells us which words stung him. Not like all the nations but give us a king to judge us, because judging Israel is what he has done every year of his adult life. They are asking for a replacement, to his face, in his own house, while he is still doing the work.

What he does with the sting is the best thing about him. He prays. He does not argue with the delegation or defend his record or point out that he has never taken a bribe, all of which he will say in chapter 12, and all of which would be true. He takes it to God first.

God's answer is remarkable pastoral care, and it is not comfort. They have not rejected you is real consolation: forty years of faithful work have not been repudiated. Then the second half enlarges the wound rather than closing it. God relieves his servant of a personal injury by telling him the injury is his own, and greater. Samuel goes from thinking he has been sacked to understanding that he has been standing next to something much worse than his own dismissal.

There is a lesson in that for anybody in Christian work who has been passed over, replaced, criticised or quietly moved aside. The first instinct is always that it is about you. Very often it is not, and the discovery is less flattering than it sounds, because it usually means somebody is refusing God and you were merely in the way.

Now God files the request, and the folder is idolatry. Everything they have done since the exodus (every Baal, every Asherah pole, the golden calf, the whole record of forsaking me and serving other gods) and so they are also doing to you. The request for a king is not a constitutional preference God happens to dislike. It belongs on the same list as the calf at Sinai.

On the surface the two look nothing alike. Nobody here is bowing to an image; they are asking for an ordinary form of government that God himself had made provision for. What makes it the same act is not the object but the transfer. An idol is anything you put in the place where God was, to do the job God was doing. These men want somebody to go out before them and fight their battles, and God had been doing that, personally, with thunder, within living memory.

And God says yes. That is the hard thing in this chapter, and the whole book turns on it. He has just called the request a rejection of himself, and his instruction is obey their voice, three times over. No blow falls, no plague. He gives them precisely what they asked for, having told them in advance and in detail what it will cost.

The psalm that looks back on the wilderness puts this in one of the most frightening sentences in the Bible: he gave them what they asked, but sent a wasting disease among them (Ps. 106:15). Paul says it three times in one paragraph about a world that exchanged the truth for a lie: God gave them up (Rom. 1:24, 26, 28). There is a judgment that consists in being told no. And there is a heavier one that consists in being handed the thing, with a receipt.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Samuel tells them the ways of the king, and the speech runs on one verb: he will take sons, daughters, fields, a tenth of the grain, servants, flocks, until you shall be his slaves (vv. 10-17). And when they cry out because of him, the LORD will not answer (v. 18).
verseByVerse.theology: Samuel's warning names every part of a household in turn, from children to livestock. Power that answers to no one tends to take, and the ordinary family pays.
verseByVerse.examples: The warning has an everyday form too: whatever we trust in place of God, whether a leader, an institution or a plan, will ask more of us than it first appeared to.

verseByVerse.quote: So Samuel told all the words of the LORD to the people who were asking for a king from him. He said, "These will be the ways of the king who will reign over you: he will take your sons and appoint them to his chariots and to be his horsemen and to run before his chariots. And he will appoint for himself commanders of thousands and commanders of fifties, and some to plow his ground and to reap his harvest, and to make his implements of war and the equipment of his chariots. He will take your daughters to be perfumers and cooks and bakers. He will take the best of your fields and vineyards and olive orchards and give them to his servants.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Samuel does exactly what he was told, and the whole speech is built on one verb, which will appear six times in seven verses: he will take.

First the sons. Not for the harvest or the family but for the chariots, as horsemen, and as men who run before his chariots, the most expendable job in an ancient army: outriders going ahead of the king's vehicle on foot. And Israel does not have chariots. Chariots are what the Canaanites had at the Kishon. Asking for a king like the nations means asking for the nations' military, and the nations' military has to be paid for out of somebody's children.

An officer class, then a labour force, and the pronouns tell the story: his ground, his harvest, his chariots. Their sons will farm land that is no longer theirs and make weapons they will not own.

Then the daughters. The roles are palace roles; a court needs perfume and bread on a scale a village does not. And the phrasing repays hearing plainly: he will take. Nobody is applying for a position.

Then the land, and not any fields but the best, given to his servants: a class of men who did not clear that ground or plant those vines, granted them for loyalty while the families who did will watch. Vineyards and olive orchards are the detail that hurts, because neither is a one-year crop. An olive tree takes a decade to bear; a vineyard is planted by a man for his grandchildren. Confiscating them takes three generations of somebody's work in an afternoon. Ahab will do this to Naboth, and the story will be remembered as the definition of a king who takes (1 Kings 21).

Is this a charter against taxes and strong government? It is a warning about what kings do when they are like the kings of the nations. Paul says to pay taxes and honour rulers (Rom 13:6–7); the warning still teaches that power tends to take, and rulers must answer to God.

verseByVerse.quote: He will take the tenth of your grain and of your vineyards and give it to his officers and to his servants. He will take your male servants and female servants and the best of your young men and your donkeys, and put them to his work. He will take the tenth of your flocks, and you shall be his slaves. And in that day you will cry out because of your king, whom you have chosen for yourselves, but the LORD will not answer you in that day."
verseByVerse.commentary:
A tenth is the tithe: God's portion, the fraction Israel had given to the LORD since Sinai in acknowledgement that the land and its produce were his gift. The king will want the same percentage, and he will give it to his officers. Israel is about to run two tithes, and the second one buys a civil service.

By now every category a family possesses has been named: sons, daughters, fields, produce, servants, livestock. The list works systematically downward through a household until nothing is left unlisted. Then the destination: you shall be his slaves.

The Hebrew is 'abadim, the word for what Israel was in Egypt, the word in the sentence God had repeated to them for centuries: "I brought you out of the house of slaves". They came out of a country where the state owned their children and their labour. God broke it open with ten plagues and a sea. And the elders have come to Ramah to request a return, and God tells them exactly what they are requesting, in the vocabulary of Egypt.

Set the whole speech against the only king who ever came without this verb. The Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many (Mark 10:45). Six times a king takes; once a King gives, and what he gives is himself. Samuel's warning is about a man moving wealth and people towards the centre. The gospel is about a King moving the other way, who was rich and became poor, and whose one recorded act of taking was the taking of a cross and a place he did not owe.

Then the sentence that reverses the whole of the previous book. The engine of Judges was a cry: Israel did evil, God sold them into a hand, they cried out, and every time he answered, because the LORD was moved to pity by their groaning (Judg. 2:18). The cry was the one reliable thing in that miserable history. Now Samuel says the day is coming when they will cry because of the king, and God will not answer.

The reason is in the middle of the verse and it is not vindictiveness: whom you have chosen for yourselves. The oppressors of Judges were sent; this one is requested. A man may bring his misery to God when it has been done to him. It is a different thing to come complaining about a burden you signed for after reading the terms aloud.

“The LORD will not answer you in that day”: when they cried out under the king they had demanded. God does not promise to remove the consequences of a stubborn choice, though he remains merciful to those who truly repent (12:20–22).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 19–22 — That We Also May Be Like All the Nations
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The people refuse Samuel and insist on a king to be like the nations and fight their battles (vv. 19-20). God says again, obey their voice, and Samuel sends them home (vv. 21-22).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 20 explains the request at last: they want a king to go out before them and fight their battles, a job God had been doing himself.
verseByVerse.examples: There is no ceremony at the end, no thanksgiving, no covenant. God grants it, Samuel dismisses the assembly, and everybody goes home. The most consequential request in Israel's history is answered and the meeting simply ends.

verseByVerse.quote: But the people refused to obey the voice of Samuel. And they said, "No! But there shall be a king over us, that we also may be like all the nations, and that our king may judge us and go out before us and fight our battles." And when Samuel had heard all the words of the people, he repeated them in the ears of the LORD. And the LORD said to Samuel, "Obey their voice and make them a king." Samuel then said to the men of Israel, "Go every man to his city."
verseByVerse.commentary:
They have heard the whole speech and they say no. That is what makes this chapter so sober. This is not a nation stumbling into a mistake or acting on partial information. God had the terms read out in full (conscription, confiscation, the double tithe, slavery, unanswered prayer), and the elders listened to all of it and said no.

Now the reason, and the last clause is the whole of it. To be like the nations, where the request began. A king to judge them, which is fair enough. And to go out before us and fight our battles. One chapter ago, at Mizpah, the LORD thundered with a mighty sound that day against the Philistines and threw them into confusion, and they were defeated before Israel (7:10). That was within the adult memory of the men making this request. God went out before them in the open, with the whole nation watching, and the Philistines had not entered Israelite territory since. They want it done by somebody they can see.

That is the sin of the chapter, and why God filed it with idolatry. Not the office, which he had legislated for. It is the transfer of a function: taking the one thing God had been doing personally and asking for a man to do it instead, because a man can be looked at, mustered and counted. An idol has never mainly been about believing wrong things. It is about relocating a job.

Samuel takes it back to God word for word and gets the same answer. Every time God has said obey their voice he has said it after describing the request as a rejection of himself.

Now hold the long view, because the Bible does not treat this chapter as the end of the argument. Israel asked for a king to fight their battles. They were given Saul, a head taller than anyone in the country, who will spend chapter 17 doing nothing while a giant shouts at his army for forty days. Then David, a man after God's own heart, who fought their battles and won them, and who took another man's wife and had her husband killed, which is precisely the verb of verse 14 applied to a person.

Then, a thousand years later, the King the whole thing was reaching for. He came into the capital on a borrowed donkey rather than a chariot; he had no fields, no officers and nowhere to lay his head; he took nothing from anybody, and gave his life as a ransom for many. He did go out before his people and fight their battle, and he fought it alone, and he won it by dying.

Paul tells the story in exactly this order in the synagogue at Antioch: they asked for a king, God gave them Saul, then raised up David, and of this man's offspring God has brought to Israel a Savior, Jesus, as he promised (Acts 13:21–23). God's yes in chapter 8 was a judgment, and he wove it into the road to his Son. Israel got exactly the king it asked for, and eventually the one it needed.

8.theology:
Samuel repeats Eli's failure (vv. 1-3). The office was never hereditary (Judg. 8:23), and the best man in Israel made, so far as we are told, much the same mistake he had once been sent to condemn.

The office was not the sin. Deuteronomy 17:14-20 permits a king. What is condemned is like all the nations, and verse 20 says what that means.

Filed with idolatry (v. 8). An idol is anything put in the place where God was, to do the job God was doing. Israel wanted a man to fight the battles God had been fighting himself.

Obey their voice (vv. 7, 9, 22). There is a judgment that consists in being told no, and a heavier one that consists in being handed the thing you asked for (Ps. 106:15; Rom. 1:24).

He will take (vv. 11-17). Six times a king takes; once a King gives, and what he gives is himself (Mark 10:45).

The cry that is not answered (v. 18). The oppressors of Judges were sent; this one is requested. Even so, God remains merciful to those who truly repent (12:20-22).
8.examples:
Then: The elders heard the full terms read aloud and still said no, but there shall be a king over us, years after God had fought for them with thunder while the whole nation watched.

Now: Two things. The first is verse 8, and its very useful definition of an idol. Nobody in this chapter worshipped an image; they asked for an ordinary, permitted, sensible arrangement, and God called it what he had called the golden calf, because they were moving a job. Ask what God has actually been doing in your life that you have quietly handed to something you can see and count, and give it back to the King who fought your battle alone and won it by dying. The second is verse 18. There is trouble that is sent, and God always hears the cry about it. And there is trouble we chose after reading the terms, and Samuel is honest that these are not the same conversation. Even so, the door is not shut: the same Samuel will tell this people, after they confess, do not be afraid, for the LORD will not forsake them for his great name's sake (12:20–22).

9.title: Saul the Seeker
9.text: <sup>1</sup>There was a man of Benjamin whose name was Kish, the son of Abiel, son of Zeror, son of Becorath, son of Aphiah, a Benjaminite, a man of wealth.<sup>2</sup>And he had a son whose name was Saul, a handsome young man. There was not a man among the people of Israel more handsome than he. From his shoulders upward he was taller than any of the people.<sup>3</sup>Now the donkeys of Kish, Saul's father, were lost. So Kish said to Saul his son, "Take one of the young men with you, and arise, go and look for the donkeys."<sup>4</sup>And he passed through the hill country of Ephraim and passed through the land of Shalishah, but they did not find them. And they passed through the land of Shaalim, but they were not there. Then they passed through the land of Benjamin, but did not find them.<sup>5</sup>When they came to the land of Zuph, Saul said to his servant who was with him, "Come, let us go back, lest my father cease to care about the donkeys and become anxious about us."<sup>6</sup>But he said to him, "Behold, there is a man of God in this city, and he is a man who is held in honor; all that he says comes true. So now let us go there. Perhaps he can tell us the way we should go."<sup>7</sup>Then Saul said to his servant, "But if we go, what can we bring the man? For the bread in our sacks is gone, and there is no present to bring to the man of God. What do we have?"<sup>8</sup>The servant answered Saul again, "Here, I have with me a quarter of a shekel of silver, and I will give it to the man of God to tell us our way."<sup>9</sup>(Formerly in Israel, when a man went to inquire of God, he said, "Come, let us go to the seer," for today's "prophet" was formerly called a seer.)<sup>10</sup>And Saul said to his servant, "Well said; come, let us go." So they went to the city where the man of God was.<sup>11</sup>As they went up the hill to the city, they met young women coming out to draw water and said to them, "Is the seer here?"<sup>12</sup>They answered, "He is; behold, he is just ahead of you. Hurry. He has come just now to the city, because the people have a sacrifice today on the high place.<sup>13</sup>As soon as you enter the city you will find him, before he goes up to the high place to eat. For the people will not eat till he comes, since he must bless the sacrifice; afterward those who are invited will eat. Now go up, for you will meet him immediately."<sup>14</sup>So they went up to the city. As they were entering the city, they saw Samuel coming out toward them on his way up to the high place.<sup>15</sup>Now the day before Saul came, the LORD had revealed to Samuel:<sup>16</sup>"Tomorrow about this time I will send to you a man from the land of Benjamin, and you shall anoint him to be prince over my people Israel. He shall save my people from the hand of the Philistines. For I have seen my people, because their cry has come to me."<sup>17</sup>When Samuel saw Saul, the LORD told him, "Here is the man of whom I spoke to you! He it is who shall restrain my people."<sup>18</sup>Then Saul approached Samuel in the gate and said, "Tell me where is the house of the seer?"<sup>19</sup>Samuel answered Saul, "I am the seer. Go up before me to the high place, for today you shall eat with me, and in the morning I will let you go and will tell you all that is on your mind.<sup>20</sup>As for your donkeys that were lost three days ago, do not set your mind on them, for they have been found. And for whom is all that is desirable in Israel? Is it not for you and for all your father's house?"<sup>21</sup>Saul answered, "Am I not a Benjaminite, from the least of the tribes of Israel? And is not my clan the humblest of all the clans of the tribe of Benjamin? Why then have you spoken to me in this way?"<sup>22</sup>Then Samuel took Saul and his young man and brought them into the hall and gave them a place at the head of those who had been invited, who were about thirty persons.<sup>23</sup>And Samuel said to the cook, "Bring the portion I gave you, of which I said to you, 'Put it aside.'"<sup>24</sup>So the cook took up the leg and what was on it and set them before Saul. And Samuel said, "See, what was kept is set before you. Eat, because it was kept for you until the hour appointed, that you might eat with the guests." So Saul ate with Samuel that day.<sup>25</sup>And when they came down from the high place into the city, a bed was spread for Saul on the roof, and he lay down to sleep.<sup>26</sup>Then at the break of dawn Samuel called to Saul on the roof, "Up, that I may send you on your way." So Saul arose, and both he and Samuel went out into the street.<sup>27</sup>As they were going down to the outskirts of the city, Samuel said to Saul, "Tell the servant to pass on before us, and when he has passed on, stop here yourself for a while, that I may make known to you the word of God."
9.overview:
Israel asked for a king like the nations, and God introduces the best-looking man in the country, a head taller than anyone. Then the monarchy begins with lost livestock: a farmer's son looks for strayed donkeys, his servant suggests asking the man of God, and as the two walk in through the town gate Samuel walks out through it.

The narrator steps back a day: the LORD had told Samuel to expect him. Everything that read as a chain of small accidents was an itinerary. Saul protests that he is from the least of the tribes, and is seated at the head of the table and served a portion kept for him before he arrived.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–2 — The Tallest Man in Israel
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Kish, a wealthy Benjaminite, is introduced with his pedigree (v. 1), and his son Saul as the most handsome man in Israel and a head taller than anyone (v. 2).
verseByVerse.theology: God gives Israel the king it specified. The rest of the book will show that a king chosen for his appearance is not the same as a king after God's own heart.
verseByVerse.examples: We still choose leaders by the outside: height, presence, how they look on a platform. The chapter does not say such gifts are bad, only that they are not what God looks at.

verseByVerse.quote: There was a man of Benjamin whose name was Kish, the son of Abiel, son of Zeror, son of Becorath, son of Aphiah, a Benjaminite, a man of wealth. And he had a son whose name was Saul, a handsome young man. There was not a man among the people of Israel more handsome than he. From his shoulders upward he was taller than any of the people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The book opens a new section the way it opened the first: a certain man, with a genealogy and a home town. Elkanah was introduced with four generations behind him (1:1), and the reader is meant to hear the formula. But Kish is a man of wealth, or of standing. Elkanah was simply a man from Ramah.

If you have come from Judges you cannot read the name Benjamin neutrally. It is the tribe that sheltered the men of Gibeah, went to war with the other eleven over it, and was cut down to six hundred survivors hiding on a rock for four months (Judg. 20:47). Its women were replaced by the massacre of Jabesh-gilead and an abduction at a festival. Israel's first king will come out of the tribe that almost ceased to exist.

Now read the description against the request just made. Israel wanted a king like all the nations, one who would go out before us and fight our battles (8:20): somebody impressive, who would look right at the head of an army and whom the neighbours would take seriously. Here he is, the best-looking man in the country by the narrator's explicit comparison, and a head taller than everybody else.

Every word is about the outside of a person. Nothing about his courage, judgment, faith or character; a face and a height. God is giving Israel exactly what it specified, down to the last inch.

Hold the verse. Seven chapters on, Samuel will look at Jesse's eldest and think surely the LORD's anointed is before him, and be told: do not look on his appearance or on the height of his stature... for the LORD sees not as man sees: man looks on the outward appearance, but the LORD looks on the heart (16:7). That sentence is written against this one.

And it reaches further than David. Of the King God finally gave, Isaiah wrote that he had no form or majesty that we should look at him, and no beauty that we should desire him (Isa. 53:2). Israel chose by height and looks, and was given a king who could be measured. God's chosen King came without anything that would have impressed the elders at Ramah, and was rejected for the lack of it. The heart that the LORD looks on was, in him, perfect.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Saul and a servant search four districts for Kish's lost donkeys (vv. 3-5). The servant knows of a man of God nearby and has a coin to bring him (vv. 6-10). Girls at the well direct them, and at the gate they meet Samuel (vv. 11-14).
verseByVerse.theology: God's guidance here comes through the ordinary: a lost animal, a failed search, a servant's suggestion. Nothing in the episode looks like guidance until it is over.
verseByVerse.examples: Saul takes a servant's advice and is the better for it. Wise counsel often comes from the person beside us whom we least expect to have it.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the donkeys of Kish, Saul's father, were lost. So Kish said to Saul his son, "Take one of the young men with you, and arise, go and look for the donkeys." And he passed through the hill country of Ephraim and passed through the land of Shalishah, but they did not find them. And they passed through the land of Shaalim, but they were not there. Then they passed through the land of Benjamin, but did not find them. When they came to the land of Zuph, Saul said to his servant who was with him, "Come, let us go back, lest my father cease to care about the donkeys and become anxious about us." But he said to him, "Behold, there is a man of God in this city, and he is a man who is held in honor; all that he says comes true. So now let us go there. Perhaps he can tell us the way we should go." Then Saul said to his servant, "But if we go, what can we bring the man? For the bread in our sacks is gone, and there is no present to bring to the man of God. What do we have?" The servant answered Saul again, "Here, I have with me a quarter of a shekel of silver, and I will give it to the man of God to tell us our way."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The monarchy of Israel begins with lost livestock. No vision, no angel, no summons: a wealthy farmer's animals have wandered off and he sends his son with a farmhand to look for them, the least remarkable errand in agricultural life.

The sentence about the search is built to feel like the walking: passed through, did not find, passed through, not there. Three days of it, we learn later: two young men working steadily through the hill country and finding nothing, in a search entirely wasted from their point of view. Every step is taking Saul towards a town he has no intention of visiting.

Saul's one contribution so far is a decent instinct, and it deserves noting because there will not be many. He wants to turn round not because he is tired but because he can see the moment coming when his father stops caring about the animals and starts worrying about the boy. And Zuph is where Elkanah's family came from (1:1): Saul has walked, without knowing it, into Samuel's home district.

The servant is the one who knows. He knows there is a man of God in the town and his reputation, all that he says comes true, which is the narrator's own commendation of Samuel in 3:19. And it is his idea to go. The future king is standing in Samuel's district and does not appear to know he lives there.

Saul's objection is practical: you did not visit a prophet empty-handed, and the bread in their sacks is gone. The servant has money, a quarter of a shekel, not a gift for a great prophet, just what a working man happens to be carrying, offered without being asked. The pattern holds all the way to the town gate. Every step that moves Saul towards his anointing is proposed by the hired man walking beside him.

Was consulting a seer like fortune-telling? Samuel was the LORD’s prophet, and the gift was a customary courtesy, not payment for magic; divination by other means was forbidden (Deut 18:10–14).

verseByVerse.quote: (Formerly in Israel, when a man went to inquire of God, he said, "Come, let us go to the seer," for today's "prophet" was formerly called a seer.) And Saul said to his servant, "Well said; come, let us go." So they went to the city where the man of God was. As they went up the hill to the city, they met young women coming out to draw water and said to them, "Is the seer here?" They answered, "He is; behold, he is just ahead of you. Hurry. He has come just now to the city, because the people have a sacrifice today on the high place. As soon as you enter the city you will find him, before he goes up to the high place to eat. For the people will not eat till he comes, since he must bless the sacrifice; afterward those who are invited will eat. Now go up, for you will meet him immediately." So they went up to the city. As they were entering the city, they saw Samuel coming out toward them on his way up to the high place.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The narrator's aside tells us two things. This history was written down long enough after the event for the vocabulary to have shifted. And a seer is one who sees: a plain, physical term for a man to whom things are shown.

They meet girls going out to the well, which is where you meet people in this part of the Bible: Abraham's servant found Rebekah at one, Jacob met Rachel, Moses met Zipporah.

The answer runs on for three verses and the writer clearly enjoys it. He is here, he is just ahead of you, hurry, he has only just arrived, he has to bless the sacrifice before anyone eats. It is exactly how people give directions when they are excited to be asked, and it is packed with information that turns out to matter: Samuel is in town today only, arrived within the hour, and is walking up this street now.

They walk in through the gate and he walks out through it. Count what had to happen for that sentence to be written. The donkeys had to stray on a particular day; the search had to fail in four districts in a particular order; the servant had to know about the seer and be carrying a coin; Saul had to be talked out of turning for home; the women had to be at the well at that hour; and Samuel had to have come to that town that morning. None of the people involved is doing anything unusual. And the next verse tells us God had the whole thing arranged the previous day.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The day before, the LORD had told Samuel to expect a Benjaminite to anoint as prince, because he had heard his people's cry (vv. 15-17). Saul asks Samuel the way to the seer, hears that the donkeys are found, and protests that he is from the least of the tribes (vv. 18-21).
verseByVerse.theology: God had the appointment in the diary twenty-four hours before Saul knew he was going that way. The donkeys were lost so that a young man would be in a particular street at a particular time.
verseByVerse.examples: Prayer can take heart from v. 16: the God who answers Israel's mixed-up request is the God who hears his people's cry, and we can bring him even our muddled asking.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the day before Saul came, the LORD had revealed to Samuel: "Tomorrow about this time I will send to you a man from the land of Benjamin, and you shall anoint him to be prince over my people Israel. He shall save my people from the hand of the Philistines. For I have seen my people, because their cry has come to me." When Samuel saw Saul, the LORD told him, "Here is the man of whom I spoke to you! He it is who shall restrain my people."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Twenty-four hours in advance, to the hour. That reorganises the whole chapter. Everything we read as a chain of small accidents (the straying donkeys, the fruitless districts, the empty food bag, the servant's coin, the chatty girls) was an itinerary.

Note the word for the office. Nagid is a leader or designate, and it is not the word Israel used. They demanded a melek, a king like all the nations. It is a humbler word, and probably deliberate: he will be given the crown the people asked for, but in God's own speech he is first a leader under God.

Listen to where the language comes from. At the burning bush God had said: I have surely seen the affliction of my people who are in Egypt and have heard their cry... I know their sufferings (Ex. 3:7-9). It is the vocabulary of the exodus, applied to the appointment of Saul, one chapter after God called this request a rejection of himself and filed it with centuries of idolatry. Now, in the same breath as granting it, he explains it in the words he used when he came down to rescue slaves.

God is genuinely angry about the request and genuinely moved by the people making it, and both are stated plainly a chapter apart. He is not being talked into anything. He is giving them a king because they asked wrongly, and a deliverer because he has seen them.

That is the heart that finally sent his Son. Saul would save Israel from the Philistines for a season, and lose to them in the end. The angel told Joseph of another child: he will save his people from their sins (Matt. 1:21). The same God who heard a cry from Egypt and from a Philistine-ridden Israel heard the deeper cry of a race under sin, and answered it not with the tallest man available but with himself.

Samuel does not have to work it out; God identifies him on sight. And the verb is unexpected: not lead, or save, but restrain, holding in, keeping within bounds something that would otherwise run loose. That is a fair description of what Israel needed after Judges, where every man did what was right in his own eyes. And it is a strange word to attach to a man whose reign will end the night after a visit to a medium at Endor.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Saul approached Samuel in the gate and said, "Tell me where is the house of the seer?" Samuel answered Saul, "I am the seer. Go up before me to the high place, for today you shall eat with me, and in the morning I will let you go and will tell you all that is on your mind. As for your donkeys that were lost three days ago, do not set your mind on them, for they have been found. And for whom is all that is desirable in Israel? Is it not for you and for all your father's house?" Saul answered, "Am I not a Benjaminite, from the least of the tribes of Israel? And is not my clan the humblest of all the clans of the tribe of Benjamin? Why then have you spoken to me in this way?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
He asks the seer where the seer lives. There is something almost funny about it, and something sad: a prophet known from Dan to Beersheba is standing in front of the future king, and the future king asks him for directions.

I am the seer, and then at once an invitation, a schedule and a promise to tell him everything on his mind, which is a considerable claim to make to a stranger, and the next verse cashes it. Saul has not mentioned the donkeys, his father or the three days, and the first specific thing the seer says is the exact business that brought him, with the duration attached and the outcome supplied.

Mark the pastoral order. Before a word about kingdoms, Samuel deals with the thing actually on the young man's mind: the donkeys are found; stop worrying about them. Only then does he raise anything else, and only as a hint. He does not say you are to be king. He asks who everything valuable in Israel is for, and lets it hang.

Saul's answer is the best thing he says in the book, and it is somebody else's almost word for word. A frightened young man threshing wheat in a winepress once told the angel of the LORD: my clan is the weakest in Manasseh, and I am the least in my father's house (Judg. 6:15). Two men, two calls, the same accurate inventory of their own insignificance. Here it is not modest phrasing; it is arithmetic. Benjamin had once been reduced to six hundred men and was still among the smallest of the tribes.

So the chapter has given us two facts about this man that do not sit easily together. He is the tallest and best-looking person in Israel, and he comes from the smallest clan of the smallest tribe and knows it. Both are true, and the second is the one that will not last.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 22–27 — The Portion That Was Kept
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Samuel seats Saul at the head of thirty guests and serves him the portion kept for him (vv. 22-24). Saul sleeps on the roof, and at dawn Samuel sends the servant ahead to give Saul the word of God (vv. 25-27).
verseByVerse.theology: Samuel honours a stranger because God has told him to. The honour comes before Saul has done anything to earn it.
verseByVerse.examples: God's plans for Saul arrive through an ordinary meal kindly given: thirty guests, a reserved cut of meat, a bed on the roof.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Samuel took Saul and his young man and brought them into the hall and gave them a place at the head of those who had been invited, who were about thirty persons. And Samuel said to the cook, "Bring the portion I gave you, of which I said to you, 'Put it aside.'" So the cook took up the leg and what was on it and set them before Saul. And Samuel said, "See, what was kept is set before you. Eat, because it was kept for you until the hour appointed, that you might eat with the guests." So Saul ate with Samuel that day. And when they came down from the high place into the city, a bed was spread for Saul on the roof, and he lay down to sleep. Then at the break of dawn Samuel called to Saul on the roof, "Up, that I may send you on your way." So Saul arose, and both he and Samuel went out into the street. As they were going down to the outskirts of the city, Samuel said to Saul, "Tell the servant to pass on before us, and when he has passed on, stop here yourself for a while, that I may make known to you the word of God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Thirty guests are already seated, and two men who came in off the road looking for donkeys are put at the top of the table. The servant goes up with him; Samuel seats them both.

The instruction to the cook was given before Saul arrived, on the strength of a sentence God had spoken the previous day. What comes out is the leg. Under the law the right thigh of a fellowship offering was the priest's portion (Lev. 7:32-33), the best cut, belonging to the man presiding. Samuel had it put aside for a young man he had never met.

Kept for you until the hour appointed is the theology of the whole chapter served on a plate. Saul has spent three days walking four districts after animals that were not there, getting hungrier, achieving nothing, and thinking about going home. He arrives at a table where a portion has been under a cloth since before he came, reserved by name, for an appointment he did not know he had. Everything that felt like wasted time was the journey to this seat.

(The ESV here follows the Greek Old Testament; the Hebrew says instead that Samuel talked with Saul on the roof. Either way, the night is spent in the seer's house.) They make him a bed on the roof, which is where you sleep in that country when the night is warm, and he lies down under the sky on the last ordinary night of his life.

Early, before the town is awake, the old man calls up to the roof and the two walk out into an empty street. The servant is sent ahead, and the chapter stops on the sentence before the word of God is spoken: two men on the edge of a town at first light, one of them about to be told something. It is a deliberate piece of storytelling.

Look back over the twenty-seven verses and count what God used: donkeys that wandered off, four districts of fruitless walking, an empty food sack, a servant who happened to know the prophet's reputation and to have a quarter shekel, a young man's worry about his father, girls at a well, a sacrifice scheduled that day in that town, a cook, and a cut of meat put by. Not one of those is a miracle. Every one is the sort of thing that happens on an ordinary day, and any of them could have gone differently. The day before it started, God had told Samuel what time to expect him.

9.theology:
Exactly what they asked for (v. 2). A face and a height, and nothing about courage, judgment or faith. Samuel will later be told the LORD sees not as man sees (16:7), a sentence written against this one.

From the least of the tribes (v. 21). Saul's protest is Gideon's almost word for word (Judg. 6:15), and for a Benjaminite it is arithmetic as much as modesty. The book will show what he did with it.

Nagid, not melek (v. 16). Israel demanded a king; in God's own speech Saul is first a leader under God.

Anger and pity together (v. 16). God speaks of this king in the language of the burning bush (Ex. 3:7-9), one chapter after calling the request a rejection of himself. He grants it in judgment and in compassion at once, and he is not being talked into anything.

Providence with no miracle in it. Nothing in the chapter is supernatural, and every step could have gone differently; yet God had told Samuel the day before what time to expect him.

Kept for you (v. 24). The best portion was set aside before Saul arrived. God's preparation runs ahead of our knowing, and for anyone in a season that has produced nothing, that is worth holding on to even before anything explains it.
9.examples:
Then: A young man spent three days looking for his father's donkeys, found nothing, and walked into a town where a prophet had been told the day before what time he would arrive and had already set his dinner aside.

Now: Two things. The first is the shape of the whole chapter: God very rarely announces himself in the middle of the arrangement. Every element of Saul's morning was ordinary, reversible and explicable, and the reader only learns it was an appointment because the narrator steps back a day in verse 15. You are unlikely to be given verse 15 at the time. The second is verse 24, and it is for anyone in a season that has produced nothing: the donkeys were never the point, and no amount of looking at them would have revealed that.

10.title: The Spirit of God Came Upon Him
10.text: <sup>1</sup>Then Samuel took a flask of oil and poured it on his head and kissed him and said, "Has not the LORD anointed you to be prince over his people Israel? And you shall reign over the people of the LORD and you will save them from the hand of their surrounding enemies. And this shall be the sign to you that the LORD has anointed you to be prince over his heritage.<sup>2</sup>When you depart from me today, you will meet two men by Rachel's tomb in the territory of Benjamin at Zelzah, and they will say to you, 'The donkeys that you went to seek are found, and now your father has ceased to care about the donkeys and is anxious about you, saying, "What shall I do about my son?"'<sup>3</sup>Then you shall go on from there farther and come to the oak of Tabor. Three men going up to God at Bethel will meet you there, one carrying three young goats, another carrying three loaves of bread, and another carrying a skin of wine.<sup>4</sup>And they will greet you and give you two loaves of bread, which you shall accept from their hand.<sup>5</sup>After that you shall come to Gibeath-elohim, where there is a garrison of the Philistines. And there, as soon as you come to the city, you will meet a group of prophets coming down from the high place with harp, tambourine, flute, and lyre before them, prophesying.<sup>6</sup>Then the Spirit of the LORD will rush upon you, and you will prophesy with them and be turned into another man.<sup>7</sup>Now when these signs meet you, do what your hand finds to do, for God is with you.<sup>8</sup>Then go down before me to Gilgal. And behold, I am coming down to you to offer burnt offerings and to sacrifice peace offerings. Seven days you shall wait, until I come to you and show you what you shall do."<sup>9</sup>When he turned his back to leave Samuel, God gave him another heart. And all these signs came to pass that day.<sup>10</sup>When they came to Gibeah, behold, a group of prophets met him, and the Spirit of God rushed upon him, and he prophesied among them.<sup>11</sup>And when all who knew him previously saw how he prophesied with the prophets, the people said to one another, "What has come over the son of Kish? Is Saul also among the prophets?"<sup>12</sup>And a man of the place answered, "And who is their father?" Therefore it became a proverb, "Is Saul also among the prophets?"<sup>13</sup>When he had finished prophesying, he came to the high place.<sup>14</sup>Saul's uncle said to him and to his servant, "Where did you go?" And he said, "To seek the donkeys. And when we saw they were not to be found, we went to Samuel."<sup>15</sup>And Saul's uncle said, "Please tell me what Samuel said to you."<sup>16</sup>And Saul said to his uncle, "He told us plainly that the donkeys had been found." But about the matter of the kingdom, of which Samuel had spoken, he did not tell him anything.<sup>17</sup>Now Samuel called the people together to the LORD at Mizpah.<sup>18</sup>And he said to the people of Israel, "Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel, 'I brought up Israel out of Egypt, and I delivered you from the hand of the Egyptians and from the hand of all the kingdoms that were oppressing you.'<sup>19</sup>But today you have rejected your God, who saves you from all your calamities and your distresses, and you have said to him, 'Set a king over us.' Now therefore present yourselves before the LORD by your tribes and by your thousands."<sup>20</sup>Then Samuel brought all the tribes of Israel near, and the tribe of Benjamin was taken by lot.<sup>21</sup>He brought the tribe of Benjamin near by its clans, and the clan of the Matrites was taken by lot; and Saul the son of Kish was taken by lot. But when they sought him, he could not be found.<sup>22</sup>So they inquired again of the LORD, "Is there a man still to come?" and the LORD said, "Behold, he has hidden himself among the baggage."<sup>23</sup>Then they ran and took him from there. And when he stood among the people, he was taller than any of the people from his shoulders upward.<sup>24</sup>And Samuel said to all the people, "Do you see him whom the LORD has chosen? There is none like him among all the people." And all the people shouted, "Long live the king!"<sup>25</sup>Then Samuel told the people the rights and duties of the kingship, and he wrote them in a book and laid it up before the LORD. Then Samuel sent all the people away, each one to his home.<sup>26</sup>Saul also went to his home at Gibeah, and with him went men of valor whose hearts God had touched.<sup>27</sup>But some worthless fellows said, "How can this man save us?" And they despised him and brought him no present. But he held his peace.
10.overview:
Saul is anointed on a road at dawn with no one watching, and Samuel gives him three signs. The first repeats his own private worry back to him; the third brings the Spirit on him among prophets at the hill of God, and he is turned into another man. He is also given an order to keep: wait seven days at Gilgal.

At Mizpah the lot falls on him in public, and Samuel tells the nation on coronation day that asking for a king was a rejection of God, and crowns him anyway. When the name is called, the king cannot be found. He is hiding in the luggage.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — A Flask of Oil and Three Signs
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Samuel anoints Saul prince over Israel (v. 1) and gives him three signs: news of the donkeys at Rachel's tomb, pilgrims with bread at the oak of Tabor, and prophets at Gibeath-elohim, where the Spirit will rush on him (vv. 2-6). Then two instructions: act as occasion serves, for God is with you, and wait seven days at Gilgal (vv. 7-8).
verseByVerse.theology: Samuel uses God's word for the office, prince (nagid), not the people's word, king. Saul is anointed to serve under God before he is crowned by the nation.
verseByVerse.examples: The pilgrims' bread (v. 4) was on its way to God and was handed to a hungry stranger. God's provision often reaches us like this, through what other people bring.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Samuel took a flask of oil and poured it on his head and kissed him and said, "Has not the LORD anointed you to be prince over his people Israel? And you shall reign over the people of the LORD and you will save them from the hand of their surrounding enemies. And this shall be the sign to you that the LORD has anointed you to be prince over his heritage. When you depart from me today, you will meet two men by Rachel's tomb in the territory of Benjamin at Zelzah, and they will say to you, 'The donkeys that you went to seek are found, and now your father has ceased to care about the donkeys and is anxious about you, saying, "What shall I do about my son?"' Then you shall go on from there farther and come to the oak of Tabor. Three men going up to God at Bethel will meet you there, one carrying three young goats, another carrying three loaves of bread, and another carrying a skin of wine. And they will greet you and give you two loaves of bread, which you shall accept from their hand.
verseByVerse.commentary:
It happens on a road at dawn, with one witness sent on ahead, in three actions: oil poured on the head, a kiss, and a sentence put as a question. No crowd, no ceremony; the servant has been sent up the road precisely so that nobody sees it.

The anointing gives the Bible one of its central titles. The anointed one is the mashiach, the messiah; from this morning the phrase the LORD's anointed belongs to a man, and David will refuse to lift a hand against it even when its holder is trying to kill him.

The title is the one Hannah sang about (2:10), and it will finally belong to one man in a way it never belonged to Saul. In Greek it is Christos, Christ. Jesus was anointed not from a flask on a road but by the Spirit at the Jordan, who came down and remained on him (John 1:32–33; Acts 10:38). Saul's anointing could be withdrawn, and was; the Father gives the Spirit to his Son without measure (John 3:34), and his kingdom has no end.

Now go back to 9:5: Come, let us go back, lest my father cease to care about the donkeys and become anxious about us. The sign quotes him.
