Two strangers at a tomb will say back to him, almost word for word, the sentence he spoke to his servant in a field when nobody was listening. That is remarkable pastoral care. God confirms the anointing of a king by having his private worry repeated by men who could not have heard it, and by settling the worry at the same time. The donkeys are found. Your father is anxious. Go home.

The location is chosen too. Rachel was Benjamin's mother and died giving birth to him. Israel's first king receives his first confirming sign at the grave of his tribe's ancestress.

The second sign is smaller and stranger, and the detail is exact: three men, three goats, three loaves, one skin of wine, and two of the loaves handed over. These are pilgrims taking offerings up to Bethel. The bread is holy provision on its way to God, diverted to a stranger on the road, and Saul had told his servant the day before that they had nothing left to eat (9:7).

Rachel’s tomb is placed on the border of Benjamin here, and near Bethlehem in Genesis 35:19. Zelzah lay on the road between, and “on the way to Ephrath” can describe the region.
verseByVerse.note: Anointing with oil set someone apart for God’s service; the anointed one is “messiah” in Hebrew, “christ” in Greek. The words from “over his people Israel?” to “to be prince” come from the Greek Old Testament; the Hebrew lacks them (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: After that you shall come to Gibeath-elohim, where there is a garrison of the Philistines. And there, as soon as you come to the city, you will meet a group of prophets coming down from the high place with harp, tambourine, flute, and lyre before them, prophesying. Then the Spirit of the LORD will rush upon you, and you will prophesy with them and be turned into another man. Now when these signs meet you, do what your hand finds to do, for God is with you. Then go down before me to Gilgal. And behold, I am coming down to you to offer burnt offerings and to sacrifice peace offerings. Seven days you shall wait, until I come to you and show you what you shall do."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two things in the verse do not obviously belong together. The town is Gibeath-elohim, the hill of God, and there is a Philistine garrison in it: the political situation of Israel in one place name. And coming down off that hill is a band of prophets with a small orchestra, making music and prophesying in a town with foreign troops stationed in it. Worship did not stop under occupation. It came down the hill past the garrison with a tambourine.

The verb rush is the one used of Samson: a sudden seizing, not a gentle settling. Then the promise larger than anything else in the chapter: turned into another man. Not improved, not trained, not promoted. Turned into somebody else.

The first instruction is remarkably open. No orders, no plan, no campaign. He is told to act on his own judgment in whatever comes to hand, and given the only thing that makes such freedom safe: for God is with you.

The second is the opposite, and it is the one to remember. Go to Gilgal. Wait seven days, until I come. Weigh the two together, because a king is being taught something. In most things: use your judgment, God is with you. In this one thing: do nothing until I arrive.

Mark the verse and leave it. It is the first specific order Saul receives as Israel's prince, it has a number of days attached, and three chapters from now he will stand at Gilgal watching his army melt away, wait almost the whole seven days, and offer the burnt offering himself.
verseByVerse.note: “Gibeath-elohim” means “the hill of God” (ESV note).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–16 — Is Saul Also Among the Prophets?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: As Saul turns to go, God gives him another heart, and the signs come true (v. 9). The Spirit rushes on him among the prophets, and the neighbours' astonishment becomes a proverb (vv. 10-13). To his uncle he speaks of the donkeys and not of the kingdom (vv. 14-16).
verseByVerse.theology: God gave him another heart is said of Saul, and it was given before any of the signs happened. What kind of change it was is weighed in the note on vv. 9-13.
verseByVerse.examples: The neighbours' surprise (v. 11) is a reminder that God's work in a person can be most startling to those who think they know him best.

verseByVerse.quote: When he turned his back to leave Samuel, God gave him another heart. And all these signs came to pass that day. When they came to Gibeah, behold, a group of prophets met him, and the Spirit of God rushed upon him, and he prophesied among them. And when all who knew him previously saw how he prophesied with the prophets, the people said to one another, "What has come over the son of Kish? Is Saul also among the prophets?" And a man of the place answered, "And who is their father?" Therefore it became a proverb, "Is Saul also among the prophets?" When he had finished prophesying, he came to the high place.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The moment he turns to go, it happens. Not after the signs, not once he has proved himself, not in response to anything he did on the road. He turns his back to walk away and God changes him on the spot.

God gave him another heart is one of the great sentences of the Old Testament, and it is said of Saul. Take the sentence seriously, because the end of this man's story makes it tempting not to. Something real was given to him here, in language close to the greatest promise God ever makes to his people: I will give you a new heart, and a new spirit I will put within you (Ezek. 36:26).

The people who react are the ones who have known him all his life. Not "who is this man" but what has come over the son of Kish: the neighbours he grew up in front of, watching somebody they thought they had measured do something entirely out of character.

The retort is obscure and has never been settled. The likeliest sense is that prophecy is not a family trade: nobody asks who the prophets' father is, because the gift is not inherited, so there is no reason Kish's boy should be excluded. What matters more is that the sentence stuck, the kind of thing people said when somebody turned up somewhere he had no business being.

It will be said about him once more. Nine chapters on, hunting David, Saul will send three parties of messengers to Ramah and lose every one to the Spirit, and finally go himself, and end up lying on the ground stripped and prophesying all day and night while David gets clean away. And the narrator writes: thus it is said, "Is Saul also among the prophets?" (19:24). The first time it is wonder. The second time it is a man's public humiliation while the kingdom walks out of his hands.

Was Saul given a new heart in the saving sense? “Another heart” means God equipped him for kingship, with courage and the Spirit’s power (v. 6); it is not said that he was born again, and his later life suggests he was not.

Can the Holy Spirit leave a believer? In the Old Testament the Spirit came on judges, prophets and kings to equip them for their office, and that gift could be withdrawn, as here. In the new covenant the Spirit dwells in every believer for ever (John 14:16) as the seal and guarantee of salvation (Eph 1:13–14); David’s prayer, take not your Holy Spirit from me (Ps 51:11), was the prayer of a king who had seen what happened to Saul. Saul received the Spirit’s power for his office, but his life shows no sign of saving faith.

What was this prophesying? Most likely inspired praise and speech, given with music (v. 5), a sign that God’s Spirit had come on Saul for his office; it was not new Scripture. This commentary holds that such gifts belonged to the era of revelation and that the Spirit today works through the completed word; many faithful Christians believe otherwise, and they are brothers and sisters in the same Lord.
verseByVerse.note: “Gibeah” means “the hill” (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: Saul's uncle said to him and to his servant, "Where did you go?" And he said, "To seek the donkeys. And when we saw they were not to be found, we went to Samuel." And Saul's uncle said, "Please tell me what Samuel said to you." And Saul said to his uncle, "He told us plainly that the donkeys had been found." But about the matter of the kingdom, of which Samuel had spoken, he did not tell him anything.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A relative asks the ordinary question and gets an ordinary, accurate answer, about the livestock and nothing about the crown.

The narrator offers no assessment, and readers have taken it both ways. It may be modesty: a young man who has had oil poured on his head at dawn and does not think it is his to announce. It may be prudence: Samuel had done this in private, and a man who starts telling his uncle he is to be king has not understood the arrangement. Or it may be the first appearance of something else, in the man who will shortly be found hiding in the luggage.

It is a mistake to be more certain than the text. What can be said is that Saul is consistently reticent about this kingdom in these early chapters, that the reticence is attractive, and that it does not last.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: At Mizpah Samuel reminds Israel that God saved them and that they have rejected him (vv. 17-19). The lot falls on Saul, who is found hiding among the baggage, a head taller than all (vv. 20-23), and the people shout, long live the king (v. 24).
verseByVerse.theology: Mizpah, where Israel once confessed and was rescued by God himself (7:5-10), is now where it receives the king it asked for in place of that rescue.
verseByVerse.examples: The shout long live the king (v. 24) is right in itself; the trouble is which king, and why. The church still raises it, to the King whose kingdom has no end.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Samuel called the people together to the LORD at Mizpah. And he said to the people of Israel, "Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel, 'I brought up Israel out of Egypt, and I delivered you from the hand of the Egyptians and from the hand of all the kingdoms that were oppressing you.' But today you have rejected your God, who saves you from all your calamities and your distresses, and you have said to him, 'Set a king over us.' Now therefore present yourselves before the LORD by your tribes and by your thousands."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Mizpah again, the hill where the nation had fasted and confessed and watched God break the Philistines with thunder (7:5-10). Samuel brings them back to the same place to give them a king, and opens the way God always opens, with the recital: I brought you up, I delivered you from Egypt and from every kingdom that oppressed you.

Then he says it on the day of the coronation. The nation is assembled, the lots are about to be cast, the king is in the crowd, and the presiding prophet tells them that what they are doing is a rejection of the God who saves you from all your calamities. He does not decide that the decision is made and the mood should be positive. He is going to crown the man, because God told him to, three times, and he will not pretend the request was a good one while he does it. God has granted it, and it was a rejection. Samuel obeys the first without withdrawing the second.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Samuel brought all the tribes of Israel near, and the tribe of Benjamin was taken by lot. He brought the tribe of Benjamin near by its clans, and the clan of the Matrites was taken by lot; and Saul the son of Kish was taken by lot. But when they sought him, he could not be found. So they inquired again of the LORD, "Is there a man still to come?" and the LORD said, "Behold, he has hidden himself among the baggage." Then they ran and took him from there. And when he stood among the people, he was taller than any of the people from his shoulders upward. And Samuel said to all the people, "Do you see him whom the LORD has chosen? There is none like him among all the people." And all the people shouted, "Long live the king!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The lot narrows from twelve tribes to one clan to one man, and lands where God had already landed a chapter ago. Samuel already knows who it is. The lot is so that the whole nation watches the choice fall publicly, tribe by tribe, and cannot afterwards say the prophet installed his own candidate.

The king of Israel is missing from his own coronation, and God has to tell them where he is. It is genuinely comic and genuinely uncomfortable. The name has been called and nobody comes forward. They search, they have to ask God a second question, and the answer is that the man is in among the luggage.

It has been read two ways, and the text will not settle it. It may be humility. He had told Samuel he was from the least clan of the smallest tribe and meant it; he had told his own uncle nothing; and a man who genuinely does not want this might well be found at the back among the packs. It may equally be fear. This is the man who will do nothing for forty days while a Philistine shouts at his army, dismayed and greatly afraid with everybody else (17:11). Both fit, the writer knew both fit, and he declines to tell us. The same behaviour looks like modesty at a coronation and like paralysis at a battlefield, and the man never entirely stops doing it.

They pull him out and stand him up, and the narrator repeats 9:2 almost word for word. He is very tall: the fact the book keeps giving us about him, given again at the moment he is presented to the nation, immediately after he has been discovered hiding.

Samuel's commendation is about how he looks.

Do you see him whom the LORD has chosen? The verb is see, and what there is to see is a head and shoulders above the crowd. There is none like him among all the people, which in the context of verse 23 means precisely one thing.

Israel asked for an impressive figure at the head of an army. They are looking at him and cheering, and everything they can see is exactly what they ordered.

Six chapters on, God will refuse Samuel seven of Jesse's sons in a row and say: do not look on his appearance or on the height of his stature, because I have rejected him. For the LORD sees not as man sees (16:7).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Samuel writes the rights of the kingship in a book and lays it before the LORD (v. 25). Saul goes home with men whose hearts God had touched, while worthless men despise him, and he holds his peace (vv. 26-27).
verseByVerse.theology: Israel's king begins under a written law, not above it, and that is the difference between this throne and the thrones Israel wanted to copy.
verseByVerse.examples: Some went with Saul because God had touched their hearts (v. 26). Loyalty that God gives is worth more than loyalty that is organised.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Samuel told the people the rights and duties of the kingship, and he wrote them in a book and laid it up before the LORD. Then Samuel sent all the people away, each one to his home. Saul also went to his home at Gibeah, and with him went men of valor whose hearts God had touched. But some worthless fellows said, "How can this man save us?" And they despised him and brought him no present. But he held his peace.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is precisely what the law required. When Israel had a king he was to write a copy of the law for himself and read it every day of his life, that he may learn to fear the LORD his God and that his heart may not be lifted up above his brothers (Deut. 17:18-20). So Israel now has a king who is under a text, and the text is not in his keeping. It is laid up before the LORD, where he cannot amend it. That is the crucial difference between this monarchy and every monarchy Israel was asking to imitate. The kings of the nations were the source of law. This one is subject to a document deposited where he does not control it.

Everybody goes home, including the king, who goes back to his father's house in Gibeah and, as the next chapter shows, to his ploughing. But some men go with him, and the phrase used of them is lovely: men of valor whose hearts God had touched. There is no army yet. God moved on some men and they attached themselves to the new king voluntarily. It is the first thing in this whole business that nobody organised.

Some do not go. Worthless fellows is, once again, sons of Belial, the phrase Hannah begged Eli not to apply to her and the narrator's verdict on Eli's sons. Their question is fair on the face of it: they have just watched him pulled out of a pile of luggage. And they show their contempt in the standard way, by withholding the gift that acknowledged a new ruler.

He held his peace is entirely to his credit. Publicly insulted on his coronation day, he lets it go. He does not have them seized, or answer them, or remember it out loud. The Hebrew is literally that he was "like one deaf".

A textual note: the oldest Hebrew copy of Samuel among the Dead Sea Scrolls has, at this point, a paragraph missing from later manuscripts, telling how Nahash the Ammonite had been oppressing Gad and Reuben and gouging out their right eyes. It reads with a slightly different word here, about a month later, instead of he held his peace. Some modern versions include it; the ESV and most others follow the traditional Hebrew. Nothing in the story or its teaching changes either way: the next chapter tells of Nahash's threat in full.

Nor is this a one-off. When his first victory is won and the people demand that those very men be executed, he refuses: not a man shall be put to death this day, for today the LORD has worked salvation in Israel (11:13). Keep both, because they are the high-water mark of the man. Saul begins genuinely humble, genuinely restrained, and genuinely willing to give God the credit. The tragedy of the chapters ahead is not that he was always what he became.

10.theology:
Seven days you shall wait (v. 8). Set beside do what your hand finds to do, a king is being taught the shape of obedience: use your judgment in most things, and in this one thing wait until I come. Chapter 13 is where he breaks it.

God gave him another heart (v. 9). It was real, and it should not be discounted because of how his story ends; but it was God's equipping for his office, not, so far as the text says, the new birth that Ezekiel's promise and the gospel bring.

Crowned and indicted in one speech (vv. 18-19). God has granted the request, and it was a rejection; obeying the first does not require withdrawing the second.

Hidden among the baggage (v. 22). Humility or fear: the text will not settle it, and the same behaviour reads differently at a coronation and on a battlefield (17:11).

A king under a text (v. 25). The kings of the nations were the source of law; this one is subject to a document laid up before the LORD (Deut. 17:18-20).

He held his peace (v. 27). Saul begins humble and restrained, and willing to give God the credit. The tragedy ahead is not that he was always what he became.
10.examples:
Then: A man was anointed king on an empty road at first light, changed by God as he turned to walk away, and found on his coronation day hiding among the luggage.

Now: Two things. Verse 7 and verse 8 belong together and most of Christian obedience lives between them: in the great majority of decisions, do what your hand finds to do, for God is with you, and in a few specific ones, wait, because you were told to. Knowing which is which is the whole skill, and Saul got it wrong on the one that had a number attached. The ground of both is the same: God is with you comes before anything is asked. And the Christian has more than Saul had: not a gift for an office that could be withdrawn, but the Spirit who dwells in every believer for ever, who is the power to wait as well as to act. When we fail at either, as we will, the Anointed One obeyed his Father to the end in our place, and the way back is open. And hold verse 9 against the instinct to read a person's end back into their beginning. God gave Saul another heart. Whatever happened afterwards, that sentence was true when it was written.

11.title: Saul's First Victory
11.text: <sup>1</sup>Then Nahash the Ammonite went up and besieged Jabesh-gilead, and all the men of Jabesh said to Nahash, "Make a treaty with us, and we will serve you."<sup>2</sup>But Nahash the Ammonite said to them, "On this condition I will make a treaty with you, that I gouge out all your right eyes, and thus bring disgrace on all Israel."<sup>3</sup>The elders of Jabesh said to him, "Give us seven days' respite that we may send messengers through all the territory of Israel. Then, if there is no one to save us, we will give ourselves up to you."<sup>4</sup>When the messengers came to Gibeah of Saul, they reported the matter in the ears of the people, and all the people wept aloud.<sup>5</sup>Now, behold, Saul was coming from the field behind the oxen. And Saul said, "What is wrong with the people, that they are weeping?" So they told him the news of the men of Jabesh.<sup>6</sup>And the Spirit of God rushed upon Saul when he heard these words, and his anger was greatly kindled.<sup>7</sup>He took a yoke of oxen and cut them in pieces and sent them throughout all the territory of Israel by the hand of the messengers, saying, "Whoever does not come out after Saul and Samuel, so shall it be done to his oxen!" Then the dread of the LORD fell upon the people, and they came out as one man.<sup>8</sup>When he mustered them at Bezek, the people of Israel were three hundred thousand, and the men of Judah thirty thousand.<sup>9</sup>And they said to the messengers who had come, "Thus shall you say to the men of Jabesh-gilead: 'Tomorrow, by the time the sun is hot, you shall have salvation.'" When the messengers came and told the men of Jabesh, they were glad.<sup>10</sup>Therefore the men of Jabesh said, "Tomorrow we will give ourselves up to you, and you may do to us whatever seems good to you."<sup>11</sup>And the next day Saul put the people in three companies. And they came into the midst of the camp in the morning watch and struck down the Ammonites until the heat of the day. And those who survived were scattered, so that no two of them were left together.<sup>12</sup>Then the people said to Samuel, "Who is it that said, 'Shall Saul reign over us?' Bring the men, that we may put them to death."<sup>13</sup>But Saul said, "Not a man shall be put to death this day, for today the LORD has worked salvation in Israel."<sup>14</sup>Then Samuel said to the people, "Come, let us go to Gilgal and there renew the kingdom."<sup>15</sup>So all the people went to Gilgal, and there they made Saul king before the LORD in Gilgal. There they sacrificed peace offerings before the LORD, and there Saul and all the men of Israel rejoiced greatly.
11.overview:
Nahash the Ammonite besieges Jabesh-gilead and sets a price on its surrender meant to shame the whole nation. He gives the town seven days to find help, because he does not believe anyone in Israel will come. The town has a history with Saul's tribe, Benjamin, that goes back to the last chapter of Judges, and the bond between them will close at the end of this book.

Gibeah weeps and does nothing, and the newly crowned king has to come in from the field to ask what the crying is about. Then the Spirit of God rushes upon him, the nation comes out at his summons, and Jabesh is rescued at the hour he promised. On the day he could most easily settle scores, Saul spares the men who had despised him and gives the credit to God. It is the high point of his life.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–3 — Gouge Out Every Right Eye
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Nahash the Ammonite besieges Jabesh-gilead, and the town offers to serve him (v. 1). His price is every right eye, as a disgrace on all Israel (v. 2). The elders ask for seven days to send through the land for help, and if nobody comes they will surrender (v. 3).
verseByVerse.theology: The right eye is a calculation, not merely cruelty. A man in a battle line held his shield on his left arm, covering the left side of his face, and fought with the right eye; take it from every man in the town and you have disarmed it for good, and left the shame on view for all Israel to see.
verseByVerse.examples: The reader has met Jabesh-gilead before. It is the town Israel destroyed in the last chapter of Judges, putting every man and every married woman to the sword, to supply four hundred wives for the six hundred surviving Benjaminites (Judg. 21:8-12). Saul is a Benjaminite, and there are Benjaminites in Gibeah descended from those women.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Nahash the Ammonite went up and besieged Jabesh-gilead, and all the men of Jabesh said to Nahash, "Make a treaty with us, and we will serve you." But Nahash the Ammonite said to them, "On this condition I will make a treaty with you, that I gouge out all your right eyes, and thus bring disgrace on all Israel." The elders of Jabesh said to him, "Give us seven days' respite that we may send messengers through all the territory of Israel. Then, if there is no one to save us, we will give ourselves up to you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The town does not fight. It sues for terms in the first verse: Jabesh-gilead is east of the Jordan, exposed, a long way from the hill country, and Ammon has arrived in force. The offer is the ordinary one of the ancient world: we will be your vassals, and you will not destroy us.

A textual note. One Dead Sea Scroll of Samuel has an extra paragraph before this verse: Nahash had already been gouging out the right eyes of the Gadites and Reubenites east of the Jordan, and some seven thousand men had escaped to Jabesh. A few modern translations print it. The chapter's meaning does not change either way; it simply shows that the terms in verse 2 were no idle threat.

Given the town's history with Benjamin (see above), hold on to the connection: when Saul's headless body is fastened to the wall of Beth-shan, it is the men of Jabesh-gilead who march all night, take it down, and bury it (31:11-13).

Nahash accepts the surrender and names his price, and he says what it is for: disgrace on all Israel. It is a message to a nation, written on the faces of one town.

He grants the week, which tells you how much he expects from Israel. He has just been told that runners will go through every territory appealing for help, and he agrees to wait, because in his judgment nobody will come. Given the long years of the judges, when the tribes seldom came to each other's aid, it is a reasonable assessment.
verseByVerse.note: The name seems to survive in the Wadi Yabis, which runs down to the Jordan from the eastern hills; the town stood somewhere along it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 4–11 — The Spirit Rushed Upon Saul
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The messengers reach Gibeah and the people weep aloud, and do nothing (v. 4). Saul comes in from the field behind the oxen and asks what is wrong (v. 5). The Spirit of God rushes upon him and his anger is greatly kindled (v. 6); he summons Israel and they come out as one man (v. 7). They muster at Bezek, promise Jabesh deliverance by the heat of the day, and Saul destroys the Ammonites in the morning watch (vv. 8-11).
verseByVerse.theology: From first to last the rescue is God's. The Spirit seizes Saul, and it is the dread of the LORD, not the king's authority, that brings the people out.
verseByVerse.examples: Saul's summons in v. 7 copies the worst page of Judges, where a Levite sent pieces of a woman's body through Israel and the tribes came out as one man to make war on Benjamin (Judg. 19:29; 20:1). This time the same summons raises an army to save a town.

verseByVerse.quote: When the messengers came to Gibeah of Saul, they reported the matter in the ears of the people, and all the people wept aloud. Now, behold, Saul was coming from the field behind the oxen. And Saul said, "What is wrong with the people, that they are weeping?" So they told him the news of the men of Jabesh. And the Spirit of God rushed upon Saul when he heard these words, and his anger was greatly kindled. He took a yoke of oxen and cut them in pieces and sent them throughout all the territory of Israel by the hand of the messengers, saying, "Whoever does not come out after Saul and Samuel, so shall it be done to his oxen!" Then the dread of the LORD fell upon the people, and they came out as one man.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The town hears the news and cries, and that is all. Nobody musters. Nobody sends to the king, who lives here. A whole community weeps about an atrocity two days' march away and goes on standing in the street.

The king of Israel is behind a plough. He has been anointed privately on a road at dawn and proclaimed with a shout at Mizpah, and he is coming in from a day's work on his father's land. He has no court, no palace, no standing army and apparently no intelligence service; the news has to be explained to him by somebody at the gate. Whatever Israel thought it was getting in chapter 8, what it has at this moment is a very tall farmer walking home behind his oxen.

Then the sentence that changes the afternoon. The Spirit of God rushed upon Saul: the same verb as for Samson and in chapter 10, a sudden seizing. And immediately, his anger was greatly kindled. A man heard that a town of his countrymen was about to have its eyes cut out to shame the nation, and something took hold of him and he was furious. Anger has a poor reputation, and this instance is entirely good.

He butchers his own plough team. Those are the oxen he was walking behind ten minutes ago, a farmer's most valuable possession and next year's ploughing. He gives up his own livelihood before asking anybody else for anything.

Any Israelite would have known where the gesture came from. At the end of Judges a Levite cut up the body of his concubine and sent the pieces throughout all the territory of Israel (Judg. 19:29). It was the recognised summons to national action, and the result was a civil war that nearly destroyed Benjamin. Saul uses the identical summons, with oxen instead of a woman, to save a town instead of destroying a tribe. A Benjaminite is redeeming the gesture that once destroyed Benjamin.

The phrase at the end comes from the same passage, where the congregation assembled as one man (Judg. 20:1) to make war on its own people. Here they come out as one man to rescue. And the credit for the muster is given plainly: the dread of the LORD fell upon the people. It was not Saul's authority, and not the horror of the parcels. God moved on the country.

verseByVerse.quote: When he mustered them at Bezek, the people of Israel were three hundred thousand, and the men of Judah thirty thousand. And they said to the messengers who had come, "Thus shall you say to the men of Jabesh-gilead: 'Tomorrow, by the time the sun is hot, you shall have salvation.'" When the messengers came and told the men of Jabesh, they were glad. Therefore the men of Jabesh said, "Tomorrow we will give ourselves up to you, and you may do to us whatever seems good to you." And the next day Saul put the people in three companies. And they came into the midst of the camp in the morning watch and struck down the Ammonites until the heat of the day. And those who survived were scattered, so that no two of them were left together.
verseByVerse.commentary:
That is three hundred and thirty thousand men, from a nation whose king's own town had just stood in the street and wept. Israel and Judah are counted separately because Judah was the largest tribe and often stood apart, which is how they will still be counted in Kings and a crack that will one day become a border. The 330,000 may be literal, or “thousand” may mean a military unit.

Bezek is the mustering ground, west of the Jordan opposite Jabesh. The message to Jabesh is short and has a deadline in it. It does not say “help is coming”, which is what frightened people are usually told; it says that by the time the sun is hot tomorrow, it will be over. He names the hour, and he will keep it.

The men of Jabesh play their part with some nerve. Knowing the relief column is coming at dawn, they tell Nahash they will give themselves up tomorrow, which keeps the Ammonites in camp and off guard on the last night they have. It was a stratagem of war against an enemy who meant to gouge out their eyes (v. 2), not the kind of lying Scripture condemns among neighbours.

Three companies and the morning watch are Gideon's plan: he divided the 300 men into three companies and came to the camp at the beginning of the middle watch (Judg. 7:16, 19). Saul fights his first battle out of the book the reader has just finished. The promise is kept to the hour: they fight until the heat of the day. The last clause is a small masterpiece of reporting. The survivors are scattered so that no two of them were left together: the Ammonite force has ceased to exist as an army, and its men are running singly across country with nobody beside them. It is more than a retreat or a rout.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–15 — Not a Man Shall Be Put to Death This Day
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The people demand the death of the men who had despised Saul (v. 12); he refuses, giving God the credit (v. 13). At Gilgal they renew the kingdom with peace offerings and great rejoicing (vv. 14-15).
verseByVerse.theology: This is the high point of Saul's life, and the chapter should be allowed to say so. He is magnanimous on the day he could most easily have settled scores, and he gives God the credit in the same breath.
verseByVerse.examples: The decline begins two chapters later at this same Gilgal, where he will not wait seven days.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the people said to Samuel, "Who is it that said, 'Shall Saul reign over us?' Bring the men, that we may put them to death." But Saul said, "Not a man shall be put to death this day, for today the LORD has worked salvation in Israel." Then Samuel said to the people, "Come, let us go to Gilgal and there renew the kingdom." So all the people went to Gilgal, and there they made Saul king before the LORD in Gilgal. There they sacrificed peace offerings before the LORD, and there Saul and all the men of Israel rejoiced greatly.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The victory is barely over and the people want a purge. They mean the worthless fellows of 10:27, who asked how can this man save us? The question has been answered in front of the whole country, and the crowd wants the men who asked it killed. It is the people who demand this, not Saul. The mob is ahead of the king.

Saul is at the height of his power, the nation is demanding blood, and the men had publicly humiliated him. Every incentive runs one way, and he refuses at once.

The reason is what makes the mercy possible: for today the LORD has worked salvation in Israel. He does not say “I have won and can afford to be generous.” He says God did this, and a man who believes the day was God's work does not treat it as capital to spend on his own grievances.

Gilgal is where the twelve stones came out of the Jordan and the reproach of Egypt was rolled away. They go there to renew the kingdom, confirming what Mizpah began now that the doubters have their answer, and they eat peace offerings in company with their king. That is the last sentence of Saul's good days, and it deserves a stop. He began humble, hid from his own coronation, held his peace when insulted, and then rose to this. Two chapters from now he will stand at this same Gilgal, watching his army drain away, and on the seventh day offer the burnt offering himself. The prophet will arrive as he finishes and tell him his kingdom will not continue. Everything after this chapter is decline, and nobody at the peace offerings could have known it.

11.theology:
Anger produced by the Spirit (v. 6). The two halves of the verse belong together: the Spirit rushed on him and his anger was greatly kindled. The anger is not the opposite of the Spirit here; it is what the Spirit produced. There is a way of being calm about atrocity that is not godliness but distance. All Gibeah was weeping and none of them was angry; one man was angry and the town was saved. This is no licence for temper: the anger is for others, not for his own pride, and it goes straight into rescue.

The gesture redeemed (v. 7). The summons that once launched a war against Benjamin now, in a Benjaminite's hands, raises an army to save a town; and even so the muster is credited to God, not to the summons.

Mercy and credit come together (v. 13). The reason Saul gives for sparing his critics is the reason he can spare them. People who take credit for what God has done are usually the same people who cannot let an insult go, because if the victory is yours then so is the honour, and the honour has been damaged.

Saul was once this. The Spirit rushed on him; he was angry at the right thing when everyone else only wept; he gave up his own property to raise an army; he kept his word to the hour; he gave God the public credit; and he spared the men who insulted him. There is no reading of this chapter in which he is not admirable. The tragedy of Saul is not that he was always what he became, but that he was once this, and that makes the rest of the book harder rather than easier.

The Spirit-anointed deliverer. Saul at his best is a sketch of what Israel needed: a king on whom the Spirit comes, who is moved by his people's misery, who saves them from an enemy they could not resist, and who spares those who despised him. The sketch does not hold; within two chapters he is failing. But the prophets went on promising a King on whom the Spirit would rest and remain (Isaiah 11:1-2; 61:1), and Jesus read the second of those passages in the synagogue at Nazareth and said it was fulfilled (Luke 4:18-21). On the day of his own victory, at the cross, he did not demand the death of those who mocked him as unable to save; he prayed for them (Luke 23:34).
11.examples:
Then: The man who did something about Jabesh came in late from ploughing and had to ask what the noise was, and when it was over he refused to let anybody settle scores on the strength of his victory.

Now: Two things. In a culture that treats composure as maturity, the Spirit's arrival in this chapter produced fury, and the weeping crowd was not more spiritual than the angry farmer. Ask what you have grown calm about that ought still to make you angry, and remember that the same Spirit who seized Saul now lives in every believer, not to inflame our pride but to move us toward the people who need rescue. And verse 13 gives the test for whether you believe a success was God's: not what you say in the thanksgiving, but whether you then spend it on your own grievances. The King who prayed for his mockers has already forgiven us far more than any insult we carry.

12.title: Samuel's Farewell Charge
12.text: <sup>1</sup>And Samuel said to all Israel, "Behold, I have obeyed your voice in all that you have said to me and have made a king over you.<sup>2</sup>And now, behold, the king walks before you, and I am old and gray; and behold, my sons are with you. I have walked before you from my youth until this day.<sup>3</sup>Here I am; testify against me before the LORD and before his anointed. Whose ox have I taken? Or whose donkey have I taken? Or whom have I defrauded? Whom have I oppressed? Or from whose hand have I taken a bribe to blind my eyes with it? Testify against me and I will restore it to you."<sup>4</sup>They said, "You have not defrauded us or oppressed us or taken anything from any man's hand."<sup>5</sup>And he said to them, "The LORD is witness against you, and his anointed is witness this day, that you have not found anything in my hand." And they said, "He is witness."<sup>6</sup>And Samuel said to the people, "The LORD is witness, who appointed Moses and Aaron and brought your fathers up out of the land of Egypt.<sup>7</sup>Now therefore stand still that I may plead with you before the LORD concerning all the righteous deeds of the LORD that he performed for you and for your fathers.<sup>8</sup>When Jacob went into Egypt, and the Egyptians oppressed them, then your fathers cried out to the LORD and the LORD sent Moses and Aaron, who brought your fathers out of Egypt and made them dwell in this place.<sup>9</sup>But they forgot the LORD their God. And he sold them into the hand of Sisera, commander of the army of Hazor, and into the hand of the Philistines, and into the hand of the king of Moab. And they fought against them.<sup>10</sup>And they cried out to the LORD and said, 'We have sinned, because we have forsaken the LORD and have served the Baals and the Ashtaroth. But now deliver us out of the hand of our enemies, that we may serve you.'<sup>11</sup>And the LORD sent Jerubbaal and Barak and Jephthah and Samuel and delivered you out of the hand of your enemies on every side, and you lived in safety.<sup>12</sup>And when you saw that Nahash the king of the Ammonites came against you, you said to me, 'No, but a king shall reign over us,' when the LORD your God was your king.<sup>13</sup>And now behold the king whom you have chosen, for whom you have asked; behold, the LORD has set a king over you.<sup>14</sup>If you will fear the LORD and serve him and obey his voice and not rebel against the commandment of the LORD, and if both you and the king who reigns over you will follow the LORD your God, it will be well.<sup>15</sup>But if you will not obey the voice of the LORD, but rebel against the commandment of the LORD, then the hand of the LORD will be against you and your king.<sup>16</sup>Now therefore stand still and see this great thing that the LORD will do before your eyes.<sup>17</sup>Is it not wheat harvest today? I will call upon the LORD, that he may send thunder and rain. And you shall know and see that your wickedness is great, which you have done in the sight of the LORD, in asking for yourselves a king."<sup>18</sup>So Samuel called upon the LORD, and the LORD sent thunder and rain that day, and all the people greatly feared the LORD and Samuel.<sup>19</sup>And all the people said to Samuel, "Pray for your servants to the LORD your God, that we may not die, for we have added to all our sins this evil, to ask for ourselves a king."<sup>20</sup>And Samuel said to the people, "Do not be afraid; you have done all this evil. Yet do not turn aside from following the LORD, but serve the LORD with all your heart.<sup>21</sup>And do not turn aside after empty things that cannot profit or deliver, for they are empty.<sup>22</sup>For the LORD will not forsake his people, for his great name's sake, because it has pleased the LORD to make you a people for himself.<sup>23</sup>Moreover, as for me, far be it from me that I should sin against the LORD by ceasing to pray for you, and I will instruct you in the good and the right way.<sup>24</sup>Only fear the LORD and serve him faithfully with all your heart. For consider what great things he has done for you.<sup>25</sup>But if you still do wickedly, you shall be swept away, both you and your king."
12.overview:
Samuel steps back from public leadership, and he does it by submitting to an audit: he invites the nation to name one thing he ever took from them, and they cannot. Then he pleads God's case from Israel's history, charges them with asking for a king when the LORD was already their king, and sets out the terms for the future. Those terms are the covenant of Sinai, unchanged, except that the king now stands inside them with everyone else.

Thunder and rain on the wheat harvest confirm his words. When the frightened people beg him to pray, he answers with two things that most of us cannot hold together, do not be afraid and you have done all this evil, and promises never to stop praying for the people who replaced him.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — Whose Ox Have I Taken?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Samuel reports that he has done what they asked and made them a king (v. 1). He is old and grey, his sons are among them, and he has walked before them since his youth (v. 2). Then he submits to a public audit and offers restitution for anything they can name (v. 3). They acquit him, and he calls the LORD and his anointed as witnesses (vv. 4-5).
verseByVerse.theology: A farewell can be a speech of self-defence or a speech of self-praise. Samuel's is neither: it is an open invitation to anyone he ever wronged to come forward.
verseByVerse.examples: The audit has a shadow over it. His sons, whose bribe-taking gave the elders their occasion in chapter 8, are standing in the crowd, and he says so.

verseByVerse.quote: And Samuel said to all Israel, "Behold, I have obeyed your voice in all that you have said to me and have made a king over you. And now, behold, the king walks before you, and I am old and gray; and behold, my sons are with you. I have walked before you from my youth until this day. Here I am; testify against me before the LORD and before his anointed. Whose ox have I taken? Or whose donkey have I taken? Or whom have I defrauded? Whom have I oppressed? Or from whose hand have I taken a bribe to blind my eyes with it? Testify against me and I will restore it to you." They said, "You have not defrauded us or oppressed us or taken anything from any man's hand." And he said to them, "The LORD is witness against you, and his anointed is witness this day, that you have not found anything in my hand." And they said, "He is witness."
verseByVerse.commentary:
He begins by stating that he did what he was asked, and the phrase he chooses is God's. Three times in chapter 8 God told him obey their voice (8:7, 9, 22), and Samuel reports back in exactly those words. He is not claiming to have approved; he is stating that the instruction was carried out.

Three beholds, and the third is painful. The king walks before you; I am old and grey; and behold, my sons are with you. These are the men whose corruption gave the elders their occasion in chapter 8: they turned aside after gain. They took bribes and perverted justice (8:3). Samuel does not defend them, explain them or leave them out. He says they are here.

Now listen to the verb. When Samuel warned them what a king would do, the speech was built on one word used six times in seven verses: he will take your sons, your daughters, your fields, your grain, your servants, your flocks (8:11-17). Here he applies it to himself, as a question. The man who has led Israel for a lifetime invites the nation to name one thing he ever took from them, and the king they have just been given will take, as a matter of policy, from everybody.

The two animals matter too. An ox and a donkey are the working stock of a small farm, the plough team and the transport. He does not ask whether he has taken anybody's silver; he asks about the things whose loss would actually ruin somebody. And he submits to the audit before two named witnesses, God and the king, with an offer of restitution. That is not a defence; it is an invitation to prosecute.

They acquit him, unanimously. He has judged this nation on circuit for a working lifetime, at Bethel and Gilgal and Mizpah and Ramah, and standing in front of everyone he ever ruled against he asks for a single complaint, and there is not one. He has it formally attested, which is a lawyer's instinct and a wise one: you have not found anything in my hand. Samuel plainly wanted it on the record precisely because his sons had made the family name a byword.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–15 — The LORD Your God Was Your King
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Samuel pleads the case, and the case is a history: Egypt and Moses and Aaron; forgetting and being sold; crying out and confessing, and the LORD sending Jerubbaal, Barak, Jephthah and Samuel (vv. 6-11). Then the charge: when Nahash came they asked for a king, when the LORD your God was your king (v. 12). And the terms: if you and the king fear the LORD, it will be well; if you rebel, his hand will be against you and your king (vv. 13-15).
verseByVerse.theology: The cycle he recites is the book of Judges in six verses, and its engine is a cry that was always answered. Verse 12 says what broke it: this time they did not cry, they asked for somebody else.
verseByVerse.examples: Watch for the king in verses 14-15. He is named in the promise and named again in the threat.

verseByVerse.quote: And Samuel said to the people, "The LORD is witness, who appointed Moses and Aaron and brought your fathers up out of the land of Egypt. Now therefore stand still that I may plead with you before the LORD concerning all the righteous deeds of the LORD that he performed for you and for your fathers. When Jacob went into Egypt, and the Egyptians oppressed them, then your fathers cried out to the LORD and the LORD sent Moses and Aaron, who brought your fathers out of Egypt and made them dwell in this place. But they forgot the LORD their God. And he sold them into the hand of Sisera, commander of the army of Hazor, and into the hand of the Philistines, and into the hand of the king of Moab. And they fought against them. And they cried out to the LORD and said, 'We have sinned, because we have forsaken the LORD and have served the Baals and the Ashtaroth. But now deliver us out of the hand of our enemies, that we may serve you.' And the LORD sent Jerubbaal and Barak and Jephthah and Samuel and delivered you out of the hand of your enemies on every side, and you lived in safety.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The word is a legal one. He is going to plead with them, and the evidence in this trial is all the righteous deeds of the LORD. Israel is in the dock.

The pattern is stated once, cleanly: oppression, a cry, a man sent, deliverance. Then the same pattern in reverse, with the verb Judges used constantly: they forgot. Israel did not formally reject or renounce God; they mislaid him. The three hands he names are three of that book's oppressors, Sisera at the Kishon, the Philistines, Eglon of Moab, and he sold them is Judges' own word (Judg. 2:14; 3:8; 4:2; 10:7). The cry that follows has the confession in it, which is what Judges 10 finally produced after earlier cries with none recorded.

Readers of the King James Version or the New King James Version will find Bedan where the ESV has Barak. Bedan is the Hebrew reading, but no judge of that name appears in the book of Judges, so the ESV follows the Greek Old Testament and the Syriac, which read Barak; some Greek manuscripts also read Samson for Samuel. The point of the list is untouched: every time they cried, God sent somebody.

Jerubbaal is Gideon, called by the nickname he was given after he pulled down his father's altar, let Baal contend (Judg. 6:32). Barak won at the Kishon, and Jephthah came from Gilead. The fourth name is Samuel, who is standing in front of them saying it. He includes himself without embarrassment, and he is entitled to: the last deliverance was at Mizpah under his prayers and God's thunder, and the men listening were there.

The point of the recital is in the last clause. You lived in safety. The system they have just replaced worked. Every time they cried, somebody came.

verseByVerse.quote: And when you saw that Nahash the king of the Ammonites came against you, you said to me, 'No, but a king shall reign over us,' when the LORD your God was your king. And now behold the king whom you have chosen, for whom you have asked; behold, the LORD has set a king over you. If you will fear the LORD and serve him and obey his voice and not rebel against the commandment of the LORD, and if both you and the king who reigns over you will follow the LORD your God, it will be well. But if you will not obey the voice of the LORD, but rebel against the commandment of the LORD, then the hand of the LORD will be against you and your king.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Here is the charge, and it comes with a date attached: the demand was made when you saw that Nahash... came against you. It was not a considered constitutional reform; it was a reaction to a threat on the border. They looked east, saw an Ammonite army, and asked for a man. Chapter 8 gives Samuel’s age and his sons’ corruption as the reason for the request; here Samuel adds the threat from Nahash, which was the fear behind it. Both were true.

The closing clause is the whole indictment: when the LORD your God was your king. That office was not vacant, and it is what makes the request what God called it in 8:7. They did not choose a king instead of anarchy; they chose one instead of him. And there is an irony Samuel does not spell out: when Nahash actually came, what saved Jabesh-gilead was not the institution of monarchy but the Spirit of God rushing on a farmer who was still behind his oxen.

Both halves of the next sentence are true and are held together without any attempt to resolve them. The king whom you have chosen: this was your doing. And the LORD has set a king over you: it was his.

Now the terms, which are the theological centre of the chapter. What has changed in the covenant? Nothing. Fear the LORD, serve him, obey his voice, do not rebel: the conditions of Sinai and of Deuteronomy, unaltered, and given to a people the LORD had already brought out of Egypt and saved again and again. The only new element is both you and the king who reigns over you. The king does not stand outside the arrangement administering it. He stands inside it, under the same terms as the farmers, named in the promise and named again in the threat.

Israel wanted a king so that things would be different: somebody to fight their battles, an arrangement like the nations had. Samuel tells them, on the day of the inauguration, that the arrangement changes nothing. If the nation rebels, the king goes down with them.

There was never a mechanism to be had. A mechanism is what Israel had been shopping for since chapter 4, when they sent for the ark; it is what Micah wanted when he hired a Levite; and it is what the elders wanted when they asked for a crown: something in place of a relationship. Every time, God gives them the thing and tells them plainly that it will not do what they want it to do.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–19 — Thunder in the Wheat Harvest
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Samuel calls them to stand and see a great thing: on the day of wheat harvest he will call on the LORD for thunder and rain, so that they will know their wickedness in asking for a king (vv. 16-17). It comes, the people greatly fear the LORD and Samuel (v. 18), and they beg him to pray for them, confessing that they have added this evil to all their sins (v. 19).
verseByVerse.theology: Samuel deliberately chooses a sign that will cost the nation something, and the cost is part of the message.
verseByVerse.examples: It is the third thunder in the book. Hannah sang that God would thunder against his adversaries when there was no war and nobody listening (2:10); he did it at Mizpah while Samuel was still at the altar (7:10); and here Samuel asks for it against Israel.

verseByVerse.quote: Now therefore stand still and see this great thing that the LORD will do before your eyes. Is it not wheat harvest today? I will call upon the LORD, that he may send thunder and rain. And you shall know and see that your wickedness is great, which you have done in the sight of the LORD, in asking for yourselves a king." So Samuel called upon the LORD, and the LORD sent thunder and rain that day, and all the people greatly feared the LORD and Samuel. And all the people said to Samuel, "Pray for your servants to the LORD your God, that we may not die, for we have added to all our sins this evil, to ask for ourselves a king."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The question is it not wheat harvest today? is not conversational. It is the sign. Everybody plans the year around rain not coming at wheat harvest, because rain on cut grain spoils it and rain on standing grain flattens it. He asks for a storm on the harvest so that the nation will understand what it has done, and the telling will be written across the crop. The sign is not free. It will damage the year's food, and it is chosen for exactly that reason: a sign that costs nothing proves nothing.

It works. They ask for prayer and they name the offence: we have added to all our sins this evil. They are not pretending it was their only fault, or that they were misled. They place it on top of a pile they acknowledge is already there.

And they ask the man they have just replaced to intercede for them, calling the LORD your God while doing it, which is frightened, and honest, and exactly wrong. Samuel is about to correct it: in verse 24 he will call the LORD theirs again.
verseByVerse.note: Compare Proverbs 26:1, where rain in harvest is a byword for something out of place.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 20–25 — Far Be It From Me That I Should Cease to Pray
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Samuel tells the people not to be afraid, though they have done all this evil, and not to turn aside from the LORD after empty things (vv. 20-21). Their security is God's own name and pleasure (v. 22). He will not sin by ceasing to pray for them (v. 23). He ends with a call to fear the LORD and a warning that persistent wickedness will sweep away both them and their king (vv. 24-25).
verseByVerse.theology: Comfort and honesty about sin are given together here, and neither is softened to make room for the other.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 23 is the sentence to take out of the chapter, and the people it is about are the ones who have just replaced him.

verseByVerse.quote: And Samuel said to the people, "Do not be afraid; you have done all this evil. Yet do not turn aside from following the LORD, but serve the LORD with all your heart. And do not turn aside after empty things that cannot profit or deliver, for they are empty. For the LORD will not forsake his people, for his great name's sake, because it has pleased the LORD to make you a people for himself. Moreover, as for me, far be it from me that I should sin against the LORD by ceasing to pray for you, and I will instruct you in the good and the right way. Only fear the LORD and serve him faithfully with all your heart. For consider what great things he has done for you. But if you still do wickedly, you shall be swept away, both you and your king."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everything pastoral in this chapter is in the opening sentence. Do not be afraid. And in the same breath, you have done all this evil.

The sin is not denied in order to comfort them. That is the cheap way, and the common one: tell frightened people it was not as bad as they think, that they were only doing their best. Samuel says none of it. Nor will he let the evil drive them away; he does not use their terror to extract anything, or leave them in it a while for their own good. You did it, and do not be afraid.

The instruction that follows is the one nobody expects: keep going. The danger for a person who has just discovered the size of his sin is not usually that he will take it lightly. It is that he will conclude he has forfeited the right to serve, and quietly withdraw. Samuel heads it off: do not turn aside; serve the LORD with all your heart, starting now, as the people who did this.

The empty things are tohu: formlessness, waste, the word for the earth before God spoke in Genesis 1:2. No argument is offered against them. The reason not to follow them is simply what they are.

Now the ground of the whole thing. The LORD will not forsake his people, and neither reason given is Israel. For his great name's sake: his own reputation is bound up with them. And because it has pleased the LORD to make you a people for himself: because he wanted to. That is the entire security of Israel, stated on the day they have been told their latest decision was wicked. It does not rest on their record, which is a disgrace, or on their promises, which they have broken continuously since Sinai, but on his name and his pleasure. The command to serve comes after it and rests on it.

Then the sentence to carry out of this chapter. This is the man they told to his face he was too old and his sons were no good, publicly superseded, with every human reason to withdraw and several respectable ones. He says that not praying for them would be a sin against the LORD: not a failure of duty or a thing beneath him, but a sin, and against God rather than against them. And with it the second half of his job: I will instruct you in the good and the right way. Prayer and teaching, both continued, for the people who replaced him.

Most of us have never put prayerlessness in that category. We think of intercession as something offered when we have the energy and the affection for it, and its absence as a shortfall. Samuel treats the people who have hurt him as a charge laid on him by God, so that to stop praying would be to disobey.

The motive he leaves them with is not fear of the storm but memory: consider what great things he has done for you. It is the argument of the stone at Ebenezer, and of the recital of the judges earlier in this chapter. Look at what he has done, and serve accordingly.

The last words are a warning with the king in them again, for the third time: you and your king (vv. 14, 15, 25). Israel asked for something that would change the terms, and Samuel ends his public ministry by telling them that nothing has changed at all.

12.theology:
The verb turned on himself (v. 3). The king Israel asked for will take (8:11-17); the prophet they set aside asks whose ox have I taken? The contrast is the whole argument of chapter 8 in one question, and the people's own verdict confirms it.

The office was not vacant (v. 12). They did not choose a king instead of anarchy; they chose one when the LORD your God was your king, and they chose him out of fear of a border raid.

Nothing has changed (vv. 14-15, 25). The covenant terms are Sinai's, unaltered, with the king inserted inside them, named in the promise and in the threat, three times over. A crown cannot replace a relationship, any more than the ark could.

Do not be afraid; you have done all this evil (v. 20). He refuses the cheap comfort of denying the sin, and refuses to let the sin drive them off, and then tells them to keep serving. The danger for someone who has just seen the size of his sin is rarely that he will take it lightly; it is that he will conclude he has forfeited the right to serve and quietly withdraw.

His name and his pleasure (v. 22). The security of Israel is stated on the day they are told their latest decision was wicked, and neither reason is Israel. For his great name's sake, and because it has pleased the LORD to make you a people for himself. Paul reaches for the same ground: the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable (Rom. 11:29). To the anxious believer who has worked out that God has every reason to be finished with him: he does have every reason, and he has given two of his own, and they are not about you.

Prayerlessness as sin (v. 23). Samuel puts the failure to pray for others, even for those who have hurt us, among the things that are sins against God, not merely shortfalls in our kindness.

The Intercessor who does not stop. Samuel stands between a guilty people and the storm, and promises never to cease praying for those who rejected him; Scripture names him with Moses as one of Israel's great intercessors (Jeremiah 15:1; Psalm 99:6). But Samuel is old, and he will die. The New Testament names the Intercessor who will not: Christ always lives to make intercession for those who draw near to God through him (Hebrews 7:25), and he prayed for the people who were crucifying him. And verses 14 and 15, with the king standing under the covenant like everyone else, wait for a King who would keep its terms. Israel's kings failed them one after another. Jesus, the Son of David, kept those terms in full and bore the covenant's curse for those who had not.
12.examples:
Then: An old man stood in front of everyone he had ever ruled against and was acquitted unanimously. Then he called down a storm on their harvest to tell them their new king was a sin, and promised to go on praying for them.

Now: Three things. Verse 3 is a standard for anyone in any kind of trust: could you invite the people you have led to name one thing you took? Verse 20 is the model for how to speak to somebody who has just realised what they have done: both halves, neither softened, and then “keep serving”. And verse 23 is the sharpest. Think of the person who has most recently passed you over, replaced you, or made it clear they would rather have somebody else. Samuel calls ceasing to pray for such people a sin against God, and he is not exaggerating for effect.

None of us has kept these terms: not the audit of verse 3, not the prayer of verse 23, not the fear and wholehearted service of verse 24. The ground Samuel gave is still the ground: the LORD has made us his own for his name's sake, and Christ, the King who kept the covenant in full, obeyed in our place and still intercedes for us. So the way back is the one this chapter shows, confession and mercy, and then not turning aside but serving again, by the Spirit he has given to those who are his.

13.title: Saul's Presumptuous Sacrifice
13.text: <sup>1</sup>Saul lived for one year and then became king, and when he had reigned for two years over Israel,<sup>2</sup>Saul chose three thousand men of Israel. Two thousand were with Saul in Michmash and the hill country of Bethel, and a thousand were with Jonathan in Gibeah of Benjamin. The rest of the people he sent home, every man to his tent.<sup>3</sup>Jonathan defeated the garrison of the Philistines that was at Geba, and the Philistines heard of it. And Saul blew the trumpet throughout all the land, saying, "Let the Hebrews hear."<sup>4</sup>And all Israel heard it said that Saul had defeated the garrison of the Philistines, and also that Israel had become a stench to the Philistines. And the people were called out to join Saul at Gilgal.<sup>5</sup>And the Philistines mustered to fight with Israel, thirty thousand chariots and six thousand horsemen and troops like the sand on the seashore in multitude. They came up and encamped in Michmash, to the east of Beth-aven.<sup>6</sup>When the men of Israel saw that they were in trouble (for the people were hard pressed), the people hid themselves in caves and in holes and in rocks and in tombs and in cisterns,<sup>7</sup>and some Hebrews crossed the fords of the Jordan to the land of Gad and Gilead. Saul was still at Gilgal, and all the people followed him trembling.<sup>8</sup>He waited seven days, the time appointed by Samuel. But Samuel did not come to Gilgal, and the people were scattering from him.<sup>9</sup>So Saul said, "Bring the burnt offering here to me, and the peace offerings." And he offered the burnt offering.<sup>10</sup>As soon as he had finished offering the burnt offering, behold, Samuel came. And Saul went out to meet him and greet him.<sup>11</sup>Samuel said, "What have you done?" And Saul said, "When I saw that the people were scattering from me, and that you did not come within the days appointed, and that the Philistines had mustered at Michmash,<sup>12</sup>I said, 'Now the Philistines will come down against me at Gilgal, and I have not sought the favor of the LORD.' So I forced myself, and offered the burnt offering."<sup>13</sup>And Samuel said to Saul, "You have done foolishly. You have not kept the command of the LORD your God, with which he commanded you. For then the LORD would have established your kingdom over Israel forever.<sup>14</sup>But now your kingdom shall not continue. The LORD has sought out a man after his own heart, and the LORD has commanded him to be prince over his people, because you have not kept what the LORD commanded you."<sup>15</sup>And Samuel arose and went up from Gilgal. The rest of the people went up after Saul to meet the army; they went up from Gilgal to Gibeah of Benjamin. And Saul numbered the people who were present with him, about six hundred men.<sup>16</sup>And Saul and Jonathan his son and the people who were present with them stayed in Geba of Benjamin, but the Philistines encamped in Michmash.<sup>17</sup>And raiders came out of the camp of the Philistines in three companies. One company turned toward Ophrah, to the land of Shual;<sup>18</sup>another company turned toward Beth-horon; and another company turned toward the border that looks down on the Valley of Zeboim toward the wilderness.<sup>19</sup>Now there was no blacksmith to be found throughout all the land of Israel, for the Philistines said, "Lest the Hebrews make themselves swords or spears."<sup>20</sup>But every one of the Israelites went down to the Philistines to sharpen his plowshare, his mattock, his axe, or his sickle,<sup>21</sup>and the charge was two-thirds of a shekel for the plowshares and for the mattocks, and a third of a shekel for sharpening the axes and for setting the goads.<sup>22</sup>So on the day of the battle there was neither sword nor spear found in the hand of any of the people with Saul and Jonathan, but Saul and Jonathan his son had them.<sup>23</sup>And the garrison of the Philistines went out to the pass of Michmash.
13.overview:
Israel has a standing army for the first time, and Jonathan enters the book with a command and no introduction. His raid on a Philistine garrison is announced as his father's victory, and Saul, who two chapters ago gave all the credit to God, lets it stand. The Philistines come up in force, and the nation that asked for a king to fight its battles goes into hiding on the first day a battle comes.

Saul is at Gilgal, where he was told on the day of his anointing to wait seven days for Samuel. He waits almost all of it, then offers the burnt offering himself as his army drains away, and Samuel arrives as he finishes. His reasons are all true, but one sentence in his defence gives him away. The kingdom is taken from his line, and the LORD has already sought out a man after his own heart, a boy in Bethlehem whom the reader will meet three chapters later. The chapter closes on an army with only two swords.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Saul keeps three thousand men and sends the rest home (vv. 1-2). Jonathan defeats the Philistine garrison at Geba, and the trumpet announces that Saul had defeated it (vv. 3-4). The Philistines muster in overwhelming force at Michmash (v. 5). Israel goes to ground, some cross the Jordan, and Saul is at Gilgal with the people following him trembling (vv. 6-7).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 4 is the first crack in Saul, and nobody in it tells a lie.
verseByVerse.examples: The narrator lists five hiding places in a single verse (v. 6), and he means the reader to count them.

verseByVerse.quote: Saul lived for one year and then became king, and when he had reigned for two years over Israel, Saul chose three thousand men of Israel. Two thousand were with Saul in Michmash and the hill country of Bethel, and a thousand were with Jonathan in Gibeah of Benjamin. The rest of the people he sent home, every man to his tent. Jonathan defeated the garrison of the Philistines that was at Geba, and the Philistines heard of it. And Saul blew the trumpet throughout all the land, saying, "Let the Hebrews hear." And all Israel heard it said that Saul had defeated the garrison of the Philistines, and also that Israel had become a stench to the Philistines. And the people were called out to join Saul at Gilgal.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The first verse of this chapter is damaged, and the honest thing is to say so once and move on.

The Hebrew reads, literally, “Saul was a son of a year when he began to reign, and he reigned two years over Israel.” That is the standard formula used for kings in Samuel and Kings, but a one-year-old king is impossible and Saul plainly reigned longer than two years, so the numbers seem to have been lost in copying. Translations handle the gap differently. The ESV and the King James Version render the Hebrew as best they can (“Saul lived for one year and then became king”; “Saul reigned one year”), and the ESV footnote notes that a few late Greek manuscripts give his age as thirty; the NIV supplies thirty years of age and forty-two years of reign. Paul gives the length of the reign as about forty years (Acts 13:21).

Nothing in the chapter depends on it. A lost number in one verse is exactly the kind of copying slip that the careful comparison of manuscripts exists to notice, and it has been noticed openly for centuries; the history the chapter tells is not in doubt.

For the first time Israel has a standing army: not a levy raised in a crisis and sent home, but soldiers kept under arms. There are two thousand under the king and a thousand under his son, and Jonathan enters the book here, with a command and no introduction.

Jonathan attacks and Saul announces it. Jonathan defeated the garrison; all Israel heard that Saul had. Saul blew the trumpet and the country drew the obvious conclusion from who was doing the announcing. The credit moved in the ordinary way credit moves, and the man it moved to did not correct it. Two chapters ago, with the crowd demanding blood, he refused to take anything for himself and said today the LORD has worked salvation in Israel. He is now taking his son's. The narrator gives it one clause. Most collapses begin at about this size.

And Israel had become a stench to the Philistines is not a victory report but a warning. Jonathan's raid has provoked the occupying power, and everybody knows what is coming.
verseByVerse.note: Geba and Michmash stood on opposite sides of a steep valley; the pass between them is the setting of chapter 14.

verseByVerse.quote: And the Philistines mustered to fight with Israel, thirty thousand chariots and six thousand horsemen and troops like the sand on the seashore in multitude. They came up and encamped in Michmash, to the east of Beth-aven. When the men of Israel saw that they were in trouble (for the people were hard pressed), the people hid themselves in caves and in holes and in rocks and in tombs and in cisterns, and some Hebrews crossed the fords of the Jordan to the land of Gad and Gilead. Saul was still at Gilgal, and all the people followed him trembling.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Chariots and horsemen are what Israel does not have and cannot answer, and like the sand on the seashore means uncountable. The chariot figure is very large and some Greek and Syriac manuscripts read three thousand, which fits the horsemen better. Either way a first-class army has arrived, and Israel has three thousand men and, as verse 22 will tell us, almost no weapons.

The writer takes his time over the hiding places. A cistern is a bell-shaped pit cut in rock for water, and a man who climbs into one cannot get out without help; a tomb is a hole full of the dead. These are not defensive positions. They are places to be not-found. This is the nation that asked for a king to go out before us and fight our battles, on the first day the battle comes. They have the king, and they are in the cisterns.

Those who cross the river are called Hebrews, the word foreigners use about Israel in this book, used here of men going over to sit out the war on the other side.

And the reader should hear the name Gilgal. This is where Samuel told Saul, on the morning he was anointed, to wait seven days until he came (10:8), and where the nation renewed the kingdom after Jabesh (11:14-15). He is in the right place, doing the right thing, with an army that is trembling.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Saul waits the seven days Samuel appointed, but Samuel does not come and the army drains away (v. 8). He offers the burnt offering himself, and as he finishes, Samuel arrives (vv. 9-10). Saul gives his reasons (vv. 11-12). Samuel's verdict is that he has not kept the LORD's command, his kingdom will not continue, and the LORD has sought out a man after his own heart (vv. 13-14).
verseByVerse.theology: This is what makes the chapter so uncomfortable: it is not defiance but obedience that failed in the last hour, with the enemy massed, the army melting, and every excuse available and true.
verseByVerse.examples: Notice how much rests on a single sentence spoken on a road three chapters earlier (10:8). Samuel treats it as God's own word.

verseByVerse.quote: He waited seven days, the time appointed by Samuel. But Samuel did not come to Gilgal, and the people were scattering from him. So Saul said, "Bring the burnt offering here to me, and the peace offerings." And he offered the burnt offering. As soon as he had finished offering the burnt offering, behold, Samuel came. And Saul went out to meet him and greet him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A great deal depends on the first four words. He waited seven days. This is not a man who ignored the instruction or decided it did not apply. He held his position for almost the whole appointed period with a first-class army massed at Michmash and his own force draining into the hills by the hour.

Try to feel the seventh day. The prophet has not come. The Philistines are a few hours' march off with chariots. Every hour another handful of men slips away; by verse 15 he will have six hundred left out of three thousand. He has done everything he was told and it has produced nothing but a smaller army. On the last day, he does it himself.

Be precise about the offence. It is not simply that a king performed a sacrifice; David and Solomon will offer sacrifices and neither is condemned for it (2 Sam. 6:17; 1 Kings 8:62-63). Saul had one specific standing order, wait at Gilgal seven days until I come, and on the seventh day he stopped waiting.

Then the most painful sentence in the chapter: as soon as he had finished. Samuel walks into Gilgal at the moment the fire is lit. He had always been coming, and Saul missed him by the length of a sacrifice. The writer adds nothing; he puts the two clauses side by side and lets the reader do the arithmetic.

verseByVerse.quote: Samuel said, "What have you done?" And Saul said, "When I saw that the people were scattering from me, and that you did not come within the days appointed, and that the Philistines had mustered at Michmash, I said, 'Now the Philistines will come down against me at Gilgal, and I have not sought the favor of the LORD.' So I forced myself, and offered the burnt offering." And Samuel said to Saul, "You have done foolishly. You have not kept the command of the LORD your God, with which he commanded you. For then the LORD would have established your kingdom over Israel forever. But now your kingdom shall not continue. The LORD has sought out a man after his own heart, and the LORD has commanded him to be prince over his people, because you have not kept what the LORD commanded you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Samuel's question is the one God asked in the garden and the angel asked at Bochim (Gen. 3:13; Judg. 2:2). It is never a request for information.

Here is the difficulty with this chapter: every one of Saul's three reasons is true. The people were scattering; the narrator said so in verse 8. Samuel had not come on the seventh day. The Philistines had mustered. Saul is not inventing excuses; he gives an accurate account of his situation, and any officer in that position would have given the same one.

Then the sentence that gives him away, and it is his own: so I forced myself. This was not a decision he was at peace with; he had to push himself over the edge into it, which means he knew. A man who believed the sacrifice was permitted would not have needed to force himself into it.
