Saul is telling the prophet, without meaning to, that his conscience was against him and he overrode it.

And the anxiety he names, I have not sought the favor of the LORD, is a real and pious concern, and exactly what the seven days were designed to provide: Samuel was coming to offer those sacrifices himself. He disobeyed a direct command to obtain the very thing obedience would have given him, one sacrifice-length before it arrived.

You have done foolishly is not about low intelligence; folly in these books is a moral category, the condition of a man who will not reckon with God. And the seven days are classified as the command of the LORD your God: not Samuel's scheduling, but God's word, given in a single sentence at the end of a private conversation on a road (10:8), and binding. The phrase also names the ground Saul forgot. The God who gave the order was his God, who had chosen him, anointed him and given him Jabesh; the order was given by one who had already shown him favour.

The cost is enormous: forever. A dynasty, of the kind that will be promised to David in 2 Samuel 7, was available to Saul, and it went in the time it took to burn one animal.

Readers reasonably feel the sentence is severe here, and it should be faced rather than softened. He waited six days and most of a seventh, under real pressure, with true reasons, in a crisis, and the kingdom is taken from his line for it.

Two things can be said, and neither of them makes it comfortable.

The first is that a king in Israel was under a text, and this was the test of it. Israel had asked for a king like the nations, and the whole difference between that king and theirs was that theirs took orders. The first specific order was wait. Everything about the office turned on whether he would.

The second is I forced myself. It was not a misunderstanding. The chapter records a man overriding his own conscience under pressure, and pressure is precisely the condition under which obedience actually counts for something. Waiting when Samuel had arrived on day two would have proved nothing.

Here, unnamed, is David, at this moment a boy in Bethlehem with sheep. Paul quotes the phrase in Pisidian Antioch: I have found in David the son of Jesse a man after my heart, who will do all my will (Acts 13:22). It is often heard as a compliment about David's feelings, but the contrast here is with a man who did not keep what he was commanded, and Paul's second half supplies the sense. The title is prince again, nagid, the word used of Saul on the road (9:16; 10:1). The office is not being abolished; it is being given to somebody else.

How can David be “a man after his own heart” when he committed adultery and murder? The phrase first means the man of God’s choosing, as opposed to the people’s; and David’s heart, for all his sins, turned back to God in repentance (Ps 51), where Saul made excuses. God does not choose sinless men; he chooses sinners and makes them his.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Samuel leaves, and Saul numbers what is left: about six hundred men (v. 15). Philistine raiders go out in three companies (vv. 17-18). The narrator then explains the strategic position: the Philistines had allowed no blacksmith in Israel, so every Israelite went down to them to have his tools sharpened, at a price, and on the day of battle only Saul and Jonathan had sword or spear (vv. 19-22).
verseByVerse.theology: Israel was not merely occupied; it was disarmed by an industrial policy, and paid the occupier to sharpen its own tools.
verseByVerse.examples: Hannah's song is about to be tested: not by might shall a man prevail (2:9). Chapter 14 opens with one of the two swordsmen walking off alone.

verseByVerse.quote: And Samuel arose and went up from Gilgal. The rest of the people went up after Saul to meet the army; they went up from Gilgal to Gibeah of Benjamin. And Saul numbered the people who were present with him, about six hundred men. And Saul and Jonathan his son and the people who were present with them stayed in Geba of Benjamin, but the Philistines encamped in Michmash. And raiders came out of the camp of the Philistines in three companies. One company turned toward Ophrah, to the land of Shual; another company turned toward Beth-horon; and another company turned toward the border that looks down on the Valley of Zeboim toward the wilderness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Samuel delivers the sentence and leaves: no discussion, no appeal, no comfort. The prophet who came to offer the sacrifices does not offer them.

Three thousand men at the start of the chapter; six hundred now. And six hundred is what remained of Benjamin after the civil war, the survivors on the rock of Rimmon (Judg. 20:47). Saul is a Benjaminite, standing in Gibeah, the town that war was fought over, with six hundred men.

The Philistines do not even bother to attack. They send raiders north to Ophrah, west to Beth-horon and east towards the wilderness, and strip the country while the king watches from Geba. Three companies is Gideon's number, and Saul's own at Jabesh (Judg. 7:16; 1 Sam. 11:11): the formation that won Israel's battles is being used by the enemy on Israel's farms.

verseByVerse.quote: Now there was no blacksmith to be found throughout all the land of Israel, for the Philistines said, "Lest the Hebrews make themselves swords or spears." But every one of the Israelites went down to the Philistines to sharpen his plowshare, his mattock, his axe, or his sickle, and the charge was two-thirds of a shekel for the plowshares and for the mattocks, and a third of a shekel for sharpening the axes and for setting the goads. So on the day of the battle there was neither sword nor spear found in the hand of any of the people with Saul and Jonathan, but Saul and Jonathan his son had them. And the garrison of the Philistines went out to the pass of Michmash.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the strategic situation, which the writer has held back. There is not one blacksmith in the country. The Philistines had a monopoly on ironworking and enforced it as policy, lest the Hebrews make swords or spears. You do not need to take a nation's weapons if you own the only forge.

They charged for it, and the narrator knows the prices: two thirds of a shekel for a ploughshare, a third for an axe. Every farmer walked down to a Philistine town once a season to have his own tools sharpened by the people occupying his country. It is a humiliation administered a hundred times a year in every village, and quiet enough that nobody would call it a war.

Six hundred men, and two swords between them, both in the royal family. Set that beside chapter 8: they wanted a king to fight their battles like all the nations, and the nations' armies were exactly what the Philistines have at Michmash, chariots, horsemen, iron and a professional smith. Here is the army the request produced.

The chapter ends with everything pointing one way: no dynasty, four fifths of the army gone, no weapons, and a garrison on the high ground. But Hannah sang, with nothing to go on, the bows of the mighty are broken, but the feeble bind on strength (2:4). The very next verse has one man and his armour-bearer walking towards that pass.
verseByVerse.note: The price in v. 21 is a pim. Stone weights inscribed with the word have been dug up, which settled the meaning of a term that had puzzled older translators.

13.theology:
The first crack (vv. 3-4). Credit moves in the ordinary way credit moves, and it is not corrected. Set it against 11:13, where at the height of his power Saul refused to take anything for himself. Few people fall in one great step; most begin by accepting something small that was not theirs.

The sin was not the sacrifice. Kings could offer sacrifices without blame (2 Sam. 6:17). Saul's sin was breaking one specific standing order with a number of days on it (10:8), which Samuel calls the command of the LORD your God.

He disobeyed to get what obedience was bringing. His stated anxiety was that he had not sought the LORD's favour, which is precisely what the seven days existed to supply. Samuel was on the road with those sacrifices, and Saul missed him by the length of one offering. And his own words, so I forced myself, show that his conscience was against him and he overrode it.

Why so severe? Two things, and neither makes it comfortable. A king in Israel was a king under a text, and the whole difference between him and the kings of the nations was that he took orders; the first specific order was wait, and everything about the office turned on it. And pressure is exactly the condition under which obedience counts for anything; waiting when the prophet arrived on day two would have proved nothing. A word to the tender conscience: the sentence here concerns a king's dynasty, and giving way under pressure is not the end for those who come back. Peter denied Christ three times under pressure, and Christ restored him (John 21:15-17).

The man after God's heart, and his Son. Paul does not stop at David. His very next sentence is: Of this man's offspring God has brought to Israel a Savior, Jesus, as he promised (Acts 13:23). Saul broke under pressure on the seventh day, and David, for all his heart, would fail too. The Son of David met a far heavier pressure in Gethsemane and did not force himself past the Father's word: not my will, but yours, be done (Luke 22:42). His is the obedience Saul's kingdom needed, and it is counted to everyone who trusts him.
13.examples:
Then: A king held his position for nearly seven days as ordered, watched four fifths of his army disappear while he did it, gave way in the last hour with every reason on his side, and the prophet walked into camp as the fire was still burning.

Now: Two things. The first is I forced myself, and it is the most useful diagnostic in the chapter. When a course of action requires you to override something in yourself before you can take it, that resistance is usually information rather than weakness, and Saul's own word for it convicted him faster than any of Samuel's. The second is the timing. He was one sacrifice short. There is no way to know, in the seventh hour of waiting, how close the answer is, which is exactly why the instruction had a number on it and not a condition. We will all fail at some seventh hour. When we do, Saul's excuses are not the way back; David's confession is, to the God whose Son waited perfectly in our place, and whose Spirit gives the patience to wait again.

14.title: Jonathan's Faith and Saul's Folly
14.text: <sup>1</sup>One day Jonathan the son of Saul said to the young man who carried his armor, "Come, let us go over to the Philistine garrison on the other side." But he did not tell his father.<sup>2</sup>Saul was staying in the outskirts of Gibeah in the pomegranate cave at Migron. The people who were with him were about six hundred men,<sup>3</sup>including Ahijah the son of Ahitub, Ichabod's brother, son of Phinehas, son of Eli, the priest of the LORD in Shiloh, wearing an ephod. And the people did not know that Jonathan had gone.<sup>4</sup>Within the passes, by which Jonathan sought to go over to the Philistine garrison, there was a rocky crag on the one side and a rocky crag on the other side. The name of the one was Bozez, and the name of the other Seneh.<sup>5</sup>The one crag rose on the north in front of Michmash, and the other on the south in front of Geba.<sup>6</sup>Jonathan said to the young man who carried his armor, "Come, let us go over to the garrison of these uncircumcised. It may be that the LORD will work for us, for nothing can hinder the LORD from saving by many or by few."<sup>7</sup>And his armor-bearer said to him, "Do all that is in your heart. Do as you wish. Behold, I am with you heart and soul."<sup>8</sup>Then Jonathan said, "Behold, we will cross over to the men, and we will show ourselves to them.<sup>9</sup>If they say to us, 'Wait until we come to you,' then we will stand still in our place, and we will not go up to them.<sup>10</sup>But if they say, 'Come up to us,' then we will go up, for the LORD has given them into our hand. And this shall be the sign to us."<sup>11</sup>So both of them showed themselves to the garrison of the Philistines. And the Philistines said, "Look, Hebrews are coming out of the holes where they have hidden themselves."<sup>12</sup>And the men of the garrison hailed Jonathan and his armor-bearer and said, "Come up to us, and we will show you a thing." And Jonathan said to his armor-bearer, "Come up after me, for the LORD has given them into the hand of Israel."<sup>13</sup>Then Jonathan climbed up on his hands and feet, and his armor-bearer after him. And they fell before Jonathan, and his armor-bearer killed them after him.<sup>14</sup>And that first strike, which Jonathan and his armor-bearer made, killed about twenty men within as it were half a furrow's length in an acre of land.<sup>15</sup>And there was a panic in the camp, in the field, and among all the people. The garrison and even the raiders trembled, the earth quaked, and it became a very great panic.<sup>16</sup>And the watchmen of Saul in Gibeah of Benjamin looked, and behold, the multitude was dispersing here and there.<sup>17</sup>Then Saul said to the people who were with him, "Count and see who has gone from us." And when they had counted, behold, Jonathan and his armor-bearer were not there.<sup>18</sup>So Saul said to Ahijah, "Bring the ark of God here." For the ark of God went at that time with the people of Israel.<sup>19</sup>Now while Saul was talking to the priest, the tumult in the camp of the Philistines increased more and more. So Saul said to the priest, "Withdraw your hand."<sup>20</sup>Then Saul and all the people who were with him rallied and went into the battle. And behold, every Philistine's sword was against his fellow, and there was very great confusion.<sup>21</sup>Now the Hebrews who had been with the Philistines before that time and who had gone up with them into the camp, even they also turned to be with the Israelites who were with Saul and Jonathan.<sup>22</sup>Likewise, when all the men of Israel who had hidden themselves in the hill country of Ephraim heard that the Philistines were fleeing, they too followed hard after them in the battle.<sup>23</sup>So the LORD saved Israel that day. And the battle passed beyond Beth-aven.<sup>24</sup>And the men of Israel had been hard pressed that day, so Saul had laid an oath on the people, saying, "Cursed be the man who eats food until it is evening and I am avenged on my enemies." So none of the people had tasted food.<sup>25</sup>Now when all the people came to the forest, behold, there was honey on the ground.<sup>26</sup>And when the people entered the forest, behold, the honey was dropping, but no one put his hand to his mouth, for the people feared the oath.<sup>27</sup>But Jonathan had not heard his father charge the people with the oath, so he put out the tip of the staff that was in his hand and dipped it in the honeycomb and put his hand to his mouth, and his eyes became bright.<sup>28</sup>Then one of the people said, "Your father strictly charged the people with an oath, saying, 'Cursed be the man who eats food this day.'" And the people were faint.<sup>29</sup>Then Jonathan said, "My father has troubled the land. See how my eyes have become bright because I tasted a little of this honey.<sup>30</sup>How much better if the people had eaten freely today of the spoil of their enemies that they found. For now the defeat among the Philistines has not been great."<sup>31</sup>They struck down the Philistines that day from Michmash to Aijalon. And the people were very faint.<sup>32</sup>The people pounced on the spoil and took sheep and oxen and calves and slaughtered them on the ground. And the people ate them with the blood.<sup>33</sup>Then they told Saul, "Behold, the people are sinning against the LORD by eating with the blood." And he said, "You have dealt treacherously; roll a great stone to me here."<sup>34</sup>And Saul said, "Disperse yourselves among the people and say to them, 'Let every man bring his ox or his sheep and slaughter them here and eat, and do not sin against the LORD by eating with the blood.'" So every one of the people brought his ox with him that night and they slaughtered them there.<sup>35</sup>And Saul built an altar to the LORD; it was the first altar that he built to the LORD.<sup>36</sup>Then Saul said, "Let us go down after the Philistines by night and plunder them until the morning light; let us not leave a man of them." And they said, "Do whatever seems good to you." But the priest said, "Let us draw near to God here."<sup>37</sup>And Saul inquired of God, "Shall I go down after the Philistines? Will you give them into the hand of Israel?" But he did not answer him that day.<sup>38</sup>And Saul said, "Come here, all you leaders of the people, and know and see how this sin has arisen today.<sup>39</sup>For as the LORD lives who saves Israel, though it be in Jonathan my son, he shall surely die." But there was not a man among all the people who answered him.<sup>40</sup>Then he said to all Israel, "You shall be on one side, and I and Jonathan my son will be on the other side." And the people said to Saul, "Do what seems good to you."<sup>41</sup>Therefore Saul said, "O LORD God of Israel, why have you not answered your servant this day? If this guilt is in me or in Jonathan my son, O LORD, God of Israel, give Urim. But if this guilt is in your people Israel, give Thummim." And Jonathan and Saul were taken, but the people escaped.<sup>42</sup>Then Saul said, "Cast the lot between me and my son Jonathan." And Jonathan was taken.<sup>43</sup>Then Saul said to Jonathan, "Tell me what you have done." And Jonathan told him, "I tasted a little honey with the tip of the staff that was in my hand. Here I am; I will die."<sup>44</sup>And Saul said, "God do so to me and more also; you shall surely die, Jonathan."<sup>45</sup>Then the people said to Saul, "Shall Jonathan die, who has worked this great salvation in Israel? Far from it! As the LORD lives, there shall not one hair of his head fall to the ground, for he has worked with God this day." So the people ransomed Jonathan, so that he did not die.<sup>46</sup>Then Saul went up from pursuing the Philistines, and the Philistines went to their own place.<sup>47</sup>When Saul had taken the kingship over Israel, he fought against all his enemies on every side, against Moab, against the Ammonites, against Edom, against the kings of Zobah, and against the Philistines. Wherever he turned he routed them.<sup>48</sup>And he did valiantly and struck the Amalekites and delivered Israel out of the hands of those who plundered them.<sup>49</sup>Now the sons of Saul were Jonathan, Ishvi, and Malchi-shua. And the names of his two daughters were these: the name of the firstborn was Merab, and the name of the younger Michal.<sup>50</sup>And the name of Saul's wife was Ahinoam the daughter of Ahimaaz. And the name of the commander of his army was Abner the son of Ner, Saul's uncle.<sup>51</sup>Kish was the father of Saul, and Ner the father of Abner was the son of Abiel.<sup>52</sup>There was hard fighting against the Philistines all the days of Saul. And when Saul saw any strong man, or any valiant man, he attached him to himself.
14.overview:
The chapter is built as a contrast, and every scene keeps it. Jonathan takes his armour-bearer and climbs into a pass towards a Philistine garrison, trusting that nothing can hinder the LORD from saving by many or by few. Two men break an army, and the narrator gives the victory to God.

Saul, meanwhile, sits on the edge of Gibeah, begins to consult God and breaks off when events start moving, and binds the army with a rash oath that starves it in the middle of a battle. By nightfall the oath has produced a national sin, God has gone silent, and the king has sworn to put his own son to death, until the army refuses and ransoms him. The chapter closes with a fair summary of Saul's reign: whatever his failings, he was a successful soldier.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — He Did Not Tell His Father
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jonathan sets out with his armour-bearer towards the Philistine garrison, but he did not tell his father (v. 1). Saul is staying on the edge of Gibeah with six hundred men and a priest wearing an ephod (vv. 2-3). The ground between is described: two rocky crags facing each other across a pass, named Bozez and Seneh (vv. 4-5).
verseByVerse.theology: Saul has the army, the priest and the ephod; Jonathan has one servant and a conviction about God. The chapter will show which matters.
verseByVerse.examples: Neither man knows what the other is doing, and that silence between father and son will matter before the day is out.

verseByVerse.quote: One day Jonathan the son of Saul said to the young man who carried his armor, "Come, let us go over to the Philistine garrison on the other side." But he did not tell his father. Saul was staying in the outskirts of Gibeah in the pomegranate cave at Migron. The people who were with him were about six hundred men, including Ahijah the son of Ahitub, Ichabod's brother, son of Phinehas, son of Eli, the priest of the LORD in Shiloh, wearing an ephod. And the people did not know that Jonathan had gone. Within the passes, by which Jonathan sought to go over to the Philistine garrison, there was a rocky crag on the one side and a rocky crag on the other side. The name of the one was Bozez, and the name of the other Seneh. The one crag rose on the north in front of Michmash, and the other on the south in front of Geba.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The last clause of verse 1 is the one the chapter will keep coming back to: he did not tell his father. Jonathan is nowhere criticised for it; it is simply a fact, and it tells us something about the household. The king's son is going out to do something that matters and does not think it worth mentioning to the king.

Older translations put Saul under a pomegranate tree; the ESV reads a pomegranate cave (the Hebrew word is Rimmon, “pomegranate”), and the words allow either. The detail is not flattering. Israel is occupied, raiders are stripping the country in three directions, and the king is sitting at the outskirts.

The priest's pedigree should stop the reader at Ichabod's brother. This is Eli's family: Phinehas who died the day the ark was taken, the son born as his mother named him the glory has departed, and now Phinehas's other son's son, standing beside Saul in an ephod. God's judgments are frequently slower than readers expect; the house sentenced in chapter 2 holds the priesthood a long time yet, until Saul destroys most of it at Nob and Solomon finishes it (22:18-19; 1 Kings 2:27).

The writer names the crags, which means people knew this place: two cliffs across a narrow pass, with a garrison on the far one. It is the hardest possible approach, a defended height reached by climbing a rock face in full view, and it is the route Jonathan has chosen.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–15 — By Many or by Few
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jonathan proposes the attack, trusting that God can save by many or by few (v. 6), and his armour-bearer commits himself wholeheartedly (v. 7). They agree a sign: if the garrison calls them up, God has given it over (vv. 8-10). The Philistines jeer and call them up (vv. 11-12). Jonathan climbs, about twenty men fall (vv. 13-14), and a panic spreads through the whole Philistine force (v. 15).
verseByVerse.theology: Faith is not solitary here. The armour-bearer commits himself to Jonathan as wholeheartedly as Jonathan commits himself to God.
verseByVerse.examples: The sign he chooses is the difficult option. If the garrison comes down, they stand still; if it calls them up, they climb a cliff into it. And he goes up on hands and feet, which means he arrives unable to hold a weapon.

verseByVerse.quote: Jonathan said to the young man who carried his armor, "Come, let us go over to the garrison of these uncircumcised. It may be that the LORD will work for us, for nothing can hinder the LORD from saving by many or by few." And his armor-bearer said to him, "Do all that is in your heart. Do as you wish. Behold, I am with you heart and soul." Then Jonathan said, "Behold, we will cross over to the men, and we will show ourselves to them. If they say to us, 'Wait until we come to you,' then we will stand still in our place, and we will not go up to them. But if they say, 'Come up to us,' then we will go up, for the LORD has given them into our hand. And this shall be the sign to us."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Here is the sentence the whole book has been building towards, spoken by a young man about to climb a cliff with one servant. Read it against the end of the last chapter: no blacksmith in Israel, two swords in the army, chariots and a garrison on the other side. Jonathan says the arithmetic is not the relevant category. Many or few is a distinction that matters to generals and does not constrain God at all. It is Hannah's line in prose: the bows of the mighty are broken, but the feeble bind on strength (2:4). She sang it with nothing to go on; her son's generation is about to see it in a pass.

The two words at the front are the making of the sentence: it may be. Jonathan has had no word from God, no prophet, no sign. He does not say the LORD will work for us; he says it may be that he will, for this is the kind of God he is. Certainty about the outcome is comfortable and usually unavailable. What Jonathan has is confidence about God's character and a willingness to act without knowing how it will go. That is a harder faith than certainty, and a better one, and it is what the three men in Babylon had when they said God was able to deliver them, but if not, be it known to you, O king, that we will not serve your gods (Dan. 3:17-18).

The armour-bearer is not named and gets one of the best lines in the book: literally, “behold, I am with you according to your heart”. He is not being told a plan; he is agreeing to a man, and he knows exactly what he is agreeing to, because he is going up the same cliff.

Mark which way round the test is set. If the garrison offers to come down to fight on level ground, they will stand still. If it tells them to come up, they will climb into a defended position under the eyes of the men holding it. He has arranged a test in which God's yes costs him considerably more than God's no.

verseByVerse.quote: So both of them showed themselves to the garrison of the Philistines. And the Philistines said, "Look, Hebrews are coming out of the holes where they have hidden themselves." And the men of the garrison hailed Jonathan and his armor-bearer and said, "Come up to us, and we will show you a thing." And Jonathan said to his armor-bearer, "Come up after me, for the LORD has given them into the hand of Israel." Then Jonathan climbed up on his hands and feet, and his armor-bearer after him. And they fell before Jonathan, and his armor-bearer killed them after him. And that first strike, which Jonathan and his armor-bearer made, killed about twenty men within as it were half a furrow's length in an acre of land. And there was a panic in the camp, in the field, and among all the people. The garrison and even the raiders trembled, the earth quaked, and it became a very great panic.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They stand up in the open and the enemy laughs at them, and the jeer about Hebrews coming out of their holes stings because it is true (13:6). Come up to us, and we will show you a thing is a taunt with a threat inside it, and it is the exact sentence Jonathan asked for. The sign arrives out of the mouths of men who are mocking and are also, without knowing it, telling him that God has handed them over.

He goes up on hands and feet. Climbing on all fours, a soldier cannot hold a weapon or a shield; he arrives winded, in front of a garrison that has watched him come the whole way. There is no worse way to enter a fight. They fall before him, and the armour-bearer, coming up behind, finishes them.

Half a furrow is a farmer's measurement, the length a plough team covers in a short run. This was not a battle; it was two men in a confined space at the top of a rock. Then the writer widens the frame: the camp, the field, all the people, the raiders of chapter 13, and the ground itself. The phrase at the end is, in Hebrew, “a panic of God”, a terror not accounted for by anything on the ground. Twenty men died at the top of a crag, and an army came apart. Nothing on the ground explains it; the writer means us to see whose work it was.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Saul's watchmen see the enemy dispersing, and Saul orders a roll call to find who is missing: Jonathan and his armour-bearer (vv. 16-17). He tells the priest to bring the ark, and then, as the tumult grows, withdraw your hand (vv. 18-19). Israel goes in, and finds every Philistine's sword against his fellow (v. 20). The Hebrews who had gone over to the Philistines change sides, and the men hiding in the hill country come out and join the pursuit (vv. 21-22). So the LORD saved Israel that day (v. 23).
verseByVerse.theology: Saul starts to enquire of God and cancels it mid-sentence because the situation is moving. It is the same instinct as Gilgal: the pressure of events overrules the consultation, and the consultation is the thing that was commanded.
verseByVerse.examples: The men who had hidden in the hills come out once the tide turns, and the narrator welcomes them rather than scorning them.

verseByVerse.quote: And the watchmen of Saul in Gibeah of Benjamin looked, and behold, the multitude was dispersing here and there. Then Saul said to the people who were with him, "Count and see who has gone from us." And when they had counted, behold, Jonathan and his armor-bearer were not there. So Saul said to Ahijah, "Bring the ark of God here." For the ark of God went at that time with the people of Israel. Now while Saul was talking to the priest, the tumult in the camp of the Philistines increased more and more. So Saul said to the priest, "Withdraw your hand." Then Saul and all the people who were with him rallied and went into the battle. And behold, every Philistine's sword was against his fellow, and there was very great confusion. Now the Hebrews who had been with the Philistines before that time and who had gone up with them into the camp, even they also turned to be with the Israelites who were with Saul and Jonathan. Likewise, when all the men of Israel who had hidden themselves in the hill country of Ephraim heard that the Philistines were fleeing, they too followed hard after them in the battle. So the LORD saved Israel that day. And the battle passed beyond Beth-aven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The first Saul knows of it is that the enemy army is falling to pieces in front of his watchmen, and his first action is a roll call. An enemy army is disintegrating on the hillside opposite and the king of Israel orders a head count. It is not unreasonable, since he wants to know what has happened, and it is a very long way from the Spirit of God rushed upon Saul.

He sends for the ark, or, on another reading of the text, for the ephod, which was the instrument for enquiring of God. Either way the intention is right: before committing, ask. Then he cancels it in the middle. The noise from the camp is increasing, and Saul decides there is no longer time to ask God anything. At Gilgal he waited almost seven days and gave way in the last hour because the army was scattering; here he begins to enquire and breaks off because the battle is starting. Twice the pressure of the moment has overruled the thing he was supposed to do, and both times he was very close. The consultation he drops is the very thing that was commanded.

They arrive to find the enemy killing each other. It is Gideon's valley again: the LORD set every man's sword against his comrade (Judg. 7:22). Israel's part in both battles is to turn up after God has done it.

The Israelites serving in the Philistine army, conscripts or men who had made an arrangement, turn with the tide, and the men from the holes and cisterns of 13:6 come out and join the chase. They hear the enemy is running and they come out. It would be easy to be sour about that, and the writer is not. They came out. The nation that was hiding in the ground at the start of the chapter is pursuing a beaten army by the end of it, and it began with one man saying it may be.

And the verdict names nobody: not Jonathan, not the armour-bearer, not Saul or the six hundred or the returning deserters. The LORD saved Israel that day.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 24–35 — Cursed Be the Man Who Eats
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Saul had put the army under an oath not to eat until evening (v. 24). They come into a forest running with honey and nobody touches it (vv. 25-26). Jonathan, who had not heard, eats and is refreshed, and when told of the oath he says his father has troubled the land (vv. 27-30). By evening the famished people slaughter the spoil on the ground and eat it with the blood (vv. 31-32). Saul stops it and builds an altar, the first he has built (vv. 33-35).
verseByVerse.theology: The oath is sworn for the king's own vengeance, and it does to Israel what Achan's sin did at Ai.
verseByVerse.examples: And it manufactured the sin it then punished. Men who have fought all day without food eventually eat meat with the blood in it, which the law forbids (Lev. 17:10-14), and Saul, who starved them, rebukes them for it.

verseByVerse.quote: And the men of Israel had been hard pressed that day, so Saul had laid an oath on the people, saying, "Cursed be the man who eats food until it is evening and I am avenged on my enemies." So none of the people had tasted food. Now when all the people came to the forest, behold, there was honey on the ground. And when the people entered the forest, behold, the honey was dropping, but no one put his hand to his mouth, for the people feared the oath. But Jonathan had not heard his father charge the people with the oath, so he put out the tip of the staff that was in his hand and dipped it in the honeycomb and put his hand to his mouth, and his eyes became bright. Then one of the people said, "Your father strictly charged the people with an oath, saying, 'Cursed be the man who eats food this day.'" And the people were faint. Then Jonathan said, "My father has troubled the land. See how my eyes have become bright because I tasted a little of this honey. How much better if the people had eaten freely today of the spoil of their enemies that they found. For now the defeat among the Philistines has not been great."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The narrator goes back to fill in what Saul had been doing while Jonathan was climbing. He had put the army under a curse, and the reason is in the last words: until... I am avenged on my enemies. My vengeance, my enemies. There is no mention of God in the oath, and the men who will go hungry all day are fighting for the king's satisfaction. His son an hour earlier said the LORD has given them into the hand of Israel (v. 12). The same battle, and one man is thinking about the LORD and Israel while the other is thinking about his enemies and himself.

The picture is deliberate and almost unbearable: wild honey running on the ground in front of an exhausted army, free, provided, requiring nothing but a hand, and not a man touches it.

Jonathan had not heard; he was in the pass. The detail the narrator chooses is physical: his eyes became bright. It is the visible difference between an army that has eaten and one that has not, recorded in one man's face, with the narrator's own clause beside it: and the people were faint.

Jonathan's verdict is a single heavy verb. Troubled is 'akar, and every Israelite knew where it came from: Joshua said to Achan, why did you bring trouble on us? The LORD brings trouble on you today, and the place was called the Valley of Achor (Josh. 7:25-26). His father's oath has done to Israel what a thief's sin did at Ai. And the cost is stated by the man who won the battle: a starving army stopped early, and the Philistines got away.

That is the mark of the rash vow throughout Scripture. It sounds serious, it is made in God's presence, it costs the people who did not make it, and it damages the very thing it was meant to protect. Jephthah's vow was the same shape, and it cost him a daughter (Judg. 11:35).

Was Saul bound by his rash oath? A vow to do wrong must not be kept (cf. Lev 5:4); the people rightly refused to let Jonathan die (v. 45). Rash vows should be avoided, and repented of when they would require sin (Eccl 5:2–6).

verseByVerse.quote: They struck down the Philistines that day from Michmash to Aijalon. And the people were very faint. The people pounced on the spoil and took sheep and oxen and calves and slaughtered them on the ground. And the people ate them with the blood. Then they told Saul, "Behold, the people are sinning against the LORD by eating with the blood." And he said, "You have dealt treacherously; roll a great stone to me here." And Saul said, "Disperse yourselves among the people and say to them, 'Let every man bring his ox or his sheep and slaughter them here and eat, and do not sin against the LORD by eating with the blood.'" So every one of the people brought his ox with him that night and they slaughtered them there. And Saul built an altar to the LORD; it was the first altar that he built to the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A day's fighting across nearly twenty miles of country on nothing at all. At sunset, when the oath expires, they pounced, butchering the beasts where they stood and eating the meat with the blood still in it.

It is a real offence, not a technicality. The prohibition on blood is one of the oldest in the law: you shall not eat flesh with its life, that is, its blood (Gen. 9:4); the life of the flesh is in the blood, and I have given it for you on the altar to make atonement for your souls (Lev. 17:11, 14). Blood belonged to God and to the altar.

Saul is properly appalled and acts at once and correctly: he calls it treachery, has a great stone rolled up so the animals can be bled properly, and sends word through the camp. It is the right response and it is efficiently done. He seems not to notice that he caused it. Saul swore the oath; the oath starved the army; the starving army ate meat with the blood; Saul rebukes them for sinning against the LORD. There is no sign anywhere that the connection occurred to him.

The last clause of verse 35 is quiet and lands hard: the first altar that he built. He is well into his reign: anointed, crowned, given Jabesh, confirmed at Gilgal and rejected at Gilgal, and this is the first altar he ever built. Gideon built one before he fought anybody; Samuel built one at Ramah when he went home. Saul builds his first in a field at night, to fix a problem he created.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 36–46 — Though It Be in Jonathan My Son
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Saul proposes a night pursuit, but the priest urges that they ask God first (v. 36). God does not answer (v. 37). Saul looks for the guilty man and swears to kill him even if it is Jonathan, and the army says nothing (vv. 38-39). The lot falls on Jonathan, who tells what he did and accepts death (vv. 40-43). Saul confirms the sentence (v. 44), but the people refuse and ransom him (v. 45).
verseByVerse.theology: Set verse 44 beside 11:13. On the day of his first victory Saul refused to execute the men who had publicly despised him, because today the LORD has worked salvation in Israel. Here, on the day of another victory, he insists on executing his own son, and the people use his own sentence back at him.
verseByVerse.examples: The army overrules the king to save the man God used. It is the only thing that stands between Jonathan and a sentence pronounced in the name of the LORD, and the writer records it without a word of criticism for anybody but Saul.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Saul said, "Let us go down after the Philistines by night and plunder them until the morning light; let us not leave a man of them." And they said, "Do whatever seems good to you." But the priest said, "Let us draw near to God here." And Saul inquired of God, "Shall I go down after the Philistines? Will you give them into the hand of Israel?" But he did not answer him that day. And Saul said, "Come here, all you leaders of the people, and know and see how this sin has arisen today. For as the LORD lives who saves Israel, though it be in Jonathan my son, he shall surely die." But there was not a man among all the people who answered him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do whatever seems good to you. Some hear in it an echo of the refrain that closes Judges, everyone doing what was right in his own eyes. Whether or not that is meant, an army that says this to its king is not offering counsel. Nobody in the command tent has suggested asking God, and it takes the priest to raise it, with a rebuke wrapped in a suggestion.

Then God says nothing, and the clause is left standing: no refusal, no rebuke, no explanation. It will happen again at the very end, on the night before Gilboa, when the LORD did not answer him, either by dreams, or by Urim, or by prophets, and he goes looking for a medium at Endor (28:6). The silence begins here.

Saul's response to God's silence is to look for somebody to blame. It is not an unreasonable inference; unanswered enquiry could indicate sin in the camp, as at Ai. But he swears a second oath in one day, committing himself in advance to execute whoever is found, and names his own son before there is any evidence. He invokes God as the God who saves, in the act of promising to kill the man God used to save them that morning.

The army says nothing. Somebody told Jonathan about the oath in the forest, so the story has been round the camp all day. The whole army knows what happened and not one man will say it, and their silence in front of the king is its own comment on him.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he said to all Israel, "You shall be on one side, and I and Jonathan my son will be on the other side." And the people said to Saul, "Do what seems good to you." Therefore Saul said, "O LORD God of Israel, why have you not answered your servant this day? If this guilt is in me or in Jonathan my son, O LORD, God of Israel, give Urim. But if this guilt is in your people Israel, give Thummim." And Jonathan and Saul were taken, but the people escaped. Then Saul said, "Cast the lot between me and my son Jonathan." And Jonathan was taken. Then Saul said to Jonathan, "Tell me what you have done." And Jonathan told him, "I tasted a little honey with the tip of the staff that was in my hand. Here I am; I will die." And Saul said, "God do so to me and more also; you shall surely die, Jonathan." Then the people said to Saul, "Shall Jonathan die, who has worked this great salvation in Israel? Far from it! As the LORD lives, there shall not one hair of his head fall to the ground, for he has worked with God this day." So the people ransomed Jonathan, so that he did not die. Then Saul went up from pursuing the Philistines, and the Philistines went to their own place.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He divides the nation from his own household, which means he already suspects. This is the one place in Scripture where we watch a question actually being framed for the Urim and Thummim, which were kept in the high priest's breastpiece and everywhere else simply named. (The fuller wording of v. 41, which names both, follows the Greek; the Hebrew here is shorter.) Two alternatives are assigned in advance, one to each object: a sacred lot with a yes-or-no answer, cast with the whole nation watching.

Jonathan's answer is one of the most dignified speeches in the Old Testament, and one of the shortest. He does not plead that he had not heard the oath, which is true (v. 27) and would be a complete defence. He does not point out that he won the battle or appeal to the army, who are plainly on his side. He states exactly what he did, a little honey on the tip of a staff, and submits: here I am, the words Samuel said in the dark at Shiloh.

His father confirms it with a third oath, and the writer has built Saul's story so that we would set this beside 11:13. Then, on the day of his first victory, he spared men who had publicly despised him because today the LORD has worked salvation in Israel. Now, on the day of this one, he will kill the son through whom God saved Israel. It is the same king and the same kind of day, and the reverse in every particular.

The army stops him with Saul's own principle: who has worked this great salvation in Israel is the language of Jabesh. You do not execute men on a day God has saved Israel; you said so yourself. They swear an oath of their own, as the LORD lives, and give the reason that settles it: he has worked with God this day.

Then: so the people ransomed Jonathan. The text does not say what the ransom was, and guessing is a distraction. A man condemned under an oath sworn in God's name was not executed, because somebody else paid.

Note the shape without pressing it into an allegory the text does not make. One man went alone into the pass and worked a great salvation for a nation hiding in caves, and that nation found him under sentence of death and ransomed him. The gospel runs the other way round, and that is the point of the comparison. Jonathan was ransomed by the people he had saved. Christ ransomed the people who condemned him, and there was no army to intervene and no substitute offered, because he was the substitute.

The night attack never happens and the enemy walks home. A day that began with two men routing an army ends with the king having starved his troops, manufactured a national sin, tried to kill his own son, been overruled by his own army, and let the Philistines go.

Why did the lot fall on Jonathan, who did not know about the oath? The lot exposed who had broken the vow, not who was guilty before God; Jonathan was innocent of rebellion, and the people saved him.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The chapter closes with a favourable summary of the reign. Saul fought enemies on every side and routed them, struck the Amalekites, and delivered Israel from its plunderers (vv. 47-48). Then the household is listed (vv. 49-51), and a last note: there was hard fighting with the Philistines all his days, and Saul recruited every strong or valiant man he saw (v. 52).
verseByVerse.theology: This is a real assessment and it should be allowed to stand. Saul was not a failure as a soldier. He secured the borders on every side and broke the raiders who had been eating Israel's harvests since the book of Judges.
verseByVerse.examples: The last clause is how the rest of the book begins. A king who recruited every strong man he saw is going to see a shepherd from Bethlehem come up out of a valley carrying a giant's head.

verseByVerse.quote: When Saul had taken the kingship over Israel, he fought against all his enemies on every side, against Moab, against the Ammonites, against Edom, against the kings of Zobah, and against the Philistines. Wherever he turned he routed them. And he did valiantly and struck the Amalekites and delivered Israel out of the hands of those who plundered them. Now the sons of Saul were Jonathan, Ishvi, and Malchi-shua. And the names of his two daughters were these: the name of the firstborn was Merab, and the name of the younger Michal. And the name of Saul's wife was Ahinoam the daughter of Ahimaaz. And the name of the commander of his army was Abner the son of Ner, Saul's uncle. Kish was the father of Saul, and Ner the father of Abner was the son of Abiel. There was hard fighting against the Philistines all the days of Saul. And when Saul saw any strong man, or any valiant man, he attached him to himself.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This needs saying clearly, because a reader who has just watched the honey and the oath will not expect it: Saul was a successful soldier. Five enemies on every frontier, Moab and Ammon east, Edom south, Zobah far north, the Philistines west, and the narrator says in his own voice he did valiantly. Delivered Israel out of the hands of those who plundered them is the language of the judges, the thing Israel had needed since Midian camped on the harvests. Saul did it, and the raids stopped. The Amalekites are mentioned in passing, and the next chapter is about them.

Almost everybody in the household will matter. Jonathan will love David and die beside his father on Gilboa, and Malchi-shua with him. Merab will be promised to David and given to somebody else. Michal will love David, be given to him, be taken away, be given back, and despise him at the end. And Abner, the king's cousin and general, will hold Saul's house together for years after Gilboa and then be murdered in a gateway.

The last sentence is how the rest of the book gets started. For a king with no standing army worth the name it is sensible policy: recruit every capable man you meet. It is also exactly how a shepherd from Bethlehem ends up at court, and three chapters from now Saul will see a young man come up out of a valley with a giant's head in his hand and attach him to himself. He will do what this verse says he always did. That will be the beginning of the end of him.

14.theology:
By many or by few (v. 6). Hannah sang it twelve chapters earlier with nothing to go on (2:4, 9); chapter 13 supplied the arithmetic; Jonathan says the arithmetic does not constrain God. His it may be claims no promise, only a confidence in what God is like, and it is the same faith as that of the three men at the furnace.

Withdraw your hand (v. 19). Saul begins to enquire and stops halfway because the opportunity seems to be opening. It is the second time the pressure of the moment has overruled what he was told to do.

The rash vow (vv. 24, 29-30). Sworn for my vengeance and my enemies, with God nowhere in it, while his son at the top of the crag was saying the LORD has given them into the hand of Israel, the oath starved the army and then produced the very sin Saul condemned. That is the shape of the rash vow everywhere in Scripture: it sounds serious, it is made in God's presence, it costs the people who did not make it, and it damages the thing it meant to protect.

He did not answer him that day (v. 37). No refusal, no rebuke, no explanation. It happens again on the last night of his life, when the LORD answers neither by dreams nor Urim nor prophets and he goes to Endor (28:6). The silence begins here.

The exact reversal of 11:13. On the day of his first victory Saul spared men who despised him because the LORD had saved Israel. Here he would kill the son through whom the LORD saved Israel, and the army stops him by quoting his own principle back: shall Jonathan die, who has worked this great salvation in Israel?

Ransomed (v. 45). Jonathan was ransomed by the people he had saved. The gospel runs the other way: Christ ransomed the people who condemned him, and was himself the price.

He did valiantly (vv. 47-48). Give this its full weight. Five frontiers, wherever he turned he routed them, and the language of the judges: he delivered Israel out of the hands of those who plundered them. Saul was not a failure as a soldier, and the book says so in its own voice.
14.examples:
Then: Two men climbed a cliff on their hands and feet towards a garrison that had just jeered at them and broke an army, while the king sat on the edge of Gibeah, ordered a head count, cancelled his consultation of God halfway through, and had already sworn an oath that would starve his troops past a forest floor running with honey.

Now: Three things. Verse 6 is the model for acting without certainty: it may be is not weak faith but honest faith, and it is built on what God is like rather than on a guarantee nobody gave you. Verse 19 is the warning: the moment when consulting God starts to feel like a delay you cannot afford is precisely the moment the consultation matters. And verses 24 to 33 are the anatomy of a rash commitment: made in God's name, costing people who never agreed to it, forcing them into the very failure it was supposed to prevent, and leaving the man who made it genuinely unable to see that he caused it. Where we have made such commitments, the way out is not to keep them at others' cost but to confess them, and the God who saved Israel that day without Saul's help is the God who forgives his people for Christ's sake and gives his Spirit to make us more like Jonathan than like his father.

15.title: To Obey Is Better Than Sacrifice
15.text: <sup>1</sup>And Samuel said to Saul, "The LORD sent me to anoint you king over his people Israel; now therefore listen to the words of the LORD.<sup>2</sup>Thus says the LORD of hosts, 'I have noted what Amalek did to Israel in opposing them on the way when they came up out of Egypt.<sup>3</sup>Now go and strike Amalek and devote to destruction all that they have. Do not spare them, but kill both man and woman, child and infant, ox and sheep, camel and donkey.'"<sup>4</sup>So Saul summoned the people and numbered them in Telaim, two hundred thousand men on foot, and ten thousand men of Judah.<sup>5</sup>And Saul came to the city of Amalek and lay in wait in the valley.<sup>6</sup>Then Saul said to the Kenites, "Go, depart; go down from among the Amalekites, lest I destroy you with them. For you showed kindness to all the people of Israel when they came up out of Egypt." So the Kenites departed from among the Amalekites.<sup>7</sup>And Saul defeated the Amalekites from Havilah as far as Shur, which is east of Egypt.<sup>8</sup>And he took Agag the king of the Amalekites alive and devoted to destruction all the people with the edge of the sword.<sup>9</sup>But Saul and the people spared Agag and the best of the sheep and of the oxen and of the fattened calves and the lambs, and all that was good, and would not utterly destroy them. All that was despised and worthless they devoted to destruction.<sup>10</sup>The word of the LORD came to Samuel:<sup>11</sup>"I regret that I have made Saul king, for he has turned back from following me and has not performed my commandments." And Samuel was angry, and he cried to the LORD all night.<sup>12</sup>And Samuel rose early to meet Saul in the morning. And it was told Samuel, "Saul came to Carmel, and behold, he set up a monument for himself and turned and passed on and went down to Gilgal."<sup>13</sup>And Samuel came to Saul, and Saul said to him, "Blessed be you to the LORD. I have performed the commandment of the LORD."<sup>14</sup>And Samuel said, "What then is this bleating of the sheep in my ears and the lowing of the oxen that I hear?"<sup>15</sup>Saul said, "They have brought them from the Amalekites, for the people spared the best of the sheep and of the oxen to sacrifice to the LORD your God, and the rest we have devoted to destruction."<sup>16</sup>Then Samuel said to Saul, "Stop! I will tell you what the LORD said to me this night." And he said to him, "Speak."<sup>17</sup>And Samuel said, "Though you are little in your own eyes, are you not the head of the tribes of Israel? The LORD anointed you king over Israel.<sup>18</sup>And the LORD sent you on a mission and said, 'Go, devote to destruction the sinners, the Amalekites, and fight against them until they are consumed.'<sup>19</sup>Why then did you not obey the voice of the LORD? Why did you pounce on the spoil and do what was evil in the sight of the LORD?"<sup>20</sup>And Saul said to Samuel, "I have obeyed the voice of the LORD. I have gone on the mission on which the LORD sent me. I have brought Agag the king of Amalek, and I have devoted the Amalekites to destruction.<sup>21</sup>But the people took of the spoil, sheep and oxen, the best of the things devoted to destruction, to sacrifice to the LORD your God in Gilgal."<sup>22</sup>And Samuel said, "Has the LORD as great delight in burnt offerings and sacrifices, as in obeying the voice of the LORD? Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice, and to listen than the fat of rams.<sup>23</sup>For rebellion is as the sin of divination, and presumption is as iniquity and idolatry. Because you have rejected the word of the LORD, he has also rejected you from being king."<sup>24</sup>Saul said to Samuel, "I have sinned, for I have transgressed the commandment of the LORD and your words, because I feared the people and obeyed their voice.<sup>25</sup>Now therefore, please pardon my sin and return with me that I may bow before the LORD."<sup>26</sup>And Samuel said to Saul, "I will not return with you. For you have rejected the word of the LORD, and the LORD has rejected you from being king over Israel."<sup>27</sup>As Samuel turned to go away, Saul seized the skirt of his robe, and it tore.<sup>28</sup>And Samuel said to him, "The LORD has torn the kingdom of Israel from you this day and has given it to a neighbor of yours, who is better than you.<sup>29</sup>And also the Glory of Israel will not lie or have regret, for he is not a man, that he should have regret."<sup>30</sup>Then he said, "I have sinned; yet honor me now before the elders of my people and before Israel, and return with me, that I may bow before the LORD your God."<sup>31</sup>So Samuel turned back after Saul, and Saul bowed before the LORD.<sup>32</sup>Then Samuel said, "Bring here to me Agag the king of the Amalekites." And Agag came to him cheerfully. Agag said, "Surely the bitterness of death is past."<sup>33</sup>And Samuel said, "As your sword has made women childless, so shall your mother be childless among women." And Samuel hacked Agag to pieces before the LORD in Gilgal.<sup>34</sup>Then Samuel went to Ramah, and Saul went up to his house in Gibeah of Saul.<sup>35</sup>And Samuel did not see Saul again until the day of his death, but Samuel grieved over Saul. And the LORD regretted that he had made Saul king over Israel.
15.overview:
Samuel brings Saul a commission to carry out God's long-sworn judgment on Amalek, and the chapter faces honestly what that order contains. Saul does the military work well and warns the Kenites clear on exactly the right principle, but he and the people keep the best of the livestock and the Amalekite king. He then raises a monument to himself and greets Samuel with the claim that he has obeyed, while the sheep can be heard behind him.

Samuel's answer is one of the great sentences of the Old Testament: to obey is better than sacrifice. Saul is rejected as king. His confession, when it comes, is accurate, but what he asks for next is to be honoured before the elders. The chapter ends on two griefs, the prophet's and God's, and neither is Saul's.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Samuel comes with a commission, and it begins by establishing authority: the LORD sent me to anoint you, so listen (v. 1). The charge is historical, what Amalek did to Israel on the way up from Egypt (v. 2). And the order is total (v. 3).
verseByVerse.theology: The ground of the sentence is not who Amalek were but what they did, and the commentary below sets out what Scripture says about it.
verseByVerse.examples: This is one of the hardest commands in the Old Testament, and the commentary does not pretend otherwise.

verseByVerse.quote: And Samuel said to Saul, "The LORD sent me to anoint you king over his people Israel; now therefore listen to the words of the LORD. Thus says the LORD of hosts, 'I have noted what Amalek did to Israel in opposing them on the way when they came up out of Egypt. Now go and strike Amalek and devote to destruction all that they have. Do not spare them, but kill both man and woman, child and infant, ox and sheep, camel and donkey.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
He establishes the chain of authority before he says anything else. The LORD sent me; I anointed you; now listen. Saul holds the office at somebody's pleasure, and the man in front of him is the one through whom the orders come.

The commission opens with a reason, and the reason is a specific historical act. It is not that Amalek are Amalekites, nor that they occupy land Israel wants. It happened at Rephidim, a few weeks out of Egypt (Ex. 17:8-16), and Deuteronomy records it like a charge sheet: he attacked you on the way when you were faint and weary, and cut off your tail, those who were lagging behind you, and he did not fear God (Deut. 25:17-18). Amalek did not attack the armed men at the front; they came at the stragglers, freed slaves with children and old people at the rear. Moses built an altar there and said: the LORD will have war with Amalek from generation to generation (Ex. 17:16).

Then the order, which must be read as it stands. Devote to destruction is the herem, the ban: a thing placed entirely under God's judgment, not to be taken as plunder or profited from. And the list includes the words no reader gets past easily: child and infant.

Set out what Scripture itself says about this, and then be honest about what it does not settle.

The ground is moral rather than ethnic: an act, named, with the manner of it on record. Four hundred years lie between the crime and the sentence, which is a long patience and not a hot temper. In the interval Amalek did not stop; they came with Eglon of Moab, and with Midian year after year to camp on the harvests like locusts, and they are named again and again in Judges alone (Judg. 3:13; 6:3; 7:12; 10:12). This was a standing, four-century aggression. And the ban means nobody profits; the whole arrangement exists so that this cannot become a raid for cattle, which is the point Saul misses.

Now the honest half. None of that makes child and infant a comfortable sentence, and it is not faithlessness to feel the weight of it. Scripture does not ask readers to pretend. What it does is refuse to let the reader think the judgment was arbitrary, or racial, or hasty, and it insists throughout that Israel deserved no better and was told so plainly (Deut. 9:4-6).

One thing more, and it is not a template. This is a specific command, to one king, at one moment, about one nation under a sworn judgment. Nothing in the New Testament permits a Christian to reason from it to anything, and Paul closes the door explicitly: the weapons of our warfare are not of the flesh (2 Cor. 10:4).

Three more things can be said to a reader who still finds this hard, and none is a trick. The God who gave this order gives every life and has the right to take it, and Scripture insists he is never unjust: shall not the Judge of all the earth do what is just? (Genesis 18:25). Judgment on a nation is not the last word about its little ones: the Westminster Confession of Faith teaches that elect infants dying in infancy are saved by Christ (Westminster 10.3), and many Christians have held, gladly, that God's mercy to such children is wide. And the ban points beyond this valley, to the final judgment on all evil and to the cross, where Christ redeemed his people from the curse by becoming a curse for us (Galatians 3:13), so that those who trust him are never devoted to destruction.
verseByVerse.note: Rephidim, where Amalek attacked, lay on Israel's route from Egypt to Sinai (Ex. 17:1, 8).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Saul musters his army and lies in wait (vv. 4-5). First he warns the Kenites clear, because they showed kindness to Israel on the way up from Egypt (v. 6). He defeats Amalek and takes Agag alive (vv. 7-8). But he and the people spare Agag and the best of the livestock, all that was good, and destroy what was despised and worthless (v. 9).
verseByVerse.theology: Saul's reasoning about the Kenites shows he understood the principle of the judgment perfectly on the morning of the battle.
verseByVerse.examples: That is what makes verse 9 so telling: the obedience stopped exactly where the value began.

verseByVerse.quote: So Saul summoned the people and numbered them in Telaim, two hundred thousand men on foot, and ten thousand men of Judah. And Saul came to the city of Amalek and lay in wait in the valley. Then Saul said to the Kenites, "Go, depart; go down from among the Amalekites, lest I destroy you with them. For you showed kindness to all the people of Israel when they came up out of Egypt." So the Kenites departed from among the Amalekites.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two hundred and ten thousand men, and Judah counted separately again. He musters, moves, and sets an ambush in the valley; whatever else this chapter shows, Saul was competent at this.

The Kenites are Jethro's people, Moses' father-in-law's clan, who came up with Judah and settled among Israel (Judg. 1:16); Jael, who put a tent peg through Sisera's head, was a Kenite. Saul's reasoning is exactly right. Amalek is under judgment for what it did to Israel on the way up from Egypt; the Kenites showed kindness on the same journey. The period was the same, the conduct opposite, and so the treatment is opposite. The judgment is not about who these people are but about what they did, and he sends a warning ahead so they can get clear.

Nothing in this book shows Saul thinking more clearly than he does in verse 6, which is exactly why the next three verses are what they are.

verseByVerse.quote: And Saul defeated the Amalekites from Havilah as far as Shur, which is east of Egypt. And he took Agag the king of the Amalekites alive and devoted to destruction all the people with the edge of the sword. But Saul and the people spared Agag and the best of the sheep and of the oxen and of the fattened calves and the lambs, and all that was good, and would not utterly destroy them. All that was despised and worthless they devoted to destruction.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The campaign is a success across a great sweep of desert country, and the whole chapter is in the comparison of the two halves of verse 9.

That is not a man who found the order too hard. It is not squeamishness about killing; he killed everything without economic value, and did it thoroughly. It is a valuation. Somebody went through the herds picking out the fat calves and the good breeding stock, and put the sword through the scrawny ones. The word for what he would not do is utterly destroy, the ban again, whose whole purpose was that nobody should profit from the judgment. Saul kept the profit and executed the rubbish.

Note who is named first: Saul and the people. In a few verses he will put the people first and himself nowhere.

He went where he was sent, fought whom he was told to fight, won, spared the Kenites correctly, destroyed the Amalekites as commanded, and kept the good livestock. On any ordinary reckoning that is ninety-five per cent of the instruction. The chapter is about the five per cent, and about what selecting it reveals.

Saul “devoted all the people”, yet Amalekites appear again (27:8; 30:1). Saul struck the Amalekites in his campaign, but many escaped elsewhere; the language describes his victory, not the end of every Amalekite.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–15 — The Bleating of the Sheep
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God tells Samuel he regrets making Saul king, and Samuel cries to the LORD all night (vv. 10-11). Saul has set up a monument for himself at Carmel (v. 12). He greets Samuel claiming to have performed the commandment (v. 13), and Samuel asks about the bleating of the sheep (v. 14).
verseByVerse.theology: The monument is the tell: the man who once hid among the baggage now raises a stone to himself.
verseByVerse.examples: Listen for the three moves in Saul's defence (v. 15); they will come round again.

verseByVerse.quote: The word of the LORD came to Samuel: "I regret that I have made Saul king, for he has turned back from following me and has not performed my commandments." And Samuel was angry, and he cried to the LORD all night. And Samuel rose early to meet Saul in the morning. And it was told Samuel, "Saul came to Carmel, and behold, he set up a monument for himself and turned and passed on and went down to Gilgal."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God says he regrets it, and the sentence has troubled readers for a long time. Verse 29 will appear to deny it in the same chapter, and both are dealt with there. What matters here is the reason, in two clauses: Saul has turned back from following me, and he has not performed my commandments. He has changed direction, and he has left his duty undone.

The prophet is angry, and the text does not say with whom. And he spends the night crying out to God, which suggests he spent it pleading for the man. Samuel had opposed the monarchy from the start, was personally rejected in the asking of it, and had called the whole thing a sin. He has every reason to feel vindicated. Instead he is up all night, and the last verse of the chapter says this never stopped.

Then the detail that tells us where the man has got to. The monument is literally a hand, a standing stone raised to keep a name alive; Absalom will put one up for the same reason, I have no son to keep my name in remembrance (2 Sam. 18:18). On the day of his coronation this man was hiding among the baggage. He told his uncle nothing about the kingdom and held his peace under insult. He is now erecting a monument to himself on the road home from a battle he did not finish.

The stones in this book have all been about God up to now. Samuel set one up at Mizpah and called it till now the LORD has helped us (7:12). Saul's stone has his own name on it.

Can God regret? Verse 29 says he is not a man, that he should have regret. God’s purposes never change; “regret” here expresses his real grief and his changed dealing with Saul, in human terms.

verseByVerse.quote: And Samuel came to Saul, and Saul said to him, "Blessed be you to the LORD. I have performed the commandment of the LORD." And Samuel said, "What then is this bleating of the sheep in my ears and the lowing of the oxen that I hear?" Saul said, "They have brought them from the Amalekites, for the people spared the best of the sheep and of the oxen to sacrifice to the LORD your God, and the rest we have devoted to destruction."
verseByVerse.commentary:
He greets the prophet with a blessing and a report, and the report is false. The question is whether he knows it. He has just built a monument to a victory, the Amalekites are destroyed, and the livestock behind him has been earmarked for sacrifice. It is entirely possible that Saul believed this sentence when he said it, which is what makes the next verse so devastating.

Samuel does not dispute the claim or reason from the law. He simply mentions what can be heard from where they are standing. The evidence has been making a noise in the background of the conversation the whole time. Some things cannot be argued away because they are audible.

The defence has three moves in a single sentence. First, they brought them, the people spared them: verse 9 said Saul and the people, and the king has removed himself from his own sentence. Second, to sacrifice to the LORD: the disobedience is re-described as piety, an excess of devotion rather than a failure of obedience. Third, and quietest, the LORD your God. Talking to the prophet about a command he was given directly, he refers to God as Samuel's. It is the smallest movement in the sentence and the most revealing.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–23 — To Obey Is Better Than Sacrifice
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Samuel cuts him off with what the LORD said in the night (v. 16). He names Saul's real problem and charges him with pouncing on the spoil (vv. 17-19). Saul insists he has obeyed and describes the disobedience in the next breath (vv. 20-21). Then the oracle: to obey is better than sacrifice, and because Saul has rejected the word of the LORD, the LORD has rejected him from being king (vv. 22-23).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 17 is the diagnosis of the whole man: a smallness that was once humility has become an excuse.
verseByVerse.examples: Saul will end his life consulting a medium at Endor (ch. 28), doing literally what Samuel says in v. 23 he is already doing in spirit.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Samuel said to Saul, "Stop! I will tell you what the LORD said to me this night." And he said to him, "Speak." And Samuel said, "Though you are little in your own eyes, are you not the head of the tribes of Israel? The LORD anointed you king over Israel. And the LORD sent you on a mission and said, 'Go, devote to destruction the sinners, the Amalekites, and fight against them until they are consumed.' Why then did you not obey the voice of the LORD? Why did you pounce on the spoil and do what was evil in the sight of the LORD?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Stop. Samuel will not let the explanation run further, and what he has to say is not his own assessment but what the LORD said to me this night. The verdict was reached before the conversation started.

Then the diagnosis of the whole man, in one question. His smallness was true, and once his best quality: the least clan of the smallest tribe (9:21), hiding among the baggage (10:22), saying nothing to his uncle or to the men who insulted him. Samuel is not praising it here. He is naming it as the problem, because it has stopped being humility and become an excuse. A man who thinks of himself as little does not have to answer for what happens on his watch; the people wanted the sheep, and who is he to stop them? Verse 24 will have him say it: I feared the people.

A self-image of insignificance looks like modesty and functions as an exemption. Are you not the head of the tribes of Israel? You were made responsible, and being frightened of the people you are responsible for is not humility.

And the verb in the second question, why did you pounce on the spoil?, is the word used of the starving army on the day of the oath, who ate the meat with the blood (14:32). Saul rebuked them for it. Samuel uses the same verb of the king, and there is no excuse of hunger this time.

verseByVerse.quote: And Saul said to Samuel, "I have obeyed the voice of the LORD. I have gone on the mission on which the LORD sent me. I have brought Agag the king of Amalek, and I have devoted the Amalekites to destruction. But the people took of the spoil, sheep and oxen, the best of the things devoted to destruction, to sacrifice to the LORD your God in Gilgal."
verseByVerse.commentary:
He says it again, with the evidence. There are four first-person claims in three sentences, I have obeyed, gone, brought, devoted, and one of the four is the disobedience itself, I have brought Agag, offered as proof of compliance.

Then but, and the exception describes exactly what he was accused of. He knows the animals were under the ban; he uses the technical term. And the same three moves as in verse 15 come round again.

This is worse than lying. A man who lies knows what he is covering. Saul appears able to say I have obeyed and then narrate the disobedience without the two colliding, because the exception has been filed under something else, the people's doing and a religious purpose, and once filed there it does not count against the claim. Anyone who has given an honest account of a matter and left one thing in a different category will recognise the mechanism.

verseByVerse.quote: And Samuel said, "Has the LORD as great delight in burnt offerings and sacrifices, as in obeying the voice of the LORD? Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice, and to listen than the fat of rams. For rebellion is as the sin of divination, and presumption is as iniquity and idolatry. Because you have rejected the word of the LORD, he has also rejected you from being king."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the summit of the chapter, and one of the great sentences of the Old Testament.

It is not a rejection of sacrifice. Samuel has offered burnt offerings all his life, and the whole system was God's own arrangement. What is attacked is the idea that the form can buy off the substance. Saul's plan was to take what God had placed under the ban and put it on God's altar: to disobey and then worship with the proceeds. Does the LORD delight in offerings as much as in being obeyed?

The prophets will keep saying it because it keeps being needed. I desire steadfast love and not sacrifice, the knowledge of God rather than burnt offerings (Hos. 6:6). What does the LORD require of you but to do justice, and to love kindness, and to walk humbly with your God? (Mic. 6:8). The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit (Ps. 51:17). And Jesus quotes Hosea twice into arguments with the Pharisees (Matt. 9:13; 12:7). Religion is the most convenient thing in the world to substitute for obedience: measurable, public, felt as devotion, and capable of being increased. A man who will not do the thing God has said can always do something else for God instead, and can generally do it generously.

Then a comparison that ought to stop anybody. Rebellion, not idolatry or blasphemy but declining to do what God said, is as the sin of divination. Divination is the attempt to get something out of the spiritual world on your own terms: to secure an outcome or manage a god without submitting to him. That is precisely what Saul has done, keeping what God put under the ban and proposing to hand some of it back. And the man told here that rebellion is like divination will finish his life in a house at Endor after dark, asking a medium to bring up a dead prophet, because the LORD did not answer him, either by dreams, or by Urim, or by prophets (28:6). Samuel names the character of his sin; Saul eventually performs it literally.

Then the sentence, built as an exchange: you rejected, he has rejected. Hear it against 8:7, they have rejected me from being king over them. Israel rejected God as king and asked for a man; the man has now rejected God's word and is himself rejected. The whole experiment has come round in seven chapters.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Saul confesses that he feared the people and obeyed their voice (v. 24), but asks Samuel to return with him (v. 25). Samuel refuses (v. 26). Saul seizes his robe and it tears, and Samuel makes it the sign: the kingdom is torn from Saul and given to a better neighbour (vv. 27-28). And the Glory of Israel will not lie or have regret (v. 29).
verseByVerse.theology: He was told to obey the voice of the LORD and he obeyed the voice of the people: the exact inversion of his office, in his own words.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 29 stands eighteen verses after I regret that I have made Saul king, from the same prophet. The commentary on vv. 27-29 explains why the two belong together.

verseByVerse.quote: Saul said to Samuel, "I have sinned, for I have transgressed the commandment of the LORD and your words, because I feared the people and obeyed their voice. Now therefore, please pardon my sin and return with me that I may bow before the LORD." And Samuel said to Saul, "I will not return with you. For you have rejected the word of the LORD, and the LORD has rejected you from being king over Israel."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now he says it, and the analysis is exactly right: no the people took this time, no your God, and the truest sentence Saul speaks in the chapter, because I feared the people and obeyed their voice. He was told at the outset to listen to the words of the LORD (v. 1) and obeyed the people instead: the precise inversion of the job. And the writer surely intends the irony. Three times in chapter 8 God told Samuel to obey their voice and give them a king; now the king explains his ruin with the same words.
