Fear of people is the most respectable of the ruling passions, because it can always be described as consideration. Saul is not accused of arrogance or cruelty. He was frightened of the men he was supposed to lead, and it cost him a kingdom.

Pardon my sin is right. Return with me is about being seen; he wants the prophet beside him when he bows, and verse 30 will say why. Samuel refuses and repeats the verdict without softening a word.

Saul said he had sinned, as David did (2 Sam 12:13). Why was David forgiven? Saul’s confession was full of excuses, because I feared the people, and he cared most to be honoured before the elders (v. 30). David blamed no one. Forgiveness was not lost to Saul, but the kingdom was, and his life showed no turning. If you fear you have gone as far as Saul, notice that the fear is itself a good sign: Saul worried about his honour, not his sin. And Christ's promise stands for anyone who comes: whoever comes to me I will never cast out (John 6:37).

verseByVerse.quote: As Samuel turned to go away, Saul seized the skirt of his robe, and it tore. And Samuel said to him, "The LORD has torn the kingdom of Israel from you this day and has given it to a neighbor of yours, who is better than you. And also the Glory of Israel will not lie or have regret, for he is not a man, that he should have regret."
verseByVerse.commentary:
He grabs at the old man's coat as he walks off and a piece comes away in his hand: an accident, the desperate action of somebody who cannot let a conversation end. And Samuel turns it into the sign, with the word that has just happened in the air between them.

Keep this scene, because the robe comes back. Nine chapters from now David will creep up on Saul in a cave and cut off the skirt of Saul's robe, and then his heart will strike him for doing even that much to the LORD's anointed (24:4-5). The same garment, the same gesture, and the two men the opposite way round. And a neighbour of yours, who is better than you is not named and is already living somewhere in the same country. Saul will spend the rest of his life trying to find out who.

Now the difficulty, which should be faced rather than managed. God said I regret that I have made Saul king (v. 11), and the last verse will say it again (v. 35). Here, in the middle, the same prophet says God does not have regret because he is not a man. The word is the same in all three places; the writer has put the contradiction inside a single chapter deliberately, and the two statements answer different questions.

Verse 29 denies that God is like a man. Men change their minds because they were misinformed, or talked round, or inconsistent; men make promises and then wish they had not. God cannot be argued out of a position or surprised into one, and what he has sworn stands. Verses 11 and 35 say that God is not indifferent. He is not a mechanism running a plan with nothing in it; something in him turns when a man he raised up turns away, and the word for it is grief.

Take one alone and you get a God who is either fickle or frozen, and the Bible presents neither. The unchangeableness is applied to the verdict: the kingdom is gone and there is no point asking again. The regret is applied to the person. God's sentence on Saul is settled, his sorrow over Saul is real, and the chapter ends on the sorrow.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Saul asks to be honoured before the elders (v. 30), and Samuel goes back with him (v. 31). Agag comes cheerfully, thinking death is past, and Samuel hacks him to pieces before the LORD (vv. 32-33). Prophet and king part and do not meet again (v. 34). But Samuel grieved over Saul, and the LORD regretted that he had made him king (v. 35).
verseByVerse.theology: The confession in v. 30 is real, and the concern underneath it has not moved.
verseByVerse.examples: Agag's name returns centuries later in the book of Esther.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he said, "I have sinned; yet honor me now before the elders of my people and before Israel, and return with me, that I may bow before the LORD your God." So Samuel turned back after Saul, and Saul bowed before the LORD. Then Samuel said, "Bring here to me Agag the king of the Amalekites." And Agag came to him cheerfully. Agag said, "Surely the bitterness of death is past." And Samuel said, "As your sword has made women childless, so shall your mother be childless among women." And Samuel hacked Agag to pieces before the LORD in Gilgal.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Here is the whole man in one sentence. He begins with a real confession, I have sinned, said for the second time with nothing to soften it. Then yet, and what follows is what he actually wants. He does not ask for help, or for prayer, or what he should do. He has just been told the kingdom is torn from him, and his concern is that the prophet should not be seen walking away from him in front of the leadership. And once more, the LORD your God.

It would be easy to conclude that the confession was therefore false, and that is probably too quick. He knows he has sinned and says so twice, and he cannot stop thinking about how it looks. Most people are that mixture; Saul is a man whose version of it was recorded.

Samuel goes with him, which is the last kindness he does him. He had refused (v. 26), and he goes anyway, standing beside a rejected king while he worships. He does not withdraw the verdict, and he does not humiliate him in public.

Then the prophet finishes the job the king would not. Agag, a captive king kept back from the slaughter, has evidently concluded that he is going to live. The sentence is exact and judicial: as your sword has made women childless. This is not the execution of a prisoner of war for being on the losing side; it is the last act of a four-hundred-year case, and the charge is what Agag's own sword did. The verb is brutal and the text does not soften it: an old prophet butchers a king at a sanctuary before the LORD. It is hard reading and it is meant to be. The ban was not a formality to be quietly dropped once the fighting was over; Saul had treated it as one, and somebody had to do what he would not.

A long shadow falls here. Centuries later, in a Persian palace, a man sets out to exterminate every Jew in a hundred and twenty-seven provinces, and the writer gives his name with a label: Haman the Agagite (Esth. 3:1). The label most likely ties him to Agag's royal house, and so the old enemy of Rephidim, spared by Saul's half-obedience, comes close to finishing what it started.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Samuel went to Ramah, and Saul went up to his house in Gibeah of Saul. And Samuel did not see Saul again until the day of his death, but Samuel grieved over Saul. And the LORD regretted that he had made Saul king over Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two men go home in opposite directions, and the working relationship between prophet and king is over. The town is Gibeah of Saul: it carries his name, as the monument at Carmel does (cf. 11:4).

They never meet again, in the sense that Samuel never again sought him out and there was no further dealing between them as prophet and king; Saul does appear before Samuel at Ramah in chapter 19, and something of Samuel appears to Saul at Endor in chapter 28.

Then four words that change the tone of the whole chapter. This is the man Saul replaced, who warned against the monarchy and was proved right in every particular. He mourned him instead, until God had to tell him to stop: how long will you grieve over Saul, since I have rejected him from being king over Israel? (16:1). Samuel had said that ceasing to pray for these people would be a sin against the LORD (12:23); this is what that looks like when the person has failed beyond recovery.

And the last sentence of the chapter is God's grief, not his anger. The verdict of verse 23 does not move, but the chapter ends on the word it used in verse 11, the word for something turning inside a person. That should govern how the rest of Saul's story is read. He is not written off with contempt by the God who rejected him. He is grieved over.

Now follow the great sentence of this chapter to the end of the Bible. To obey is better than sacrifice. Israel's tragedy, restated by prophet after prophet, is that the two kept coming apart: a nation offering rams while doing as it pleased, and kings building monuments to themselves on the way home from half-finished obedience.

They came together once. Hebrews puts Psalm 40 into the mouth of Christ at his coming into the world: sacrifices and offerings you have not desired, but a body have you prepared for me... Behold, I have come to do your will, O God. And the writer draws the conclusion: he does away with the first in order to establish the second. And by that will we have been sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all (Heb. 10:5-10). Obedience and sacrifice, which Saul tried to trade against each other, turn out in the end to be the same act, performed by one person, once, in the place of people who have all obeyed by halves.

15.theology:
The ban, honestly. The commentary on vv. 1-3 sets out the case Scripture makes and what it leaves hard. Two things bear repeating: the whole point of the herem is that nobody profits, which is exactly what Saul missed; and the command is not a template for anyone, since the weapons of our warfare are not of the flesh (2 Cor. 10:4).

A partial obedience (v. 9). On any ordinary reckoning Saul obeyed most of the instruction. The chapter is about the part he left out, and about what choosing it reveals.

Little in your own eyes (v. 17). It was once his best quality, and it has become an exemption. Fear of people is the most respectable of the ruling passions, because it can always be described as consideration.

To obey is better than sacrifice (v. 22). This is not a rejection of sacrifice, which was God's own arrangement, but of using the form to buy off the substance. The prophets say it for centuries because it keeps being needed (Hos. 6:6; Mic. 6:8; Ps. 51:16-17). And the obedience asked of Saul was asked of a man God had already chosen, anointed and given victory; the command came after the kindness, as it always had for Israel.

Regret, and no regret (vv. 11, 29, 35). God cannot be misinformed, talked round or surprised, and what he has sworn stands; and he is not indifferent, for something in him turns when a man he raised up turns away. The unchangeableness is applied to the verdict, the regret to the person.

Where it ends. The chapter closes not on the sentence but on two griefs, and neither is Saul's. And the great sentence has an end in the New Testament: obedience and sacrifice, which Saul tried to trade against each other, are the same act in Christ, who did the Father's will perfectly and offered himself once for all (Heb. 10:5-10). His obedience is counted to those who trust him, which is why a believer who has obeyed by halves can come back, as Saul would not, without excuses.
15.examples:
Then: A king warned the innocent clear on exactly the right principle, destroyed everything that had no resale value, kept the good breeding stock for a sacrifice, put up a monument to himself on the way home, and told the prophet he had obeyed while the sheep were bleating behind him.

Now: Three things. Verse 14 is the test for any account of yourself that has been carefully constructed: some things cannot be argued away because they are audible. Verse 17 is the uncomfortable one: a low view of yourself can function as an exemption from responsibility, and being frightened of the people you are answerable for is not humility. And verse 22 is the standing danger of a religious life: when God has said something you will not do, there is always something else you can do for him instead. None of us obeys wholly. The answer is not Saul's filing of exceptions but plain confession to the God who has already made us his own, trusting Christ's whole obedience in place of our partial one, and asking the Spirit, who now lives in his people, for the courage to fear God more than the people around us.

16.title: The LORD Looks on the Heart
16.text: <sup>1</sup>The LORD said to Samuel, "How long will you grieve over Saul, since I have rejected him from being king over Israel? Fill your horn with oil, and go. I will send you to Jesse the Bethlehemite, for I have provided for myself a king among his sons."<sup>2</sup>And Samuel said, "How can I go? If Saul hears it, he will kill me." And the LORD said, "Take a heifer with you and say, 'I have come to sacrifice to the LORD.'<sup>3</sup>And invite Jesse to the sacrifice, and I will show you what you shall do. And you shall anoint for me him whom I declare to you."<sup>4</sup>Samuel did what the LORD commanded and came to Bethlehem. The elders of the city came to meet him trembling and said, "Do you come peaceably?"<sup>5</sup>And he said, "Peaceably; I have come to sacrifice to the LORD. Consecrate yourselves, and come with me to the sacrifice." And he consecrated Jesse and his sons and invited them to the sacrifice.<sup>6</sup>When they came, he looked on Eliab and thought, "Surely the LORD's anointed is before him."<sup>7</sup>But the LORD said to Samuel, "Do not look on his appearance or on the height of his stature, because I have rejected him. For the LORD sees not as man sees: man looks on the outward appearance, but the LORD looks on the heart."<sup>8</sup>Then Jesse called Abinadab and made him pass before Samuel. And he said, "Neither has the LORD chosen this one."<sup>9</sup>Then Jesse made Shammah pass by. And he said, "Neither has the LORD chosen this one."<sup>10</sup>And Jesse made seven of his sons pass before Samuel. And Samuel said to Jesse, "The LORD has not chosen these."<sup>11</sup>Then Samuel said to Jesse, "Are all your sons here?" And he said, "There remains yet the youngest, but behold, he is keeping the sheep." And Samuel said to Jesse, "Send and get him, for we will not sit down till he comes here."<sup>12</sup>And he sent and brought him in. Now he was ruddy and had beautiful eyes and was handsome. And the LORD said, "Arise, anoint him, for this is he."<sup>13</sup>Then Samuel took the horn of oil and anointed him in the midst of his brothers. And the Spirit of the LORD rushed upon David from that day forward. And Samuel rose up and went to Ramah.<sup>14</sup>Now the Spirit of the LORD departed from Saul, and a harmful spirit from the LORD tormented him.<sup>15</sup>And Saul's servants said to him, "Behold now, a harmful spirit from God is tormenting you.<sup>16</sup>Let our lord now command your servants who are before you to seek out a man who is skillful in playing the lyre, and when the harmful spirit from God is upon you, he will play it, and you will be well."<sup>17</sup>So Saul said to his servants, "Provide for me a man who can play well and bring him to me."<sup>18</sup>One of the young men answered, "Behold, I have seen a son of Jesse the Bethlehemite, who is skillful in playing, a man of valor, a man of war, prudent in speech, and a man of good presence, and the LORD is with him."<sup>19</sup>Therefore Saul sent messengers to Jesse and said, "Send me David your son, who is with the sheep."<sup>20</sup>And Jesse took a donkey laden with bread and a skin of wine and a young goat and sent them by David his son to Saul.<sup>21</sup>And David came to Saul and entered his service. And Saul loved him greatly, and he became his armor-bearer.<sup>22</sup>And Saul sent to Jesse, saying, "Let David remain in my service, for he has found favor in my sight."<sup>23</sup>And whenever the harmful spirit from God was upon Saul, David took the lyre and played it with his hand. So Saul was refreshed and was well, and the harmful spirit departed from him.
16.overview:
God tells Samuel to stop mourning Saul and sends him to Bethlehem, where he has already seen for himself a king among Jesse's sons. Seeing is what this chapter is about. The prophet looks at the eldest son and makes exactly the mistake the nation made with Saul, and God corrects him with one of the great sentences of the Old Testament: man looks on the outward appearance, but the LORD looks on the heart.

Seven sons pass, and the one chosen is the youngest, whom his father had not even brought. The Spirit rushes on David from that day forward, and in the very next sentence departs from Saul; neither man knows. The chapter ends with the rejected king soothed by the music of his replacement, whom he has made his armour-bearer and loves greatly.
16.theology:
The LORD looks on the heart (v. 7). The commentary on vv. 6-7 draws out both the comfort and the discomfort of this verse. Set it in the book as a whole and it closes a circle. Saul was the people's choice, made by the eye, and the narrator gave us his height twice. David is God's choice, and in chapter 13 Samuel had already called him a man after his own heart. That does not mean David's heart was flawless; the rest of his story shows otherwise. It means God chose him, and that when David sinned his heart turned back to God in repentance. God does not use the opposite criterion from ours, preferring the unimpressive; he uses a different one altogether, which nobody in the room could see, and the heart he looks for is one that he himself makes clean.

The LORD's anointed (vv. 6, 13). Samuel's first guess was surely the LORD's anointed is before him, and the Hebrew word for anointed, mashiach, is the word behind Messiah; its Greek equivalent is Christos. Here Israel's hope begins to take the shape of a son of Jesse anointed with oil and filled with the Spirit from that day forward. Isaiah promised a shoot from the stump of Jesse on whom the Spirit of the LORD would rest (Isaiah 11:1-2), and John saw the Spirit descend on Jesus and remain (John 1:32-33). The title Christ means exactly this: the Anointed One, David's greater Son.

A harmful spirit from the LORD (v. 14). Scripture holds together a God who governs even what opposes him and a God who is never the author of evil (Jas. 1:13), without explaining the mechanism. This verse describes a specific judgment on a specific man, and must not be used to read depression or mental illness as demonic oppression.

Saul loved him greatly (v. 21). It is easy to read the coming chapters as though Saul were an enemy from the start. He was not. What came between them began as jealousy, growing in the empty place where the Spirit had been, towards a man he genuinely loved.
16.examples:
Then: A father consecrated seven sons for the prophet's sacrifice and did not send for the eighth, because somebody had to mind the sheep, and the prophet refused to sit down until the boy was fetched in from the field.

Now: Three things. Verse 7 cuts both ways and both should be felt: God is not using the instrument the world uses on you, and he is using one you cannot manage. The answer to the second is not a tidier heart but the one David prayed for, and in Christ God has promised it: he gives his Spirit to make the heart new. Verse 11 is for anyone who has been the person not sent for; David was not sulking about it but doing the job he had been left with, which is where the messenger found him. And verse 21 is the warning: Saul's ruin did not begin in hatred. It began with a man he genuinely loved doing well.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — How Long Will You Grieve?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God tells Samuel to stop grieving over Saul and to fill his horn and go to Jesse of Bethlehem, for he has provided a king among his sons (v. 1). Samuel fears Saul will kill him; God gives him a sacrifice to conduct and promises to show him what to do (vv. 2-3). The elders of Bethlehem come out trembling (v. 4).
verseByVerse.theology: God has already chosen before the prophet sets out; the rest of the chapter is about learning to see what he has seen.
verseByVerse.examples: Two details tell you the state of the country. The prophet of Israel is afraid the king will murder him, and the elders of a small town tremble when he arrives, because a prophet turning up unannounced generally meant somebody was in trouble.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD said to Samuel, "How long will you grieve over Saul, since I have rejected him from being king over Israel? Fill your horn with oil, and go. I will send you to Jesse the Bethlehemite, for I have provided for myself a king among his sons." And Samuel said, "How can I go? If Saul hears it, he will kill me." And the LORD said, "Take a heifer with you and say, 'I have come to sacrifice to the LORD.' And invite Jesse to the sacrifice, and I will show you what you shall do. And you shall anoint for me him whom I declare to you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The last verse of the previous chapter said Samuel grieved over Saul, and God now interrupts it. Not to rebuke him for having a heart; the grief was right, and God's own regret is recorded in the same verse. But there is work to do and Samuel has stopped. Grief has a proper length and can outlast its usefulness, and the question how long is put kindly and firmly, and followed at once by an errand.

Keep the verb provided, literally "I have seen for myself a king among his sons", because seeing is what this chapter is about. God has already looked at Jesse's household and chosen before Samuel has filled the horn. And note for myself: the last king was provided for Israel, because Israel asked. This one God has seen for his own purposes.

Then the prophet is frightened of the king. Samuel anointed this man, crowned him, rebuked him twice and pronounced his rejection to his face, and he says plainly that if Saul learns of this journey he will be murdered. He is not being cowardly but accurate. The man who will shortly throw a spear at a boy playing the lyre, and one day order the slaughter of eighty-five priests and their town, is entirely capable of it.

God gives him a way to travel safely, and it is not a lie. Samuel really does take a heifer, sacrifice, and invite Jesse; when the elders ask why he has come he tells them the truth. What he does not do is announce the second purpose to a hostile court. There is a difference between deceiving a man and declining to brief him, and here God himself draws it.

And Samuel is told very little: go to Jesse, one of his sons, I will show you what you shall do. He sets out knowing the town and the family and nothing else, and will get the name only when the boy is standing in front of him.

verseByVerse.quote: Samuel did what the LORD commanded and came to Bethlehem. The elders of the city came to meet him trembling and said, "Do you come peaceably?" And he said, "Peaceably; I have come to sacrifice to the LORD. Consecrate yourselves, and come with me to the sacrifice." And he consecrated Jesse and his sons and invited them to the sacrifice.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The prophet is afraid of the king, and the elders of a small country town are afraid of the prophet, because a man like Samuel arriving unannounced usually meant somebody was in trouble. He has, after all, recently hacked a king to pieces at Gilgal.

He reassures them and gives them something to do. Consecrate yourselves is a real instruction, washing, clean clothes, abstinence, the ordinary preparation for coming near holy things. Then he consecrates Jesse and his sons personally, and the next paragraphs turn on a name missing from that phrase.

Bethlehem has appeared in this history before: the Levite's concubine came from it, and Ruth the Moabite came to glean there, and her great-grandson is at this moment out with the sheep.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–13 — Man Looks on the Outward Appearance
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Samuel sees Eliab and is sure he is the LORD's anointed (v. 6), but God corrects him: the LORD looks on the heart (v. 7). Seven sons pass and none is chosen (vv. 8-10). The youngest is with the sheep; they send for him and Samuel anoints him among his brothers, and the Spirit rushes on David from that day forward (vv. 11-13).
verseByVerse.theology: The prophet's mistake in v. 6 is the nation's mistake in chapter 8, and God corrects it in words borrowed from the description of Saul.
verseByVerse.examples: Jesse did not bring him. Seven sons were consecrated and invited and the eighth was left with the sheep, and his own father did not think him worth mentioning until asked directly. Then a prophet, a town's elders and a family stood and waited for a boy to be fetched in from a field.

verseByVerse.quote: When they came, he looked on Eliab and thought, "Surely the LORD's anointed is before him." But the LORD said to Samuel, "Do not look on his appearance or on the height of his stature, because I have rejected him. For the LORD sees not as man sees: man looks on the outward appearance, but the LORD looks on the heart."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The prophet takes one look at the eldest and is certain, and it is not a foolish conclusion. Eliab is the firstborn, which counted for a great deal; he is evidently impressive; and Samuel is the best-qualified man in Israel to make this judgment. He is also making exactly the mistake the whole nation made in chapter 8.

Hear the echo in God's phrase. When Saul was introduced, from his shoulders upward he was taller than any of the people (9:2), and the narrator repeated it at the coronation (10:23). Height is the one physical fact this book keeps giving us about the king just rejected. So God is not offering a general reflection on vanity. He is correcting the criterion that produced Saul, to the man who anointed Saul, using Saul's own description. And I have rejected him is the verb of chapter 15 (15:23, 26): Eliab is turned down in the same words.

Then one of the load-bearing sentences of the Old Testament. Man looks on the outward appearance is literally "to the eyes", to what is available to the eyes. That is not a wickedness peculiar to Israel; it is how human assessment works, said to a prophet who has just done it. The LORD looks on the heart, and two things follow that pull in opposite directions.

The first is comfort, and it is enormous. God is not assessing you on the things everybody else assesses you on: height, looks, presence, birth order, all working for Eliab and none of them counting. The people the world does not look at twice are not overlooked by God, because he never used that instrument.

The second is not comfortable at all. If God looks on the heart, he is looking at the one part of you nobody else has seen. A reputation can be managed; the heart cannot be tidied for a visit. David, chosen by this standard, will fail catastrophically by it, and will ask for the only remedy: create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within me (Ps. 51:10). It is a prayer, not a resolution; the clean heart is God's gift before it is our task.

And Samuel does not acquire the ability. Told the principle in verse 7, he still has to be told the answer in verse 12. Seeing the heart is God's work, not a skill a spiritual man develops.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Jesse called Abinadab and made him pass before Samuel. And he said, "Neither has the LORD chosen this one." Then Jesse made Shammah pass by. And he said, "Neither has the LORD chosen this one." And Jesse made seven of his sons pass before Samuel. And Samuel said to Jesse, "The LORD has not chosen these."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The writer gives the next two refusals the same sentence twice, and the repetition is doing something: this is a slow, public, increasingly awkward procession, a prophet saying no to one promising young man after another.

Seven is the number of completeness in this literature. Jesse has produced the full set, every son he thought worth bringing, and the answer is no to all of them. Put yourself in the room: the sacrifice made, the family standing there, nobody left. By any ordinary reckoning the errand has failed and somebody has misheard God.

Jesse had eight sons (17:12), but 1 Chronicles 2:13–15 lists seven, with David the seventh. One son probably died young and is left out of the later list.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Samuel said to Jesse, "Are all your sons here?" And he said, "There remains yet the youngest, but behold, he is keeping the sheep." And Samuel said to Jesse, "Send and get him, for we will not sit down till he comes here." And he sent and brought him in. Now he was ruddy and had beautiful eyes and was handsome. And the LORD said, "Arise, anoint him, for this is he." Then Samuel took the horn of oil and anointed him in the midst of his brothers. And the Spirit of the LORD rushed upon David from that day forward. And Samuel rose up and went to Ramah.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The answer is the most revealing sentence in the chapter. Jesse was told to consecrate himself and his sons for a sacrifice conducted by the most important man in Israel, and he did not send for this one. The boy was not brought, not consecrated, not invited, and not mentioned until the prophet asked directly whether that was everybody.

The word rendered youngest also carries the sense of smallest, least. And the reason, that somebody has to mind the sheep, is true, and is the kind of true reason that gets given about the member of a family nobody thinks of as a candidate for anything. David's own father did not consider him worth including in the shortlist of his own sons.

The whole gathering waits: the prophet, the elders, Jesse and seven grown men, while somebody runs to fetch the boy who was not asked. Nobody sits down. The sacrifice is on hold.

He arrives, and the narrator describes his appearance five verses after saying appearance is not the criterion. The tension should be named rather than smoothed over. The chapter is not saying that God prefers unattractive people, or that David was chosen despite being good-looking. Appearance is not the instrument. David happened also to be handsome, and it was not why; Eliab was probably handsome too, and was refused on a ground nobody in the room could see.

Note the vessel. Saul was anointed from a flask of oil (10:1), a small pottery jar. David is anointed from the horn of oil, and a horn is the picture of strength all through this book, from Hannah's song: my horn is exalted in the LORD... he will exalt the horn of his anointed (2:1, 10). And it happens in the midst of his brothers: the seven who were invited watch the one left with the sheep have oil poured on his head. Eliab is there, and when his little brother turns up at the valley of Elah he will lose his temper with him in front of everyone (17:28). This scene is presumably somewhere behind that.

The verb is the one used of Samson and Saul, a sudden seizing, but the phrase attached has not been used before in this book: from that day forward. The Spirit rushed on Samson repeatedly and left; it clothed itself with Gideon for a campaign; it came on Saul in bursts, for occasions. Here it comes and stays. John the Baptist reaches for the same thing when he explains how he knew Jesus: I saw the Spirit descend from heaven like a dove, and it remained on him (John 1:32). The sign was not the descending but the staying.

Then Samuel goes home to Ramah, and the anticlimax is deliberate. There is no ceremony and no proclamation. Samuel anoints a shepherd boy in a Bethlehem courtyard and goes home, and David goes back to the sheep.
verseByVerse.note: David is named here for the first time in the book, only after the oil has been poured.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Spirit departs from Saul and a harmful spirit from the LORD torments him (v. 14). His servants propose music, and Saul agrees (vv. 15-17). A young man describes David in six phrases, ending and the LORD is with him (v. 18), and Saul sends to Jesse for him (v. 19).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 14 is set against verse 13 on purpose: the same Spirit, moving in opposite directions, in consecutive sentences.
verseByVerse.examples: The servant's list ends where it matters. Five of the six items are accomplishments; the last is the LORD is with him, which is as high a thing as this book says about anybody and the only thing on the list nobody can acquire.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the Spirit of the LORD departed from Saul, and a harmful spirit from the LORD tormented him. And Saul's servants said to him, "Behold now, a harmful spirit from God is tormenting you. Let our lord now command your servants who are before you to seek out a man who is skillful in playing the lyre, and when the harmful spirit from God is upon you, he will play it, and you will be well."
verseByVerse.commentary:
This verse and the one before are a matched pair. The kingdom changes hands in the space between them, and neither man knows it: David has gone back to the flock and Saul is on his throne.

The second clause is one of the hardest in the book. Scripture is willing to speak this way more than once. Micaiah sees a spirit volunteer to be a lying spirit in the mouth of all his prophets to entice Ahab, and God saying you are to entice him, and you shall succeed (1 Kings 22:19-23). Satan afflicts Job only within limits God sets (Job 1:12; 2:6). What Scripture never says is that God is the author of evil: God cannot be tempted with evil, and he himself tempts no one (Jas. 1:13). The picture is of a sovereign who governs even what opposes him and is never implicated in it, held without explaining the mechanism.

What the verse makes plain is the order. The Spirit left, and then something else occupied the space; Saul is tormented because the place is empty. Jesus describes the same shape in a parable about a house swept and left unoccupied (Matt. 12:43-45).

And it matters pastorally that this verse not be used to read depression or mental illness as demonic oppression. Saul's case is a specific judgment on a specific man following a rejection announced by a prophet; nothing here licenses a general diagnosis of anybody's darkness, and much harm has been done by people who thought it did. Note what the remedy turns out to be: not an exorcism, but music. His household names the trouble accurately and proposes something practical: find a man with a lyre and keep him at hand.

Can the Holy Spirit leave a believer? In the Old Testament the Spirit came on judges, prophets and kings to equip them for their office, and that gift could be withdrawn, as here. In the new covenant the Spirit dwells in every believer for ever (John 14:16) as the seal and guarantee of salvation (Eph 1:13–14); David’s prayer, take not your Holy Spirit from me (Ps 51:11), was the prayer of a king who had seen what happened to Saul. Saul received the Spirit’s power for his office, but his life shows no sign of saving faith.

Does God send evil spirits? Saul had rejected God, and God gave him over to a tormenting spirit as judgment (16:14), as he later sent a lying spirit to Ahab (1 Kgs 22:22). God is never the author of sin (Jas 1:13), but even evil spirits are under his rule, and he uses them to judge those who have turned from him.

verseByVerse.quote: So Saul said to his servants, "Provide for me a man who can play well and bring him to me." One of the young men answered, "Behold, I have seen a son of Jesse the Bethlehemite, who is skillful in playing, a man of valor, a man of war, prudent in speech, and a man of good presence, and the LORD is with him." Therefore Saul sent messengers to Jesse and said, "Send me David your son, who is with the sheep."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Provide for me a man uses the verb of verse 1, literally "see". God saw a king for himself; Saul asks his servants to see him a musician; and it is the same person.

Five of the servant's six phrases are accomplishments any recruiting officer would welcome. The sixth, the LORD is with him, is as high as this book says of anybody. It was said of Samuel (3:19) and will be said of David repeatedly from here on, and it is the one item nobody can acquire, train for or fake. A servant had noticed it about a teenager who looked after sheep.

A word about a man of war, because it sits oddly before the next chapter, where David arrives at the army as a boy bringing bread and Saul asks whose son he is. The likeliest explanation is the simplest: these narratives are arranged by theme as much as by clock, and chapter 16 introduces David as the man he is going to be. And what Saul asks in 17:55-58 is not "who is this" but whose son is this, a question about family, asked because the young man's father is about to be exempted from tax (17:25). Nothing in either chapter needs forcing.

And the phrase again: who is with the sheep. It is how his father described him (v. 11), and now how the king identifies him in an official summons. The anointing has happened and the Spirit has come, and to everybody he is still the one out with the flock.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 20–23 — And Saul Loved Him Greatly
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesse sends David to Saul with a present (v. 20). Saul loves him greatly and makes him his armour-bearer (v. 21), asks to keep him (v. 22), and whenever the harmful spirit comes, David plays and Saul is refreshed (v. 23).
verseByVerse.theology: Saul loved him greatly. Everything that follows, the spear, the pursuit, the three thousand men in the wilderness, the cave, the medium at Endor, begins here, with a king who loved the boy who would replace him and did not know it.
verseByVerse.examples: The armour-bearer stands at the king's shoulder, close enough to be run through.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesse took a donkey laden with bread and a skin of wine and a young goat and sent them by David his son to Saul. And David came to Saul and entered his service. And Saul loved him greatly, and he became his armor-bearer. And Saul sent to Jesse, saying, "Let David remain in my service, for he has found favor in my sight." And whenever the harmful spirit from God was upon Saul, David took the lyre and played it with his hand. So Saul was refreshed and was well, and the harmful spirit departed from him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesse's present of bread, wine and a young goat is almost exactly what the three pilgrims were carrying at the oak of Tabor on the day of Saul's anointing (10:3).

Four words then govern the rest of the book: Saul loved him greatly. It is easy to read the coming chapters as though Saul were an enemy from the start. He was not. He met this young man, loved him, and gave him the position of closest personal trust. An armour-bearer carried a man's weapons, stood beside him in battle and slept near him: the job Jonathan's servant had at Michmash, the man at your shoulder. Everything that follows, the spear at the wall, the daughter used as a trap, the three thousand men combing the wilderness, the priests of Nob, Endor, begins with a king who loved him.

He has found favour in my sight: in Saul's eyes. The man whose eyes were the problem has looked at David and approved of him, and he is right, and he does not know what he is looking at.

The position at the close of the chapter is one of the strangest in Scripture. A rejected king, tormented in the empty place where the Spirit used to be, is kept well by the music of the boy anointed to replace him. And this is the pattern of David's life: anointed king by the prophet of Israel, he could say so, and instead carries another man's weapons, plays for him when the darkness comes, and waits, holding a right he does not grasp at. It is a faint early sketch of his greater Son, who did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped but took the form of a servant (Philippians 2:6-7). For a while, and not a short one, the man who has lost everything is soothed nightly by the man who is going to receive it.

And the chapter's great verse has an end that is not in this book. God looked past seven consecrated sons and sent for a boy nobody had invited: God chose what is low and despised in the world, even things that are not, to bring to nothing things that are (1 Cor. 1:28). A thousand years later, in the fields outside this same town, the birth of the true King was announced to shepherds. And he himself was somebody the eye would pass over: he had no form or majesty that we should look at him, and no beauty that we should desire him (Isa. 53:2). Man looks on the outward appearance. Everybody did, and missed him.

17.title: The Battle Is the LORD's
17.text: <sup>1</sup>Now the Philistines gathered their armies for battle. And they were gathered at Socoh, which belongs to Judah, and encamped between Socoh and Azekah, in Ephes-dammim.<sup>2</sup>And Saul and the men of Israel were gathered, and encamped in the Valley of Elah, and drew up in line of battle against the Philistines.<sup>3</sup>And the Philistines stood on the mountain on the one side, and Israel stood on the mountain on the other side, with a valley between them.<sup>4</sup>And there came out from the camp of the Philistines a champion named Goliath of Gath, whose height was six cubits and a span.<sup>5</sup>He had a helmet of bronze on his head, and he was armed with a coat of mail, and the weight of the coat was five thousand shekels of bronze.<sup>6</sup>And he had bronze armor on his legs, and a javelin of bronze slung between his shoulders.<sup>7</sup>The shaft of his spear was like a weaver's beam, and his spear's head weighed six hundred shekels of iron. And his shield-bearer went before him.<sup>8</sup>He stood and shouted to the ranks of Israel, "Why have you come out to draw up for battle? Am I not a Philistine, and are you not servants of Saul? Choose a man for yourselves, and let him come down to me.<sup>9</sup>If he is able to fight with me and kill me, then we will be your servants. But if I prevail against him and kill him, then you shall be our servants and serve us."<sup>10</sup>And the Philistine said, "I defy the ranks of Israel this day. Give me a man, that we may fight together."<sup>11</sup>When Saul and all Israel heard these words of the Philistine, they were dismayed and greatly afraid.<sup>12</sup>Now David was the son of an Ephrathite of Bethlehem in Judah, named Jesse, who had eight sons. In the days of Saul the man was already old and advanced in years.<sup>13</sup>The three oldest sons of Jesse had followed Saul to the battle. And the names of his three sons who went to the battle were Eliab the firstborn, and next to him Abinadab, and the third Shammah.<sup>14</sup>David was the youngest. The three eldest followed Saul,<sup>15</sup>but David went back and forth from Saul to feed his father's sheep at Bethlehem.<sup>16</sup>For forty days the Philistine came forward and took his stand, morning and evening.<sup>17</sup>And Jesse said to David his son, "Take for your brothers an ephah of this parched grain, and these ten loaves, and carry them quickly to the camp to your brothers.<sup>18</sup>Also take these ten cheeses to the commander of their thousand. See if your brothers are well, and bring some token from them."<sup>19</sup>Now Saul and they and all the men of Israel were in the Valley of Elah, fighting with the Philistines.<sup>20</sup>And David rose early in the morning and left the sheep with a keeper and took the provisions and went, as Jesse had commanded him. And he came to the encampment as the host was going out to the battle line, shouting the war cry.<sup>21</sup>And Israel and the Philistines drew up for battle, army against army.<sup>22</sup>And David left the things in charge of the keeper of the baggage and ran to the ranks and went and greeted his brothers.<sup>23</sup>As he talked with them, behold, the champion, the Philistine of Gath, Goliath by name, came up out of the ranks of the Philistines and spoke the same words as before. And David heard him.<sup>24</sup>All the men of Israel, when they saw the man, fled from him and were much afraid.<sup>25</sup>And the men of Israel said, "Have you seen this man who has come up? Surely he has come up to defy Israel. And the king will enrich the man who kills him with great riches and will give him his daughter and make his father's house free in Israel."<sup>26</sup>And David said to the men who stood by him, "What shall be done for the man who kills this Philistine and takes away the reproach from Israel? For who is this uncircumcised Philistine, that he should defy the armies of the living God?"<sup>27</sup>And the people answered him in the same way, "So shall it be done to the man who kills him."<sup>28</sup>Now Eliab his eldest brother heard when he spoke to the men. And Eliab's anger was kindled against David, and he said, "Why have you come down? And with whom have you left those few sheep in the wilderness? I know your presumption and the evil of your heart, for you have come down to see the battle."<sup>29</sup>And David said, "What have I done now? Was it not but a word?"<sup>30</sup>And he turned away from him toward another, and spoke in the same way, and the people answered him again as before.<sup>31</sup>When the words that David spoke were heard, they repeated them before Saul, and he sent for him.<sup>32</sup>And David said to Saul, "Let no man's heart fail because of him. Your servant will go and fight with this Philistine."<sup>33</sup>And Saul said to David, "You are not able to go against this Philistine to fight with him, for you are but a youth, and he has been a man of war from his youth."<sup>34</sup>But David said to Saul, "Your servant used to keep sheep for his father. And when there came a lion, or a bear, and took a lamb from the flock,<sup>35</sup>I went after him and struck him and delivered it out of his mouth. And if he arose against me, I caught him by his beard and struck him and killed him.<sup>36</sup>Your servant has struck down both lions and bears, and this uncircumcised Philistine shall be like one of them, for he has defied the armies of the living God."<sup>37</sup>And David said, "The LORD who delivered me from the paw of the lion and from the paw of the bear will deliver me from the hand of this Philistine." And Saul said to David, "Go, and the LORD be with you!"<sup>38</sup>Then Saul clothed David with his armor. He put a helmet of bronze on his head and clothed him with a coat of mail,<sup>39</sup>and David strapped his sword over his armor. And he tried in vain to go, for he had not tested them. Then David said to Saul, "I cannot go with these, for I have not tested them." So David put them off.<sup>40</sup>Then he took his staff in his hand and chose five smooth stones from the brook and put them in his shepherd's pouch. His sling was in his hand, and he approached the Philistine.<sup>41</sup>And the Philistine moved forward and came near to David, with his shield-bearer in front of him.<sup>42</sup>And when the Philistine looked and saw David, he disdained him, for he was but a youth, ruddy and handsome in appearance.<sup>43</sup>And the Philistine said to David, "Am I a dog, that you come to me with sticks?" And the Philistine cursed David by his gods.<sup>44</sup>The Philistine said to David, "Come to me, and I will give your flesh to the birds of the air and to the beasts of the field."<sup>45</sup>Then David said to the Philistine, "You come to me with a sword and with a spear and with a javelin, but I come to you in the name of the LORD of hosts, the God of the armies of Israel, whom you have defied.<sup>46</sup>This day the LORD will deliver you into my hand, and I will strike you down and cut off your head. And I will give the dead bodies of the host of the Philistines this day to the birds of the air and to the wild beasts of the earth, that all the earth may know that there is a God in Israel,<sup>47</sup>and that all this assembly may know that the LORD saves not with sword and spear. For the battle is the LORD's, and he will give you into our hand."<sup>48</sup>When the Philistine arose and came and drew near to meet David, David ran quickly toward the battle line to meet the Philistine.<sup>49</sup>And David put his hand in his bag and took out a stone and slung it and struck the Philistine on his forehead. The stone sank into his forehead, and he fell on his face to the ground.<sup>50</sup>So David prevailed over the Philistine with a sling and with a stone, and struck the Philistine and killed him. There was no sword in the hand of David.<sup>51</sup>Then David ran and stood over the Philistine and took his sword and drew it out of its sheath and killed him and cut off his head with it. When the Philistines saw that their champion was dead, they fled.<sup>52</sup>And the men of Israel and Judah rose with a shout and pursued the Philistines as far as Gath and the gates of Ekron, so that the wounded Philistines fell on the way from Shaaraim as far as Gath and Ekron.<sup>53</sup>And the people of Israel came back from chasing the Philistines, and they plundered their camp.<sup>54</sup>And David took the head of the Philistine and brought it to Jerusalem, but he put his armor in his tent.<sup>55</sup>As soon as Saul saw David go out against the Philistine, he said to Abner, the commander of the army, "Abner, whose son is this youth?" And Abner said, "As your soul lives, O king, I do not know."<sup>56</sup>And the king said, "Inquire whose son the boy is."<sup>57</sup>And as soon as David returned from the striking down of the Philistine, Abner took him, and brought him before Saul with the head of the Philistine in his hand.<sup>58</sup>And Saul said to him, "Whose son are you, young man?" And David answered, "I am the son of your servant Jesse the Bethlehemite."
17.overview:
Two armies face each other across the valley of Elah, and a Philistine champion comes out every morning and evening to challenge Israel to single combat. Nobody goes down to meet him, not even Saul, the king Israel asked for so that he would fight its battles. After forty days a shepherd boy arrives on an errand for his father, hears the challenge, and asks the question nobody else has asked: who is this man, to defy the armies of the living God?

His brother scorns him, the king doubts him and the giant laughs at him. David goes down with a sling and five stones, trusting the God who had delivered him before, and the giant falls. The chapter is the best-known story in the Old Testament, and its shape is the shape of the gospel: one champion fights alone for a people who cannot fight for themselves, and they share in a victory they did nothing to win.
17.theology:
The living God (v. 26). The question in this valley was never whether a boy can beat a giant. It is whether the God whose armies these are is alive, and David is the only person in the chapter who frames it that way.

Arguing from the record (v. 37). David's confidence rests on what God has already done, not on his own nerve. That kind of reasoning requires no special temperament, only a memory and the honesty to keep the record.

Untested armour (v. 39). The best equipment in the kingdom, offered kindly, would have got him killed. God's servants are sent out with what he has trained them to use.

The battle is the LORD's (v. 47). This does not mean David can stay on the hill. It means the outcome is not decided by the inventory of verses 5 to 7, and it is a word for people who are about to act, not for people standing still.

The champion, and how to read this chapter. Two nations, one representative each, and whatever happens to him happens to everybody. That is how the chapter is built, and the closing comment on vv. 55-58 follows it to its end in Christ.
17.examples:
Then: An army stood on a hillside for six weeks under a giant's taunts, with a generous reward on offer that nobody claimed, until a shepherd on an errand asked why nobody had answered him.

Now: Three things. First, verse 37 is the most transferable sentence in the chapter, and it is not about courage: David reasoned from what God had actually done, in private, years earlier, with nobody watching. Keep the record; you will want it. Second, verse 39: when somebody offers you their armour, the question is not whether it is good but whether you have ever moved in it. And third, verse 28. Eliab's attack was a claim to know a motive, and it was confident and false, and David did not argue with it, correct it, or produce the one fact that would have ended it. He turned and asked somebody else the same question. All three are easier for someone who knows the battle has already been won for him: the Son of David has fought the enemy we could not face, and his Spirit gives his people the courage to walk into the valleys that are ours to walk.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Two armies face each other across the valley of Elah (vv. 1-3). A Philistine champion comes out, itemised like an inventory (vv. 4-7), and proposes single combat, winner takes the nation (vv. 8-10). Saul and all Israel are dismayed and greatly afraid (v. 11).
verseByVerse.theology: The scene is set up so that, by any human reckoning, Israel has no answer.
verseByVerse.examples: Watch whose name comes first among the frightened in v. 11.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the Philistines gathered their armies for battle. And they were gathered at Socoh, which belongs to Judah, and encamped between Socoh and Azekah, in Ephes-dammim. And Saul and the men of Israel were gathered, and encamped in the Valley of Elah, and drew up in line of battle against the Philistines. And the Philistines stood on the mountain on the one side, and Israel stood on the mountain on the other side, with a valley between them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two armies face each other from two hills, and neither will come down.

That is why nothing happens for six weeks. Whoever descends into the valley of Elah gives up the high ground and attacks uphill. Neither commander will do it, so the two forces sit and look at each other across a few hundred yards of open ground.

The place names are real and the country is still there. Socoh and Azekah are on the western edge of the Judean hills, where the highlands drop towards the Philistine plain, and the valley of Elah is one of the roads into Judah. This is a fight about a doorway.
verseByVerse.note: The Valley of Elah lies about 15 miles south-west of Jerusalem.

verseByVerse.quote: And there came out from the camp of the Philistines a champion named Goliath of Gath, whose height was six cubits and a span. He had a helmet of bronze on his head, and he was armed with a coat of mail, and the weight of the coat was five thousand shekels of bronze. And he had bronze armor on his legs, and a javelin of bronze slung between his shoulders. The shaft of his spear was like a weaver's beam, and his spear's head weighed six hundred shekels of iron. And his shield-bearer went before him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A word about the number, once, and then it can be left alone.

Six cubits and a span is about nine feet nine inches, and that is what the Hebrew text has. The oldest Greek translation, a Dead Sea scroll of Samuel and Josephus all read four cubits and a span, which is about six feet nine. The ESV prints six, and the difference does not affect anything in the chapter: the average man of that time and place stood around five feet three, so either figure describes somebody who towers over every soldier on the field.

The narrator takes an inventory like a quartermaster: a bronze helmet; a coat of mail weighing five thousand shekels, something over a hundred and twenty pounds of metal, worn; bronze greaves on the legs; a bronze javelin slung across his back; and a spear with a shaft the thickness of a weaver's beam and a head of fifteen pounds of iron.

Count the material. There is bronze four times, and iron once, and iron is the point of the spear. Israel, we were told four chapters ago, has no blacksmith in the entire country, and two swords in its whole army (13:19-22). The man coming down the hill is carrying more metal on his body than Israel's army possesses.

The last item on the list is a person: the giant does not carry his own shield; a man walks in front of him holding it. The description is designed to do to the reader exactly what the sight of him did to the army, and it works. By the end of verse 7 there is no sensible answer to this man.

Who killed Goliath? Second Samuel 21:19 says Elhanan struck down Goliath the Gittite, but 1 Chronicles 20:5 says Elhanan killed Lahmi the brother of Goliath. The text of 2 Samuel was most likely damaged in copying, and David killed Goliath, as this chapter says.
verseByVerse.note: Goliath came from Gath (v. 4), one of the five Philistine cities, where the ark had once brought plague on the town (5:8-9).

verseByVerse.quote: He stood and shouted to the ranks of Israel, "Why have you come out to draw up for battle? Am I not a Philistine, and are you not servants of Saul? Choose a man for yourselves, and let him come down to me. If he is able to fight with me and kill me, then we will be your servants. But if I prevail against him and kill him, then you shall be our servants and serve us." And the Philistine said, "I defy the ranks of Israel this day. Give me a man, that we may fight together." When Saul and all Israel heard these words of the Philistine, they were dismayed and greatly afraid.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Single combat was a recognised way of settling a war. Rather than two armies destroying each other, each side puts up a champion and the nations abide by the result. It saved lives, and it worked because both sides believed the outcome expressed something more than muscle.

Note how he describes Israel: are you not servants of Saul? He does not call them servants of the LORD. He defines them by their king, which is precisely what they asked to be defined by in chapter 8, and it is exactly the wrong description, as David will point out in eighteen verses.

The stakes are the nation. Keep the shape of it, because it is the shape of the whole story: a single representative stands for everybody, and what happens to him happens to them.

The verb to follow through the chapter is I defy. It means to taunt, to reproach, to hold up to contempt. It comes back in verse 25, twice on David's lips in verses 26 and 36, and finally in his speech to Goliath himself: the God of the armies of Israel, whom you have defied (v. 45). Everybody uses the word. The question of the chapter is who is being defied.

Here is the answer to chapter 8, and the name at the front of the sentence is the point. Saul, who stood head and shoulders above everyone else (9:2), was requested so that he might go out before us and fight our battles (8:20). There is a man in this army closer to Goliath's size than anybody else in the country, and he is listed first among the frightened.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The narrator reintroduces David, going back and forth between court and sheep (vv. 12-15), while the Philistine comes out morning and evening for forty days (v. 16). Jesse sends David with provisions for his brothers (vv. 17-18). David leaves the sheep with a keeper, arrives as the army goes out shouting, leaves the supplies with the baggage-keeper and runs to the ranks (vv. 19-22).
verseByVerse.theology: The narrator pauses the standoff to reintroduce David, as if we had never met him.
verseByVerse.examples: Nobody in the chapter is less obviously a hero than the supply runner who arrives in v. 20.

verseByVerse.quote: Now David was the son of an Ephrathite of Bethlehem in Judah, named Jesse, who had eight sons. In the days of Saul the man was already old and advanced in years. The three oldest sons of Jesse had followed Saul to the battle. And the names of his three sons who went to the battle were Eliab the firstborn, and next to him Abinadab, and the third Shammah. David was the youngest. The three eldest followed Saul, but David went back and forth from Saul to feed his father's sheep at Bethlehem. For forty days the Philistine came forward and took his stand, morning and evening.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The narrator stops the battle and reintroduces David as though we had not met him. Chapter 16 showed us the anointing and the court; this chapter starts him again from the village, because the whole point of what follows is that nobody at the valley of Elah knows who he is.

Verse 15 holds the two chapters together. David is not a permanent fixture at court. He went back and forth, up to Gibeah when the king needed music, home to Bethlehem when he did not. He is a part-time musician and a full-time shepherd, and at this moment he is at home.

Twice a day for forty days is eighty times. Every morning the army of Israel forms up, and the giant walks out and shouts, and they go back to their tents. Every evening the same happens, for nearly six weeks.

Forty is the number of testing in this literature: forty days of rain, forty years in the wilderness, forty days on the mountain, and forty days in another wilderness a thousand years later. This is Israel's examination, conducted twice daily in public, and the nation is failing it.

There is something worse in the repetition than in the threat. A crisis that lasts an afternoon can be survived by nerve. Six weeks of it is long enough for fear to become a routine, for a whole army to organise its day around a humiliation and simply live with it.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesse said to David his son, "Take for your brothers an ephah of this parched grain, and these ten loaves, and carry them quickly to the camp to your brothers. Also take these ten cheeses to the commander of their thousand. See if your brothers are well, and bring some token from them." Now Saul and they and all the men of Israel were in the Valley of Elah, fighting with the Philistines. And David rose early in the morning and left the sheep with a keeper and took the provisions and went, as Jesse had commanded him. And he came to the encampment as the host was going out to the battle line, shouting the war cry. And Israel and the Philistines drew up for battle, army against army. And David left the things in charge of the keeper of the baggage and ran to the ranks and went and greeted his brothers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everything in the errand is ordinary. There are twenty pounds of roasted grain and ten loaves for the boys, and ten cheeses for their commanding officer, which is a father sweetening the man his sons serve under. And then the real request, which is why he is sending anybody at all: see if your brothers are well, and bring some token from them.

He wants proof they are alive. And David rose early. He left the sheep with a keeper; he does not simply walk off and leave them, and this fact will matter in eight verses when his brother accuses him of exactly that. And he went as Jesse had commanded him.

The young man who has been anointed king of Israel is running an errand for his father and doing it properly.

He arrives as the army is forming up and shouting. Mark the war cry, because it is the same noise Israel made when the ark arrived at Aphek, a shout that made the earth resound, from an army that lost thirty thousand men in the battle that followed (4:5, 10). Israel is good at the shouting.

He hands over the supplies to the man whose job it is, and runs: the second time in three verses that he has made proper arrangements for something in his care before doing the next thing. And there is a small irony in the location: the last person this book found among the baggage was Saul, hiding from his own coronation (10:22). David drops his parcels there and goes forward.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–30 — The Armies of the Living God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: David sees the army flee from Goliath (vv. 23-24) and hears of the reward (v. 25). He asks what will be done for the man who kills him, and who this uncircumcised Philistine is to defy the armies of the living God (v. 26). Eliab's anger flares and he claims to know David's heart (v. 28). David answers mildly and turns to somebody else (vv. 29-30).
verseByVerse.theology: David's first recorded words in the Bible contain two questions, and the second changes the chapter.
verseByVerse.examples: Eliab's accusation in v. 28 is confident, personal and false: v. 20 says David left the sheep with a keeper.

verseByVerse.quote: As he talked with them, behold, the champion, the Philistine of Gath, Goliath by name, came up out of the ranks of the Philistines and spoke the same words as before. And David heard him. All the men of Israel, when they saw the man, fled from him and were much afraid. And the men of Israel said, "Have you seen this man who has come up? Surely he has come up to defy Israel. And the king will enrich the man who kills him with great riches and will give him his daughter and make his father's house free in Israel." And David said to the men who stood by him, "What shall be done for the man who kills this Philistine and takes away the reproach from Israel? For who is this uncircumcised Philistine, that he should defy the armies of the living God?" And the people answered him in the same way, "So shall it be done to the man who kills him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The flight of the army establishes that David sees exactly what everybody else sees. He is not spared the sight, and he is not too young to understand it. The giant comes out, the army of Israel breaks and runs, and a teenager who has just left his provisions with the baggage-keeper watches his nation flee.

The reward is substantial, money, the king's daughter and tax exemption for the man's household, and it is common knowledge in the ranks and nobody has taken it. The prize has been on offer for weeks, and every day men have decided it is not enough.

These are the first words David speaks in the Bible, and there are two questions in them. The first is practical: what does the man get? He asks it first, and again in verse 30, while an army is too frightened to move. Was he in it for the prize? The narrator does not say so, does not criticise him, and that silence is the answer. The reward had been publicly offered by the king; wanting it was not shameful, and a young man might reasonably be interested. What the chapter shows is that the prize was on offer to every soldier in Israel for six weeks and not one of them took it, which means the reward was never what was lacking.

Scripture is generally more relaxed about mixed motives than we are. Moses was looking to the reward (Heb. 11:26), and the Lord himself endured the cross for the joy that was set before him (Heb. 12:2). Wanting what God has attached to obedience is not mercenary. It becomes mercenary when it is the only thing in the sentence, and here it is followed at once by something nobody in that valley had said aloud in forty days.

The second question is the one that changes the chapter. Everybody at the valley of Elah has been doing arithmetic for six weeks: nine feet tall, a hundred and twenty-five pounds of bronze, a fifteen-pound spearhead, forty days, two armies. The sums have been done and re-done and they come out the same way every time.

David does a different sum entirely, and it has two terms in it that nobody else has been using. The man is uncircumcised: outside the covenant, with no claim on anybody. And the army he is shouting at belongs to the living God.

That phrase is the hinge. David does not say “our God” or “the God of Israel”, but the God who is alive, which in this book is a loaded word. The last god to be mentioned in these pages, Dagon of the Philistines, had to be picked up off the floor of his own temple by his own priests, and then his head and hands were found on the doorstep (5:3-4).

So the question is not whether a boy can beat a giant. It is whether the God whose armies these are is alive. David has framed it correctly and everybody else has framed it wrongly, and that is the whole difference between him and the army.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Eliab his eldest brother heard when he spoke to the men. And Eliab's anger was kindled against David, and he said, "Why have you come down? And with whom have you left those few sheep in the wilderness? I know your presumption and the evil of your heart, for you have come down to see the battle." And David said, "What have I done now? Was it not but a word?" And he turned away from him toward another, and spoke in the same way, and the people answered him again as before.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Every part of Eliab's attack repays taking apart. First, who is speaking. Eliab is the son Samuel looked at and thought surely the LORD's anointed is before him, and God said no, and gave the reason (16:6-7). He was in the room when the oil was poured on his youngest brother's head.

Second, the sneer: those few sheep in the wilderness. It is contempt for the job, and through the job for the boy. And it is inaccurate as well as unkind; David left the flock with a keeper before he came (v. 20).

Third, and this is the extraordinary part: I know your presumption and the evil of your heart.

Read that against 16:7, where God told Samuel that man looks on the outward appearance but the LORD looks on the heart. Eliab claims to have done the one thing that verse says belongs to God alone, and he claims it about the brother God actually chose, having himself been passed over on exactly that ground.

It is a very common form of attack and it is unanswerable by design. It does not say “you are wrong”, which can be discussed, but “I know why you are really doing this”: a claim about motive, made confidently, by somebody who cannot possibly know.

Something else is probably underneath it. Eliab is a soldier who has stood in this valley for forty days and not gone down. His little brother has been here twenty minutes and is asking why nobody has dealt with the Philistine. Anger of that kind usually has shame somewhere behind it.

The answer is mild, and the small word in the middle tells a story: what have I done now? That is the sentence of a younger brother with some history, somebody used to being the one at fault, who knows this tone of voice.

There is no self-defence, no correction of the falsehood about the sheep, no mention of the anointing, which would have ended the argument permanently. He says he only asked a question, and turns round and asks somebody else the same thing. He does not win the argument with Eliab, and he does not leave. He simply declines to be diverted by it and goes back to the question that matters.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 31–40 — I Cannot Go With These
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Saul sends for David, who offers to fight (vv. 31-32). Saul refuses: he is only a youth (v. 33). David answers with the lion and the bear, and argues that the LORD who delivered him then will deliver him now (vv. 34-37). He cannot walk in Saul's armour, which he has not tested (vv. 38-39), and takes his staff, five smooth stones and his sling (v. 40).
verseByVerse.theology: David's case to Saul in v. 37 rests on what God has done, not on what David can do.
verseByVerse.examples: David goes into the fight with what he knows how to use.

verseByVerse.quote: When the words that David spoke were heard, they repeated them before Saul, and he sent for him. And David said to Saul, "Let no man's heart fail because of him. Your servant will go and fight with this Philistine." And Saul said to David, "You are not able to go against this Philistine to fight with him, for you are but a youth, and he has been a man of war from his youth."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Word reaches the king. Before he volunteers, he addresses the morale of the army, which is a strange thing for a teenage supply runner to say to a king, and it is the sentence of somebody who has been watching men be afraid and thinks it unnecessary.

Saul makes exactly the assessment chapter 16 warned about. He looks at David and measures him: too young, insufficiently experienced, physically outmatched by a professional. Every word of it is true, and it is the same instrument that had approved of Saul himself (height, bearing, obvious capacity) and that God had refused to use at Bethlehem.

Note also the phrase he ends on: a man of war from his youth. It is a soldier's verdict, and it is being pronounced by a king who has not gone down into that valley either.

verseByVerse.quote: But David said to Saul, "Your servant used to keep sheep for his father. And when there came a lion, or a bear, and took a lamb from the flock, I went after him and struck him and delivered it out of his mouth. And if he arose against me, I caught him by his beard and struck him and killed him. Your servant has struck down both lions and bears, and this uncircumcised Philistine shall be like one of them, for he has defied the armies of the living God." And David said, "The LORD who delivered me from the paw of the lion and from the paw of the bear will deliver me from the hand of this Philistine." And Saul said to David, "Go, and the LORD be with you!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
David answers the objection with his job. Saul has said he is a shepherd rather than a soldier, as though those were opposites, and David explains what shepherding actually involved. A predator takes a lamb; the shepherd goes after it, strikes it, and takes the animal out of its mouth. If it turns on him, he catches it by the beard and kills it.

Read that slowly, because familiarity has flattened it. He put his hand into a lion's mouth for one sheep, and he did it more than once, and he did it for animals that were not his: your servant used to keep sheep for his father.

It is the answer to those few sheep in the wilderness, and the man who will write the LORD is my shepherd learned the trade at the sharp end. And the reason he puts the giant in the same category as an animal is not confidence but the defying.

He does not say “I killed a lion, therefore I can kill a Philistine”. Look at the subject of the verb. The LORD who delivered me... will deliver me. The lion and the bear are not evidence about David's strength; they are evidence about God's record.

That is the logic of Ebenezer. After God routed the Philistines at Mizpah, Samuel set up a stone between Mizpah and Shen and named it Ebenezer, “stone of help”, saying till now the LORD has helped us (7:12). It was not a prediction, but a fact placed in the landscape so that the next time trouble came there would be something to argue from.

David is arguing from his own two remembered deliverances, in a field, with nobody watching, years ago. What has God actually done? Start there, and reason forward. The king lets him go, with a blessing.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Saul clothed David with his armor. He put a helmet of bronze on his head and clothed him with a coat of mail, and David strapped his sword over his armor. And he tried in vain to go, for he had not tested them. Then David said to Saul, "I cannot go with these, for I have not tested them." So David put them off. Then he took his staff in his hand and chose five smooth stones from the brook and put them in his shepherd's pouch. His sling was in his hand, and he approached the Philistine.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Saul dresses him in his own equipment, kindly and absurdly. Saul is the tallest man in Israel. The armour is built for a body a head and shoulders above everybody else, and it is being fastened onto a teenager.

Note the detail: David strapped his sword over his armor. That is one of the two swords in the entire army (13:22).

He cannot walk in it, and the objection is not size but unfamiliarity. Whatever the protection is worth, he has never moved in it, and a man about to fight for his life is not going to learn a new set of equipment on the way down the hill.

It is a small scene with a large principle in it. David has just argued from what God has done through him before, with what he knows how to use. Saul offers him the best equipment in the kingdom and it would have killed him.

Every item he takes instead is a shepherd's: staff, pouch, sling, and ammunition out of the water. His weapons come from the brook rather than the armoury.

Something should be said about the sling, because a modern reader hears something a child plays with. It was a serious military weapon and every army had specialists in it. Judges has already described some: Benjamin fielded seven hundred picked left-handed slingers who could sling a stone at a hair and not miss (Judg. 20:16). A stone from a practised sling travels fast enough to kill at a distance, and it far outranges the one distance weapon Goliath is carrying, the javelin slung between his shoulders (v. 6). That means the boy with no armour is the one man in that valley who never has to come within reach of a fifteen-pound spearhead.

A last word about the five, since people ask. The text does not say why. The suggestion that Goliath had four brothers is a guess built on a much later verse (2 Sam. 21:22), and the simplest answer is that a slinger carries spares. Nothing in the chapter turns on it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 41–47 — The Battle Is the LORD's
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Goliath comes on, sees David, and disdains him as ruddy and handsome in appearance (vv. 41-42), cursing him by his gods (vv. 43-44). David answers that he comes in the name of the LORD of hosts, so that all the earth and all this assembly may know that the battle is the LORD's (vv. 45-47).
verseByVerse.theology: Goliath is the third man in this chapter to misjudge David by what his eyes can see.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 47 puts the message of the whole book into a single sentence.

verseByVerse.quote: And the Philistine moved forward and came near to David, with his shield-bearer in front of him. And when the Philistine looked and saw David, he disdained him, for he was but a youth, ruddy and handsome in appearance. And the Philistine said to David, "Am I a dog, that you come to me with sticks?" And the Philistine cursed David by his gods. The Philistine said to David, "Come to me, and I will give your flesh to the birds of the air and to the beasts of the field."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The shield-bearer is mentioned again, and by now it is almost comic. And ruddy and handsome in appearance is what the narrator wrote when the boy was brought in from the sheep for Samuel to look at: he was ruddy and had beautiful eyes and was handsome (16:12).

Goliath looks at David and sees exactly what the text told us was there, and draws the wrong conclusion, because he is reading appearance.

That makes three men in one chapter. Eliab looked at him and saw presumption. Saul looked at him and saw a youth who was not able. Goliath looks at him and sees somebody not worth the trouble. Every assessment in this chapter is made by the eyes, and every one is wrong, and the reader has been told why since 16:7.

He sees the staff and not the sling. David is carrying a shepherd's staff in one hand and a sling in the other, and the giant registers the stick. A man in full bronze armour looks down at what he assumes is a boy come to shoo him like an animal.

Then he curses him by his gods.

Remember the threat, because David is about to hand it back with the plural changed.

verseByVerse.quote: Then David said to the Philistine, "You come to me with a sword and with a spear and with a javelin, but I come to you in the name of the LORD of hosts, the God of the armies of Israel, whom you have defied. This day the LORD will deliver you into my hand, and I will strike you down and cut off your head. And I will give the dead bodies of the host of the Philistines this day to the birds of the air and to the wild beasts of the earth, that all the earth may know that there is a God in Israel, and that all this assembly may know that the LORD saves not with sword and spear.
