For the battle is the LORD's, and he will give you into our hand."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The great speech is built on a single contrast, three weapons against one name: Goliath's inventory is recited back to him, sword, spear, javelin, and set against the name of the LORD of hosts.

That title has a history in this book, and this is where it arrives at its destination. It appeared for the first time in the whole Bible in a sentence about an ordinary man walking up to Shiloh once a year (1:3). The first person recorded praying by it was a childless woman asking for a baby (1:11). And now it is a war cry in a valley, shouted a few decades later at an armoured champion.

LORD of hosts means the LORD of armies, of every army there is, in heaven and on earth. David is telling a professional soldier that he has miscounted the forces present.

The last clause identifies the actual offence: the God of the armies of Israel, whom you have defied. The taunting was aimed at God, not merely at Israel's honour, whatever Goliath thought he was doing.

He returns the threat, enlarged from one body to an army. Note the order of the verbs, because it is the theology of the whole speech in miniature. The LORD will deliver you into my hand, and I will strike you down. God does the delivering; the boy does the striking. Both are in the sentence and neither swallows the other.

Two purposes, two audiences. One is what you would expect: that all the earth may know that there is a God in Israel. The nations are watching, and the question raised by weeks of unanswered blasphemy is whether Israel's God is real.

Then that all this assembly may know: his own side, standing behind him on the hill, needs to learn that the battle is the LORD's. With that a set of three is complete, the spine of this book. Hannah sang the first, in a corrupt sanctuary, with no war on and nobody listening, having just handed over a toddler: the bows of the mighty are broken, but the feeble bind on strength... not by might shall a man prevail (2:4, 9).

Jonathan said the second at the bottom of a cliff with one servant and no promise: nothing can hinder the LORD from saving by many or by few (14:6). David says the third in a valley, in front of two armies. Three people, none of them in authority, a countrywoman, a king's son acting without orders, and a shepherd on an errand, say the same thing across fifteen chapters while the nation asks for a king to fight its battles.

The last clause turns the whole thing round: he will give you into our hand. David is about to fight alone, and he says the victory belongs to everybody on the hill behind him.

Ask what the battle is the LORD's actually meant that afternoon, because it is a sentence Christians say about situations in which nothing then happens.

It did not mean David could stay on the hill. Three verses from now he runs at an armoured man with a leather strap and a stone, and if the stone misses he dies. Nothing about the LORD's ownership of the battle removed one step of the walk down into that valley.

What it meant was that the outcome was not being decided by the inventory in verses 5 to 7. David still had to sling; God decided where the stone went. It is not an alternative to acting but a statement about who determines what the acting produces, which is why it could be said by a man about to run at a giant and could not be said by an army standing still.

Does this chapter teach us to face our giants? David is not first a model for our courage; he is the anointed champion who fights for a terrified people, as Christ fought for us. Our part is Israel’s: to trust the one who won the battle. The battle is the LORD’s does not mean sitting back, but trusting God as we obey.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 48–54 — There Was No Sword in the Hand of David
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: David runs to meet the Philistine; the stone sinks into his forehead and he falls on his face (vv. 48-49). There is no sword in David's hand, so he kills him with Goliath's own (vv. 50-51). Israel pursues and plunders the camp (vv. 52-53), and David takes the head to Jerusalem (v. 54).
verseByVerse.theology: The fight that six weeks of dread had built up is over in a single verse.
verseByVerse.examples: Notice whose sword finishes the giant.

verseByVerse.quote: When the Philistine arose and came and drew near to meet David, David ran quickly toward the battle line to meet the Philistine. And David put his hand in his bag and took out a stone and slung it and struck the Philistine on his forehead. The stone sank into his forehead, and he fell on his face to the ground. So David prevailed over the Philistine with a sling and with a stone, and struck the Philistine and killed him. There was no sword in the hand of David. Then David ran and stood over the Philistine and took his sword and drew it out of its sheath and killed him and cut off his head with it. When the Philistines saw that their champion was dead, they fled.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He runs at him. Day after day the men of Israel have looked at this man and gone backwards; verse 24 says they fled from him. The first movement David makes is forward, and it is fast.

Tactically it is also right. A slinger needs distance and needs to be moving; the last thing he wants is to let an armoured man close on him slowly. But the writer is not reporting tactics. He is reporting that one person on that field advanced.

Five verbs and it is over: put, took, slung, struck, sank. For all the helmet, the coat of mail and the shield carried before him by another man, the stone found his forehead. And the reader of this book has seen a Philistine fall on his face before. Twice, in the temple at Ashdod, the Philistines came in the morning and found Dagon fallen face downward on the ground before the ark of the LORD (5:3-4). The second time his head was off.

Philistia's god went down on his face in front of the LORD, and lost his head. Philistia's champion goes down on his face in front of the LORD's anointed, and loses his.

The narrator stops to say there was no sword in David's hand, and he did not have to. The one sword David had been offered he took off with Saul's armour.

The nation that had no blacksmith did not need one.

He finishes it with Goliath's own sword. The weapon that was going to take David's head takes Goliath's. The man had promised to give the boy's flesh to the birds, and the instrument of that promise is drawn out of its sheath by the boy and used on him.

The Bible comes back to that shape at the very end. Christ shared our flesh and blood that through death he might destroy the one who has the power of death, that is, the devil (Heb. 2:14). Death was the thing held over everybody's head, and it was through death that the one holding it was undone.
verseByVerse.note: The text does not say how the stone got past the helmet; it says only that it found the one place that mattered.

verseByVerse.quote: And the men of Israel and Judah rose with a shout and pursued the Philistines as far as Gath and the gates of Ekron, so that the wounded Philistines fell on the way from Shaaraim as far as Gath and Ekron. And the people of Israel came back from chasing the Philistines, and they plundered their camp. And David took the head of the Philistine and brought it to Jerusalem, but he put his armor in his tent.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the army moves. They have been standing on that hill for six weeks. One man went down and won, and the whole force rises with a shout and chases a beaten enemy west to the gates of their own cities.

The text carries no criticism of them, and there should not be much in the reading either. This is how it works: the champion fights, and the people enter into what he won. They did nothing to earn the victory and they share in it entirely, and the pursuit is real work and theirs to do.

They take the spoil, which none of them fought for. Then two objects and two destinations, and one is a surprise. Jerusalem at this moment is not Israelite. It is a Jebusite town that Benjamin failed to take in the first chapter of Judges and that will not be captured for another generation, when this same man walks up and takes it and makes it his capital (2 Sam. 5:6-9). Why bring the head there? The text does not say. Perhaps the writer means where it finally came to rest once Jerusalem was David's city, or perhaps it was shown at a hostile town's gate as a warning; it is wiser to leave the puzzle open than to invent an answer.

The armour he keeps. And the sword later turns up at the sanctuary at Nob, wrapped in a cloth behind the ephod, where David will collect it years later when he is running for his life from Saul, and where that visit will cost eighty-five priests their lives (21:8-9; 22:18).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 55–58 — Whose Son Is This Youth?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: As David goes out, Saul asks Abner whose son he is, and Abner does not know (v. 55). The king repeats it: inquire whose son the boy is (v. 56). When David comes back with the head still in his hand, Saul asks him directly, and David answers: I am the son of your servant Jesse the Bethlehemite (vv. 57-58).
verseByVerse.theology: The chapter ends not with a victory speech but with a father's name and a village.
verseByVerse.examples: From this day Saul will keep David at court and not let him go home (18:2).

verseByVerse.quote: As soon as Saul saw David go out against the Philistine, he said to Abner, the commander of the army, "Abner, whose son is this youth?" And Abner said, "As your soul lives, O king, I do not know." And the king said, "Inquire whose son the boy is." And as soon as David returned from the striking down of the Philistine, Abner took him, and brought him before Saul with the head of the Philistine in his hand. And Saul said to him, "Whose son are you, young man?" And David answered, "I am the son of your servant Jesse the Bethlehemite."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The king asks his general who the boy's father is, and the general does not know.

Readers have long noticed that Saul appears not to recognise a young man who was his own armour-bearer in the previous chapter, and it is worth a sentence rather than an argument. The question asked here, three times, is not “who is this” but whose son is this, and there is a reason for it in verse 25, which promised that the man who killed Goliath would have his father's house made free in Israel. Saul needs to know which household to exempt, and Abner, who has not met the family, cannot tell him.

A textual note belongs here. The oldest complete manuscript of the Greek Old Testament (the Septuagint) has a much shorter form of this story, without verses 12 to 31 and 55 to 58 and parts of chapter 18. Many scholars think the Hebrew text has joined two accounts of David's arrival; others think the Greek translators shortened the story to ease the very difficulty readers notice. The Hebrew is the text the church has received, and its parts can be read together sensibly once Saul's question is heard as one about David's father.

Hold the picture as the chapter closes: a teenager walked in to the king by the commander of the army, carrying a severed head, and the last words are a village and a family. He does not mention the anointing, or the lion and the bear; he gives a father's name and a small town in Judah.

Now stand back from the whole chapter, because its shape is the reason it has never been forgotten, and the shape is older and larger than a story about courage.

Two nations stood on two hills, and between them a single man offered terms: one champion each, and whatever happens to him happens to everybody. Israel had no answer. For forty days the whole people stood paralysed by one enemy they could not face, and the arrangement was entirely fair and entirely hopeless.

Then somebody came who was not part of the army. He came from Bethlehem on his father's errand. Nobody recognised him; his own brother despised him; the king assessed him and found him inadequate; the enemy looked at him and laughed. He went out with none of the equipment the situation appeared to require, alone, in front of everybody, and he fought the battle in the name of the LORD and not with a sword. And when he had won it, the people who had contributed nothing rose with a shout and entered into it.

That is not an illustration somebody has imposed on the passage. It is how the passage is built, and it is why the New Testament can speak the way it does about a representative who partook of the same things, that is, our flesh and blood (Heb. 2:14).

The usual way of reading this chapter is that we are David and our problems are Goliath, and that is exactly backwards. In this valley there is only one person who can fight, and everybody else is on the hill. The good news of the passage is not that you can be David. It is that somebody has been. Jesus, the Son of David, went down alone into the valley his people could not enter, and the victory he won is theirs.

18.title: Jonathan's Covenant and Saul's Jealousy
18.text: <sup>1</sup>As soon as he had finished speaking to Saul, the soul of Jonathan was knit to the soul of David, and Jonathan loved him as his own soul.<sup>2</sup>And Saul took him that day and would not let him return to his father's house.<sup>3</sup>Then Jonathan made a covenant with David, because he loved him as his own soul.<sup>4</sup>And Jonathan stripped himself of the robe that was on him and gave it to David, and his armor, and even his sword and his bow and his belt.<sup>5</sup>And David went out and was successful wherever Saul sent him, so that Saul set him over the men of war. And this was good in the sight of all the people and also in the sight of Saul's servants.<sup>6</sup>As they were coming home, when David returned from striking down the Philistine, the women came out of all the cities of Israel, singing and dancing, to meet King Saul, with tambourines, with songs of joy, and with musical instruments.<sup>7</sup>And the women sang to one another as they celebrated, "Saul has struck down his thousands, and David his ten thousands."<sup>8</sup>And Saul was very angry, and this saying displeased him. He said, "They have ascribed to David ten thousands, and to me they have ascribed thousands, and what more can he have but the kingdom?"<sup>9</sup>And Saul eyed David from that day on.<sup>10</sup>The next day a harmful spirit from God rushed upon Saul, and he raved within his house while David was playing the lyre, as he did day by day. Saul had his spear in his hand.<sup>11</sup>And Saul hurled the spear, for he thought, "I will pin David to the wall." But David evaded him twice.<sup>12</sup>Saul was afraid of David because the LORD was with him but had departed from Saul.<sup>13</sup>So Saul removed him from his presence and made him a commander of a thousand. And he went out and came in before the people.<sup>14</sup>And David had success in all his undertakings, for the LORD was with him.<sup>15</sup>And when Saul saw that he had great success, he stood in fearful awe of him.<sup>16</sup>But all Israel and Judah loved David, for he went out and came in before them.<sup>17</sup>Then Saul said to David, "Here is my elder daughter Merab. I will give her to you for a wife. Only be valiant for me and fight the LORD's battles." For Saul thought, "Let not my hand be against him, but let the hand of the Philistines be against him."<sup>18</sup>And David said to Saul, "Who am I, and who are my relatives, my father's clan in Israel, that I should be son-in-law to the king?"<sup>19</sup>But at the time when Merab, Saul's daughter, should have been given to David, she was given to Adriel the Meholathite for a wife.<sup>20</sup>Now Saul's daughter Michal loved David. And they told Saul, and the thing pleased him.<sup>21</sup>Saul thought, "Let me give her to him, that she may be a snare for him and that the hand of the Philistines may be against him." Therefore Saul said to David a second time, "You shall now be my son-in-law."<sup>22</sup>And Saul commanded his servants, "Speak to David in private and say, 'Behold, the king has delight in you, and all his servants love you. Now then become the king's son-in-law.'"<sup>23</sup>And Saul's servants spoke those words in the ears of David. And David said, "Does it seem to you a little thing to become the king's son-in-law, since I am a poor man and have no reputation?"<sup>24</sup>And the servants of Saul told him, "Thus and so did David speak."<sup>25</sup>Then Saul said, "Thus shall you say to David, 'The king desires no bride-price except a hundred foreskins of the Philistines, that he may be avenged of the king's enemies.'" Now Saul thought to make David fall by the hand of the Philistines.<sup>26</sup>And when his servants told David these words, it pleased David well to be the king's son-in-law. Before the time had expired,<sup>27</sup>David arose and went, along with his men, and killed two hundred of the Philistines. And David brought their foreskins, which were given in full number to the king, that he might become the king's son-in-law. And Saul gave him his daughter Michal for a wife.<sup>28</sup>But when Saul saw and knew that the LORD was with David, and that Michal, Saul's daughter, loved him,<sup>29</sup>Saul was even more afraid of David. So Saul was David's enemy continually.<sup>30</sup>Then the commanders of the Philistines came out to battle, and as often as they came out David had more success than all the servants of Saul, so that his name was highly esteemed.
18.overview:
The chapter opens with the crown prince loving David, making a covenant with him, and handing him the robe of the heir and his own sword. Then the women sing, and Saul hears only the arithmetic and reaches, out of jealousy rather than revelation, the correct conclusion: what more can he have but the kingdom? The spear follows, and verse 12 gives the diagnosis of everything after it: the LORD was with David and had departed from Saul.

After that, every device backfires. Promotion makes the country love him; a daughter offered as a snare becomes a wife who saves his life; a bride-price of a hundred Philistine foreskins, designed to kill him, is paid double and early.

The New Testament knows this pattern: the LORD's anointed is loved by the people and hunted by the reigning power. So the rulers in Jerusalem reasoned about Jesus: If we let him go on like this, everyone will believe in him (John 11:48); and the church read Psalm 2's kings who set themselves against the LORD's Anointed as fulfilled in Herod and Pilate (Acts 4:25–27). David's road to the throne runs through suffering, and so does the road of the Son of David. Jonathan shows the right answer to God's chosen King: not to guard your own throne against him, but to give him the robe gladly.
18.theology:
Jonathan's robe (v. 4). The robe runs through the book as the sign of the kingdom: torn from Saul (15:27-28), handed over freely by Jonathan here, and cut in a cave by David, whose heart then struck him for it (24:4-5). What Saul loses by disobedience, Jonathan gives away in love, and David will refuse to seize.

Knowing without yielding (vv. 12, 28). What frightened Saul was not David's ambition but that the LORD was with him. Saul saw that more clearly than anyone, and the knowledge produced only fear, because what he wanted was not God but the position. It is possible to be entirely right about where God is at work and still refuse to bow to it.

Piety used as a weapon (vv. 17, 25). Saul twice dresses murder in good words: the LORD's battles in verse 17, and vengeance on the king's enemies in verse 25. Religious language is never more dangerous than in the mouth of a man who wants someone dead, and the book does not exempt its hero from the warning (see v. 17).
18.examples:
Then: The heir to the throne of Israel took off his robe, his armour and one of the country's only two swords and gave them to the shepherd who was going to replace him — while his father, in the same week, worked out that the same young man would have the kingdom and began watching him with a spear in his hand.

Now: Jonathan is the model nobody imitates: he had everything to lose and handed it over gladly, before being asked, to the person whose rise meant his own eclipse. Ask what you would have to take off. We are more like Saul than we admit, guarding what is ours and souring at another's blessing. But the Son of David laid aside far more than a robe for us (Philippians 2:7), and in him we are already given everything; his Spirit is the one who loosens our grip and makes room for gladness at another's rise. Verse 8 adds a warning about a habit of hearing: a man who can extract an insult from a compliment will never run short of insults.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — He Stripped Himself of the Robe
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jonathan loves David, makes a covenant with him and gives him his robe and weapons (vv. 1-4). David succeeds wherever he is sent, and it pleases everybody (v. 5).
verseByVerse.theology: Jonathan's gift is the first sign that the kingdom will pass to David as a gift freely given, not as a prize seized.
verseByVerse.examples: The covenant made here is the one both men will call on in chapter 20, and David will keep it to Jonathan's son long after both of them are gone (2 Sam. 9).

verseByVerse.quote: As soon as he had finished speaking to Saul, the soul of Jonathan was knit to the soul of David, and Jonathan loved him as his own soul. And Saul took him that day and would not let him return to his father's house. Then Jonathan made a covenant with David, because he loved him as his own soul. And Jonathan stripped himself of the robe that was on him and gave it to David, and his armor, and even his sword and his bow and his belt. And David went out and was successful wherever Saul sent him, so that Saul set him over the men of war. And this was good in the sight of all the people and also in the sight of Saul's servants.
verseByVerse.commentary:
It happens in the room where the last chapter ended, with the head still in David's hand.

Their souls were knit — bound, tied together, the word used of Jacob's life being bound up with Benjamin's (Gen. 44:30). And the measure given twice in five verses is as his own soul: Jonathan loved David the way he loved himself, which is the standard the law sets for loving a neighbour and which almost nobody meets.

Consider who this is. Jonathan is the king's eldest son and the heir to the throne. He is also the man who went up a cliff with one servant and broke a Philistine army while his father sat under a tree. He has every reason to resent the boy who has just done in one day what he did at Michmash, and to see him as a rival for a throne that is his.

The part-time musician becomes a permanent fixture. He no longer goes back and forth to Bethlehem as he did (17:15); he lives at court.

Then Jonathan makes a covenant with him. In this world a covenant was a formal, sworn, binding promise, more like a treaty than a friendship, and it is Jonathan who makes the first move.

It is a remarkable act, and it is performed without a word of explanation.

The robe comes first. In this book a robe stands for an office. Samuel wore one and Saul tore it and was told the LORD has torn the kingdom of Israel from you this day (15:27-28). The heir's robe was probably the visible mark of the succession.

Jonathan takes it off and puts it on David.

Then the rest of the list, and the writer builds it: his armour, and even his sword and his bow and his belt. The even is the narrator's, and it points at the sword.

At Michmash, because the Philistines allowed no blacksmith in the country, only Saul and Jonathan had a sword (13:22). One chapter ago the narrator went out of his way to say there was no sword in the hand of David (17:50).

Jonathan hands him his.

Put the whole gesture together. The crown prince strips off the mark of his succession, his protection and his own sword, and gives them to the young man everybody in the room can see is going to replace him — and he does it out of love, before anybody has asked him for anything.

Everyone else in this book fights over the kingdom. Israel demands it, Saul clings to it and throws spears to keep it, and Jonathan takes his coat off and hands it over. He is the only person in the story who does gladly the thing the others will destroy themselves resisting.

For one verse everybody is pleased, and the writer lists them: the people, the servants, and by implication the king who did the promoting.

It is the last time in this book that everybody is on the same side.

Was the love of David and Jonathan homosexual? Nothing in the text says so, and the suggestion reads a modern category into an ancient covenant. The language of souls knit together is covenant language of loyalty (18:3), the kiss was a normal greeting between men in that culture (cf. 2 Sam 15:5), and both men married. Scripture forbids same-sex intercourse (Lev 18:22); it also honours deep friendship between men, and this is one of its finest examples.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The women's song makes Saul jealous and watchful (vv. 6-9). He hurls a spear at David (vv. 10-11), fears him because the LORD is with him (v. 12), and promotes him away from court, which only makes all Israel and Judah love him (vv. 13-16).
verseByVerse.theology: The section turns on one question Saul asks, what more can he have but the kingdom?, and one fact he cannot change: the LORD was with David (v. 12).
verseByVerse.examples: Notice that David does nothing to win this contest. He plays the lyre, goes where he is sent and comes back; the growth is God's doing, and David's part is to stay faithful in the post he has been given.

verseByVerse.quote: As they were coming home, when David returned from striking down the Philistine, the women came out of all the cities of Israel, singing and dancing, to meet King Saul, with tambourines, with songs of joy, and with musical instruments. And the women sang to one another as they celebrated, "Saul has struck down his thousands, and David his ten thousands." And Saul was very angry, and this saying displeased him. He said, "They have ascribed to David ten thousands, and to me they have ascribed thousands, and what more can he have but the kingdom?" And Saul eyed David from that day on.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The women come out to meet the king, and they come out of every town.

This is what Israel did after a victory: Miriam at the sea, Deborah after the Kishon, Jephthah's daughter at the door. Tambourines and dancing and a song made up for the occasion.

Now look carefully at the song, because everything depends on how it is heard.

It is a victory song for Saul. The women came out to meet King Saul; he is named first; he is credited with thousands. It is, on any ordinary reading, a compliment to the king with a nice line about the young man who killed the champion.

Hebrew poetry also works in pairs that escalate — thousands, then ten thousands — and the second line is often simply a heightening of the first rather than a comparison. The women are not conducting an assessment. They are singing.

Saul hears only the arithmetic.

He reduces a national celebration to a comparison between two numbers, and he gets the numbers the right way round, and he is right that his is the smaller. That is the whole of what he takes from the day.

There is a way of listening that can extract an insult from a compliment, and it is not a failure of hearing. It is a condition of the man doing it.

Then his conclusion, which is a genuine piece of political insight: what more can he have but the kingdom?

He is correct. That is exactly what David is going to have, and it was decided in a Bethlehem courtyard two chapters ago and Saul has no idea. He has arrived at the truth by the wrong road, from jealousy rather than revelation, and it will govern the rest of his life.

Verse 9 is a single clause, and it is the beginning of everything.

The verb means to watch with suspicion, to keep under observation. And in a book that has made so much of eyes — the LORD looks on the heart, man looks on the outward appearance — the king's contribution is a sidelong look that never stops.

From that day on. Not an outburst; a settled practice, beginning on the afternoon of a national celebration and running until the day he dies on Gilboa.

verseByVerse.quote: The next day a harmful spirit from God rushed upon Saul, and he raved within his house while David was playing the lyre, as he did day by day. Saul had his spear in his hand. And Saul hurled the spear, for he thought, "I will pin David to the wall." But David evaded him twice. Saul was afraid of David because the LORD was with him but had departed from Saul.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The verb is the terrible one.

Rushed. It is the word used when the Spirit of the LORD came on Samson, and on Saul at Gibeah, and on Saul at Jabesh when his anger was kindled for a town about to lose its eyes, and on David at his anointing. It is this book's word for God taking hold of a man suddenly.

Here it is used of what fills the space the Spirit left.

Then the detail that says everything about David in this period: he is playing the lyre as he did day by day. This is routine. Every day, the king is tormented, and every day the young man he is watching with suspicion sits down and plays for him.

The last clause is put at the end of the sentence like a loaded gun on a table. Saul had his spear in his hand.

A king's spear was his sceptre — the thing he held while sitting, the mark of office. It is also, at close range, a weapon.

He throws it, and the intention is recorded: to pin a man to a wall like an insect.

The last word matters: twice.

David evaded him twice, which most naturally means that after the first spear he came back. He picked up the lyre, sat down in the same room as the man who had just tried to kill him, and went on playing.

Here is the diagnosis of the entire rest of the book, in one sentence.

Three things are stated. Saul was afraid of David. The LORD was with David. The LORD had departed from Saul.

The middle clause is the cause of the first. It was not David's ambition that frightened him — David has done nothing but win his battles and play for him when he was ill. What frightened Saul was that God was with the young man, and he could see it.

That is a terrible position to be in and it should be named exactly. He is not afraid of the wrong thing. He has correctly identified the most important fact in the situation, which is that the LORD is with David. And the evidence that ought to have brought him to his knees drives him to a spear instead.

A note on the text: the main early manuscript of the Greek Old Testament (the Septuagint) has a shorter form of chapters 17 and 18, without verses 10–11 and 17–19 here among others. Scholars debate whether the translators shortened the story or the Hebrew combines two tellings; our Bibles follow the Hebrew, and nothing the chapter teaches hangs on the difference.

Does God send evil spirits? Saul had rejected God, and God gave him over to a tormenting spirit as judgment (16:14), as he later sent a lying spirit to Ahab (1 Kgs 22:22). God is never the author of sin (Jas 1:13), but even evil spirits are under his rule, and he uses them to judge those who have turned from him.

verseByVerse.quote: So Saul removed him from his presence and made him a commander of a thousand. And he went out and came in before the people. And David had success in all his undertakings, for the LORD was with him. And when Saul saw that he had great success, he stood in fearful awe of him. But all Israel and Judah loved David, for he went out and came in before them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He solves the problem by promoting him, which is what frightened men in authority generally do.

Removing David from court gets him out of the room. Making him a field commander sends him where Philistines are, which is the same calculation Saul will make explicitly in four verses. And he went out and came in before the people is the standard phrase for leading an army in public.

Every measure backfires in the same way, and the narrator gives the reason each time: for the LORD was with him.

Saul now stands in fearful awe of a young officer in his own army. The word is stronger than nervousness; it is dread.

The promotion meant to remove him makes the whole country love him.

Note the two names, kept separate: all Israel and Judah. The book counts them apart at musters and it counts them apart here, and one day the crack will become a border. For the moment both halves love the same man.

Everything Saul does to reduce David enlarges him. He is not being outmanoeuvred by a clever rival; David has made no move at all. He is being defeated by the fact stated in verse 12.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Saul offers Merab, hoping the Philistines will kill David (v. 17). David protests his lowliness (v. 18), and Merab is given to somebody else (v. 19).
verseByVerse.theology: The reward promised at the valley of Elah (17:25) becomes another trap, and then is simply withheld.
verseByVerse.examples: David's humility here is not a pose. He takes the broken promise in silence and leaves his cause with God, as he will for years to come.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Saul said to David, "Here is my elder daughter Merab. I will give her to you for a wife. Only be valiant for me and fight the LORD's battles." For Saul thought, "Let not my hand be against him, but let the hand of the Philistines be against him." And David said to Saul, "Who am I, and who are my relatives, my father's clan in Israel, that I should be son-in-law to the king?" But at the time when Merab, Saul's daughter, should have been given to David, she was given to Adriel the Meholathite for a wife.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The offer is the reward promised at the valley of Elah, and the condition attached to it is a piece of blasphemy.

Fight the LORD's battles. That is the language of this book at its highest — the battle is the LORD's, said in a valley in front of two armies one chapter ago. Saul puts it in a marriage contract as a way of getting a man killed.

The narrator opens the king's head and shows us what is in it.

The calculation is precise and it is the calculation of a coward: not "I will not kill him" but "my hand must not be the one". He wants the outcome and not the responsibility.

It is exactly what David will one day arrange for Uriah, and he will do it, and it will be the ruin of his house (2 Sam. 11:15). This book does not spare anybody.

David's answer is Saul's own sentence.

When Samuel first hinted at the kingdom, the young man from Gibeah said: am I not a Benjaminite, from the least of the tribes of Israel? And is not my clan the humblest of all the clans of the tribe of Benjamin? (9:21).

Family, clan, insignificance. The same protest, from the same kind of young man — and the one who made it first is now sitting on the other side of the room calculating how to have him killed.

Then the promise is simply broken, publicly, at the appointed time.

There is no explanation. The girl who was promised to the national hero in front of the army is married to somebody else on the day, and David says nothing about it.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Saul offers Michal as a snare and names a deadly bride-price (vv. 20-25). David pays double (vv. 26-27), and Saul, seeing the LORD is with him, fears him more (vv. 28-30).
verseByVerse.theology: Saul's last scheme in the chapter uses his own daughter, and like the others it turns against him: Michal's love for David will save his life in the next chapter (19:11-17).
verseByVerse.examples: The schemes grow steadily darker, from a spear to a broken promise to a daughter used as bait, and every one ends in David's greater honour.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Saul's daughter Michal loved David. And they told Saul, and the thing pleased him. Saul thought, "Let me give her to him, that she may be a snare for him and that the hand of the Philistines may be against him." Therefore Saul said to David a second time, "You shall now be my son-in-law." And Saul commanded his servants, "Speak to David in private and say, 'Behold, the king has delight in you, and all his servants love you. Now then become the king's son-in-law.'" And Saul's servants spoke those words in the ears of David. And David said, "Does it seem to you a little thing to become the king's son-in-law, since I am a poor man and have no reputation?" And the servants of Saul told him, "Thus and so did David speak." Then Saul said, "Thus shall you say to David, 'The king desires no bride-price except a hundred foreskins of the Philistines, that he may be avenged of the king's enemies.'" Now Saul thought to make David fall by the hand of the Philistines.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two sentences, and everything wrong with this household is between them.

Michal loved David. The phrase is small and it is unusual: the narrator states a woman's love for a man, which he almost never does in these histories. He puts it down plainly and without decoration.

Her father is pleased — not because his daughter is happy, but for the reason the next verse gives.

The word is snare.

It is a loaded word in these books. God used it at Bochim about the gods Israel refused to drive out — their gods shall be a snare to you (Judg. 2:3). It is what Gideon's golden ephod became to him and his family (Judg. 8:27). It is the word for the thing that catches you.

Saul applies it to his own daughter, in his own thoughts, about the man she loves. Anyone who has been used by a parent as a pawn may see that Scripture names the thing for what it is, and lays the blame on the father, not the child.

He runs it through intermediaries, with a script, and the script is all warmth.

The king delights in you. All his servants love you. Neither statement is true of the man who wrote it, and both are being said by employees who have been told what to say.

David's objection is money and standing.

A marriage required a bride-price, and a royal marriage required a considerable one. He says he is poor and — literally — lightly esteemed, which is a striking thing for the most celebrated soldier in Israel to say about himself, and it uses the same root as the word in the man of God's oracle to Eli for those who despise God and are lightly esteemed in return (2:30).

Saul names a price designed to be fatal.

The demand is grotesque and it is meant to be. A hundred Philistine foreskins cannot be collected at a distance; every one requires a man dead at close quarters and then handled. It is a hundred separate opportunities to be killed. Foreskins, grim as it is, were probably chosen because only they proved the dead were uncircumcised Philistines, and the narrator states the purpose in the last sentence so that nobody misses it.

Note the pretext: that he may be avenged of the king's enemies. He is dressing an assassination as patriotism, exactly as he dressed it as piety in verse 17.

verseByVerse.quote: And when his servants told David these words, it pleased David well to be the king's son-in-law. Before the time had expired, David arose and went, along with his men, and killed two hundred of the Philistines. And David brought their foreskins, which were given in full number to the king, that he might become the king's son-in-law. And Saul gave him his daughter Michal for a wife. But when Saul saw and knew that the LORD was with David, and that Michal, Saul's daughter, loved him, Saul was even more afraid of David. So Saul was David's enemy continually. Then the commanders of the Philistines came out to battle, and as often as they came out David had more success than all the servants of Saul, so that his name was highly esteemed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He brings double, and early.

A hundred was the price. David delivers two hundred and does it before the deadline, which tells us something about the young man and also removes any possibility of dispute over the count.

Note along with his men. David has men now. The commander of a thousand has a following of his own, and that fact will matter for the next twelve chapters.

Given in full number to the king. They are counted out in front of him.

The scene is deliberately grim. A king who wanted a young man dead has to sit and watch two hundred proofs that he is not, counted onto the floor, and then hand over his daughter.

Here is the mechanism of his ruin, stated as plainly as it can be.

It is the strangest thing about Saul, and it is not rare. The evidence that ought to have stopped him is the thing that drove him on. Every proof that God was with David — the giant, the campaigns, the two hundred, his own daughter's love — made him more determined, because he was not asking whether God was with David. He was asking whether the throne was safe.

Verse 29 then gives the settled state in one sentence.

Not angry, not suspicious, not watchful. Continually. It has stopped being an episode and become the shape of his life, and it will remain so through thirteen chapters, three thousand men, two caves and a medium, until the day the Philistines find him on Mount Gilboa.

The chapter ends where it began: David succeeding, and everybody noticing.

The last phrase is highly esteemed — and it is the exact opposite of what David called himself in verse 23, when he said he was lightly esteemed. The book that told us those who honor me I will honor, and those who despise me shall be lightly esteemed (2:30) is quietly showing the promise working itself out in two men at the same court.

Saul asked for a hundred foreskins and David brought two hundred; in 2 Samuel 3:14 David speaks of a hundred, because he is naming the price Saul set, not contradicting the count he paid. (The Greek Old Testament reads a hundred here too.)

19.title: The Hunter and the Hunted
19.text: <sup>1</sup>And Saul spoke to Jonathan his son and to all his servants, that they should kill David. But Jonathan, Saul's son, delighted much in David.<sup>2</sup>And Jonathan told David, "Saul my father seeks to kill you. Therefore be on your guard in the morning. Stay in a secret place and hide yourself.<sup>3</sup>And I will go out and stand beside my father in the field where you are, and I will speak to my father about you. And if I learn anything I will tell you."<sup>4</sup>And Jonathan spoke well of David to Saul his father and said to him, "Let not the king sin against his servant David, because he has not sinned against you, and because his deeds have brought good to you.<sup>5</sup>For he took his life in his hand and he struck down the Philistine, and the LORD worked a great salvation for all Israel. You saw it, and rejoiced. Why then will you sin against innocent blood by killing David without cause?"<sup>6</sup>And Saul listened to the voice of Jonathan. Saul swore, "As the LORD lives, he shall not be put to death."<sup>7</sup>And Jonathan called David, and Jonathan reported to him all these things. And Jonathan brought David to Saul, and he was in his presence as before.<sup>8</sup>And there was war again. And David went out and fought with the Philistines and struck them with a great blow, so that they fled before him.<sup>9</sup>Then a harmful spirit from the LORD came upon Saul, as he sat in his house with his spear in his hand. And David was playing the lyre.<sup>10</sup>And Saul sought to pin David to the wall with the spear, but he eluded Saul, so that he struck the spear into the wall. And David fled and escaped that night.<sup>11</sup>Saul sent messengers to David's house to watch him, that he might kill him in the morning. But Michal, David's wife, told him, "If you do not escape with your life tonight, tomorrow you will be killed."<sup>12</sup>So Michal let David down through the window, and he fled away and escaped.<sup>13</sup>Michal took an image and laid it on the bed and put a pillow of goats' hair at its head and covered it with the clothes.<sup>14</sup>And when Saul sent messengers to take David, she said, "He is sick."<sup>15</sup>Then Saul sent the messengers to see David, saying, "Bring him up to me in the bed, that I may kill him."<sup>16</sup>And when the messengers came in, behold, the image was in the bed, with the pillow of goats' hair at its head.<sup>17</sup>Saul said to Michal, "Why have you deceived me thus and let my enemy go, so that he has escaped?" And Michal answered Saul, "He said to me, 'Let me go. Why should I kill you?'"<sup>18</sup>Now David fled and escaped, and he came to Samuel at Ramah and told him all that Saul had done to him. And he and Samuel went and lived at Naioth.<sup>19</sup>And it was told Saul, "Behold, David is at Naioth in Ramah."<sup>20</sup>Then Saul sent messengers to take David, and when they saw the company of the prophets prophesying, and Samuel standing as head over them, the Spirit of God came upon the messengers of Saul, and they also prophesied.<sup>21</sup>When it was told Saul, he sent other messengers, and they also prophesied. And Saul sent messengers again the third time, and they also prophesied.<sup>22</sup>Then he himself went to Ramah and came to the great well that is in Secu. And he asked, "Where are Samuel and David?" And one said, "Behold, they are at Naioth in Ramah."<sup>23</sup>And he went there to Naioth in Ramah. And the Spirit of God came upon him also, and as he went he prophesied until he came to Naioth in Ramah.<sup>24</sup>And he too stripped off his clothes, and he too prophesied before Samuel and lay naked all that day and all that night. Thus it is said, "Is Saul also among the prophets?"
19.overview:
The killing of David becomes official policy, and Jonathan argues for him so well that Saul swears in the name of the LORD. The oath lasts one campaign: a victory triggers the spear, and David leaves the court for good. The daughter Saul gave as a snare lowers him out of a window, and the chapter ends with three arrest parties and the king himself seized by the Spirit at Naioth while the man they came for walks away.

Jonathan's plea names the heart of it: David is hunted without cause. David's own psalms of the innocent sufferer, hated without a cause (Psalms 35:19; 69:4), are words Jesus said were fulfilled in him (John 15:25), and the heading of Psalm 59 sets one of them on this very night. The Son of David was hated for the same reason David was, because God was plainly with him. But where David slipped out through a window, Jesus did not escape. He let the arrest party take him, and his innocent blood was shed for the guilty.
19.theology:
Reached, but not changed (vv. 4-6). Jonathan's plain words about sin got through: Saul heard them and swore in the name of the LORD. He was not beyond reach. But an oath sworn under the pressure of a good argument is not the same as a changed heart, and it lasted one campaign.

The Spirit who rules even his enemies (vv. 20-24). The Spirit who came on Saul at the beginning to make him another man (10:6) now comes on him to stop him. God's Spirit is not a power a king can use or lose at will. He goes where God sends him, to equip or to restrain, and in this chapter he protects the LORD's anointed without a blow being struck.

Four hunts, and no rescue anybody would have designed. There is no battle in this chapter, no miracle performed for David, no angel and no fire. A brother-in-law argues, a wife lowers a rope, and three arrest parties and a king are stopped by being made to worship. The manhunt is defeated without a blow, and the man at the centre does nothing but run, which is what he will do for the next twelve chapters. The LORD's anointed spends a third of this book as a fugitive, and at no point is he abandoned.
19.examples:
Then: A king sent three separate arrest parties after one fugitive and lost every one of them to a prayer meeting, went himself, was seized by the Spirit on the road, and spent a day and a night lying stripped on the ground in front of the prophet who had told him his kingdom was gone — while the man he came for walked quietly out of town.

Now: Two things. Jonathan's speech is the best model in Scripture for defending an absent person to someone determined against them: name the thing honestly, state the facts, argue their own interest, and make them remember what they themselves once felt. It is not manipulation; every element of it is true. Jonathan could risk his father's anger because his own standing rested on the LORD's covenant, not on the throne, and those whom Christ has spoken for before the Father are freed to speak up for others. And verse 10 is for anyone who has been told that staying is always the godlier option. David went back three times. Then he left, and the book does not criticise him for it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — Why Will You Sin Against Innocent Blood?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Saul orders David's death; Jonathan warns him and pleads his case (vv. 1-5). Saul listens and swears, and David comes back (vv. 6-7).
verseByVerse.theology: Jonathan does what the rest of the court will not: he tells the king to his face that what he plans is sin.
verseByVerse.examples: Jonathan's courage costs him something. He is arguing against his own father and, though he never says so, against his own succession.

verseByVerse.quote: And Saul spoke to Jonathan his son and to all his servants, that they should kill David. But Jonathan, Saul's son, delighted much in David. And Jonathan told David, "Saul my father seeks to kill you. Therefore be on your guard in the morning. Stay in a secret place and hide yourself. And I will go out and stand beside my father in the field where you are, and I will speak to my father about you. And if I learn anything I will tell you." And Jonathan spoke well of David to Saul his father and said to him, "Let not the king sin against his servant David, because he has not sinned against you, and because his deeds have brought good to you. For he took his life in his hand and he struck down the Philistine, and the LORD worked a great salvation for all Israel. You saw it, and rejoiced. Why then will you sin against innocent blood by killing David without cause?" And Saul listened to the voice of Jonathan. Saul swore, "As the LORD lives, he shall not be put to death." And Jonathan called David, and Jonathan reported to him all these things. And Jonathan brought David to Saul, and he was in his presence as before.
verseByVerse.commentary:
It is now official policy, given to the household as an instruction.

Up to this point the attempts have been private — a spear in a room, a bride-price designed to be fatal — and deniable. Saul now tells his court, including his son, to kill the man.

The writer names the obstacle in the same verse, twice identifying whose son he is: but Jonathan, Saul's son, delighted much in David.

He warns him first and argues afterwards, which is the right order.

The arrangement is careful. He will stand in the field where David is hiding, so that David can hear the conversation, and he undertakes to report whatever he learns.

Now the plea, and it is a model of how to speak for somebody who is not in the room.

He opens with the category. Let not the king sin. Not "do not make a mistake", not "you will regret this" — the proposal is named as sin, to the man's face, in the first clause.

Then the facts: he has not sinned against you. There is no charge. Nothing David has done constitutes an offence, and Jonathan says so flatly.

Then the benefit to the accuser: his deeds have brought good to you. He argues Saul's own interest, which is not flattery but relevance.

Then the five best words in the speech: you saw it, and rejoiced.

He reminds his father of his own gladness. There was a day when Saul stood on that hillside and watched a boy come back with a head in his hand, and he was delighted, and the whole country sang. Jonathan makes him look at it.

He also describes the victory in his father's words: the LORD worked a great salvation for all Israel. That is Saul's own sentence from his best day — today the LORD has worked salvation in Israel (11:13), spoken when he refused to execute men who had insulted him. His son is quoting him back to himself.

Last, the moral name for the proposal, twice: sin against innocent blood, and without cause.

It works.

That should be said before anything else. Saul hears the argument, accepts it, and swears an oath in the name of the LORD that David will not be killed. He is not beyond reach; a son speaking plainly to him about sin got through.

David comes back to court on his brother-in-law's word, and everything is as it was.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–10 — The Spear in the Wall
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: War returns, David wins again, and Saul's spear misses him a last time; David leaves the court for good (vv. 8-10).
verseByVerse.theology: The last night under Saul's roof begins like every other, with David serving the king who wants him dead.
verseByVerse.examples: David leaves with nothing: no house, no wife beside him, no post at court. Everything that follows in the wilderness he will receive from God's hand.

verseByVerse.quote: And there was war again. And David went out and fought with the Philistines and struck them with a great blow, so that they fled before him. Then a harmful spirit from the LORD came upon Saul, as he sat in his house with his spear in his hand. And David was playing the lyre. And Saul sought to pin David to the wall with the spear, but he eluded Saul, so that he struck the spear into the wall. And David fled and escaped that night.
verseByVerse.commentary:
One campaign. That is how long the oath lasts, and the thing that breaks it is a victory.

The scene is 18:10 again, staged identically: the house, the spirit, the spear in the hand, the young man playing.

David is at the lyre again. After two spears he had come back and played; after the plot with the bride-price he had come back and played; after his father-in-law's oath he came back and played. The narrator does not comment on it and the repetition is the comment.

This time the spear goes into the plaster.

Picture the room afterwards: an overturned lyre, a king, and a spear standing in the wall where a man's chest had been a second earlier.

Then David fled and escaped that night. That is the end of it. He has absorbed three attempts and gone on serving; the fourth ends the arrangement, and he never lives at that court again.

There is a point at which a person has to leave, and it is not a failure of patience or of grace. David had endured this repeatedly and returned each time. What ended it was not a change in his character but a spear in the wall, and the writer does not suggest he should have stayed for a fifth. Anyone whose home has become dangerous may take this to heart: seeking safety is not a lack of faith.

Why does the narrator say the spirit came from the LORD? Saul had rejected God, and the tormenting spirit was God giving him over in judgment (16:14), as he later allowed a lying spirit to deceive Ahab (1 Kings 22:22). God is never the author of sin (James 1:13), but no spirit, good or evil, is outside his rule, and he can use even this one to judge a man who has turned from him.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–17 — Let Down Through the Window
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Michal warns David, lowers him through the window and deceives Saul's men with a household image (vv. 11-16). Confronted, she blames David (v. 17).
verseByVerse.theology: Saul's own household turns against his plan: his son argued for David, and now his daughter saves him.
verseByVerse.examples: The heading of Psalm 59 sets that psalm on this night, and it is worth reading alongside the chapter: a man in a watched house, praying.

verseByVerse.quote: Saul sent messengers to David's house to watch him, that he might kill him in the morning. But Michal, David's wife, told him, "If you do not escape with your life tonight, tomorrow you will be killed." So Michal let David down through the window, and he fled away and escaped. Michal took an image and laid it on the bed and put a pillow of goats' hair at its head and covered it with the clothes. And when Saul sent messengers to take David, she said, "He is sick." Then Saul sent the messengers to see David, saying, "Bring him up to me in the bed, that I may kill him." And when the messengers came in, behold, the image was in the bed, with the pillow of goats' hair at its head. Saul said to Michal, "Why have you deceived me thus and let my enemy go, so that he has escaped?" And Michal answered Saul, "He said to me, 'Let me go. Why should I kill you?'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The house is watched, and the person who sees it is the king's daughter.

Remember what her father said when he arranged this marriage: let me give her to him, that she may be a snare for him (18:21). The trap married David, found out what her father was doing, and warned him.

She lets him down through a window, at night, past the men posted at the door.

It is a small escape with a long history in Scripture: Rahab let the spies down by a rope through a window in the wall of Jericho, and centuries later the disciples in Damascus lowered Paul over the wall in a basket when the gates were being watched (Josh. 2:15; Acts 9:25). God's people have quite often left a city by the window.

She makes a dummy, and the material matters.

The word is teraphim — a household idol, of the kind Rachel stole from her father's house and sat on (Gen. 31:19, 34), and of the kind Micah kept in his shrine in the hills of Ephraim (Judg. 17:5). There is one in David's house, and this one is evidently large enough, with the goats' hair at its head, to pass for a man under bedclothes in a dim room.

The narrator says nothing about it. He reports it, and moves on, and a reader is left to notice what is standing in the bedroom of the LORD's anointed.

Her father's answer to the news that his son-in-law is ill is that they should carry the bed to him so that he can kill the man in it.

A king has been told that a sick man is lying in his daughter's house, and his instruction is that the bed be brought so that he can do it himself. There is no pretence left in him now.

Here Michal says something that is not true, and the shape of it matters.

She tells her father that David threatened her — that he said, in effect, help me or I will kill you. Nothing in the account suggests it. She warned him and she lowered him and she made the dummy, and the whole plan appears to have been hers.

Both things are true of her, and the narrator lets both stand. She risked her life to save her husband. And when the risk arrived, she got out from under it by putting the blame on him, and she left in her father's mind a picture of David as a man who would threaten to murder his own wife.

She was in an impossible position, and people in impossible positions do this. It is also the beginning of a distance between these two that never closes. David will take other wives; Michal is given away by her father to another man; and the last we ever hear of her, years later when the ark comes into Jerusalem, is that she despised him in her heart (2 Sam. 6:16).

Why was there an idol in David’s house at all? The image was probably Michal’s rather than David’s, brought from a home where such things were kept, and its presence in the king’s daughter’s house shows how far Israel had drifted. The narrator does not excuse it; he lets it stand as a quiet rebuke.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–24 — Is Saul Also Among the Prophets?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: David flees to Samuel at Naioth (v. 18). Three arrest parties and then Saul himself are seized by the Spirit and prophesy (vv. 19-24).
verseByVerse.theology: David's first move as a fugitive is to go to the prophet, and there God protects him by the Spirit's power alone.
verseByVerse.examples: It is a fearful thing to set yourself against God, and a mercy that he can stop us before we do what we intend.

verseByVerse.quote: Now David fled and escaped, and he came to Samuel at Ramah and told him all that Saul had done to him. And he and Samuel went and lived at Naioth. And it was told Saul, "Behold, David is at Naioth in Ramah." Then Saul sent messengers to take David, and when they saw the company of the prophets prophesying, and Samuel standing as head over them, the Spirit of God came upon the messengers of Saul, and they also prophesied. When it was told Saul, he sent other messengers, and they also prophesied. And Saul sent messengers again the third time, and they also prophesied. Then he himself went to Ramah and came to the great well that is in Secu. And he asked, "Where are Samuel and David?" And one said, "Behold, they are at Naioth in Ramah." And he went there to Naioth in Ramah. And the Spirit of God came upon him also, and as he went he prophesied until he came to Naioth in Ramah. And he too stripped off his clothes, and he too prophesied before Samuel and lay naked all that day and all that night. Thus it is said, "Is Saul also among the prophets?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
He runs to the old man who anointed him.

It is the first thing David does as a fugitive, and it is a good instinct: he goes to the prophet and told him all that Saul had done to him. The two of them then go and live at Naioth, which appears to be the prophets' settlement at Ramah.

This is also, as far as the book records, the last time these two are ever together. Samuel dies in chapter 25.

The arrest party walks into a prayer meeting and never makes the arrest.

They see the prophets and Samuel at their head, and the Spirit of God comes on them, and they join in. No blow is struck. Nobody argues with them or bars the door.

He sends a second party, and the same thing happens. He sends a third.

There is something close to comedy in the repetition, and it is entirely at the king's expense. Three times he despatches men to bring back a fugitive, and three times they arrive and are absorbed into a company of worshippers.

So he goes himself, and it happens to him before he even arrives.

As he went he prophesied — the Spirit takes him on the road, and he comes into Naioth already prophesying, which is not what he set out to do.

He ends on the floor.

The stripping is probably the removal of his outer robes and armour rather than nakedness as we would mean it; the point is that a king is lying on the ground without the marks of his office, in front of the prophet who told him the kingdom was torn from him, for a day and a night, while the man he came to arrest walks away.

Then the proverb, and it is the bookend of Saul's life.

The first time it was asked, the Spirit had just come on a young farmer from Gibeah on the day he was anointed, and the neighbours who had known him all his life said in astonishment: what has come over the son of Kish? Is Saul also among the prophets? (10:11-12). It was wonder. It meant that God had done something unaccountable with an ordinary man.

Here the same words are said over a king stripped on the ground, and they mean the opposite. The Spirit that once made him another man now simply immobilises him.

Between the two askings lies everything: the waiting at Gilgal, the oath at Michmash, the Amalekite livestock, the monument at Carmel, the spear, and the arrest parties.

What God has done in this chapter is easily missed in the strangeness of the ending.

David is hunted four times in this chapter and never once defended by force, and yet he is never caught (see the theology above).

What was this prophesying, and why did Saul lie naked? The Spirit overpowered Saul so that he could not carry out his plan, stripping him of his royal robes and leaving him helpless before Samuel. It was not a sign of salvation but of God’s power over a king who opposed him; the Spirit can come on a man for a moment without dwelling in him (cf. Num 24:2). It is no pattern for worship today.

20.title: Covenant Friendship
20.text: <sup>1</sup>Then David fled from Naioth in Ramah and came and said before Jonathan, "What have I done? What is my guilt? And what is my sin before your father, that he seeks my life?"<sup>2</sup>And he said to him, "Far from it! You shall not die. Behold, my father does nothing either great or small without disclosing it to me. And why should my father hide this from me? It is not so."<sup>3</sup>But David vowed again, saying, "Your father knows well that I have found favor in your eyes, and he thinks, 'Do not let Jonathan know this, lest he be grieved.' But truly, as the LORD lives and as your soul lives, there is but a step between me and death."<sup>4</sup>Then Jonathan said to David, "Whatever you say, I will do for you."<sup>5</sup>David said to Jonathan, "Behold, tomorrow is the new moon, and I should not fail to sit at table with the king. But let me go, that I may hide myself in the field till the third day at evening.<sup>6</sup>If your father misses me at all, then say, 'David earnestly asked leave of me to run to Bethlehem his city, for there is a yearly sacrifice there for all the clan.'<sup>7</sup>If he says, 'Good!' it will be well with your servant, but if he is angry, then know that harm is determined by him.<sup>8</sup>Therefore deal kindly with your servant, for you have brought your servant into a covenant of the LORD with you. But if there is guilt in me, kill me yourself, for why should you bring me to your father?"<sup>9</sup>And Jonathan said, "Far be it from you! If I knew that it was determined by my father that harm should come to you, would I not tell you?"<sup>10</sup>Then David said to Jonathan, "Who will tell me if your father answers you roughly?"<sup>11</sup>And Jonathan said to David, "Come, let us go out into the field." So they both went out into the field.<sup>12</sup>And Jonathan said to David, "The LORD, the God of Israel, be witness! When I have sounded out my father, about this time tomorrow, or the third day, behold, if he is well disposed toward David, shall I not then send and disclose it to you?<sup>13</sup>But should it please my father to do you harm, the LORD do so to Jonathan and more also if I do not disclose it to you and send you away, that you may go in safety. May the LORD be with you, as he has been with my father.<sup>14</sup>If I am still alive, show me the steadfast love of the LORD, that I may not die;<sup>15</sup>and do not cut off your steadfast love from my house forever, when the LORD cuts off every one of the enemies of David from the face of the earth."<sup>16</sup>And Jonathan made a covenant with the house of David, saying, "May the LORD take vengeance on David's enemies."<sup>17</sup>And Jonathan made David swear again by his love for him, for he loved him as he loved his own soul.<sup>18</sup>Then Jonathan said to him, "Tomorrow is the new moon, and you will be missed, because your seat will be empty.<sup>19</sup>On the third day go down quickly to the place where you hid yourself when the matter was in hand, and remain beside the stone heap.<sup>20</sup>And I will shoot three arrows to the side of it, as though I shot at a mark.<sup>21</sup>And behold, I will send the boy, saying, 'Go, find the arrows.' If I say to the boy, 'Look, the arrows are on this side of you, take them,' then you are to come, for, as the LORD lives, it is safe for you and there is no danger.<sup>22</sup>But if I say to the youth, 'Look, the arrows are beyond you,' then go, for the LORD has sent you away.<sup>23</sup>And as for the matter of which you and I have spoken, behold, the LORD is between you and me forever."<sup>24</sup>So David hid himself in the field. And when the new moon came, the king sat down to eat food.<sup>25</sup>The king sat on his seat, as at other times, on the seat by the wall. Jonathan sat opposite, and Abner sat by Saul's side, but David's place was empty.<sup>26</sup>Yet Saul did not say anything that day, for he thought, "Something has happened to him. He is not clean; surely he is not clean."<sup>27</sup>But on the second day, the day after the new moon, David's place was empty. And Saul said to Jonathan his son, "Why has not the son of Jesse come to the meal, either yesterday or today?"<sup>28</sup>Jonathan answered Saul, "David earnestly asked leave of me to go to Bethlehem.<sup>29</sup>He said, 'Let me go, for our clan holds a sacrifice in the city, and my brother has commanded me to be there. So now, if I have found favor in your eyes, let me get away and see my brothers.' For this reason he has not come to the king's table."<sup>30</sup>Then Saul's anger was kindled against Jonathan, and he said to him, "You son of a perverse, rebellious woman, do I not know that you have chosen the son of Jesse to your own shame, and to the shame of your mother's nakedness?<sup>31</sup>For as long as the son of Jesse lives on the earth, neither you nor your kingdom shall be established. Therefore send and bring him to me, for he shall surely die."<sup>32</sup>Then Jonathan answered Saul his father, "Why should he be put to death? What has he done?"<sup>33</sup>But Saul hurled his spear at him to strike him. So Jonathan knew that his father was determined to put David to death.<sup>34</sup>And Jonathan rose from the table in fierce anger and ate no food the second day of the month, for he was grieved for David, because his father had disgraced him.<sup>35</sup>In the morning Jonathan went out into the field to the appointment with David, and with him a little boy.<sup>36</sup>And he said to his boy, "Run and find the arrows that I shoot." As the boy ran, he shot an arrow beyond him.<sup>37</sup>And when the boy came to the place of the arrow that Jonathan had shot, Jonathan called after the boy and said, "Is not the arrow beyond you?"<sup>38</sup>And Jonathan called after the boy, "Hurry! Be quick! Do not stay!" So Jonathan's boy gathered up the arrows and came to his master.<sup>39</sup>But the boy knew nothing. Only Jonathan and David knew the matter.<sup>40</sup>And Jonathan gave his weapons to his boy and said to him, "Go and carry them to the city."<sup>41</sup>And as soon as the boy had gone, David rose from beside the stone heap and fell on his face to the ground and bowed three times. And they kissed one another and wept with one another, David weeping the most.<sup>42</sup>Then Jonathan said to David, "Go in peace, because we have sworn both of us in the name of the LORD, saying, 'The LORD shall be between me and you, and between my offspring and your offspring, forever.'" And he rose and departed, and Jonathan went into the city.
20.overview:
David arrives asking to be shown the charge against him, and there is none (vv. 1-4). Jonathan cannot yet believe his father means murder, but he puts himself at David's disposal anyway, and the two arrange a test at the new moon feast (vv. 5-11).

In the field they renew their covenant, and the heir asks the fugitive to show kindness to his children when the kingdom changes hands, which Jonathan speaks of as certain (vv. 12-23). At the feast Saul's anger breaks out, and a spear thrown at his own son settles the question (vv. 24-34). The two friends meet once more in the field, weep, and part with the LORD between them (vv. 35-42).
20.theology:
Making peace with the coming king (vv. 14-16). Jonathan asks for kindness to his house when, not if, the LORD cuts off every one of David's enemies, though his own father is chief among them and he is the heir. He sees what Psalm 2 would later say to the kings of the earth: the LORD's anointed will reign, so make your peace with him while there is time. The New Testament applies that psalm, and the promise that the King's enemies will be put under his feet, to Jesus (Acts 2:34–35; 1 Corinthians 15:25). Jonathan also asks for steadfast love for the house of David forever, and God himself later promised that house a throne for ever (2 Samuel 7:16), a promise the angel says Jesus inherits (Luke 1:32–33). Many Christians have seen in the lame grandson at David's table a picture of the gospel: a child of the rebel house, unable to walk, seated with the king's sons for the sake of another. That is the grace of the Son of David to sinners.

The LORD between them (vv. 23, 42). The covenant rests not on affection, which cools, but on the LORD, who does not. That is why it could outlast both men, and why Jonathan can promise only what has been sworn and who guarantees it.
20.examples:
Then: Two young men arranged a signal with three arrows and a boy who would never know what he was carrying — and when it came to it the signal was unnecessary, and they met in the open and wept, and the heir to the throne asked the fugitive to spare his children when the kingdom changed hands.

Now: Three things. Verse 1 is for anyone who has looked hard for the offence and cannot find it — sometimes there is not one, and the search for a fault to correct is itself the trap. Verse 4 is Jonathan's: he committed himself to David before he was persuaded, which is what this kind of loyalty looks like from the inside. And verses 14-15 are the hardest and best. He could see that his family's future depended entirely on the mercy of the man his father was hunting, and he asked for mercy instead of fighting.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — There Is But a Step Between Me and Death
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: David asks what his guilt is; Jonathan cannot believe his father means it, but puts himself at David's disposal (vv. 1-4). David proposes a test at the new moon feast (vv. 5-8).
verseByVerse.theology: Jonathan is loyal to his father and committed to David, and this chapter is where he learns how far apart those two loyalties have drifted.
verseByVerse.examples: David's questions in verse 1 are a prayer as much as a protest. The psalms ask God the same thing: if I have done this, if there is wrong in my hands (Ps. 7:3).

verseByVerse.quote: Then David fled from Naioth in Ramah and came and said before Jonathan, "What have I done? What is my guilt? And what is my sin before your father, that he seeks my life?" And he said to him, "Far from it! You shall not die. Behold, my father does nothing either great or small without disclosing it to me. And why should my father hide this from me? It is not so." But David vowed again, saying, "Your father knows well that I have found favor in your eyes, and he thinks, 'Do not let Jonathan know this, lest he be grieved.' But truly, as the LORD lives and as your soul lives, there is but a step between me and death." Then Jonathan said to David, "Whatever you say, I will do for you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Three questions, and they are the questions of a man who genuinely cannot account for what is happening to him.

He is not protesting his general innocence; he is asking to be shown the charge, because he has looked for it and cannot find one.

He cannot, because there is not one. He killed the giant, won the campaigns, married into the family, played the lyre through the bad nights and came back after the spears. The reader knows the answer and David does not: it is not anything he has done. It is that the LORD was with him but had departed from Saul (18:12).

That is one of the harder things about being on the receiving end of this kind of hatred. There is no fault to correct, so there is no way to fix it.

His friend will not believe it, and the reason is touching and out of date.

My father does nothing either great or small without disclosing it to me. It had been true. In chapter 19 Saul told Jonathan openly to kill David, which is how Jonathan came to warn him in the first place (19:1-2).

What Jonathan does not yet know is that his father has learned from that. The openness he is appealing to was withdrawn the day it cost Saul an assassination.

There is something else in the denial as well, and anybody who has had to hear hard truth about a parent will recognise it. It is not so. He is not weighing evidence. He is refusing a picture of his father that he cannot yet hold.

David has read the situation exactly, including Saul's motive for the concealment.

Saul, he says, is keeping it quiet lest he be grieved. Even here, David credits the man with wanting to spare his son pain. He does not say "because your father knows you would stop him", which is also true and would be the sharper reading.

His sentence about the single step between him and death is a picture of a man walking along an edge, and it is the settled condition of the next twelve chapters of his life.

He is not being dramatic. He has had a spear thrown at him three times, escaped through a window, and been hunted by three arrest parties in quick succession.

Jonathan hands him a blank cheque.

He has not accepted the argument — he still thinks his father is not capable of this. He puts himself at David's disposal anyway, before he is convinced, which is what friendship of this kind looks like from the inside.

verseByVerse.quote: David said to Jonathan, "Behold, tomorrow is the new moon, and I should not fail to sit at table with the king. But let me go, that I may hide myself in the field till the third day at evening. If your father misses me at all, then say, 'David earnestly asked leave of me to run to Bethlehem his city, for there is a yearly sacrifice there for all the clan.' If he says, 'Good!' it will be well with your servant, but if he is angry, then know that harm is determined by him. Therefore deal kindly with your servant, for you have brought your servant into a covenant of the LORD with you. But if there is guilt in me, kill me yourself, for why should you bring me to your father?" And Jonathan said, "Far be it from you! If I knew that it was determined by my father that harm should come to you, would I not tell you?" Then David said to Jonathan, "Who will tell me if your father answers you roughly?" And Jonathan said to David, "Come, let us go out into the field." So they both went out into the field.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Attendance at the king's table at the new moon was expected of his officers and family.

So David's absence will be conspicuous by design. That is the point of choosing this occasion: it forces a reaction.

The cover story, and it should be reported honestly rather than defended.

Part of it is true: David has just asked Jonathan to let him go (v. 5), though to hide, not to go to Bethlehem. The annual clan sacrifice at Bethlehem is probably also real. What is untrue is the implication that David has gone there, and the whole thing is arranged to produce a false impression in Saul's mind.

The narrator does not comment, and neither should a reader go much beyond him. Scripture records a good many people concealing things from men who intend murder — the midwives in Egypt, Rahab on the wall, Samuel with his heifer on the Bethlehem road (16:2) — and it does not stop to lecture any of them.

The test is well designed: one absence, two possible reactions, and the reaction is the verdict.

He appeals to the covenant of chapter 18, and to the word hesed — the loyal love that keeps its promises when it does not have to. It will be used three times in this chapter.

Note also who initiated that covenant. You have brought your servant into a covenant. David did not ask for it; Jonathan made it, in the room where the giant's head was still in his hand.

Here is the measure of the two men.

David tells Jonathan that if there really is a charge against him, Jonathan should execute him personally rather than hand him over.
