He is not expecting it — the first four verses have established that he cannot find any guilt in himself. He is putting his life in his friend's hands in the plainest form available, and doing it as an argument: you can have it if it is owed.

They leave the buildings. Everything that follows in this chapter happens in the open, away from the house, and that is a comment on the house.
verseByVerse.note: The new moon was a monthly festival with a sacrificial meal.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–23 — The LORD Be With You, As He Has Been With My Father
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jonathan swears to warn David (vv. 12-13), asks him to show steadfast love to his house (vv. 14-17), and arranges the signal of the arrows (vv. 18-23).
verseByVerse.theology: Here the covenant of chapter 18 is widened from two men to two houses, and its terms are kindness, hesed, both ways.
verseByVerse.examples: The arrows are a sad necessity. Friends who cannot be seen to talk must speak in code, and the plan shows how dangerous loyalty to David has become, even for the king's son.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jonathan said to David, "The LORD, the God of Israel, be witness! When I have sounded out my father, about this time tomorrow, or the third day, behold, if he is well disposed toward David, shall I not then send and disclose it to you? But should it please my father to do you harm, the LORD do so to Jonathan and more also if I do not disclose it to you and send you away, that you may go in safety. May the LORD be with you, as he has been with my father. If I am still alive, show me the steadfast love of the LORD, that I may not die; and do not cut off your steadfast love from my house forever, when the LORD cuts off every one of the enemies of David from the face of the earth." And Jonathan made a covenant with the house of David, saying, "May the LORD take vengeance on David's enemies." And Jonathan made David swear again by his love for him, for he loved him as he loved his own soul.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He swears with God as witness, and the undertaking is exact: either way, David will be told.

He calls down a curse on himself if he fails to warn the man his father wants dead.

If the verdict is harm, Jonathan will actively assist the escape of the person his father has identified as the obstacle to Jonathan's own throne. He is swearing, under oath, to work against his family's interest.

The tenses carry it. May the LORD be with you — future, a blessing. As he has been with my father — past, and finished.

Saul is alive and reigning. His son says, in a single sentence, that the LORD was with him and prays that he will be with David instead. There is no bitterness in it and no announcement; it is simply what Jonathan has understood and his father has spent five chapters refusing to.

Now the most remarkable request in the chapter. Take the assumption inside it first. When the LORD cuts off every one of the enemies of David from the face of the earth — not if. Jonathan states the future as settled: David will have the kingdom, and everyone opposing him will be removed.

His father is at this moment the chief of those enemies, and Jonathan is his heir.

So what he asks for is mercy. Show me hesed while I live, and do not cut it off from my house forever. He is negotiating, in advance, for the survival of his children under the regime that will replace his own.

That is an act of extraordinary clear sight and extraordinary humility together. He can see the whole thing — that the throne is going, that his line will be at the mercy of the man he loves, that his father's resistance is futile — and his response is to ask for kindness rather than to fight.

It was kept. Years later, when David is secure in Jerusalem and every rival house would normally be destroyed, he asks: is there still anyone left of the house of Saul, that I may show him kindness for Jonathan's sake? They bring him a man lame in both feet, Jonathan's son, and David seats him at the king's table for the rest of his life (2 Sam. 9:1-13). Later still, when the Gibeonites demanded Saul's descendants, David spared him because of the oath of the LORD sworn here (2 Sam. 21:7).

A promise made in a field by two young men in trouble was honoured many years later to a crippled grandson of the man who had been hunting them.

He makes the covenant not with David but with the house of David — a dynasty that does not exist yet, in a family with no throne, on behalf of his own descendants.

Was Jonathan right to oppose his father? Honouring parents does not mean helping them commit murder. Jonathan stayed loyal to his father as king and died at his side (31:2), but he would not betray an innocent man or resist God’s choice.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Jonathan said to him, "Tomorrow is the new moon, and you will be missed, because your seat will be empty. On the third day go down quickly to the place where you hid yourself when the matter was in hand, and remain beside the stone heap. And I will shoot three arrows to the side of it, as though I shot at a mark. And behold, I will send the boy, saying, 'Go, find the arrows.' If I say to the boy, 'Look, the arrows are on this side of you, take them,' then you are to come, for, as the LORD lives, it is safe for you and there is no danger. But if I say to the youth, 'Look, the arrows are beyond you,' then go, for the LORD has sent you away. And as for the matter of which you and I have spoken, behold, the LORD is between you and me forever."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The practical arrangements begin, and they are careful and unhurried.

A hiding place they have used before, a stone heap for a landmark, and an archery practice that will look entirely ordinary to anyone watching from the town.

The signal is spoken to a child who will have no idea what he is carrying.

The plan is a good one. Two men who cannot be seen speaking to each other arrange to have their message delivered in public, at volume, to somebody else.

Note the phrasing of the bad outcome: then go, for the LORD has sent you away. Not "my father has driven you out". If David has to run, Jonathan has already decided how to describe it.

The LORD is between you and me forever. It is the sentence he will repeat as his farewell in verse 42, and it is the whole basis of the arrangement: not affection, which can cool, but a third party who does not.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 24–34 — Why Has Not the Son of Jesse Come?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Saul passes over David's absence on the first day and asks on the second (vv. 24-29). He erupts at Jonathan and throws a spear at him (vv. 30-34).
verseByVerse.theology: The feast is a test with only one possible result, and Saul fails it on the second day.
verseByVerse.examples: Jonathan tells the agreed story without wavering, though he knows what his father may do to him for it.

verseByVerse.quote: So David hid himself in the field. And when the new moon came, the king sat down to eat food. The king sat on his seat, as at other times, on the seat by the wall. Jonathan sat opposite, and Abner sat by Saul's side, but David's place was empty. Yet Saul did not say anything that day, for he thought, "Something has happened to him. He is not clean; surely he is not clean." But on the second day, the day after the new moon, David's place was empty. And Saul said to Jonathan his son, "Why has not the son of Jesse come to the meal, either yesterday or today?" Jonathan answered Saul, "David earnestly asked leave of me to go to Bethlehem. He said, 'Let me go, for our clan holds a sacrifice in the city, and my brother has commanded me to be there. So now, if I have found favor in your eyes, let me get away and see my brothers.' For this reason he has not come to the king's table."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The narrator seats everybody and then shows us the gap.

Saul is on his usual seat by the wall — and this is the man who threw a spear at a wall with David in front of it. Jonathan opposite. Abner beside the king. And an empty place.

He says nothing, and the narrator lets us hear him talking himself into an explanation.

The repetition is the giveaway: he is not clean; surely he is not clean. A man who was genuinely unconcerned would think it once. Saul is working at it.

Ritual uncleanness would be a real and sufficient reason to miss a sacrificial meal, so the explanation is a good one. It lasts a day.

Here is a small thing that runs to the end of the book: he does not use the name.

The son of Jesse. Not David, whom he loved greatly and made his armour-bearer and his son-in-law. From here on it is almost always this: the son of Jesse, to Jonathan, to his officers at Gibeah, to Ahimelech at Nob. Nabal will use it too, as an insult (22:7-13; 25:10). Only when Saul is shamed does he say my son David again (24:16; 26:17).

It is what people do with somebody they have decided to destroy. The name goes first.

Jonathan gives the agreed answer, and adds a detail of his own — my brother has commanded me to be there — which was not in the script.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Saul's anger was kindled against Jonathan, and he said to him, "You son of a perverse, rebellious woman, do I not know that you have chosen the son of Jesse to your own shame, and to the shame of your mother's nakedness? For as long as the son of Jesse lives on the earth, neither you nor your kingdom shall be established. Therefore send and bring him to me, for he shall surely die." Then Jonathan answered Saul his father, "Why should he be put to death? What has he done?" But Saul hurled his spear at him to strike him. So Jonathan knew that his father was determined to put David to death. And Jonathan rose from the table in fierce anger and ate no food the second day of the month, for he was grieved for David, because his father had disgraced him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He goes for his son through his son's mother, and it is the sentence of a man with nothing left to lose.

The insult is aimed at Jonathan and lands on Ahinoam, Saul's own wife, who has done nothing and is not present. It is a common enough move and it is always the same move: hurt the person in front of you by defiling somebody they love.

The charge itself is that Jonathan has chosen David. Which is exactly right. He chose him in chapter 18 and took off his robe to prove it.

Here is what Saul thinks he is fighting for.

Neither you nor your kingdom. He is arguing for Jonathan's inheritance. Everything — the spears, the arrest parties, the manhunt about to consume the rest of his life — is being done, in his own account of it, for his son.

His son gave the kingdom away two chapters ago, voluntarily, with his own robe and his own sword, to the man his father wants killed.

There is a particular grief in that, and it is not rare. A man destroying himself on behalf of somebody who does not want what he is fighting for, and cannot say so in a way that will be heard.

Jonathan asks David's question.

It is verse 1 almost word for word: what have I done? What is my guilt? The friend puts the innocent man's question to the king, and there is no answer to it, because there is no charge.

He also asked it in chapter 19 and it worked; Saul listened and swore an oath. He tries it again.

The answer is a spear.

Two throws at David in 18:11, one more in 19:10, and now one at his own son across a festival table in front of Abner and the court.

The spear finally accomplishes what argument could not: so Jonathan knew. The argument had not convinced him. His father's own weapon, thrown at his own head, did.

He leaves the table furious and does not eat.

The anger is right, and it is the second time in this book that a man of Saul's house has been angry at the correct thing — the Spirit of God rushed on Saul at Jabesh and his anger was greatly kindled for a town about to lose its eyes (11:6). The father was capable of this once.

The grief is for the other man. Jonathan has just been called the son of a perverse, rebellious woman and had a spear thrown at him, and the narrator says he was grieved for David.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jonathan gives the signal with the arrows (vv. 35-40); the two friends meet and weep (v. 41), and part with the LORD between them (v. 42).
verseByVerse.theology: Friendship of this kind costs both men dearly, and the parting is told without a word wasted.
verseByVerse.examples: For anyone who has said goodbye to a friend they would not see again, this scene is honest. The tears are not a lack of faith, and the parting is held in God's hand.

verseByVerse.quote: In the morning Jonathan went out into the field to the appointment with David, and with him a little boy. And he said to his boy, "Run and find the arrows that I shoot." As the boy ran, he shot an arrow beyond him. And when the boy came to the place of the arrow that Jonathan had shot, Jonathan called after the boy and said, "Is not the arrow beyond you?" And Jonathan called after the boy, "Hurry! Be quick! Do not stay!" So Jonathan's boy gathered up the arrows and came to his master. But the boy knew nothing. Only Jonathan and David knew the matter. And Jonathan gave his weapons to his boy and said to him, "Go and carry them to the city." And as soon as the boy had gone, David rose from beside the stone heap and fell on his face to the ground and bowed three times. And they kissed one another and wept with one another, David weeping the most. Then Jonathan said to David, "Go in peace, because we have sworn both of us in the name of the LORD, saying, 'The LORD shall be between me and you, and between my offspring and your offspring, forever.'" And he rose and departed, and Jonathan went into the city.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He keeps the appointment, and he shoots the arrow that means run.

The agreed words, shouted across a field to a child, and then three more that were not in the plan.

Hurry. Be quick. Do not stay. On the face of it he is chivvying a boy after an arrow. Behind a stone heap a man is listening to his friend telling him to run.

The narrator points at it so that we do not miss the double meaning.

Then he sends the child home, and the whole elaborate system becomes unnecessary.

He comes out, and the first thing he does is put his face in the dirt.

Three times, which is the full formal obeisance offered to a king. And it is being offered by the man God has anointed to be king, to the heir who has just given up the throne for him.

Two men in a field, kissing and weeping, and the narrator adds a detail nobody asked him for: David wept the most.

It is a strange, small, entirely human observation, and it is the kind of detail that gets into a story only because somebody was there. And it is a fair question why it was David.

Jonathan is losing a friend and going back to a house where his father throws spears at him. David is losing everything at once: his position, his wife, his home, his standing, the court where he was loved, and the only man in it who was ever safe. He is walking into the wilderness with nothing, and he will not have a settled address for years.

The farewell is a covenant, not a goodbye.

Go in peace is what you say to somebody you may not see again. And then he gives the reason it can be said: they have sworn, in God's name, and the LORD is between them, and it extends to their children, and it is forever.

He does not promise to see David again. He does not promise to protect him, which is beyond his power. He states what has been sworn and who guarantees it.

One goes out into the country and one goes back into the town, and the sentence is as bare as that.

They will meet once more. In three chapters, in the wilderness of Ziph, Jonathan will come out and find David in the woods and strengthen his hand in God, and say the thing his father could never say: you shall be king over Israel, and I shall be next to you (23:16-17). That is the last conversation they ever have.

After that, Jonathan appears once more in this book, dead on Mount Gilboa beside his father (31:2). And David will say over him the words that end their story: I am distressed for you, my brother Jonathan; very pleasant have you been to me (2 Sam. 1:26).

The covenant made in this field outlived both of them, because two young men in serious trouble swore something to each other in the open air, with God between them, and one of them remembered.

Do the kissing and weeping here, or David's later lament that Jonathan's love surpassed the love of women (2 Samuel 1:26), mean their love was sexual? Nothing in the text says so. Their bond is described in covenant language of sworn loyalty (18:3; 20:42); men kissed in greeting and farewell in that culture (2 Samuel 15:5; 19:39); and both men married. David's lament compares the faithfulness of a friend who gave up a throne for him with every other love he had known. Scripture forbids same-sex intercourse (Leviticus 18:22); it also honours deep friendship between men, and this is one of its finest examples.

21.title: David at Nob
21.text: <sup>1</sup>Then David came to Nob, to Ahimelech the priest. And Ahimelech came to meet David, trembling, and said to him, "Why are you alone, and no one with you?"<sup>2</sup>And David said to Ahimelech the priest, "The king has charged me with a matter and said to me, 'Let no one know anything of the matter about which I send you, and with which I have charged you.' I have made an appointment with the young men for such and such a place.<sup>3</sup>Now then, what do you have on hand? Give me five loaves of bread, or whatever is here."<sup>4</sup>And the priest answered David, "I have no common bread on hand, but there is holy bread— if the young men have kept themselves from women."<sup>5</sup>And David answered the priest, "Truly women have been kept from us as always when I go on an expedition. The vessels of the young men are holy even when it is an ordinary journey. How much more today will their vessels be holy?"<sup>6</sup>So the priest gave him the holy bread, for there was no bread there but the bread of the Presence, which is removed from before the LORD, to be replaced by hot bread on the day it is taken away.<sup>7</sup>Now a certain man of the servants of Saul was there that day, detained before the LORD. His name was Doeg the Edomite, the chief of Saul's herdsmen.<sup>8</sup>Then David said to Ahimelech, "Then have you not here a spear or a sword at hand? For I have brought neither my sword nor my weapons with me, because the king's business required haste."<sup>9</sup>And the priest said, "The sword of Goliath the Philistine, whom you struck down in the Valley of Elah, behold, it is here wrapped in a cloth behind the ephod. If you will take that, take it, for there is none but that here." And David said, "There is none like that; give it to me."<sup>10</sup>And David rose and fled that day from Saul and went to Achish the king of Gath.<sup>11</sup>And the servants of Achish said to him, "Is not this David the king of the land? Did they not sing to one another of him in dances, 'Saul has struck down his thousands, and David his ten thousands'?"<sup>12</sup>And David took these words to heart and was much afraid of Achish the king of Gath.<sup>13</sup>So he changed his behavior before them and pretended to be insane in their hands and made marks on the doors of the gate and let his spittle run down his beard.<sup>14</sup>Then Achish said to his servants, "Behold, you see the man is mad. Why then have you brought him to me?<sup>15</sup>Do I lack madmen, that you have brought this fellow to behave as a madman in my presence? Shall this fellow come into my house?"
21.overview: David comes to Nob alone and lies to the priest, and the lie is what puts the priest in danger. Ahimelech gives him the holy bread, and the Son of God later cites the incident without blame: I desire mercy, and not sacrifice. An Edomite named Doeg is watching, and everything in chapter 22 comes out of it. Then David carries Goliath's sword to Goliath's town, is much afraid, and saves his life by feigning madness, the day behind Psalm 34.
21.theology:
The cost of a convenient lie (v. 2). David's lie protected him for an afternoon and cost eighty-five lives. A priest who believed he was helping the king helped freely. Scripture records it without excuse, and in the end so does David.

Mercy and not sacrifice (vv. 4-6). All three of the first Gospels record Jesus' use of this incident (Matt. 12:3-7; Mark 2:25-26; Luke 6:3-4). As the note on vv. 1-6 shows, he admits the irregularity and still approves the mercy: Ahimelech's choice fits the Lord's own reading of the law.

Someone greater than David (Matthew 12:6, 8). Jesus' argument is more than a point about rules. He sets himself beside David: the LORD's anointed, not yet on the throne, hungry with his followers, and accused by the religious leaders of his day. Then he goes further than David ever could: something greater than the temple is here, and the Son of Man is lord of the Sabbath. If David's need could open the holy bread, the need and authority of David's greater Son reach further still, for the temple and its bread pointed to him. (Christians differ on how the Sabbath carries over: this commentary holds that it is fulfilled in Christ and that the Lord's Day is a glad gift rather than a binding law, while many godly believers, with the Westminster Confession and the 1689 London Baptist Confession, hold a Lord's-Day Sabbath.)

Fear and faith in the same man (vv. 10-15). The man who ran at a giant was much afraid, and Scripture does not hide it. The psalms that grew out of that day (see the note on vv. 10-15) put fear and trust in the same sentence, which is where most believers actually live.
21.examples:
Then: The most famous soldier in Israel walked into a country priest's yard alone and hungry, told him a lie to get bread, took the sword he had captured as a boy off a hook behind the ephod, and carried it into the home town of the man he had killed with it — where he saved his life by pretending to be insane.

Now: Two things, and they pull against each other, which is why the chapter needs both. Ahimelech is the model for what to do when a rule and a hungry person meet in the same room, and the Lord Jesus' use of the story bears him out. And David is the warning about what a convenient falsehood costs when other people are standing in the room while you tell it. Yet he is also the way back: he named his sin without excuse (22:22), and the God of Psalm 34, who is near to the brokenhearted, did not cast him off. There is mercy for liars who own what they did, and David's greater Son, who never spoke a false word, is the one whose truthfulness covers ours.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — The Bread of the Presence
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: David comes alone to Nob, lies about a royal errand, and asks for bread (vv. 1-3). The priest gives him the holy bread (vv. 4-6).
verseByVerse.theology: Ahimelech has to decide on the spot between a holy rule and a hungry man, and he decides for the man.
verseByVerse.examples: Ahimelech acted in good faith on what he was told, and that good faith will cost him his life. The blame for it lies with the man who lied and the king who killed, not with him.

verseByVerse.quote: Then David came to Nob, to Ahimelech the priest. And Ahimelech came to meet David, trembling, and said to him, "Why are you alone, and no one with you?" And David said to Ahimelech the priest, "The king has charged me with a matter and said to me, 'Let no one know anything of the matter about which I send you, and with which I have charged you.' I have made an appointment with the young men for such and such a place. Now then, what do you have on hand? Give me five loaves of bread, or whatever is here." And the priest answered David, "I have no common bread on hand, but there is holy bread— if the young men have kept themselves from women." And David answered the priest, "Truly women have been kept from us as always when I go on an expedition. The vessels of the young men are holy even when it is an ordinary journey. How much more today will their vessels be holy?" So the priest gave him the holy bread, for there was no bread there but the bread of the Presence, which is removed from before the LORD, to be replaced by hot bread on the day it is taken away.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The priest is frightened before a word is said.

Nob was probably where the tabernacle had been re-established after Shiloh fell, and the man in charge is a great-grandson of Eli. What he sees coming up the road is the king's son-in-law, the captain of the bodyguard, the most famous soldier in Israel — unarmed, and by himself.

His question is the right one and it goes straight to the trouble: why are you alone? Men in David's position do not travel alone. Something has gone very wrong, and Ahimelech can see it.

David lies to him.

It should be said plainly, because David himself will say it plainly in the next chapter. There is no secret royal errand. He is running for his life, and he invents a commission to explain himself, and the invention is what puts the priest in danger — because a man who has been told he is helping the king will help freely and without asking further questions.

In the next chapter, when eighty-five priests are dead, David will say: I have occasioned the death of all the persons of your father's house (22:22).

He is hungry, and that is the whole of the request.

There is nothing in the building but the bread of the Presence.

The law is specific about it. Twelve loaves in two rows on a table of pure gold before the LORD, replaced every Sabbath, and the old loaves shall be for Aaron and his sons, and they shall eat it in a holy place, since it is for him a most holy portion (Lev. 24:5-9).

Ahimelech knows this perfectly well; he is the priest. And he weighs it, attaches the one condition that seems to him to matter, and hands it over.

This small transaction is famous because of what happened about a thousand years later. On a Sabbath, some Pharisees watch Jesus' disciples pulling heads of grain as they walk through a field, and object. And he answers them with this chapter.

Have you never read what David did when he was in need and was hungry, he and those who were with him: how he entered the house of God... and ate the bread of the Presence, which it is not lawful for any but the priests to eat, and also gave it to those who were with him? (Mark 2:25-26).

He does not say the bread was not holy, or that the rule did not apply, or that David was technically within his rights. He says it is not lawful for any but the priests to eat. The irregularity is admitted.

Then, in Matthew's account, he draws the conclusion out of the prophets: if you had known what this means, "I desire mercy, and not sacrifice," you would not have condemned the guiltless (Matt. 12:7).

That is Hosea 6:6, and it is Samuel's principle at Gilgal six chapters ago: to obey is better than sacrifice (15:22). The same order of things. God is not indifferent to his own arrangements, and he is not served by a use of them that leaves a hungry man hungry.

Ahimelech got it right. Faced with a starving man and twelve consecrated loaves that had just been taken off the table (v. 6), he fed him — and the Son of God cited the incident without blame in an argument with the most careful rule-keepers of his generation.

One footnote, since readers meet it. Mark's version says this happened in the time of Abiathar the high priest (Mark 2:26), and the priest here is Ahimelech, Abiathar's father. Abiathar was probably present at Nob; he escapes the massacre in the next chapter and becomes the well-known high priest of the period (22:20). So the phrase most likely locates the incident in his era, or in the section of Scripture associated with his name, as Mark elsewhere says in the passage about the bush for a part of Exodus (Mark 12:26). Not every reader finds these answers fully satisfying, and it is honest to say so; but nothing in either account depends on it.

“The vessels of the young men are holy”: their bodies and gear were ritually clean, for they had abstained from sexual relations, as soldiers on campaign did (cf. 2 Sam 11:11). That made them fit to eat the holy bread.
verseByVerse.note: 1 Samuel 21:1–15 is 21:2–16 in the Hebrew numbering (ESV note).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Doeg the Edomite is at the sanctuary (v. 7). David asks for a weapon and is given Goliath's sword (vv. 8-9).
verseByVerse.theology: Two things leave the sanctuary with David: a sword, and a witness who will use what he saw.
verseByVerse.examples: God gave David victory in the valley without a sword in his hand. Now he has the sword, and he is more afraid than he ever was in the valley.

verseByVerse.quote: Now a certain man of the servants of Saul was there that day, detained before the LORD. His name was Doeg the Edomite, the chief of Saul's herdsmen. Then David said to Ahimelech, "Then have you not here a spear or a sword at hand? For I have brought neither my sword nor my weapons with me, because the king's business required haste." And the priest said, "The sword of Goliath the Philistine, whom you struck down in the Valley of Elah, behold, it is here wrapped in a cloth behind the ephod. If you will take that, take it, for there is none but that here." And David said, "There is none like that; give it to me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
One verse, dropped in, with no comment at all.

The narrator interrupts a conversation about bread to tell us that somebody else was in the building, and then goes straight back to the bread. He gives us the man's nationality, his employer, and his job, and says nothing about what he is doing there beyond a phrase that probably means he was fulfilling some religious obligation.

An Edomite — a foreigner, from Esau's people — who is Saul's chief herdsman, at the sanctuary, watching the king's fugitive son-in-law take holy bread and a weapon from the high priest.

Everything in the next chapter comes out of this verse, and the writer plants it without underlining.

The lie continues, and he asks for a weapon.

The detail is true even if the reason is not: he has nothing. He left the court through a window at night with what he stood up in.

The last thing the narrator told us about that sword was that David took it off the giant's body and used it to cut off his head (17:51), and that he put the armour in his tent. The sword itself came here, to the sanctuary, and has been lying wrapped in cloth behind the ephod ever since — a relic of the day God saved Israel by a boy with a sling.

It is handed back to him on the worst day of his life so far.

One sentence, and it can be read two ways at once.

Practically, it is the only weapon in the building and he takes it. But he says more than that: there is none like that. He is holding the sword he took when he had none, given by a God who saves not with sword and spear, on a day when he has nothing else at all.

His best day's trophy is the equipment of his worst.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: David flees to Gath and is recognised (vv. 10-11). Afraid, he feigns madness, and Achish dismisses him (vv. 12-15).
verseByVerse.theology: He has run to the enemy's capital carrying the enemy champion's sword, and the first thing the courtiers do is quote the song that started all his trouble. There is nowhere left for him inside Israel and nowhere safe outside it.
verseByVerse.examples: If you have done something undignified out of fear, notice that God did not wait for David to recover his dignity before he heard him.

verseByVerse.quote: And David rose and fled that day from Saul and went to Achish the king of Gath. And the servants of Achish said to him, "Is not this David the king of the land? Did they not sing to one another of him in dances, 'Saul has struck down his thousands, and David his ten thousands'?" And David took these words to heart and was much afraid of Achish the king of Gath. So he changed his behavior before them and pretended to be insane in their hands and made marks on the doors of the gate and let his spittle run down his beard. Then Achish said to his servants, "Behold, you see the man is mad. Why then have you brought him to me? Do I lack madmen, that you have brought this fellow to behave as a madman in my presence? Shall this fellow come into my house?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Remember what he is carrying.

Gath is Goliath's town. It is named as his in the first description of him — a champion named Goliath of Gath (17:4) — and David is walking into it with the man's sword on his hip.

It is either the boldest thing in the book or the most desperate, and verse 12 tells us which.

They know him at once, and they quote the song.

That song has now followed him everywhere. It made Saul watch him with suspicion, it was in Saul's mouth when he raged at Jonathan, and here it is in a Philistine court, sung back at him by the servants of the king whose champion he killed. Everybody in that room can recite it.

They also call him the king of the land, which is not his title and is a shrewd guess by men who have been keeping an eye on Israel.

The narrator says it without any softening: much afraid.

This is the man who ran at a giant. He is now standing in that giant's home town, recognised, in a foreign court, with no army and no plan, and he is frightened.

So the anointed king of Israel scratches at a gate and drools into his beard.

Nothing here can be made dignified and the writer does not try. Madness probably afforded a man some protection in that world, since many thought the mad were under a god's hand and left them alone, so it is a calculated performance and it works. It is also the lowest point of his life so far, and it is recorded in detail.

The king's irritation is entirely about the inconvenience, and the contempt is total.

Do I lack madmen? He is not even worth a decision. They throw him out.

What makes this chapter worth reading twice is not in the chapter.

Two psalms carry headings that point to this day. The first is Psalm 56 — when the Philistines seized him in Gath — and it says: when I am afraid, I put my trust in you... in God I trust; I shall not be afraid. What can flesh do to me? (Ps. 56:3-4). He was much afraid, verse 12 says so, and the psalm does not pretend otherwise; it puts the fear and the trust in the same sentence.

The second is Psalm 34, whose heading names the day when he changed his behavior before Abimelech, so that he drove him out. And that psalm is one of the most-loved in the book. I sought the LORD, and he answered me and delivered me from all my fears... this poor man cried, and the LORD heard him and saved him out of all his troubles... oh, taste and see that the LORD is good! (Ps. 34:4-8).

Somebody wrote taste and see that the LORD is good about the day he stood in an enemy gateway with saliva running into his beard because it was the only thing he could think of to stay alive.

Hold that, if your own worst day would not look like a testimony from the outside. The psalm did not come from the throne. It came from the gate at Gath.

And the psalm did not stay at Gath. Peter takes its best-known line and applies it to Christ: if indeed you have tasted that the Lord is good, he writes, and goes straight on, As you come to him, a living stone rejected by men (1 Peter 2:3–4). John probably hears the same psalm's not one of them is broken (34:20) at the cross (John 19:36). The song of a fugitive king, delivered from his enemies, became a song about the rejected King who was not delivered from death but through it.

Psalm 34 names the king “Abimelech”, which seems to have been a royal title among the Philistines, like Pharaoh (cf. Gen 26:1); his name was Achish.
verseByVerse.note: Achish is king of Gath here and again in 27:2, when David comes back to him with six hundred men.

22.title: The Massacre at Nob
22.text: <sup>1</sup>David departed from there and escaped to the cave of Adullam. And when his brothers and all his father's house heard it, they went down there to him.<sup>2</sup>And everyone who was in distress, and everyone who was in debt, and everyone who was bitter in soul, gathered to him. And he became commander over them. And there were with him about four hundred men.<sup>3</sup>And David went from there to Mizpeh of Moab. And he said to the king of Moab, "Please let my father and my mother stay with you, till I know what God will do for me."<sup>4</sup>And he left them with the king of Moab, and they stayed with him all the time that David was in the stronghold.<sup>5</sup>Then the prophet Gad said to David, "Do not remain in the stronghold; depart, and go into the land of Judah." So David departed and went into the forest of Hereth.<sup>6</sup>Now Saul heard that David was discovered, and the men who were with him. Saul was sitting at Gibeah under the tamarisk tree on the height with his spear in his hand, and all his servants were standing about him.<sup>7</sup>And Saul said to his servants who stood about him, "Hear now, people of Benjamin; will the son of Jesse give every one of you fields and vineyards, will he make you all commanders of thousands and commanders of hundreds,<sup>8</sup>that all of you have conspired against me? No one discloses to me when my son makes a covenant with the son of Jesse. None of you is sorry for me or discloses to me that my son has stirred up my servant against me, to lie in wait, as at this day."<sup>9</sup>Then answered Doeg the Edomite, who stood by the servants of Saul, "I saw the son of Jesse coming to Nob, to Ahimelech the son of Ahitub,<sup>10</sup>and he inquired of the LORD for him and gave him provisions and gave him the sword of Goliath the Philistine."<sup>11</sup>Then the king sent to summon Ahimelech the priest, the son of Ahitub, and all his father's house, the priests who were at Nob, and all of them came to the king.<sup>12</sup>And Saul said, "Hear now, son of Ahitub." And he answered, "Here I am, my lord."<sup>13</sup>And Saul said to him, "Why have you conspired against me, you and the son of Jesse, in that you have given him bread and a sword and have inquired of God for him, so that he has risen against me, to lie in wait, as at this day?"<sup>14</sup>Then Ahimelech answered the king, "And who among all your servants is so faithful as David, who is the king's son-in-law, and captain over your bodyguard, and honored in your house?<sup>15</sup>Is today the first time that I have inquired of God for him? No! Let not the king impute anything to his servant or to all the house of my father, for your servant has known nothing of all this, much or little."<sup>16</sup>And the king said, "You shall surely die, Ahimelech, you and all your father's house."<sup>17</sup>And the king said to the guard who stood about him, "Turn and kill the priests of the LORD, because their hand also is with David, and they knew that he fled and did not disclose it to me." But the servants of the king would not put out their hand to strike the priests of the LORD.<sup>18</sup>Then the king said to Doeg, "You turn and strike the priests." And Doeg the Edomite turned and struck down the priests, and he killed on that day eighty-five persons who wore the linen ephod.<sup>19</sup>And Nob, the city of the priests, he put to the sword; both man and woman, child and infant, ox, donkey and sheep, he put to the sword.<sup>20</sup>But one of the sons of Ahimelech the son of Ahitub, named Abiathar, escaped and fled after David.<sup>21</sup>And Abiathar told David that Saul had killed the priests of the LORD.<sup>22</sup>And David said to Abiathar, "I knew on that day, when Doeg the Edomite was there, that he would surely tell Saul. I have occasioned the death of all the persons of your father's house.<sup>23</sup>Stay with me; do not be afraid, for he who seeks my life seeks your life. With me you shall be in safekeeping."
22.overview: The distressed, the indebted and the bitter gather to David in a cave, and they become the mighty men of 2 Samuel 23. Meanwhile Saul, under a tamarisk with his spear, bribes his tribe and pities himself, and Doeg the Edomite reports what he saw at Nob with the one innocent fact left out. Ahimelech's honest defence condemns him, the bodyguard refuses the order, and Doeg does it. Eighty-five men in linen ephods, and then the town: both man and woman, child and infant, ox, donkey and sheep. That is the wording of the command about Amalek which Saul would not obey (15:3). He would not do it to the enemies of God. He does it to a town of God's priests.
22.theology:
The king outside the camp. The pattern runs on to the Son of David. He too was the rightful King without a throne, and those who gathered to him were tax collectors, sinners and the weary, not the great (Matthew 11:28; 1 Corinthians 1:26–28). He calls his people to come to him outside the camp and share his reproach until his kingdom comes (Hebrews 13:13). And David's promise in verse 23, with me you shall be in safekeeping, is kept far better by Christ: no one will snatch his sheep out of his hand (John 10:28). Unlike David, whose lie brought the danger, he never once put his people at risk by his own sin; he took their danger on himself.

Two kings, two kinds of rule. Saul rules by tribe, bribe and fear, and when his own guards will not obey, by a foreigner's sword (vv. 7-18). David rules from a cave, with nothing to offer but honesty and company (vv. 22-23). The heading of Psalm 52 sets that psalm against Doeg: God's answer to the man who trusted in the abundance of his riches and boasted of evil is that God will break him down forever (52:5, 7), while the righteous flourish in the house of God.
22.examples:
Then: A king's own bodyguard stood in a ring around him and refused, without a word, to kill the priests of the LORD — so he handed the sword to a foreigner, who killed eighty-five men in their vestments and then destroyed their town down to the livestock, using the exact terms of a command from God that the same king had refused to obey against an enemy.

Now: Three things. Doeg's report is the model of the damaging truth — nothing invented, one thing left out — so ask whether any account you have given lately was accurate in that way. The guards are the model of the other kind of courage: no speech, no confrontation, simply not moving when told to do what should not be done. And David's I have occasioned the death is the hardest. He had four true things he could have said instead, and said none of them, to the one man in the world with a right to hear it. Confession like that is possible only for someone who knows that God's mercy is larger than his guilt (Psalm 32:5), and for us it rests on the one who carried the guilt we cannot undo.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — Everyone Who Was in Distress
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: At Adullam David's family and four hundred men in distress gather to him (vv. 1-2). He shelters his parents in Moab (vv. 3-4) and, at Gad's word, returns to Judah (v. 5).
verseByVerse.theology: David's first followers are not the people anyone would choose, and that is the point: God builds his king's army out of the men nobody else wanted.
verseByVerse.examples: Even on the run, David makes provision for his elderly parents. Honouring father and mother does not wait for settled times.

verseByVerse.quote: David departed from there and escaped to the cave of Adullam. And when his brothers and all his father's house heard it, they went down there to him. And everyone who was in distress, and everyone who was in debt, and everyone who was bitter in soul, gathered to him. And he became commander over them. And there were with him about four hundred men. And David went from there to Mizpeh of Moab. And he said to the king of Moab, "Please let my father and my mother stay with you, till I know what God will do for me." And he left them with the king of Moab, and they stayed with him all the time that David was in the stronghold. Then the prophet Gad said to David, "Do not remain in the stronghold; depart, and go into the land of Judah." So David departed and went into the forest of Hereth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He gets out of Philistine territory and into a cave, and the first people to arrive are his family.

Including Eliab, presumably, who told him in front of the army that he knew the evil of your heart. Whatever was between those brothers, when David was a hunted man his father's whole house came down and joined him in a hole in the ground.

Then the rest.

Everyone in distress — men under pressure, in trouble of some kind. Everyone in debt — men who could not pay, which in that world meant men facing slavery for themselves and their children. And everyone bitter in soul — the aggrieved, the disappointed, men with a grudge against how things had gone for them.

Four hundred of them, and there is not one word in the list about courage or ability or faith.

This is the beginning of David's army. Not a militia of patriots, and not veterans: the failed, the indebted and the embittered, gathering in a cave around a man with no position and a price on his head.

Within a generation these men, or their sons, are the corps listed by name at the end of 2 Samuel — the thirty and the three, the men who broke through a Philistine garrison to bring David a drink of water from the well at Bethlehem (2 Sam. 23:8-17). The distressed and the debtors became the mighty men.

The making of them is what the next ten chapters are about, and it happens in caves and wildernesses under a commander who is himself being hunted.

He gets his parents out of the country, and the country he chooses is Moab.

That is not a random choice. Jesse's grandmother was Ruth the Moabitess, who left Moab for Bethlehem and would not go back (Ruth 1:16). David is sending his elderly father and mother to his own family's other side, along a road his great-grandmother walked in the opposite direction.

The phrase he uses for his situation matters: till I know what God will do for me. Not until things settle, or until Saul dies, or until I have an army. He does not know what is coming and says so, and he expects God to do something.

A prophet appears with no introduction, and David obeys immediately.

Gad turns up here as though we know him, and he stays with David for the rest of his life; he is the one who brings him the choice of three judgments after the census, decades later (2 Sam. 24:11-14). From this point the fugitive has a prophet, and shortly he will have a priest with an ephod as well.

The instruction itself is counter-intuitive: leave the stronghold, go back into Judah, which is where Saul is looking. He goes.
verseByVerse.note: Adullam lay in the lowlands of Judah.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–16 — Hear Now, People of Benjamin
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Saul complains to his servants (vv. 6-8), Doeg reports Nob (vv. 9-10), and Ahimelech's defence is met with a death sentence (vv. 11-16).
verseByVerse.theology: Saul's speech shows the kind of king the people asked for: one who looks after his own tribe, and above all himself.
verseByVerse.examples: Ahimelech's honesty does not save him. Sometimes telling the truth costs everything, and Scripture does not pretend otherwise; it simply records that he told it.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Saul heard that David was discovered, and the men who were with him. Saul was sitting at Gibeah under the tamarisk tree on the height with his spear in his hand, and all his servants were standing about him. And Saul said to his servants who stood about him, "Hear now, people of Benjamin; will the son of Jesse give every one of you fields and vineyards, will he make you all commanders of thousands and commanders of hundreds, that all of you have conspired against me? No one discloses to me when my son makes a covenant with the son of Jesse. None of you is sorry for me or discloses to me that my son has stirred up my servant against me, to lie in wait, as at this day." Then answered Doeg the Edomite, who stood by the servants of Saul, "I saw the son of Jesse coming to Nob, to Ahimelech the son of Ahitub, and he inquired of the LORD for him and gave him provisions and gave him the sword of Goliath the Philistine."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The narrator has now placed that spear in Saul's hand three times, and it has been thrown four times. It is the thing he holds.

He opens with the tribe.

Hear now, people of Benjamin. His court is staffed with his own clansmen, and his first argument is that David is from Judah and they are not. It is the oldest appeal in politics and it is being made by a man who was anointed to lead all twelve tribes.

Then the bribe, which should be set beside the warning it echoes.

Samuel had told the nation what a king would do: he will take the best of your fields and vineyards and olive orchards and give them to his servants (8:14). That is the confiscation Israel was warned about, and here is the king naming it as the currency of loyalty — and implying, quite openly, that this is what he does for them.

The rest of the speech is self-pity, and the pronouns run one way.

Conspired against me. Discloses to me. Sorry for me. Discloses to me. Against me. Five times in one verse, from a king to his own household, complaining that nobody feels for him.

He also knows about the covenant. When my son makes a covenant with the son of Jesse — he has worked out what happened in the field, and his complaint is not that it happened but that nobody told him.

Then the Edomite speaks.

He has been waiting for this. A king has just told a room full of Benjaminites that nobody cares about him and that he is surrounded by conspirators, and the one foreigner in the room steps forward with information.

Everything he says is factually accurate and the whole report is a lie in its effect. He describes a priest giving bread, a weapon and an oracle to a fugitive, and leaves out the one thing that makes it innocent: that Ahimelech had been told David was on the king's own business.

Doeg was standing there. He heard it. He omits it.

That is how the most damaging kind of falsehood is usually told — not by inventing anything, but by reporting true things with the exculpating fact removed.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the king sent to summon Ahimelech the priest, the son of Ahitub, and all his father's house, the priests who were at Nob, and all of them came to the king. And Saul said, "Hear now, son of Ahitub." And he answered, "Here I am, my lord." And Saul said to him, "Why have you conspired against me, you and the son of Jesse, in that you have given him bread and a sword and have inquired of God for him, so that he has risen against me, to lie in wait, as at this day?" Then Ahimelech answered the king, "And who among all your servants is so faithful as David, who is the king's son-in-law, and captain over your bodyguard, and honored in your house? Is today the first time that I have inquired of God for him? No! Let not the king impute anything to his servant or to all the house of my father, for your servant has known nothing of all this, much or little." And the king said, "You shall surely die, Ahimelech, you and all your father's house."
verseByVerse.commentary:
He summons not one priest but the whole family, which tells us what he has decided before anybody arrives.

And they come. Every one of them walks to Gibeah at the king's word, because that is what you do when the king sends.

He is addressed by his father's name, not his own — the same trick Saul uses on David — and he answers here I am, which is the word Samuel said in the dark at Shiloh and Jonathan's at Michmash (14:43).

The charge is conspiracy, and Doeg's three items are recited as the evidence: bread, a sword, an oracle.

The priest's defence is the truth, delivered straight, and it is the worst thing he could possibly have said.

And every one of those facts is precisely what Saul cannot bear. The man is defending himself by listing the reasons the king wants David dead.

It is what happens when an honest man is questioned by somebody whose real motive he has not grasped. Ahimelech thinks he is answering a charge of treason and is producing character evidence. He has no idea he is standing in front of a man who has thrown four spears.

This is his real answer, and it is unanswerable: this was routine.

He has enquired of God for David before, more than once. Of course he has — David is the captain of the bodyguard, and consulting the LORD before an operation is what the priesthood is for. Nothing that happened at Nob was unusual in any way.

Then the plea: your servant has known nothing of all this, much or little. He is telling the truth, and he does not know that David lied to him, and he is about to die for a deception he was never party to.

Four words of verdict, and no engagement with the defence at all.

Saul does use his name here, which he has not done since the summons. And the sentence extends to the whole family, which is why they were all summoned.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–19 — The Servants of the King Would Not
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The guard refuses to kill the priests (v. 17); Doeg kills eighty-five of them and then Nob itself (vv. 18-19).
verseByVerse.theology: When the king's own men will not do evil, he finds someone who will. Evil seldom lacks a willing hand, which makes the refusal of the guards all the more precious.
verseByVerse.examples: For anyone who has been ordered to do wrong by someone with power over them, the guards show that quiet refusal is possible, and that God sees it.

verseByVerse.quote: And the king said to the guard who stood about him, "Turn and kill the priests of the LORD, because their hand also is with David, and they knew that he fled and did not disclose it to me." But the servants of the king would not put out their hand to strike the priests of the LORD. Then the king said to Doeg, "You turn and strike the priests." And Doeg the Edomite turned and struck down the priests, and he killed on that day eighty-five persons who wore the linen ephod. And Nob, the city of the priests, he put to the sword; both man and woman, child and infant, ox, donkey and sheep, he put to the sword.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He gives the order to his own bodyguard, and he calls them what they are while doing it: the priests of the LORD.

He is not confused about who these men are. He knows.

Here is the one clean thing in the chapter.

They refuse. Ordinary soldiers, standing in a ring around a king who has already killed for less, decline to carry out a direct royal order, and they decline it in silence — the text records no speech, no argument and no plea. They simply do not move.

The narrator does not praise them, which is his way, and the absence of comment is the comment. Somewhere in the guard of a man like Saul there were men who had worked out that there are orders you do not obey.

This is the only recorded refusal in the chapter and it comes from nobody in particular. Not Abner, the commander and the king's cousin, who is standing there. Not any of the servants named. The men without names.

So he turns to the foreigner, and the foreigner does it.

Eighty-five men in priestly dress, killed by one man on the orders of the king of Israel, in front of a bodyguard who had just refused.

The detail who wore the linen ephod is put there so that nobody can pretend these were combatants. They were dressed for the altar when they were summoned and they were dressed for the altar when they died.

Set that list beside one seven chapters back.

Now go and strike Amalek and devote to destruction all that they have. Do not spare them, but kill both man and woman, child and infant, ox and sheep, camel and donkey (15:3).

It is the same sentence. Man and woman, child and infant, and the livestock enumerated after them.

Saul was given that command by God about a nation under a centuries-old sentence for attacking the weak at the back of Israel's column, and he did not carry it out. He kept the best of the sheep and the oxen and the fattened calves and the king, and told Samuel it was for sacrifice, and lost the kingdom for it.

And here, of his own initiative, with no command from anybody, he executes it in full — against an Israelite town, the town of the priests of the LORD, down to the infants and the donkeys.

He would not do it to God's enemies. He does it to God's priests.

There is nothing to add to that and the writer adds nothing. He states the two lists seven chapters apart and lets anyone who is reading carefully put them together.

One more thing, and it is not a consolation but it is the truth. This is the fulfilment of a sentence passed long before. The man of God told Eli that God would cut off your strength and the strength of your father's house, so that there will not be an old man in your house, and that all the descendants of your house shall die by the sword of men (2:31-33). Ahimelech was Eli's great-grandson.

God's word stands, and it does not make Saul or Doeg one degree less guilty of what they chose to do. Scripture holds both of those at once, as it does at Acts 2:23, and it does not offer to resolve them.

And for anyone who reads of the children of Nob and thinks of a child of their own: God did not overlook them. He named their killer in a psalm (Psalm 52), and he has promised a day when every such deed is judged and every tear wiped away (Revelation 21:4).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 20–23 — With Me You Shall Be in Safekeeping
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Abiathar escapes to David (vv. 20-21), who owns his part without excuse (v. 22) and offers him safekeeping (v. 23).
verseByVerse.theology: Abiathar arrives with nothing but grief and the ephod, and David's first act is to take the blame that is his.
verseByVerse.examples: A priest in the cave means that the hunted king can now ask God for guidance, and he will soon do so (23:6, 9).

verseByVerse.quote: But one of the sons of Ahimelech the son of Ahitub, named Abiathar, escaped and fled after David. And Abiathar told David that Saul had killed the priests of the LORD. And David said to Abiathar, "I knew on that day, when Doeg the Edomite was there, that he would surely tell Saul. I have occasioned the death of all the persons of your father's house. Stay with me; do not be afraid, for he who seeks my life seeks your life. With me you shall be in safekeeping."
verseByVerse.commentary:
One man gets out.

He is the survivor the oracle promised. The only one of you whom I shall not cut off from my altar shall be spared to weep his eyes out to grieve his heart (2:33). Abiathar will serve David for some forty years, and Solomon will finally remove him from the priesthood — and the historian stops to say why: thus fulfilling the word of the LORD that he had spoken concerning the house of Eli in Shiloh (1 Kings 2:27).

He runs to David, which is the only direction left.

David takes it, without one word of qualification.

Every one of these excuses was available to him and every one is true. He does not say that Saul gave the order. He does not say that Doeg swung the sword. He does not say that he had no way of knowing, or that he was running for his life, or that a hungry man must eat.

He says two things. I knew on that day, when Doeg the Edomite was there, that he would surely tell Saul. He saw the man. He understood what he was, and what he would do with what he had seen, and he asked for the bread and the sword anyway.

That is a confession of the kind almost nobody makes, and it is made to the one surviving son of the family, on the day he arrives with the news. There is no attempt to share the weight out.

It does not make him the murderer; Saul gave the order and Doeg carried it out and both will answer for it. What David is owning is the lie in chapter 21 and the decision to go on with it in front of a man he knew was watching.

Then he offers the only thing he has, which is a place beside him in a cave.

The honesty of it is the striking part: he who seeks my life seeks your life. He does not promise safety, because he has none to promise. He is a hunted man offering a hunted man company, and the guarantee amounts to "whatever happens to me will happen to you".

And that turns out to be worth having. Abiathar brought the ephod down with him (23:6), and from the next chapter onward the fugitive can enquire of God directly — which is precisely what Saul, sitting on his throne under his tamarisk tree, can no longer do at all.

Saul destroyed the priests of Nob to protect his crown, and the one survivor walked out of the ruins carrying the ephod to David.

23.title: David Strengthens Himself in the LORD
23.text: <sup>1</sup>Now they told David, "Behold, the Philistines are fighting against Keilah and are robbing the threshing floors."<sup>2</sup>Therefore David inquired of the LORD, "Shall I go and attack these Philistines?" And the LORD said to David, "Go and attack the Philistines and save Keilah."<sup>3</sup>But David's men said to him, "Behold, we are afraid here in Judah; how much more then if we go to Keilah against the armies of the Philistines?"<sup>4</sup>Then David inquired of the LORD again. And the LORD answered him, "Arise, go down to Keilah, for I will give the Philistines into your hand."<sup>5</sup>And David and his men went to Keilah and fought with the Philistines and brought away their livestock and struck them with a great blow. So David saved the inhabitants of Keilah.<sup>6</sup>When Abiathar the son of Ahimelech had fled to David to Keilah, he had come down with an ephod in his hand.<sup>7</sup>Now it was told Saul that David had come to Keilah. And Saul said, "God has given him into my hand, for he has shut himself in by entering a town that has gates and bars."<sup>8</sup>And Saul summoned all the people to war, to go down to Keilah, to besiege David and his men.<sup>9</sup>David knew that Saul was plotting harm against him. And he said to Abiathar the priest, "Bring the ephod here."<sup>10</sup>Then David said, "O LORD, the God of Israel, your servant has surely heard that Saul seeks to come to Keilah, to destroy the city on my account.<sup>11</sup>Will the men of Keilah surrender me into his hand? Will Saul come down, as your servant has heard? O LORD, the God of Israel, please tell your servant." And the LORD said, "He will come down."<sup>12</sup>Then David said, "Will the men of Keilah surrender me and my men into the hand of Saul?" And the LORD said, "They will surrender you."<sup>13</sup>Then David and his men, who were about six hundred, arose and departed from Keilah, and they went wherever they could go. When Saul was told that David had escaped from Keilah, he gave up the expedition.<sup>14</sup>And David remained in the strongholds in the wilderness, in the hill country of the wilderness of Ziph. And Saul sought him every day, but God did not give him into his hand.<sup>15</sup>David saw that Saul had come out to seek his life. David was in the wilderness of Ziph at Horesh.<sup>16</sup>And Jonathan, Saul's son, rose and went to David at Horesh, and strengthened his hand in God.<sup>17</sup>And he said to him, "Do not fear, for the hand of Saul my father shall not find you. You shall be king over Israel, and I shall be next to you. Saul my father also knows this."<sup>18</sup>And the two of them made a covenant before the LORD. David remained at Horesh, and Jonathan went home.<sup>19</sup>Then the Ziphites went up to Saul at Gibeah, saying, "Is not David hiding among us in the strongholds at Horesh, on the hill of Hachilah, which is south of Jeshimon?<sup>20</sup>Now come down, O king, according to all your heart's desire to come down, and our part shall be to surrender him into the king's hand."<sup>21</sup>And Saul said, "May you be blessed by the LORD, for you have had compassion on me.<sup>22</sup>Go, make yet more sure. Know and see the place where his foot is, and who has seen him there, for it is told me that he is very cunning.<sup>23</sup>See therefore and take note of all the lurking places where he hides, and come back to me with sure information. Then I will go with you. And if he is in the land, I will search him out among all the thousands of Judah."<sup>24</sup>And they arose and went to Ziph ahead of Saul. Now David and his men were in the wilderness of Maon, in the Arabah to the south of Jeshimon.<sup>25</sup>And Saul and his men went to seek him. And David was told, so he went down to the rock and lived in the wilderness of Maon. And when Saul heard that, he pursued after David in the wilderness of Maon.<sup>26</sup>Saul went on one side of the mountain, and David and his men on the other side of the mountain. And David was hurrying to get away from Saul. As Saul and his men were closing in on David and his men to capture them,<sup>27</sup>a messenger came to Saul, saying, "Hurry and come, for the Philistines have made a raid against the land."<sup>28</sup>So Saul returned from pursuing after David and went against the Philistines. Therefore that place was called the Rock of Escape.<sup>29</sup>And David went up from there and lived in the strongholds of Engedi.
23.overview: David asks God, twice, and saves Keilah, a town that would hand him over, while the king uses his army to hunt him. Because Abiathar brought the ephod from Nob, David can ask and Saul can only infer: God has given him into my hand. The narrator answers in his own words: God did not give him into his hand. Then Jonathan comes into the wilderness and strengthened his hand in God, and when the chase closes round a hill in Maon, a messenger with news of a Philistine raid pulls Saul away. They named the rock.
23.theology:
Asking and inferring (vv. 2, 7, 9). The chapter is built on a contrast: David asks God, four times, while Saul reads God's will off his circumstances. Both men believe in providence. The difference is that one brings his plans to God and the other brings God to his plans.

Not into his hand (vv. 5, 12, 14). The shape of this chapter is the shape of the gospel turned about. The anointed king saves a town that would hand him over, and God will not let his enemy take him, because David's time had not come. The Son of David also spent himself for people who would hand him over, and more than once his enemies could not lay hands on him, because his hour had not yet come (John 7:30). But when it came, God did give him into the hands of sinners (Matthew 26:45), delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God (Acts 2:23). David was kept from Saul's hand; Christ was handed over, so that those who betrayed him could be saved.
23.examples:
Then: Two armed forces went round one hill in opposite directions, yards apart and out of sight, with the smaller one running out of ground — until a messenger reached the larger one with news of a Philistine raid, and it turned and left. They called the hill the Rock of Escape.

Now: Two things to take. Jonathan is the pattern for what to do about a discouraged Christian, and it is simpler than most people think: you do not need a new word for them, you need to say the old one out loud where they are. Go to them, and strengthen their hand in God; it is the Spirit, the Comforter, who takes such ordinary words and makes them hold. And Saul at verse 7 is the pattern to avoid — the habit of taking a convenient circumstance as divine endorsement of what you already wanted. He was doing theology, and he was hunting God's anointed while he did it.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: David asks the LORD, asks again when his men are afraid, and saves Keilah (vv. 1-5). Abiathar has brought the ephod (v. 6).
verseByVerse.theology: David's first act after the news from Nob is to protect someone else. Grief and danger have not turned him in on himself.
verseByVerse.examples: The ephod reaches David through the worst event of these chapters. God did not cause Saul's crime, but he did not let it have the last word.

verseByVerse.quote: Now they told David, "Behold, the Philistines are fighting against Keilah and are robbing the threshing floors." Therefore David inquired of the LORD, "Shall I go and attack these Philistines?" And the LORD said to David, "Go and attack the Philistines and save Keilah." But David's men said to him, "Behold, we are afraid here in Judah; how much more then if we go to Keilah against the armies of the Philistines?" Then David inquired of the LORD again. And the LORD answered him, "Arise, go down to Keilah, for I will give the Philistines into your hand." And David and his men went to Keilah and fought with the Philistines and brought away their livestock and struck them with a great blow. So David saved the inhabitants of Keilah. When Abiathar the son of Ahimelech had fled to David to Keilah, he had come down with an ephod in his hand.
verseByVerse.commentary:
What is being robbed is not treasure.

The threshing floors are where the grain harvest is separated and stored. Raiding them at harvest time is the cheapest way to make war on a farming town: you let them do the work and then take the year's food. Keilah is not facing a siege; it is facing a winter with nothing in the barn.

Keilah is a town of Judah, David's own tribe, a few miles from the hills where he is hiding. And nobody from the government is coming, because the government's army is out looking for him.

He asks first.

It happens four times in twenty-nine verses and it is the thing that distinguishes him from the man hunting him. The obvious course is to go; his tribe is being robbed and he has four hundred armed men. He asks anyway.

His men say no, and they are not being cowardly — they are being accurate.

They are wanted men in their own country. They are frightened where they are. Marching into open ground to fight the Philistine army, with Saul's forces somewhere behind them, is a plainly terrible idea, and any competent soldier would say so.

So he asks a second time, and God answers a second time, and adds something.

The first answer was an instruction. The second is an instruction with a promise inside it: I will give the Philistines into your hand. God does not rebuke him for asking twice. He gives the frightened men something to hold.

Anybody who has been told that asking again is a failure of faith may take heart. David had a clear word and his men were afraid, so he went back and asked again, and God met the second asking with more than he gave the first.

So David saves Keilah. He is a hunted man with no title, no supply line, and a price on his head, and he spends the one asset he has — four hundred men — on a town that cannot pay him, cannot shelter him, and as we are about to discover would hand him over at the first opportunity.

And Saul, who has a throne, a standing army and a commander-in-chief, is using all of it to chase one man round the hills while the Philistines rob his people's grain.

The narrator does not say which of them is behaving like a king. He does not need to.

Here is the note that explains the whole chapter.

It reads like an aside and it is the engine of everything that follows. Abiathar, the one survivor of Nob, arrived carrying the ephod — the priestly vestment used for enquiring of the LORD.

So David can ask God questions. Four times in this chapter he does, and four times he gets an answer.

Saul cannot ask anybody anything, because he killed the men who could have told him. He destroyed the priests of Nob to secure his crown, and the effect of it is that the priest and the ephod are now in the cave with his rival, and the king of Israel is left guessing.

He had already stopped hearing from God before that — the LORD did not answer him, either by dreams, or by Urim, or by prophets, as it will be put at 28:6. Nob was him closing the last door himself.

The ephod brought by Abiathar probably held the Urim and Thummim, the sacred lots by which the priest received God’s yes or no. Christians today have no ephod and need none: God has spoken fully in his Son and in the Scriptures (Hebrews 1:1–2), and we ask him for wisdom (James 1:5) rather than for a lot to fall.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–14 — God Has Given Him Into My Hand
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Saul thinks God has trapped David (vv. 7-8). David asks God, learns Keilah would betray him, and leaves (vv. 9-13); God does not give him into Saul's hand (v. 14).
verseByVerse.theology: God's answers to David here are not riddles. They are plain warnings, given so that he can act on them.
verseByVerse.examples: Being betrayed by the people you have just helped is one of the bitterest things there is. David does not take revenge on Keilah; he simply leaves.

verseByVerse.quote: Now it was told Saul that David had come to Keilah. And Saul said, "God has given him into my hand, for he has shut himself in by entering a town that has gates and bars." And Saul summoned all the people to war, to go down to Keilah, to besiege David and his men. David knew that Saul was plotting harm against him. And he said to Abiathar the priest, "Bring the ephod here." Then David said, "O LORD, the God of Israel, your servant has surely heard that Saul seeks to come to Keilah, to destroy the city on my account. Will the men of Keilah surrender me into his hand? Will Saul come down, as your servant has heard? O LORD, the God of Israel, please tell your servant." And the LORD said, "He will come down." Then David said, "Will the men of Keilah surrender me and my men into the hand of Saul?" And the LORD said, "They will surrender you." Then David and his men, who were about six hundred, arose and departed from Keilah, and they went wherever they could go. When Saul was told that David had escaped from Keilah, he gave up the expedition. And David remained in the strongholds in the wilderness, in the hill country of the wilderness of Ziph. And Saul sought him every day, but God did not give him into his hand.
verseByVerse.commentary:
It is one of the most instructive mistakes in Scripture.

Saul looks at a circumstance — his enemy is inside a walled town with gates — and he draws a theological conclusion from it: God has given him into my hand. The reasoning is not stupid. A man in a walled town is trapped; you can besiege him; that is simply true.

It is completely wrong, and the narrator will say so in his own words seven verses later. For the moment he lets it stand.

Two things in it repay attention.

The first is that Saul is doing theology. He is not a secularist; he reads events as God's providence, and he is at this moment hunting the LORD's anointed while sincerely believing the LORD is helping him do it. That is a more frightening thing to be than an atheist.

The second is the method. He has a desire, he sees a circumstance that serves it, and he calls the circumstance God's will. There is no asking involved, and there is nobody left to ask. Favourable circumstances are not, by themselves, evidence of anything at all — and the man who most needs to hear that is always the one whose plan is going well.

David's response to the same news is four words: bring the ephod here.

That is the contrast the chapter is built on, and it is put in consecutive verses. Saul infers. David asks.

The shape of the prayer comes before the questions in it.

To destroy the city on my account. His first thought is not his own neck but what his presence will cost the town he has just saved. That is the man; it is the same instinct as I have occasioned the death in the previous chapter.

Two questions, two answers, and the second one is bitter.

They will hand him over. The men whose harvest he had just saved, at the risk of every life he commands, will open the gates and give him to Saul rather than take the consequences of keeping him.

It should be said that they are not monsters. Saul had just destroyed an entire town for sheltering David — the news from Nob would have reached Keilah — and these are farmers with families inside walls that will not hold against an army. Fear does this to ordinary decent people. It does not make it less of a betrayal, and God tells David it is coming.

There is a question readers rightly ask here: if they never actually did it, in what sense was the answer true? The answer is that God told him what would happen, and the telling is why it did not. This is not God being mistaken about the future. It is God warning a man about a road so that the man does not walk down it — which is what almost every warning in Scripture is for. A father who says "that branch will break" is not proved wrong when the child comes down.

There are six hundred men now, up from four hundred, and more keep coming.

And the phrase they went wherever they could go is as bleak as it sounds. No destination, no plan; out of the town and into the hills, because staying was the one thing they knew would kill them.

There is the answer to verse 7, in Saul's own vocabulary. He said God has given him into my hand. The narrator waits seven verses and then writes the sentence with the word not in it.

And the rest of it: Saul sought him every day. Every day. This is a king spending the whole of his reign, day after day, on one man — and the reason he never finds him is not that David is clever, though he is. The reason is stated: God did not hand him over.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–18 — He Strengthened His Hand in God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jonathan comes to David at Horesh and strengthens his hand in God (vv. 15-17). They make a covenant and part (v. 18).
verseByVerse.theology: In a chapter full of informers and pursuers, one man walks into danger simply to stand beside a friend.
verseByVerse.examples: The covenant renewed in verse 18 is the third between these two men (18:3; 20:16-17), and the last.

verseByVerse.quote: David saw that Saul had come out to seek his life. David was in the wilderness of Ziph at Horesh. And Jonathan, Saul's son, rose and went to David at Horesh, and strengthened his hand in God. And he said to him, "Do not fear, for the hand of Saul my father shall not find you. You shall be king over Israel, and I shall be next to you. Saul my father also knows this." And the two of them made a covenant before the LORD. David remained at Horesh, and Jonathan went home.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is where the chapter turns, and it turns on a visit.

The verse establishes what David can see: the king is out, personally, hunting him. He is in scrub country with six hundred men and nowhere to be.

Jonathan is the crown prince. His father's army is combing that wilderness at that moment for the man he is going to see. Every step of the journey is a risk, and there is no political purpose to it, no message to carry, no negotiation to conduct.

He goes because his friend is frightened.

Then the phrase: he strengthened his hand in God.

The writer could have said he encouraged him. He could have said he brought supplies, or news, or men. He says something more exact than any of those. Jonathan took hold of David's hand — the image is of a grip going slack — and put it back on God.

He did not give him anything new. David already knew he was anointed; Samuel had poured the oil over him in his father's house. What a hunted man loses is not information but grip, and what Jonathan did was close his fingers round what he already had.

That is the whole ministry of encouragement in five words, and anyone can do it. You do not need a new revelation for a discouraged believer. You need to say, out loud, in the wilderness, the thing they already know and can no longer feel.
