There are four things in that speech, and each one costs him something.

Do not fear, for the hand of Saul my father shall not find you. He is telling his own father's hunted enemy that the hunt will fail — and he is right, and he lives in that man's house.

You shall be king over Israel. The heir to the throne of Israel says to a fugitive, in a wilderness, that the fugitive will have his crown. He has pointed to it before, in the field (20:13-15), and he says it plainly here without a flicker.

And I shall be next to you. This is the only thing he says that is not true, and it is the saddest line in the book. He pictures a future in which David reigns and Jonathan stands at his right hand, the two of them together, the friendship surviving into the kingdom. It never happens. He dies on Mount Gilboa beside his father (31:2), and David tears his clothes and sings very pleasant have you been to me; your love to me was extraordinary (2 Sam. 1:26).

Then the last: Saul my father also knows this.

Saul knows. His own son says so, plainly, as a settled fact: the king of Israel is aware that David will be king, and is hunting him anyway. He has known since the day he shouted at Jonathan that as long as the son of Jesse lives on the earth, neither you nor your kingdom shall be established (20:31), and probably since the song of the women (18:6-7).

So this is not a tragic misunderstanding, and it is not paranoia about a rival he cannot assess. It is a man who has heard the verdict of God, understood it, and decided to spend the rest of his life fighting it with an army. There is a kind of sin that goes on precisely because it knows.

Then Jonathan goes home, and home is his father's house. He walks back to Gibeah, to the table where the spear was thrown at him, and takes his place as the king's son.

He has just told a man in a wood that that man will have his throne, and now he goes back to serve the father who will die trying to prevent it, and to die with him. Jonathan is loyal to two people who cannot both be served, and he does not solve it; he carries it.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Ziphites offer to betray David, and Saul blesses them (vv. 19-23). The chase closes round a mountain in Maon (vv. 24-26), until a Philistine raid calls Saul away (vv. 27-29).
verseByVerse.theology: Even David's own tribe will sell him to the king. The only safe place left to him is God's keeping.
verseByVerse.examples: David has no move left at the end of this chapter, and that is when the rescue comes. God's help often arrives very close to the edge.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the Ziphites went up to Saul at Gibeah, saying, "Is not David hiding among us in the strongholds at Horesh, on the hill of Hachilah, which is south of Jeshimon? Now come down, O king, according to all your heart's desire to come down, and our part shall be to surrender him into the king's hand." And Saul said, "May you be blessed by the LORD, for you have had compassion on me. Go, make yet more sure. Know and see the place where his foot is, and who has seen him there, for it is told me that he is very cunning. See therefore and take note of all the lurking places where he hides, and come back to me with sure information. Then I will go with you. And if he is in the land, I will search him out among all the thousands of Judah." And they arose and went to Ziph ahead of Saul. Now David and his men were in the wilderness of Maon, in the Arabah to the south of Jeshimon. And Saul and his men went to seek him. And David was told, so he went down to the rock and lived in the wilderness of Maon. And when Saul heard that, he pursued after David in the wilderness of Maon. Saul went on one side of the mountain, and David and his men on the other side of the mountain. And David was hurrying to get away from Saul. As Saul and his men were closing in on David and his men to capture them, a messenger came to Saul, saying, "Hurry and come, for the Philistines have made a raid against the land." So Saul returned from pursuing after David and went against the Philistines. Therefore that place was called the Rock of Escape. And David went up from there and lived in the strongholds of Engedi.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Ziphites are men of Judah. David's own tribe informs on him, twice — they do it again in chapter 26 — and they travel to Gibeah to do it.

Nobody is paying them. Nobody has threatened them. They simply calculate which way the power runs and act accordingly.

According to all your heart's desire. They have taken the measure of the man exactly. They know what he wants more than anything in the world, and they say so to his face as a courtesy.

Saul pronounces a blessing in the name of the LORD on a band of informers.

He also calls what they have done compassion — compassion on him. That pronoun again. The man has been sorry for himself since the tamarisk tree, and here he describes the betrayal of a fugitive by his own tribesmen as an act of pity toward the king.

Everything he touches gets bent round to face him, including the divine name.

The last clause is telling: it is told me that he is very cunning.

David has never once acted against Saul. He played the harp, killed the giant, led the army, married the daughter, obeyed the orders, and ran. There is no cunning to report. But Saul is being told there is, by someone, and he believes it — because a man who has decided on a conclusion attracts the evidence he needs.

The sentence is left hanging in mid-air, and that is deliberate.

Picture it. One hill, and two forces going round it in opposite directions, out of sight of each other by a matter of yards. David is running out of mountain. Saul's men are extending the line to come round both sides at once, which is the classic way to take a hill, and it works.

There is nothing David can do about it. He has no clever move left. Everything in the chapter up to now has depended on his asking God and getting an answer, and here there is no time to ask anything.

A messenger arrives with bad news from somewhere else.

There is no angel, no earthquake, no answer from the ephod, and no record that anybody prayed. What happens is that the Philistines — the enemy Saul was anointed to save Israel from, and has been ignoring in order to hunt one of his own officers — choose that week to raid, and the raid pulls him off the hill at the exact moment the line was closing.

It is a piece of ordinary bad news, arriving at the only minute it could have helped. And it is the answer to God did not give him into his hand in verse 14: this is what that sentence looks like on the ground.

Most deliverance is like this. Not the parting of a sea, but a message arriving, a meeting being cancelled, a job falling through, somebody else's crisis pulling a threat away — and only afterwards does anyone see what it was.

They named the rock.

Somebody in that party understood what had just happened well enough to give the hill a name, so that the story could be told at it afterwards. Sela-hammahlekoth — the Rock of Escape, or of Divisions, since the mountain divided the two forces.

Israel had a long habit of doing this. Ebenezer, the stone Samuel set up after Mizpah, was another (7:12): till now the LORD has helped us. They put a marker on the ground at the place where God did something, because they knew perfectly well that they would forget it by next year otherwise.

Anyone reading this could stand to have a few. Not stones, but named days, written down — the ones where the messenger arrived in time.

He moves on, to a place of springs and caves above the Dead Sea. And Saul, having dealt with the Philistines, comes straight back — which is where the next chapter begins, with the king walking alone into a cave.

24.title: David Spares Saul at En-gedi
24.text: <sup>1</sup>When Saul returned from following the Philistines, he was told, "Behold, David is in the wilderness of Engedi."<sup>2</sup>Then Saul took three thousand chosen men out of all Israel and went to seek David and his men in front of the Wildgoats' Rocks.<sup>3</sup>And he came to the sheepfolds by the way, where there was a cave, and Saul went in to relieve himself. Now David and his men were sitting in the innermost parts of the cave.<sup>4</sup>And the men of David said to him, "Here is the day of which the LORD said to you, 'Behold, I will give your enemy into your hand, and you shall do to him as it shall seem good to you.'" Then David arose and stealthily cut off a corner of Saul's robe.<sup>5</sup>And afterward David's heart struck him, because he had cut off a corner of Saul's robe.<sup>6</sup>He said to his men, "The LORD forbid that I should do this thing to my lord, the LORD's anointed, to put out my hand against him, seeing he is the LORD's anointed."<sup>7</sup>So David persuaded his men with these words and did not permit them to attack Saul. And Saul rose up and left the cave and went on his way.<sup>8</sup>Afterward David also arose and went out of the cave, and called after Saul, "My lord the king!" And when Saul looked behind him, David bowed with his face to the earth and paid homage.<sup>9</sup>And David said to Saul, "Why do you listen to the words of men who say, 'Behold, David seeks your harm'?<sup>10</sup>Behold, this day your eyes have seen how the LORD gave you today into my hand in the cave. And some told me to kill you, but I spared you. I said, 'I will not put out my hand against my lord, for he is the LORD's anointed.'<sup>11</sup>See, my father, see the corner of your robe in my hand. For by the fact that I cut off the corner of your robe and did not kill you, you may know and see that there is no wrong or treason in my hands. I have not sinned against you, though you hunt my life to take it.<sup>12</sup>May the LORD judge between me and you, may the LORD avenge me against you, but my hand shall not be against you.<sup>13</sup>As the proverb of the ancients says, 'Out of the wicked comes wickedness.' But my hand shall not be against you.<sup>14</sup>After whom has the king of Israel come out? After whom do you pursue? After a dead dog! After a flea!<sup>15</sup>May the LORD therefore be judge and give sentence between me and you, and see to it and plead my cause and deliver me from your hand."<sup>16</sup>As soon as David had finished speaking these words to Saul, Saul said, "Is this your voice, my son David?" And Saul lifted up his voice and wept.<sup>17</sup>He said to David, "You are more righteous than I, for you have repaid me good, whereas I have repaid you evil.<sup>18</sup>And you have declared this day how you have dealt well with me, in that you did not kill me when the LORD put me into your hands.<sup>19</sup>For if a man finds his enemy, will he let him go away safe? So may the LORD reward you with good for what you have done to me this day.<sup>20</sup>And now, behold, I know that you shall surely be king, and that the kingdom of Israel shall be established in your hand.<sup>21</sup>Swear to me therefore by the LORD that you will not cut off my offspring after me, and that you will not destroy my name out of my father's house."<sup>22</sup>And David swore this to Saul. Then Saul went home, but David and his men went up to the stronghold.
24.overview: Saul walks alone into the cave where David's men are hiding, and they call it the day the LORD promised, though no such promise is recorded. David cuts the corner off Saul's robe instead, and his conscience strikes him for it. Then he walks out in front of three thousand soldiers, holds up the cloth, and hands the case to the LORD: my hand shall not be against you. Saul weeps, confesses, concedes the kingdom and asks for an oath about his children. Then he goes home, and David does not go with him.
24.theology:
Two men, one temptation (vv. 4, 10). In consecutive chapters Saul and David's men make the same move: a circumstance lines up with what they want, and they call it God's doing (23:7; 24:4). The difference between David and Saul is not that one is given opportunities and the other is not, but that David will not treat an opportunity as permission.

The Son of David who did not revile (vv. 12, 15). Peter describes Jesus in David's terms: when he was reviled, he did not revile in return; when he suffered, he did not threaten, but continued entrusting himself to him who judges justly (1 Peter 2:23). David spared his enemy's life in a cave; the Son of David went further and gave his life for his enemies, for while we were enemies we were reconciled to God by the death of his Son (Romans 5:10). David would not lift his hand against the LORD's anointed. At the cross the LORD's Anointed let sinful hands be lifted against him, and prayed for them. That is the root of the non-retaliation this chapter teaches: we who were spared by him can spare others.

Forgiving is not the same as trusting (v. 22). David spared Saul, swore the oath he asked for, and still did not go home with him. Anyone who has forgiven someone who harmed them may take this to heart: forgiving does not require going back into danger.
24.examples:
Then: Six hundred men watched their enemy walk unarmed into their own hiding place, and their commander crawled up behind him, cut a piece off his coat, came back, and then had to argue them out of killing him — before walking into the open in front of the man's army to show him the cloth.

Now: The chapter is for anybody holding a justified grievance and the power to act on it. Two things in it are practical. First, the test David's men failed: when a circumstance lines up perfectly with what you already wanted, and you find yourself calling it God's leading, check whether God ever actually said it — and be suspicious of any leading that ends with "and then do as seems good to you". Second, what David did instead: he did not swallow the wrong, deny it, or minimise it. He named it, asked God to judge it, and took his own hand off it. Those are not the same as letting it go, and it is the second that a person can actually do. It is not done by clenched teeth: the Spirit of the one who prayed for his enemies is given to make it possible, and when we have taken the revenge we should have left to God, the same Lord who judges justly is the one who forgives us.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — The Day of Which the LORD Said
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Saul enters the cave where David is hiding (vv. 1-3). David's men urge him on; he cuts Saul's robe instead and is struck in conscience (vv. 4-5), and he restrains his men (vv. 6-7).
verseByVerse.theology: The cave tests David at the point where he is weakest: tired, hunted, and urged on by the men who depend on him.
verseByVerse.examples: A tender conscience is a gift. David's heart struck him over a scrap of cloth; years later, after Bathsheba, it would take a prophet to wake it (2 Sam. 12:1-13).

verseByVerse.quote: When Saul returned from following the Philistines, he was told, "Behold, David is in the wilderness of Engedi." Then Saul took three thousand chosen men out of all Israel and went to seek David and his men in front of the Wildgoats' Rocks. And he came to the sheepfolds by the way, where there was a cave, and Saul went in to relieve himself. Now David and his men were sitting in the innermost parts of the cave. And the men of David said to him, "Here is the day of which the LORD said to you, 'Behold, I will give your enemy into your hand, and you shall do to him as it shall seem good to you.'" Then David arose and stealthily cut off a corner of Saul's robe. And afterward David's heart struck him, because he had cut off a corner of Saul's robe. He said to his men, "The LORD forbid that I should do this thing to my lord, the LORD's anointed, to put out my hand against him, seeing he is the LORD's anointed." So David persuaded his men with these words and did not permit them to attack Saul. And Saul rose up and left the cave and went on his way.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He deals with the Philistine raid and comes straight back to the hunt, with three thousand picked men, for six hundred fugitives and one of them in particular.

Engedi is a spring above the Dead Sea, and the cliffs behind it are riddled with caves. It is good country to hide in and impossible country to search.

The narrator writes it exactly like that, without embarrassment and without a joke.

The king of Israel, at the head of three thousand men, steps into a cave for a private moment, and six hundred armed men who want him dead are sitting in the dark at the back of it watching him. He is alone, unarmed, in the one posture in which no man is dangerous.

Look for the promise. It is not in this book. Nowhere has God said to David that he would give his enemy into his hand, and nowhere has anybody said it on his behalf. Samuel anointed him and said nothing of the kind. Jonathan told him he would be king and said nothing of the kind. There is no such oracle.

The men have, most likely, invented it.

Not cynically: they are exhausted and frightened, and here is their enemy alone in a cave. What else could it be?

It is exactly what Saul did one chapter ago. God has given him into my hand, for he has shut himself in by entering a town that has gates and bars (23:7). The same reasoning, the same confidence, about the same man — and the narrator answered Saul's version in his own words seven verses later.

Both sides of this war read the circumstances as divine endorsement of what they already wanted, and only one man in the cave declines to.

The second half of what they say matters: you shall do to him as it shall seem good to you. That is the part that gives the game away. A word from God that ends by handing you unlimited discretion is generally your own word.

He goes forward with a knife and comes back with a piece of cloth.

Here is the verse people stumble at. He did not kill him. He did not wound him. He did not so much as wake him. He cut a corner off a garment in the dark — and his conscience hit him for it.

It is not scrupulosity, and the reason is in chapter 15.

When Samuel turned to leave Gilgal, Saul grabbed the skirt of his robe and it tore, and Samuel said: the LORD has torn the kingdom of Israel from you this day and has given it to a neighbor of yours, who is better than you (15:27-28). The tearing of the robe was the sign. That is the language the kingdom changing hands is spoken in.

So when David crouches behind Saul in the dark and cuts the corner off his robe, he has just performed that sign himself, with his own hand, on the king's own coat. He has enacted the transfer of the kingdom rather than waiting for it.

Saul sees it too. In verse 20 he is staring at a piece of his own robe in David's hand when he says now, behold, I know that you shall surely be king. Both men know what the cloth means.

He says it twice in one sentence: the LORD's anointed.

This is the whole argument, and what it does not say matters as much as what it does. It does not say Saul is a good king; David knows exactly what he is. It does not say the throne is rightfully his; David has been anointed for it himself. It says that oil was poured on that man's head by Samuel at God's command, and that no reading of the circumstances gives a private citizen the right to undo it with a knife.

What God gave, God can take. David will not do God's work for him with a weapon in the dark, and this is the principle he will hold to for the next seven chapters, at enormous cost, twice.

He has to persuade them, and the Hebrew verb is probably stronger than that; elsewhere it means to tear apart, and here it likely means he rebuked them sharply. Six hundred armed men had already decided; he talked them out of it standing in the dark while the opportunity walked away.

Does “touch not the LORD’s anointed” forbid criticising leaders? David refused to kill Saul or seize his throne; he did not refuse to rebuke him, and in the very next verses he confronts Saul to his face (vv. 9–15). The verse forbids violence and rebellion against those God has placed in authority. It does not shield any pastor or leader from being tested by Scripture (Acts 17:11) or corrected when they sin (1 Tim 5:19–20).

When may believers resist a wicked ruler? David would not kill Saul, but he fled, and he refused to help him do evil; the guards who refused to kill the priests did right (22:17). We must obey God rather than men (Acts 5:29), while not taking up the sword ourselves against those God has placed in authority.
verseByVerse.note: To “relieve himself” is literally “to cover his feet” (ESV note).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–15 — A Dead Dog, a Single Flea
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: David calls after Saul, shows him the cloth (vv. 8-11), and hands the case to the LORD (vv. 12-15).
verseByVerse.theology: This is the first time in years that David and Saul have spoken face to face, and David uses it not to accuse but to plead.
verseByVerse.examples: By handing the verdict to the LORD, David takes the one course that lets him neither retaliate nor surrender.

verseByVerse.quote: Afterward David also arose and went out of the cave, and called after Saul, "My lord the king!" And when Saul looked behind him, David bowed with his face to the earth and paid homage. And David said to Saul, "Why do you listen to the words of men who say, 'Behold, David seeks your harm'? Behold, this day your eyes have seen how the LORD gave you today into my hand in the cave. And some told me to kill you, but I spared you. I said, 'I will not put out my hand against my lord, for he is the LORD's anointed.' See, my father, see the corner of your robe in my hand. For by the fact that I cut off the corner of your robe and did not kill you, you may know and see that there is no wrong or treason in my hands. I have not sinned against you, though you hunt my life to take it. May the LORD judge between me and you, may the LORD avenge me against you, but my hand shall not be against you. As the proverb of the ancients says, 'Out of the wicked comes wickedness.' But my hand shall not be against you. After whom has the king of Israel come out? After whom do you pursue? After a dead dog! After a flea! May the LORD therefore be judge and give sentence between me and you, and see to it and plead my cause and deliver me from your hand."
verseByVerse.commentary:
This takes courage.

He has just let the man go. Now he walks out into the daylight, in front of three thousand soldiers who could be on him in a minute, and calls out to make himself a target — and then puts his face on the ground.

He could have stayed in the cave and let Saul walk away not knowing. Instead he comes out, because a piece of cloth is no use as evidence unless somebody sees it.

He does not deny the providence — he denies the conclusion drawn from it. God arranged the opportunity; that is not the same as God licensing the murder. This is the distinction his men could not make and Saul cannot make, and it is the whole difference between them.

He calls him father. It is technically accurate — Saul is his father-in-law, whatever has become of that marriage — and it is also the last tenderness available to a man who has spent years being hunted by the person he is speaking to.

Then the cloth. See the corner of your robe in my hand. The evidence is unanswerable and the whole speech turns on it: I was close enough to cut this, and you are alive.

Here is the sentence to carry out of the chapter. It is not a renunciation of justice. He asks God to avenge him — he believes he has been wronged, says so, and wants it answered. What he renounces is doing the answering himself.

None of that is pretending not to mind. David minds a great deal. He simply transfers the case to a court he cannot corrupt and whose judge is not a party to it, and then takes his own hand off the matter.

Paul is standing on this ground centuries later: never avenge yourselves, but leave it to the wrath of God, for it is written, "Vengeance is mine, I will repay, says the Lord" (Rom. 12:19). The reason a Christian can let go of a grievance is not that grievances do not matter but that they are being handled.

He quotes a saying everybody in earshot knows, and he uses it carefully.

The proverb means that a wicked man's actions come out of what he is. David applies it as an argument: if I were what you say I am, you would be dead in that cave. My actions have shown you what I am. Judge by the fruit.

Then he makes himself as small as a man can make himself.

A dead dog is the most contemptible thing in that vocabulary — unclean, worthless, and not even alive. A single flea is a thing you cannot catch and would not want if you did.

It is genuine humility and it is also an extremely shrewd argument, and both at once. He is saying to the king, in front of the army: look at what you have become. Three thousand chosen men of Israel, marching round the wilderness of Engedi, after a flea. The Philistines are raiding the threshing floors and this is what the kingdom is doing.

He ends where he began, and the verbs pile up: judge, give sentence, see to it, plead my cause, deliver me.

That last one is honest. He is not asking God merely to referee. He is asking to be got out of this, because he is not enjoying it, and he says so to Saul's face.

The headings of Psalms 57 and 142 place them when he fled from Saul, in the cave. Whether Adullam or this cave at Engedi is meant is uncertain, but both psalms give the prayer behind this speech: I cry out to God Most High, to God who fulfills his purpose for me (57:2).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–22 — You Are More Righteous Than I
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Saul weeps and confesses (vv. 16-19), concedes the kingdom (v. 20), asks for an oath about his offspring, and goes home while David goes up to the stronghold (vv. 21-22).
verseByVerse.theology: Saul says everything a penitent should say, and the chapter's last verse shows why words alone are not enough.
verseByVerse.examples: Saul's fear for his children is real, and David's oath answers it. The kindness he promised here he kept, as the note below shows.

verseByVerse.quote: As soon as David had finished speaking these words to Saul, Saul said, "Is this your voice, my son David?" And Saul lifted up his voice and wept. He said to David, "You are more righteous than I, for you have repaid me good, whereas I have repaid you evil. And you have declared this day how you have dealt well with me, in that you did not kill me when the LORD put me into your hands. For if a man finds his enemy, will he let him go away safe? So may the LORD reward you with good for what you have done to me this day. And now, behold, I know that you shall surely be king, and that the kingdom of Israel shall be established in your hand. Swear to me therefore by the LORD that you will not cut off my offspring after me, and that you will not destroy my name out of my father's house." And David swore this to Saul. Then Saul went home, but David and his men went up to the stronghold.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He weeps, and there is no reason to think the tears are fake.

Is this your voice, my son David? He has to ask, which tells you they are at a distance and shouting, and he calls him my son, which he has not done in a long time. Something in the man breaks for a moment.

That is as clear a confession as anybody makes in this book.

He does not soften it or spread it about. You are more righteous than I. Good for evil, and he names which of them did which. He is entirely right about the facts and entirely honest about them.

It is a rhetorical question with an obvious answer, and Saul is the proof of it: he has found his enemy repeatedly and thrown a spear every time. He is describing the ordinary way of the world, and he has just watched somebody not do it, and he cannot account for it except by calling it righteousness.

That is what non-retaliation does when anyone actually sees it: it does not fit the way the world runs, and it makes people ask what is different.

He says it out loud, standing on a hillside, holding nothing, looking at a piece of his own robe in the hand of the man who cut it.

Everyone has now said it. Samuel said it at Gilgal with a torn robe in his fist. Jonathan said it twice, in a field and in a wood. Abigail will say it in the next chapter. And here is Saul himself, saying it in his own voice, weeping.

Not one of them changes what he does next.

This is what he is actually frightened of, and it is a reasonable fear. When a dynasty changed hands in that world the incoming king commonly killed the old king's family, and everybody knew it (as Israel's later history shows, 1 Kings 15:29; 2 Kings 10:11).

He swore it, and he kept it.

Years later, on the throne, he asks: is there still anyone left of the house of Saul, that I may show him kindness for Jonathan's sake? and they bring him Jonathan's son Mephibosheth, crippled in both feet, who calls himself a dead dog such as I (2 Sam. 9:8), the very words David used of himself here, and David gives him back all Saul's land and sits him at the royal table for the rest of his life (2 Sam. 9). The oath sworn on a hillside to a weeping enemy was still being kept a generation later by a man who had every power not to.

Now the last clause of the chapter, and it is the most important one.

David does not go with him.

He has just heard a full confession, an acknowledgment of his righteousness, a blessing, and a concession of the throne, and at the end of it he says nothing about coming back to court, and goes up into the rocks with his six hundred men.

He believes the tears were real. He does not believe they will last, and he is right; within two chapters Saul is out with three thousand men again, having heard from the Ziphites a second time.

That is a hard, useful thing to know about people, and it is not cynicism. A man can mean every word he says while he is saying it, weep genuinely, be perfectly accurate about his own sin, and be back at exactly the same behaviour within the month, because nothing underneath has changed. Real feeling is not repentance. Repentance is a turn, and Saul turns round and walks home.

25.title: Abigail: Wisdom That Stops a Fool
25.text: <sup>1</sup>Now Samuel died. And all Israel assembled and mourned for him, and they buried him in his house at Ramah. Then David rose and went down to the wilderness of Paran.<sup>2</sup>And there was a man in Maon whose business was in Carmel. The man was very rich; he had three thousand sheep and a thousand goats. He was shearing his sheep in Carmel.<sup>3</sup>Now the name of the man was Nabal, and the name of his wife Abigail. The woman was discerning and beautiful, but the man was harsh and badly behaved; he was a Calebite.<sup>4</sup>David heard in the wilderness that Nabal was shearing his sheep.<sup>5</sup>So David sent ten young men. And David said to the young men, "Go up to Carmel, and go to Nabal and greet him in my name.<sup>6</sup>And thus you shall greet him: 'Peace be to you, and peace be to your house, and peace be to all that you have.<sup>7</sup>I hear that you have shearers. Now your shepherds have been with us, and we did them no harm, and they missed nothing all the time they were in Carmel.<sup>8</sup>Ask your young men, and they will tell you. Therefore let my young men find favor in your eyes, for we come on a feast day. Please give whatever you have at hand to your servants and to your son David.'"<sup>9</sup>When David's young men came, they said all this to Nabal in the name of David, and then they waited.<sup>10</sup>And Nabal answered David's servants, "Who is David? Who is the son of Jesse? There are many servants these days who are breaking away from their masters.<sup>11</sup>Shall I take my bread and my water and my meat that I have killed for my shearers and give it to men who come from I do not know where?"<sup>12</sup>So David's young men turned away and came back and told him all this.<sup>13</sup>And David said to his men, "Every man strap on his sword!" And every man of them strapped on his sword. David also strapped on his sword. And about four hundred men went up after David, while two hundred remained with the baggage.<sup>14</sup>But one of the young men told Abigail, Nabal's wife, "Behold, David sent messengers out of the wilderness to greet our master, and he railed at them.<sup>15</sup>Yet the men were very good to us, and we suffered no harm, and we did not miss anything when we were in the fields, as long as we went with them.<sup>16</sup>They were a wall to us both by night and by day, all the while we were with them keeping the sheep.<sup>17</sup>Now therefore know this and consider what you should do, for harm is determined against our master and against all his house, and he is such a worthless man that one cannot speak to him."<sup>18</sup>Then Abigail made haste and took two hundred loaves and two skins of wine and five sheep already prepared and five seahs of parched grain and a hundred clusters of raisins and two hundred cakes of figs, and laid them on donkeys.<sup>19</sup>And she said to her young men, "Go on before me; behold, I come after you." But she did not tell her husband Nabal.<sup>20</sup>And as she rode on the donkey and came down under cover of the mountain, behold, David and his men came down toward her, and she met them.<sup>21</sup>Now David had said, "Surely in vain have I guarded all that this fellow has in the wilderness, so that nothing was missed of all that belonged to him, and he has returned me evil for good.<sup>22</sup>God do so to the enemies of David and more also, if by morning I leave so much as one male of all who belong to him."<sup>23</sup>When Abigail saw David, she hurried and got down from the donkey and fell before David on her face and bowed to the ground.<sup>24</sup>She fell at his feet and said, "On me alone, my lord, be the guilt. Please let your servant speak in your ears, and hear the words of your servant.<sup>25</sup>Let not my lord regard this worthless fellow, Nabal, for as his name is, so is he. Nabal is his name, and folly is with him. But I your servant did not see the young men of my lord, whom you sent.<sup>26</sup>Now then, my lord, as the LORD lives, and as your soul lives, because the LORD has restrained you from bloodguilt and from saving with your own hand, now then let your enemies and those who seek to do evil to my lord be as Nabal.<sup>27</sup>And now let this present that your servant has brought to my lord be given to the young men who follow my lord.<sup>28</sup>Please forgive the trespass of your servant. For the LORD will certainly make my lord a sure house, because my lord is fighting the battles of the LORD, and evil shall not be found in you so long as you live.<sup>29</sup>If men rise up to pursue you and to seek your life, the life of my lord shall be bound in the bundle of the living in the care of the LORD your God. And the lives of your enemies he shall sling out as from the hollow of a sling.<sup>30</sup>And when the LORD has done to my lord according to all the good that he has spoken concerning you and has appointed you prince over Israel,<sup>31</sup>my lord shall have no cause of grief or pangs of conscience for having shed blood without cause or for my lord working salvation himself. And when the LORD has dealt well with my lord, then remember your servant."<sup>32</sup>And David said to Abigail, "Blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel, who sent you this day to meet me!<sup>33</sup>Blessed be your discretion, and blessed be you, who have kept me this day from bloodguilt and from working salvation with my own hand!<sup>34</sup>For as surely as the LORD, the God of Israel, lives, who has restrained me from hurting you, unless you had hurried and come to meet me, truly by morning there had not been left to Nabal so much as one male."<sup>35</sup>Then David received from her hand what she had brought him. And he said to her, "Go up in peace to your house. See, I have obeyed your voice, and I have granted your petition."<sup>36</sup>And Abigail came to Nabal, and behold, he was holding a feast in his house, like the feast of a king. And Nabal's heart was merry within him, for he was very drunk. So she told him nothing at all until the morning light.<sup>37</sup>In the morning, when the wine had gone out of Nabal, his wife told him these things, and his heart died within him, and he became as a stone.<sup>38</sup>And about ten days later the LORD struck Nabal, and he died.<sup>39</sup>When David heard that Nabal was dead, he said, "Blessed be the LORD who has avenged the insult I received at the hand of Nabal, and has kept back his servant from wrongdoing. The LORD has returned the evil of Nabal on his own head." Then David sent and spoke to Abigail, to take her as his wife.<sup>40</sup>When the servants of David came to Abigail at Carmel, they said to her, "David has sent us to you to take you to him as his wife."<sup>41</sup>And she rose and bowed with her face to the ground and said, "Behold, your handmaid is a servant to wash the feet of the servants of my lord."<sup>42</sup>And Abigail hurried and rose and mounted a donkey, and her five young women attended her. She followed the messengers of David and became his wife.<sup>43</sup>David also took Ahinoam of Jezreel, and both of them became his wives.<sup>44</sup>Saul had given Michal his daughter, David's wife, to Palti the son of Laish, who was of Gallim.
25.overview:
Samuel dies in half a verse, and the writer moves straight on to a sheep farmer.

The farmer is Nabal, which means fool, and his wife is discerning and beautiful. David's request at shearing time is courteous and true, and Nabal answers in Saul's own vocabulary.

So David straps on a sword. The chapter sits between two in which he spares Saul (chs. 24 and 26), and here he swears before God to kill every male in a household by morning because a farmer was rude to his messengers.

Abigail meets him on the road with two hundred loaves and the wisest speech in the book. She takes the blame that is not hers, promises him a sure house, and argues that he will have to carry this onto the throne. David blesses God for sending her. Ten days later the LORD strikes Nabal, and David gets the outcome without the bloodguilt.
25.theology:
A sure house (vv. 28-29). A farmer's wife on a hillside names the Davidic covenant (God's sworn promise of a lasting dynasty) before Nathan carries it to the palace (2 Sam. 7:11-16). That house is made sure for ever in Jesus, to whom God gives the throne of his father David (Luke 1:32–33).

On me alone be the guilt (v. 24). Many Christians have heard in Abigail's first words an echo of the gospel: a go-between falls at the feet of the coming king and takes on herself the guilt of a household under sentence. The likeness is only partial. David's anger was not just, and Abigail could only plead; she could not pay. But it is the shape of what the Son of David did in full. God's anger against sin is entirely just, and Christ did not merely ask for the guilt to be laid on him; he bore it (2 Corinthians 5:21; 1 Peter 2:24).

The flat ending (vv. 43-44). The chapter closes by noting another wife, and Michal given to another man, without comment (see the note on vv. 39-44). Why does God allow it? He tolerated polygamy for a time, as he did divorce, because of your hardness of heart, but from the beginning it was not so (Matthew 19:4–8; Genesis 2:24); the law even forbade a king to multiply wives (Deuteronomy 17:17), and Scripture's honest record of the wreckage is its verdict.
25.examples:
Then: A woman loaded two hundred loaves and five dressed sheep onto donkeys without telling her husband, rode down a mountain track into four hundred men coming the other way with swords drawn and an oath sworn, got off the donkey, put her face on the ground, and talked their commander out of a massacre — and he thanked her for it.

Now: Two things worth taking. Abigail's method, for anyone who has to stop somebody doing something terrible: she gave him somewhere to put the offence, told the truth about the offender without defending him, spoke in his own vocabulary, and then argued from the future he wanted back into the choice in front of him. Not one word of it is flattery and not one word is a lecture. And David's response, which is rarer than her speech: he did not say he had it under control. He blessed God for sending her, admitted out loud what he would have done by morning, and said I have obeyed your voice. Thanking the person who just stopped you is harder than being stopped. And when we are David on the road, sword already on, the God who sent Abigail still sends his word and his people to turn us back, and his Spirit gives the humility to listen.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–13 — Who Is the Son of Jesse?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Samuel dies (v. 1). David asks the rich fool Nabal for provision at shearing time (vv. 2-9), Nabal insults him (vv. 10-11), and David arms four hundred men (vv. 12-13).
verseByVerse.theology: Samuel's death leaves David without the prophet who anointed him, and the very next scene shows David at his most dangerous.
verseByVerse.examples: The request is reasonable and the refusal is insulting, and David's response is still wrong. Being wronged does not make every answer right.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Samuel died. And all Israel assembled and mourned for him, and they buried him in his house at Ramah. Then David rose and went down to the wilderness of Paran. And there was a man in Maon whose business was in Carmel. The man was very rich; he had three thousand sheep and a thousand goats. He was shearing his sheep in Carmel. Now the name of the man was Nabal, and the name of his wife Abigail. The woman was discerning and beautiful, but the man was harsh and badly behaved; he was a Calebite. David heard in the wilderness that Nabal was shearing his sheep. So David sent ten young men. And David said to the young men, "Go up to Carmel, and go to Nabal and greet him in my name. And thus you shall greet him: 'Peace be to you, and peace be to your house, and peace be to all that you have. I hear that you have shearers. Now your shepherds have been with us, and we did them no harm, and they missed nothing all the time they were in Carmel. Ask your young men, and they will tell you. Therefore let my young men find favor in your eyes, for we come on a feast day. Please give whatever you have at hand to your servants and to your son David.'" When David's young men came, they said all this to Nabal in the name of David, and then they waited. And Nabal answered David's servants, "Who is David? Who is the son of Jesse? There are many servants these days who are breaking away from their masters. Shall I take my bread and my water and my meat that I have killed for my shearers and give it to men who come from I do not know where?" So David's young men turned away and came back and told him all this. And David said to his men, "Every man strap on his sword!" And every man of them strapped on his sword. David also strapped on his sword. And about four hundred men went up after David, while two hundred remained with the baggage.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Half a verse.

The boy who slept beside the ark and heard his name called in the dark. The judge who stood at Mizpah and set up a stone and called it Ebenezer. The man who anointed two kings, who tore his robe out of Saul's hand at Gilgal, who went to Bethlehem with a horn of oil and looked at seven sons before God told him to send for the eighth. The last of the judges, and the first of the prophets.

All Israel came and mourned, which is right and is more than they gave him while he lived. They had asked him for a king to be like the nations, and he had told them exactly what it would cost, and they had said no! But there shall be a king over us. Everything he warned them about has now happened, and they bury him and go home.

The writer gives him one sentence and moves straight to a story about a sheep farmer, and the abruptness is the point. Israel's great men die and God's purposes do not pause for the funeral.

The introductions are complete before either character speaks, and the reader is told who is who.

Nabal means fool. Not a simpleton — in Hebrew the nabal is the moral fool of Proverbs, the man who says in his heart there is no God, whose folly is a settled disposition rather than a lack of intelligence. He is very rich, and his character is given in two words: harsh, and badly behaved.

His wife is discerning and beautiful, and the order matters. The first word is the wisdom vocabulary. She is put in front of us as the wise woman married to the fool, which is one of Proverbs' recurring nightmares.

The request is impeccably courteous, and the timing is deliberate.

Sheep-shearing was the harvest festival of a pastoral estate: a week of feasting, and the season when a wealthy man was expected to be open-handed. Nobody sent men to ask at shearing time unless they expected a yes.

The claim is verifiable and it is true; the servant confirms every word of it in verse 15.

Six hundred armed men had been living in the same hills as Nabal's flocks through the grazing season and had taken nothing. In that country, in those years, that is a substantial service, and David is asking to be paid something for it out of a feast that is already happening.

Those are Saul's words.

The son of Jesse is Saul's phrase. It is what he calls David when he will not say his name — at the table when Jonathan defended him, under the tamarisk tree when he addressed the Benjaminites. And servants breaking away from their masters takes the king's son-in-law, the captain of the bodyguard, the man who killed Goliath, and files him as a runaway slave.

Who is David? Everybody in Judah knew who David was. Nabal is not ignorant; he is being insulting on purpose, and he is being insulting in the vocabulary of the court, which suggests he knows exactly which way the wind is blowing and has decided to be on the winning side loudly.

Count the possessives: my bread, my water, my meat.

Three possessives in one sentence, and this from a man who is about to hold a feast like the feast of a king. It is not that he cannot afford it; it is that it is his.

And from I do not know where is the last twist of the knife: not merely no, but you are nobody, and I do not know you, and I do not propose to find out.

David, who would not lift his hand against a king, straps on a sword over a bad answer from a farmer.

Four hundred men go up and two hundred stay with the baggage — and that detail tells you this is not a raid to frighten somebody. That is a battle formation.

Set this chapter between the two on either side of it. In chapter 24 he had Saul unarmed in a cave and would not touch him. In chapter 26 he will stand over him asleep with a spear in the ground and will not touch him. And in between, a man is rude to his messengers and he sets off to kill every male in the household by morning.

He can restrain himself against the king who has been hunting him for years, on principle, at mortal cost. He cannot restrain himself against a fool who insulted him at a party.

That is not a contradiction anyone should find surprising. It is easier to be magnificent about the great injury than decent about the small one, and most people who have managed the first have lost their temper over the second in the same week.
verseByVerse.note: Carmel here is a town in Judah, not the northern mountain.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–22 — One Cannot Speak to Him
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A servant tells Abigail (vv. 14-17); she loads a gift without telling Nabal (vv. 18-20), while David swears to leave no male alive (vv. 21-22).
verseByVerse.theology: A servant sees the danger first, and goes to the one person in the house who can act.
verseByVerse.examples: Wisdom here begins not with a speech but with loaded donkeys. Abigail acts quickly and generously before she says a word.

verseByVerse.quote: But one of the young men told Abigail, Nabal's wife, "Behold, David sent messengers out of the wilderness to greet our master, and he railed at them. Yet the men were very good to us, and we suffered no harm, and we did not miss anything when we were in the fields, as long as we went with them. They were a wall to us both by night and by day, all the while we were with them keeping the sheep. Now therefore know this and consider what you should do, for harm is determined against our master and against all his house, and he is such a worthless man that one cannot speak to him." Then Abigail made haste and took two hundred loaves and two skins of wine and five sheep already prepared and five seahs of parched grain and a hundred clusters of raisins and two hundred cakes of figs, and laid them on donkeys. And she said to her young men, "Go on before me; behold, I come after you." But she did not tell her husband Nabal. And as she rode on the donkey and came down under cover of the mountain, behold, David and his men came down toward her, and she met them. Now David had said, "Surely in vain have I guarded all that this fellow has in the wilderness, so that nothing was missed of all that belonged to him, and he has returned me evil for good. God do so to the enemies of David and more also, if by morning I leave so much as one male of all who belong to him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
He does not go to Nabal, and he does not go to the steward. He walks past the master of the house to the master's wife, and everyone in the story treats this as the obvious thing to do.

The servant confirms David's claim in stronger terms than David made it. Not merely that they did no harm, but that they were the reason nothing else did. Shepherds in open country at night are the most vulnerable people in the economy, and for a season they had six hundred soldiers between them and the hills.

There is the household's settled verdict on its head, delivered to his wife by a servant who does not expect to be contradicted.

One cannot speak to him. Not he will be angry, or "he will need persuading". He cannot be spoken to. Everybody who works there has already established this and made their arrangements accordingly, which is why the servant is standing in front of Abigail instead.

The word behind worthless is the Hebrew for a son of Belial. It is what the narrator calls Eli's sons (2:12), and what the malcontents were called who despised Saul at his coronation (10:27). It is not describing a bad mood. It is a category.

The size and speed of it are striking.

Two hundred loaves. Five dressed sheep. A hundred bunches of raisins, two hundred fig cakes. This is not a gesture; it is provision for six hundred men, assembled and loaded while an army is coming down the mountain. She has the whole estate moving at once.

She gives, generously and immediately, exactly what her husband refused — out of the same stores, on the same day.

She does not tell him.

The text states it flatly and does not defend it, and it needs no defending. He cannot be spoken to, there is no time, and four hundred armed men are on the road with an oath sworn to leave nobody alive. She acts to save his life, his household and his servants without his knowledge, because telling him would have cost all three.

He is talking himself into it as he rides, and the grievance is legitimate. Every word of it is true. That is what makes it dangerous.

He has put himself under an oath, before God, to commit a massacre.

Every male in the household — which means the servants who did him no wrong, the shepherds whose lives his men guarded, the boy who ran to Abigail. Not one of them insulted anybody. They are to die by morning because their employer was rude.

This is the same man who one chapter ago said may the LORD judge between me and you... but my hand shall not be against you, and who told Saul he would not so much as touch him. He is about to save himself with his own hand, and he has sworn to God that he will.

Did Abigail sin by acting behind her husband’s back? A wife’s submission to her husband is never obedience in sin (Acts 5:29), and Nabal’s folly had brought death on every man in the house (v. 17). She acted to save lives and to keep David from bloodshed, and Scripture calls her discerning and beautiful (v. 3). Her case is extraordinary, not a pattern for ordinary disagreements. And where a husband's harshness becomes abuse, Scripture never asks a wife to endure it in silence: she should seek safety at once, and the church should help her.

Was David right to break his oath? Yes: it was an oath to do evil, and it would have been sin to keep it. He thanks God for Abigail’s restraint (v. 32).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–31 — Bound in the Bundle of the Living
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Abigail falls at David's feet, takes the blame (vv. 23-25), tells him the LORD has restrained him (v. 26), promises him a sure house (vv. 27-30), and warns him against a lifelong grief of conscience (v. 31).
verseByVerse.theology: Every part of Abigail's speech points David back to God: to his restraint, his promise and his keeping.
verseByVerse.examples: She speaks to David as the future king while he is behaving like an outlaw, and that is what calls the king out of him.

verseByVerse.quote: When Abigail saw David, she hurried and got down from the donkey and fell before David on her face and bowed to the ground. She fell at his feet and said, "On me alone, my lord, be the guilt. Please let your servant speak in your ears, and hear the words of your servant. Let not my lord regard this worthless fellow, Nabal, for as his name is, so is he. Nabal is his name, and folly is with him. But I your servant did not see the young men of my lord, whom you sent. Now then, my lord, as the LORD lives, and as your soul lives, because the LORD has restrained you from bloodguilt and from saving with your own hand, now then let your enemies and those who seek to do evil to my lord be as Nabal. And now let this present that your servant has brought to my lord be given to the young men who follow my lord. Please forgive the trespass of your servant. For the LORD will certainly make my lord a sure house, because my lord is fighting the battles of the LORD, and evil shall not be found in you so long as you live. If men rise up to pursue you and to seek your life, the life of my lord shall be bound in the bundle of the living in the care of the LORD your God. And the lives of your enemies he shall sling out as from the hollow of a sling. And when the LORD has done to my lord according to all the good that he has spoken concerning you and has appointed you prince over Israel, my lord shall have no cause of grief or pangs of conscience for having shed blood without cause or for my lord working salvation himself. And when the LORD has dealt well with my lord, then remember your servant."
verseByVerse.commentary:
She puts herself between four hundred swords and a household, on the ground, and starts by taking the blame for something she did not do.

It is not grovelling and it is not flattery. It is the only opening that could work. A man riding to punish an offence has to be given somewhere to put it, and she takes it herself, immediately, before he can refuse.

What follows is one of the longest speeches by anyone in this book.

She is entirely candid about her husband, and she uses his name as the argument. Nabal is his name, and folly is with him.

She is not defending him. She is telling David that killing this man would be like being insulted by the weather and going to war with the sky.

Here she does something remarkable with the tense.

She speaks of the restraint as already accomplished — the LORD has restrained you — while the man is still on the road with his sword on. She is not asking him to stop. She is telling him that God has stopped him, and that she is the stopping, and inviting him to recognise it.

Then the phrase: from bloodguilt, and from saving with your own hand. Those two are the same sin here. Taking what is yours by your own arm, rather than waiting for the God who promised it, is exactly what he refused to do in the cave — and she names it in the language he himself would have used.

Then comes the promise of a sure house. She is standing on a mountain track in front of a fugitive with a price on his head, and she tells him God will build him a lasting dynasty. That is not a compliment. That is the promise Nathan will carry to the palace years later, in almost these words: the LORD will make you a house... and your kingdom shall be made sure forever before me (2 Sam. 7:11-16).

A sheep farmer's wife says it first, on a hillside, to a man who is at that moment riding to commit murder.

Two images, and the second is startling.

Bound in the bundle of the living. The picture is of valuables tied up in a cloth and kept close — the way a traveller carried what he could not afford to lose. Your life, she says, is in God's bundle, tied at his belt. Nothing gets at it without going through him.

Then she uses a sling, of all images, to this man.

Everyone in Israel knew what David had done with a sling in the Valley of Elah, and she picks the one image in the language guaranteed to reach him, and turns it round: you did that once, and God will do it for you now. Put the stone down.

She has taken his measure completely, and she is using it to save lives.

She keeps one line for herself, at the end, after everything else.

Here is the argument that actually lands, and here is why.

She does not tell him this would be wrong, though it would be. She does not appeal to his pity for the servants, though she could. She argues forward, into the reign he is going to have, and asks what he will have to carry into it.

There will be a throne. There will be a day when God has done everything he promised. And on that day, she says, you do not want to be a king who remembers a hillside full of dead shepherds killed over a rude answer. You will have pangs of conscience, and you will have them forever, and they will be in the room with you when you sit down.

That is the wisest thing anybody says to David in this book. She is not asking him to be nicer. She is asking him to think about the man he will have to be, and to protect that man from the man he is being today.

Keep that for the next time a person is owed something and can take it. The question is not only whether the thing is deserved. It is what you will be carrying afterwards, and for how long.
verseByVerse.note: “Nabal” means “fool” (ESV note).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 32–44 — His Heart Died Within Him
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: David blesses God for Abigail and turns back (vv. 32-35). Nabal hears the news and his heart dies within him, and the LORD strikes him (vv. 36-38). David marries Abigail (vv. 39-42), and two flat notes end the chapter (vv. 43-44).
verseByVerse.theology: In these verses David learns that God can deal with a wrong without his help, a lesson he will need in the next chapter.
verseByVerse.examples: The chapter that began with a death ends with a marriage, and with two notes showing that David's household is not yet in order.

verseByVerse.quote: And David said to Abigail, "Blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel, who sent you this day to meet me! Blessed be your discretion, and blessed be you, who have kept me this day from bloodguilt and from working salvation with my own hand! For as surely as the LORD, the God of Israel, lives, who has restrained me from hurting you, unless you had hurried and come to meet me, truly by morning there had not been left to Nabal so much as one male." Then David received from her hand what she had brought him. And he said to her, "Go up in peace to your house. See, I have obeyed your voice, and I have granted your petition." And Abigail came to Nabal, and behold, he was holding a feast in his house, like the feast of a king. And Nabal's heart was merry within him, for he was very drunk. So she told him nothing at all until the morning light. In the morning, when the wine had gone out of Nabal, his wife told him these things, and his heart died within him, and he became as a stone. And about ten days later the LORD struck Nabal, and he died.
verseByVerse.commentary:
His first word is about God.

Not an agreement, and not a word of thanks — those come next. First: who sent you. He recognises inside about ten seconds that the woman standing in the road with a hundred bunches of raisins is God's answer to a prayer nobody prayed, and he says so out loud before he says anything else.

Then her, by name and by quality — and he takes her exact phrase and repeats it back.

From bloodguilt and from working salvation with my own hand. That is her sentence from verse 26, almost word for word, and his using it is the sign that he has understood.

He is also being uncommonly honest. He does not say "I had it under control". He says this woman prevented him, and blesses her for it. There is a particular strength required to say thank you to somebody who has just stopped you doing something dreadful, and most people cannot manage it in the moment.

He confirms it. He would have done it. There is no minimising afterwards.

Then he says I have obeyed your voice. The word is the ordinary one for obeying. The commander of six hundred men tells a woman he came to kill that he has done as she said, and does not appear to find it difficult.

Set that against another man in this book who was asked whether he had obeyed a voice, and said he had, and had not (15:20-22).

Nabal's feast is like the feast of a king, so the refusal had no excuse behind it. The man who would not spare bread and water and meat for the soldiers who guarded his flocks is at that hour throwing a banquet fit for a monarch on the same supplies, and is too drunk to be told that his life was saved a few hours ago.

She tells him nothing until he is sober, which is judgment as well as prudence: there is no point saying anything true to a man in that condition.

Something breaks in him when he hears it.

The description is medical enough to be recognisable — perhaps a stroke, on hearing how close he came — and it is written in language that also says something about the man. His heart died within him. He became as a stone. The narrator has been telling us what Nabal was since verse 3, and this is the physical form of it.

The vengeance David rode out to take is taken, ten days later, by somebody else.

The writer says who did it and does not hedge: the LORD struck Nabal. That is the same verb used of God's judgments elsewhere in the book, and it settles what has just happened.

This is Abigail's whole argument proved. David wanted Nabal dead. Nabal is dead. And David's hands are clean, and he has nothing to carry to the throne, and he never had to lift a finger. He got the outcome without the guilt, purely because a woman stood in the road and he listened.

It is what Paul means: never avenge yourselves, but leave it to the wrath of God... Vengeance is mine, I will repay, says the Lord (Rom. 12:19). The promise is not that the wrong will be ignored. It is that it will be dealt with by somebody whose hands can afford it.

verseByVerse.quote: When David heard that Nabal was dead, he said, "Blessed be the LORD who has avenged the insult I received at the hand of Nabal, and has kept back his servant from wrongdoing. The LORD has returned the evil of Nabal on his own head." Then David sent and spoke to Abigail, to take her as his wife. When the servants of David came to Abigail at Carmel, they said to her, "David has sent us to you to take you to him as his wife." And she rose and bowed with her face to the ground and said, "Behold, your handmaid is a servant to wash the feet of the servants of my lord." And Abigail hurried and rose and mounted a donkey, and her five young women attended her. She followed the messengers of David and became his wife. David also took Ahinoam of Jezreel, and both of them became his wives. Saul had given Michal his daughter, David's wife, to Palti the son of Laish, who was of Gallim.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He blesses God twice, and for two different things.

For the judgment: the LORD who has avenged the insult I received. He does not pretend he did not want this. He wanted it very much and rode out with four hundred men to arrange it.

And for the restraint: has kept back his servant from wrongdoing. He is as glad about the second as the first, and the order in which he says them shows he has grasped which of the two he was closer to losing.

He asks her to marry him in the same breath.

The narrator lets the two sentences stand next to each other without a syllable of comment, and a reader can make of the speed what they like. What is certain is that David has correctly identified the most valuable person he has met in years.

She is consistent to the end: the woman who took the blame that was not hers offers to wash feet.

And she goes. Out of a large estate and a settled position, into a wilderness with a hunted man and six hundred soldiers, with five servants and no security whatever. She is taken captive at Ziklag before this is over (30:5).

She had told him on the road that God would build him a sure house. She now goes and lives as though she believed it.

The chapter ends on two flat notes and no comment at all.

There is another wife, Ahinoam, mentioned for the first time as an established fact. And Michal — who loved him, who let him down through the window with a rope and put an idol in his bed — has been handed by her father to another man, as though the marriage had never happened. Saul is dissolving the connection by force.

Both notes are reported the way this writer reports everything: what happened, without approval or disapproval. He described Gideon's ephod the same way, and Jacob's two wives, and left the reader to notice. Silence here is not endorsement. David now has three wives, one of them given away by her father in his absence, and the wreckage that multiple marriages make in his household is a large part of the story of 2 Samuel — Amnon and Absalom and Adonijah are all sons of different mothers.

It is a strange ending to a chapter about restraint, and it is honest. The man who was talked out of a massacre one week is not a finished article by the next. Scripture keeps saying this about its heroes and refuses to tidy them.

26.title: David Spares Saul Again
26.text: <sup>1</sup>Then the Ziphites came to Saul at Gibeah, saying, "Is not David hiding himself on the hill of Hachilah, which is on the east of Jeshimon?"<sup>2</sup>So Saul arose and went down to the wilderness of Ziph with three thousand chosen men of Israel to seek David in the wilderness of Ziph.<sup>3</sup>And Saul encamped on the hill of Hachilah, which is beside the road on the east of Jeshimon. But David remained in the wilderness. When he saw that Saul came after him into the wilderness,<sup>4</sup>David sent out spies and learned that Saul had indeed come.<sup>5</sup>Then David rose and came to the place where Saul had encamped. And David saw the place where Saul lay, with Abner the son of Ner, the commander of his army. Saul was lying within the encampment, while the army was encamped around him.<sup>6</sup>Then David said to Ahimelech the Hittite, and to Joab's brother Abishai the son of Zeruiah, "Who will go down with me into the camp to Saul?" And Abishai said, "I will go down with you."<sup>7</sup>So David and Abishai went to the army by night. And there lay Saul sleeping within the encampment, with his spear stuck in the ground at his head, and Abner and the army lay around him.<sup>8</sup>Then Abishai said to David, "God has given your enemy into your hand this day. Now please let me pin him to the earth with one stroke of the spear, and I will not strike him twice."<sup>9</sup>But David said to Abishai, "Do not destroy him, for who can put out his hand against the LORD's anointed and be guiltless?"<sup>10</sup>And David said, "As the LORD lives, the LORD will strike him, or his day will come to die, or he will go down into battle and perish.<sup>11</sup>The LORD forbid that I should put out my hand against the LORD's anointed. But take now the spear that is at his head and the jar of water, and let us go."<sup>12</sup>So David took the spear and the jar of water from Saul's head, and they went away. No man saw it or knew it, nor did any awake, for they were all asleep, because a deep sleep from the LORD had fallen upon them.<sup>13</sup>Then David went over to the other side and stood far off on the top of the hill, with a great space between them.<sup>14</sup>And David called to the army, and to Abner the son of Ner, saying, "Will you not answer, Abner?" Then Abner answered, "Who are you who calls to the king?"<sup>15</sup>And David said to Abner, "Are you not a man? Who is like you in Israel? Why then have you not kept watch over your lord the king? For one of the people came in to destroy the king your lord.<sup>16</sup>This thing that you have done is not good. As the LORD lives, you deserve to die, because you have not kept watch over your lord, the LORD's anointed. And now see where the king's spear is and the jar of water that was at his head."<sup>17</sup>Saul recognized David's voice and said, "Is this your voice, my son David?" And David said, "It is my voice, my lord, O king."<sup>18</sup>And he said, "Why does my lord pursue after his servant? For what have I done? What evil is on my hands?<sup>19</sup>Now therefore let my lord the king hear the words of his servant. If it is the LORD who has stirred you up against me, may he accept an offering, but if it is men, may they be cursed before the LORD, for they have driven me out this day that I should have no share in the heritage of the LORD, saying, 'Go, serve other gods.'<sup>20</sup>Now therefore, let not my blood fall to the earth away from the presence of the LORD, for the king of Israel has come out to seek a single flea like one who hunts a partridge in the mountains."<sup>21</sup>Then Saul said, "I have sinned. Return, my son David, for I will no more do you harm, because my life was precious in your eyes this day. Behold, I have acted foolishly, and have made a great mistake."<sup>22</sup>And David answered and said, "Here is the spear, O king! Let one of the young men come over and take it.<sup>23</sup>The LORD rewards every man for his righteousness and his faithfulness, for the LORD gave you into my hand today, and I would not put out my hand against the LORD's anointed.<sup>24</sup>Behold, as your life was precious this day in my sight, so may my life be precious in the sight of the LORD, and may he deliver me out of all tribulation."<sup>25</sup>Then Saul said to David, "Blessed be you, my son David! You will do many things and will succeed in them." So David went his way, and Saul returned to his place.
26.overview:
The Ziphites inform a second time, and Saul comes out again with three thousand chosen men, not long after weeping on a hillside and conceding the throne. But this chapter is not a repeat of chapter 24. At Engedi the opportunity walked into the cave where David was hiding. Here he goes looking for it, walks into the camp at night on purpose, and still refuses to strike.

Abishai, David's nephew, reads the moment as God's gift; David answers that God has his own ways of ending Saul's life and needs no help from him. Across the valley at dawn David shames Abner, pleads with Saul, and hears the clearest confession Saul ever makes. Then David went his way, and Saul returned to his place, and they never meet again.
26.theology:
A settled conviction, not a lost nerve. At Engedi David had two minutes to decide. Here he spends most of a day building the opportunity and then declines it, which settles that what he said in the cave was principle and not panic. God really had opened the door, putting the whole camp into a deep sleep from the LORD (v. 12), and the opening still did not license what Abishai wanted. Easy is not the same as right, and God is never short of ways to keep his promises without our breaking faith (v. 10).

The kingdom not seized (vv. 8-11). The Son of David faced the same offer and gave the same answer. Satan showed him all the kingdoms of the world and offered a short way to the throne, and he refused it (Matthew 4:8–10). In Gethsemane a loyal follower drew a sword as Abishai wanted to use the spear, and Jesus told him to put it away: he could have called on more than twelve legions of angels, but the Scriptures had to be fulfilled (Matthew 26:52–54). David waited for the crown God had promised; Christ received his kingdom by way of a cross, from the Father's hand. We seldom wait as well as David did here, and Christ's perfect patience is counted to those who trust him; his Spirit is the one who teaches us to wait.

Exile as idolatry (v. 19). To be squeezed out of Israel is to be squeezed away from the altar, the sacrifices and the feasts. David feels that loss as a spiritual danger and not merely a political one, which is why his move to Philistia in the next chapter is such a fall.

Knowing is not yielding (vv. 21-25). Saul understands his position better than almost anyone in Scripture. He confesses, blesses David and foretells his success, then goes home unchanged. David, for his part, answers him with courtesy and without revenge, yet keeps his distance. Mercy toward someone and trust in them are separate things, and Scripture lets us hold the first without the second.
26.examples:
Then: Two men walked into a camp of three thousand soldiers at night, stood over the sleeping king with his own spear planted beside his head, and one of them asked permission to use it. The other said no, took the spear and the water jar, and shouted across the valley at dawn to give them back.

Now: An open door is not an instruction, and the fact that something has become easy is not evidence that it has become right. The believer can afford to wait because the outcome is already in the hands of the God who has promised and kept his word to us in Christ. Verse 22 adds the other half: forgiving somebody and trusting them again are two different decisions. David spared Saul and gave him back his weapon, and sent a boy to carry it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–12 — A Deep Sleep from the LORD
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Ziphites inform on David a second time and Saul comes out again (vv. 1-2). David sends spies, confirms the camp, and goes down into it at night with Abishai, where Saul lies asleep with his spear stuck in the ground by his head (vv. 3-7). Abishai asks leave to strike once (v. 8); David refuses (vv. 9-11), and they walk out with the spear and the water jar through a camp the LORD has put to sleep (v. 12).
verseByVerse.theology: Three times in four chapters somebody reads a circumstance as a divine licence (Saul at Keilah, David's men in the cave, Abishai here), and not one of them asks God anything.
verseByVerse.examples: When something we want suddenly becomes possible, the question is still what God has said, not what the circumstances seem to say.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the Ziphites came to Saul at Gibeah, saying, "Is not David hiding himself on the hill of Hachilah, which is on the east of Jeshimon?" So Saul arose and went down to the wilderness of Ziph with three thousand chosen men of Israel to seek David in the wilderness of Ziph. And Saul encamped on the hill of Hachilah, which is beside the road on the east of Jeshimon. But David remained in the wilderness. When he saw that Saul came after him into the wilderness, David sent out spies and learned that Saul had indeed come. Then David rose and came to the place where Saul had encamped. And David saw the place where Saul lay, with Abner the son of Ner, the commander of his army. Saul was lying within the encampment, while the army was encamped around him. Then David said to Ahimelech the Hittite, and to Joab's brother Abishai the son of Zeruiah, "Who will go down with me into the camp to Saul?" And Abishai said, "I will go down with you." So David and Abishai went to the army by night. And there lay Saul sleeping within the encampment, with his spear stuck in the ground at his head, and Abner and the army lay around him. Then Abishai said to David, "God has given your enemy into your hand this day. Now please let me pin him to the earth with one stroke of the spear, and I will not strike him twice." But David said to Abishai, "Do not destroy him, for who can put out his hand against the LORD's anointed and be guiltless?" And David said, "As the LORD lives, the LORD will strike him, or his day will come to die, or he will go down into battle and perish. The LORD forbid that I should put out my hand against the LORD's anointed. But take now the spear that is at his head and the jar of water, and let us go." So David took the spear and the jar of water from Saul's head, and they went away. No man saw it or knew it, nor did any awake, for they were all asleep, because a deep sleep from the LORD had fallen upon them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Ziphites again (v. 1). The same men, the same journey, almost the same sentence as at 23:19. Nobody is paying them and nobody has threatened them; they simply keep informing on their own tribesman because he is losing and the king is not. Loyalty to the winning side dressed up as loyalty to the crown is an old habit, and the Ziphites have it badly.

Three thousand chosen men (v. 2). He has just wept on a hillside and confessed that David would certainly be king. He is out again with the same army.

David sent out spies (vv. 3-5). Here is the difference between this chapter and chapter 24. At Engedi the opportunity walked in on him and he had about two minutes to decide. Here he sends out reconnaissance, confirms the report, and personally observes where the king is sleeping and where the commander is lying beside him. He builds the opportunity himself, with care, over what must have been most of a day.

Refusing something that lands in your lap is one thing. Constructing it and then refusing it is another, and it shows that what David said in the cave was not a loss of nerve but a settled conviction about who gives kingdoms.

Abishai (v. 6). Two men are asked and one answers, David's nephew. Zeruiah is David's sister, and her sons are going to be a recurring problem for the rest of David's life: magnificent soldiers who solve every difficulty the same way. Years later David will say, these men, the sons of Zeruiah, are more severe than I (2 Sam. 3:39). Here is the first sample of it.

His spear stuck in the ground (v. 7). The narrator has had that spear in Saul's hand twice in his house, at the tamarisk tree, and flying across the table at Jonathan. Here it is planted beside his head while he sleeps, probably to mark the royal place. It is the emblem of his kingship, and it is about to be carried off by a man he is hunting, who could just as easily have driven it into the ground through him.

God has given your enemy (v. 8). Saul said it at Keilah: God has given him into my hand (23:7). David's men said it in the cave: here is the day of which the LORD said (24:4). Three different mouths on three different sides, each looking at circumstances that suit him and announcing what God is doing, while there is an ephod in David's camp through which God could have been asked.
