I will not strike him twice is a professional telling his commander that one thrust will be enough, and quietly offering to be the one who does it so that David's own hand stays clean.

Who can put out his hand (v. 9). The same principle as the cave, and no more explanation than last time. He does not argue that Saul deserves better, or that it would be impolitic, or that they would be caught. Oil was poured on that head at God's word; nobody unpours it with a spear.

The LORD will strike him (v. 10). This is new, and it is the deepest thing David says in either chapter. He is not merely refusing to kill Saul. He is saying that Saul's end is already appointed, that God has more than one way of doing it, and that not one of those ways requires David's help: God strikes him, or he simply reaches the end of his life, or he goes down in battle. The third comes true, five chapters from here: on Mount Gilboa the archers find Saul, his sons are killed around him, and he falls on his own sword (31:1-6). David names the manner of it standing over him in the dark with a spear in reach. Anybody waiting for God to deal with someone should carry that sentence. God is not short of methods, and he has never once needed a believer to break faith in order to get something done.

The spear and the jar (v. 11). He takes the two things a soldier keeps closest: his weapon and his water. Either one, shown across a valley in the morning, says more than any speech about where David could have been in the night.

A deep sleep from the LORD (v. 12). Three thousand men, a posted watch, and Abner beside the king, every one of them unconscious because God put them under, with the word used of the sleep that fell on Adam. God arranged the whole opportunity, and it still did not mean what Abishai said it meant. That is the lesson of these three chapters together, put as plainly as it can be put: God may open a door in front of you for a reason entirely different from the one you assume, and the opening is not the instruction. He set that camp asleep so that David could prove he would not do it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–20 — Like One Who Hunts a Partridge
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: David crosses the valley and shouts, first at Abner for failing to guard the king, holding up the spear as proof (vv. 13-16), then to Saul, who knows his voice. What has he done? They have driven him from the heritage of the LORD, and the king hunts a single flea like a partridge in the mountains (vv. 17-20).
verseByVerse.theology: The rebuke to Abner humiliates the commander for a genuine failure and proves David's case by the same stroke: the spear in his hand shows the king was his to take, and he did not take him.
verseByVerse.examples: Being cut off from the place of worship is a real loss, and David does not pretend otherwise. Christians kept from church by illness, distance or hostility can say so honestly to God, as he did.

verseByVerse.quote: Then David went over to the other side and stood far off on the top of the hill, with a great space between them. And David called to the army, and to Abner the son of Ner, saying, "Will you not answer, Abner?" Then Abner answered, "Who are you who calls to the king?" And David said to Abner, "Are you not a man? Who is like you in Israel? Why then have you not kept watch over your lord the king? For one of the people came in to destroy the king your lord. This thing that you have done is not good. As the LORD lives, you deserve to die, because you have not kept watch over your lord, the LORD's anointed. And now see where the king's spear is and the jar of water that was at his head." Saul recognized David's voice and said, "Is this your voice, my son David?" And David said, "It is my voice, my lord, O king." And he said, "Why does my lord pursue after his servant? For what have I done? What evil is on my hands? Now therefore let my lord the king hear the words of his servant. If it is the LORD who has stirred you up against me, may he accept an offering, but if it is men, may they be cursed before the LORD, for they have driven me out this day that I should have no share in the heritage of the LORD, saying, 'Go, serve other gods.' Now therefore, let not my blood fall to the earth away from the presence of the LORD, for the king of Israel has come out to seek a single flea like one who hunts a partridge in the mountains."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Far off on the top of the hill (v. 13). He puts a valley between himself and three thousand men before he says a word, which is simple good sense.

Will you not answer, Abner (v. 14). He addresses the commander before the king, and the whole camp is listening, and the mockery that follows is deliberate and not empty.

Are you not a man? Who is like you in Israel? Abner is the commander-in-chief and Saul's own cousin, the most senior soldier in the kingdom. And he slept while two men walked into the middle of his camp and stood over the king, close enough to have ended the reign with one thrust.

See where the king's spear is (v. 16). He calls Saul the LORD's anointed, to Abner, in front of the army, using the phrase that is his own reason for not killing him. He is telling three thousand soldiers, without saying it directly, that he holds their king's person sacred while their own commander could not stay awake. And the proof of the accusation and the proof of David's innocence are the same object: he has the spear, therefore the guard failed, therefore he could have used it, therefore he did not.

Is this your voice (v. 17). Word for word what Saul said at Engedi (24:16). The writer lays the two scenes on top of each other so that the differences show.

If it is the LORD (vv. 18-19). He divides the possibilities honestly. If God is behind this, there is sin in him somewhere he cannot see, and he will bring a sacrifice and be forgiven and the matter is closed. He is prepared to entertain that he is the problem, which is a remarkable thing for a hunted man to say to his hunter. He also knows where forgiveness is found: in the offering God appointed, not in self-justification. If it is men, the informers, let them answer for it. How could the LORD stir Saul up? David allows that God may be judging him, as God had sent a harmful spirit on Saul (16:14); God rules even the hostility of the wicked without being its author.

Go, serve other gods (v. 19). Here is the thing that actually hurts, and it is not the running or the caves. Nobody has said those words to David. But Israel is the land where the altar is, where sacrifice is offered and the feasts are kept, and to be driven out of it is to be pushed out of reach of the means of grace, into countries where every shrine belongs to somebody else. He treats the two as the same sentence, and in his world they were. Exile is not mere homesickness: he says it is as good as being ordered into idolatry, and the next chapter, where he goes to live among the Philistines, shows how real that danger was.

A single flea, a partridge (v. 20). Both images belittle him on purpose. A single flea is what he called himself at Engedi. The partridge is a picture anybody in that country would recognise: the way you take one is to chase it until it cannot fly any more, because it can only manage short bursts: you do not out-fly it, you exhaust it. He is saying in public that he is being worn out on purpose by a man with three thousand soldiers and nothing better to do.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 21–25 — So David Went His Way
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Saul confesses as plainly as he ever will (v. 21). David does not return; he tells him to send a young man for the spear (v. 22), commits himself to the LORD who rewards righteousness and faithfulness, and prays that his own life be precious in God's sight (vv. 23-24). Saul blesses him, and they part for the last time (v. 25).
verseByVerse.theology: Saul finally uses Samuel's word about himself, and it is still not repentance, because nothing changes.
verseByVerse.examples: David believes the confession enough to answer it and not enough to walk within arm's length of the man who made it, and he is right.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Saul said, "I have sinned. Return, my son David, for I will no more do you harm, because my life was precious in your eyes this day. Behold, I have acted foolishly, and have made a great mistake." And David answered and said, "Here is the spear, O king! Let one of the young men come over and take it. The LORD rewards every man for his righteousness and his faithfulness, for the LORD gave you into my hand today, and I would not put out my hand against the LORD's anointed. Behold, as your life was precious this day in my sight, so may my life be precious in the sight of the LORD, and may he deliver me out of all tribulation." Then Saul said to David, "Blessed be you, my son David! You will do many things and will succeed in them." So David went his way, and Saul returned to his place.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I have sinned (v. 21). It is the clearest thing he ever says, and every clause of it is true. Not "mistakes were made": he names it as sin, in the first person. And I have acted foolishly has a history: Samuel said it to him at Gilgal after the unlawful sacrifice, you have done foolishly. You have not kept the command of the LORD your God (13:13). By now the kingdom has been torn away, a priestly town has been massacred, and his son has told his enemy he will be king. Still nothing changes, which is why the confession is not repentance. Within two chapters he will be at a medium's house at Endor, consulting the dead, on the night before he dies.

Here is the spear (v. 22). It is the most eloquent thing in the chapter, and it is a piece of logistics. He does not walk down the hill and hand it to Saul, and he does not accept the invitation to return. Send a boy for it. He has just heard a confession he believes, from a man weeping and calling him son, and he will not come within arm's length of him. Two chapters ago he heard the same words and went up to the stronghold instead of going home. He has learned exactly what Saul's remorse is worth: real while it lasts, and worth nothing tomorrow. Discernment about a person is not bitterness toward them: complete courtesy, no revenge, and no putting himself in Saul's power again, both at once.

The LORD gave you into my hand (v. 23). He says it a second time. He never denies the providence; he only ever denied the conclusion. God really did put Saul in his hand, twice, and both times the right reading of it was a test to pass rather than a door to go through.

So may my life be precious (v. 24). The last thing David ever says to Saul is a prayer, that God would treat him the way he has just treated Saul. That is a large thing to ask, and he has earned the right to ask it twice over. It is very close to a line the Lord Jesus put into the prayer he taught: forgive us our debts, as we also have forgiven our debtors (Matt. 6:12). And deliver me out of all tribulation is honest: he is not pretending to be above it. He wants out.

David went his way (v. 25). They never see or speak to each other again. David hears about Gilboa from a stranger with torn clothes, and composes a lament for the man who hunted him and the friend he had lost. Saul's last words to David are a blessing and an accurate prophecy, which Samuel, Jonathan and Abigail had already spoken; he says it to the man's face and goes back to a kingdom he knows is not his. There is a kind of clarity that does nothing at all. Saul knows who God has chosen, he knows he is wrong, he knows he has been a fool, he can even bless the man. He goes home and dies in a battle he was warned about, having changed nothing. Knowing the truth about yourself and God is not the same as submitting to it, and Saul is the proof.

27.title: David Among the Philistines
27.text: <sup>1</sup>Then David said in his heart, "Now I shall perish one day by the hand of Saul. There is nothing better for me than that I should escape to the land of the Philistines. Then Saul will despair of seeking me any longer within the borders of Israel, and I shall escape out of his hand."<sup>2</sup>So David arose and went over, he and the six hundred men who were with him, to Achish the son of Maoch, king of Gath.<sup>3</sup>And David lived with Achish at Gath, he and his men, every man with his household, and David with his two wives, Ahinoam of Jezreel, and Abigail of Carmel, Nabal's widow.<sup>4</sup>And when it was told Saul that David had fled to Gath, he no longer sought him.<sup>5</sup>Then David said to Achish, "If I have found favor in your eyes, let a place be given me in one of the country towns, that I may dwell there. For why should your servant dwell in the royal city with you?"<sup>6</sup>So that day Achish gave him Ziklag. Therefore Ziklag has belonged to the kings of Judah to this day.<sup>7</sup>And the number of the days that David lived in the country of the Philistines was a year and four months.<sup>8</sup>Now David and his men went up and made raids against the Geshurites, the Girzites, and the Amalekites, for these were the inhabitants of the land from of old, as far as Shur, to the land of Egypt.<sup>9</sup>And David would strike the land and would leave neither man nor woman alive, but would take away the sheep, the oxen, the donkeys, the camels, and the garments, and come back to Achish.<sup>10</sup>When Achish asked, "Where have you made a raid today?" David would say, "Against the Negeb of Judah," or, "Against the Negeb of the Jerahmeelites," or, "Against the Negeb of the Kenites."<sup>11</sup>And David would leave neither man nor woman alive to bring news to Gath, thinking, "lest they should tell about us and say, 'So David has done.'" Such was his custom all the while he lived in the country of the Philistines.<sup>12</sup>And Achish trusted David, thinking, "He has made himself an utter stench to his people Israel; therefore he shall always be my servant."
27.overview:
Then David said in his heart. That is the whole of the consultation. On the largest decision of his fugitive years, a man who has a priest, an ephod and a prophet in his camp asks nothing and talks to himself, and what he tells himself is false. It comes in the week after Saul wept and swore off the hunt, when David has never had more evidence of God's care.

So he goes back to Gath, where he once escaped by pretending to be mad, and this time he is given a town and stays a year and four months. Then comes the darkest passage in the book about him. He raids and leaves neither man nor woman alive, so that nobody can reach Gath and contradict the story he is telling Achish. The lie works perfectly, and that is the trouble: Achish is sure David can never go home.
27.theology:
Fear decides alone (v. 1). Chapter 23 set a man who asked and was answered against a king who inferred and was wrong. Here David has priest, ephod and prophet, all three, precisely because Saul destroyed the priests of Nob and Abiathar ran to him, and uses none of them. Fear is a poor analyst, and it often does its best work when the pressure lifts.

Success can be a worse place (v. 4). The plan is shrewd, the safety is real, and Saul gives up. It is entirely possible to solve a problem successfully and be further from God at the end of it.

A silence that is not approval (v. 11). The writer does not comment on the killing, exactly as at Nob, and the silence is neither approval nor a space to be filled with excuses.

Why record this at all? A writer tidying up a national hero would hardly have kept verse 11. Scripture tells the truth about its heroes: Abraham lied about his wife twice, Jacob cheated his brother and his father-in-law, Moses killed a man and hid the body, Peter swore he had never met the Lord. And the same David later prayed create in me a clean heart, O God; he understood what was in him better than his readers do.

He cannot get himself out (v. 12). David has bought safety by making a Philistine king sure he can never come home. The next three chapters are God extracting him: suspicious Philistine commanders who refuse him a place in the battle line (29:3-11), and a burnt town that finally drives him to call for the ephod again (30:7). He was not rescued because he found his way back; God came after him.

The anointed who needed rescuing. This chapter is one reason Israel could never rest its hope in David himself. The anointed king, with every means of hearing God in his own camp, decides alone, lies, and sheds blood to keep the lie standing. The Son of David whom the New Testament proclaims is his opposite at each point. In his own wilderness he was offered safety and a kingdom on easier terms and would not act apart from his Father’s word (Matthew 4:1-11); he said he did nothing on his own authority (John 8:28); and when a lie would have saved his life, he told the truth and was condemned for it (Mark 14:61-64). David needed a Saviour too, and the greater David came for men like him.
27.examples:
Then: A man with a priest, an ephod and a prophet in his camp decided his future in a private conversation with himself, moved six hundred families into enemy territory, and killed every inhabitant of the villages he raided so that nobody could contradict the account he was giving his host.

Now: The decision that undid him was made in the quiet week after the crisis, alone, and the tell was that he never put it to anybody. God has not left his people to decide alone: he gives his word, prayer, and one another, and his Spirit uses all three. A decision you are reluctant to say out loud to somebody who will push back on it is usually the one that most needs saying out loud. And if, like David, you have already gone, the way back is the one he found in chapter 30: turn to the LORD your God, who has not let you go.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — David Said in His Heart
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: David decides in his heart that Saul will kill him one day and that his only escape is Philistia (v. 1). He crosses to Achish of Gath with six hundred men and their households, and Saul stops looking for him (vv. 2-4). He asks for a country town and is given Ziklag, where he stays a year and four months (vv. 5-7).
verseByVerse.theology: The verdict David reaches in private contradicts every promise he has been given, from Samuel's oil to Abigail's sure house.
verseByVerse.examples: Fear is at its most persuasive just after the danger has passed, and it is worth testing its conclusions against what God has actually said.

verseByVerse.quote: Then David said in his heart, "Now I shall perish one day by the hand of Saul. There is nothing better for me than that I should escape to the land of the Philistines. Then Saul will despair of seeking me any longer within the borders of Israel, and I shall escape out of his hand." So David arose and went over, he and the six hundred men who were with him, to Achish the son of Maoch, king of Gath. And David lived with Achish at Gath, he and his men, every man with his household, and David with his two wives, Ahinoam of Jezreel, and Abigail of Carmel, Nabal's widow. And when it was told Saul that David had fled to Gath, he no longer sought him. Then David said to Achish, "If I have found favor in your eyes, let a place be given me in one of the country towns, that I may dwell there. For why should your servant dwell in the royal city with you?" So that day Achish gave him Ziklag. Therefore Ziklag has belonged to the kings of Judah to this day. And the number of the days that David lived in the country of the Philistines was a year and four months.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Said in his heart (v. 1). Five words at the front of the verse carry the whole chapter. Count what he does not do. He does not call for Abiathar or send for the ephod. He does not ask the LORD whether to go, as he did four separate times over one operation at Keilah, and he does not ask Gad the prophet, who is somewhere in the camp. He talks to himself, and then he acts on it.

Now look at what he tells himself, because it is false: Now I shall perish one day by the hand of Saul. Saul never touches him. Not in this chapter, not in the next, not ever. In four chapters Saul will be dead on a mountain, David far away in the south, and the hand that kills Saul will be his own. The thing David is certain of does not happen.

Note the timing. This comes immediately after a hillside where Saul wept, confessed his sin, blessed him and swore off the hunt. Jonathan had told him the hand of Saul would not find him. Abigail had told him God would make him a sure house. He has just watched God put an entire army to sleep so that he could walk through it. He has never had more evidence, and this is the moment he decides he is going to die.

A man can hold together through years of being hunted and come apart in the week afterwards, when there is finally room to think, and what fills the room is not gratitude but the calculation he was too busy to make. Saul will despair is shrewd, and it works exactly as designed (v. 4); everything wrong with the plan lies upstream of its cleverness.

To Achish (v. 2). King of Gath. The last time David stood in front of this man he was alone, unarmed, recognised by the song, much afraid, and he saved his life by scratching at the gate and letting saliva run into his beard (21:12-15). He comes back with six hundred soldiers and their families, and this time he is welcomed. Remember what he said one chapter ago. To be driven out of Israel, he told Saul, was to be pushed out of the heritage of the LORD, away from the altar and the feasts and the sacrifices, and amounted to being told go, serve other gods (26:19). He knew exactly what leaving the land meant. And he goes.

Saul sought him no more (v. 4). Nothing in this chapter goes wrong for David. The safety is real, the arrangement holds, and the king of Israel gives up.

A place in the country (v. 5). The reason he gives for leaving the capital is deference. The real reason is distance: in a country town nobody watches what he does, and everything in the second half of the chapter depends on that.

Ziklag, a year and four months (vv. 6-7). He settles with six hundred households under a Philistine king, on Philistine land. The aside, therefore Ziklag has belonged to the kings of Judah to this day, is the writer reminding us that God is still working in the middle of all this. A town handed over to buy a mercenary's loyalty ends up permanently in the royal holdings of Judah. It is also where the news of Gilboa reaches David, and where he is sitting when the kingdom comes to him.
verseByVerse.note: Ziklag lay in the Negeb; it later belonged to the kings of Judah.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–12 — Lest They Should Tell About Us
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: From Ziklag David raids the Geshurites, the Girzites and the Amalekites, leaving no one alive (vv. 8-9). He tells Achish he has been raiding Judah's own territory, which is a lie (v. 10). The narrator explains the killing (v. 11), and Achish concludes that David will always be his servant (v. 12).
verseByVerse.theology: The plainest sentence in the chapter gives the motive: he leaves nobody alive because a survivor could contradict the story he is telling his patron. This is killing to protect a lie, and the writer simply records it, as he recorded Nob.
verseByVerse.examples: Amalek on the target list is not an excuse for verse 11, and the Amalekites will burn Ziklag while David is away three chapters from now.

verseByVerse.quote: Now David and his men went up and made raids against the Geshurites, the Girzites, and the Amalekites, for these were the inhabitants of the land from of old, as far as Shur, to the land of Egypt. And David would strike the land and would leave neither man nor woman alive, but would take away the sheep, the oxen, the donkeys, the camels, and the garments, and come back to Achish. When Achish asked, "Where have you made a raid today?" David would say, "Against the Negeb of Judah," or, "Against the Negeb of the Jerahmeelites," or, "Against the Negeb of the Kenites." And David would leave neither man nor woman alive to bring news to Gath, thinking, "lest they should tell about us and say, 'So David has done.'" Such was his custom all the while he lived in the country of the Philistines. And Achish trusted David, thinking, "He has made himself an utter stench to his people Israel; therefore he shall always be my servant."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Raids (v. 8). He has to live, six hundred families have to eat, and a mercenary in that arrangement fed himself by raiding. Amalek is on the list: the people Saul was commanded to devote to destruction and did not, losing the kingdom over it (15:1-23), and the people who attacked Israel at the back of the column coming out of Egypt, the stragglers and the weary first. That much looks like finishing what Saul left, but verse 11 will show that this was not David's reason. The Amalekites will come back for Ziklag in three chapters.

Against the Negeb of Judah (vv. 9-10). Every one of his answers to Achish is a lie, each chosen with care, and each names his own people. Judah is his tribe. The Kenites are the clan of Jethro, Moses' father-in-law, long friendly to Israel; Saul warned them out of the way before the Amalekite campaign (15:6). David tells the king of Gath that he has been raiding Israelites because that is the news Achish wants, and the only story that keeps him safe.

Lest they should tell (v. 11). There is the reason, given by the narrator. He kills everybody because a survivor could talk. Not for plunder, though he takes plunder. Not as judgment on Amalek, though Amalek is among them. Some defend the raids as the ban (Hebrew herem, a people devoted wholly to God in judgment) commanded against Amalek (Deuteronomy 25:17-19). But no such command is given here, and the narrator names a different motive: the ban was a sentence carried out at God’s word; this is a cover-up. Every man and every woman in those settlements dies to keep a lie standing up.

The writer does not comment, exactly as with the massacre at Nob: he states what happened, gives the reason, and moves on. There is no sentence anywhere in these five verses that softens what is described, and producing one is not a service to anybody. This is the man after God's own heart, sixteen months into a foreign country he entered without asking God a single question, killing to protect a falsehood.

Achish trusted David (v. 12). The deception is a total success, and the last verse says what it cost. Achish's reasoning is sound on the information he has: a man hated by his own nation has nowhere else to go. He shall always be my servant. So David ends the chapter secure, well supplied, trusted by his enemy, out of the land, out of reach of the altar, with the blood of whole villages behind him and no way back that he can see. He will need to be got out of it, and he cannot do it himself. The first recorded words of his enquiry after sixteen months are shall I pursue?, standing in the ashes of everything he had.

Was David’s deception of Achish wrong? He lied to a Philistine overlord, and killed every witness to protect the lie (v. 11). Scripture records it in a chapter where David has gone to live among the enemy out of fear (v. 1), and it does not commend it. Deceiving an enemy in war differs from ordinary lying, but this was a dark season in David’s life, not a model.

28.title: Saul and the Witch of Endor
28.text: <sup>1</sup>In those days the Philistines gathered their forces for war, to fight against Israel. And Achish said to David, "Understand that you and your men are to go out with me in the army."<sup>2</sup>David said to Achish, "Very well, you shall know what your servant can do." And Achish said to David, "Very well, I will make you my bodyguard for life."<sup>3</sup>Now Samuel had died, and all Israel had mourned for him and buried him in Ramah, his own city. And Saul had put the mediums and the necromancers out of the land.<sup>4</sup>The Philistines assembled and came and encamped at Shunem. And Saul gathered all Israel, and they encamped at Gilboa.<sup>5</sup>When Saul saw the army of the Philistines, he was afraid, and his heart trembled greatly.<sup>6</sup>And when Saul inquired of the LORD, the LORD did not answer him, either by dreams, or by Urim, or by prophets.<sup>7</sup>Then Saul said to his servants, "Seek out for me a woman who is a medium, that I may go to her and inquire of her." And his servants said to him, "Behold, there is a medium at En-dor."<sup>8</sup>So Saul disguised himself and put on other garments and went, he and two men with him. And they came to the woman by night. And he said, "Divine for me by a spirit and bring up for me whomever I shall name to you."<sup>9</sup>The woman said to him, "Surely you know what Saul has done, how he has cut off the mediums and the necromancers from the land. Why then are you laying a trap for my life to bring about my death?"<sup>10</sup>But Saul swore to her by the LORD, "As the LORD lives, no punishment shall come upon you for this thing."<sup>11</sup>Then the woman said, "Whom shall I bring up for you?" He said, "Bring up Samuel for me."<sup>12</sup>When the woman saw Samuel, she cried out with a loud voice. And the woman said to Saul, "Why have you deceived me? You are Saul."<sup>13</sup>The king said to her, "Do not be afraid. What do you see?" And the woman said to Saul, "I see a god coming up out of the earth."<sup>14</sup>He said to her, "What is his appearance?" And she said, "An old man is coming up, and he is wrapped in a robe." And Saul knew that it was Samuel, and he bowed with his face to the ground and paid homage.<sup>15</sup>Then Samuel said to Saul, "Why have you disturbed me by bringing me up?" Saul answered, "I am in great distress, for the Philistines are warring against me, and God has turned away from me and answers me no more, either by prophets or by dreams. Therefore I have summoned you to tell me what I shall do."<sup>16</sup>And Samuel said, "Why then do you ask me, since the LORD has turned from you and become your enemy?<sup>17</sup>The LORD has done to you as he spoke by me, for the LORD has torn the kingdom out of your hand and given it to your neighbor, David.<sup>18</sup>Because you did not obey the voice of the LORD and did not carry out his fierce wrath against Amalek, therefore the LORD has done this thing to you this day.<sup>19</sup>Moreover, the LORD will give Israel also with you into the hand of the Philistines, and tomorrow you and your sons shall be with me. The LORD will give the army of Israel also into the hand of the Philistines."<sup>20</sup>Then Saul fell at once full length on the ground, filled with fear because of the words of Samuel. And there was no strength in him, for he had eaten nothing all day and all night.<sup>21</sup>And the woman came to Saul, and when she saw that he was terrified, she said to him, "Behold, your servant has obeyed you. I have taken my life in my hand and have listened to what you have said to me.<sup>22</sup>Now therefore, you also obey your servant. Let me set a morsel of bread before you; and eat, that you may have strength when you go on your way."<sup>23</sup>He refused and said, "I will not eat." But his servants, together with the woman, urged him, and he listened to their words. So he arose from the earth and sat on the bed.<sup>24</sup>Now the woman had a fattened calf in the house, and she quickly killed it, and she took flour and kneaded it and baked unleavened bread of it,<sup>25</sup>and she put it before Saul and his servants, and they ate. Then they rose and went away that night.
28.overview:
Achish tells David to march out with the Philistines against Israel, and the bill for chapter 27 falls due. David answers with a sentence that means nothing and sounds like everything, and is promoted to bodyguard for life. He cannot get himself out of this.

Across the valley Saul looks at the Philistine army and something goes out of him. He prays, and nothing comes back. So he asks for a medium, disguises himself to hide from his own law, travels by night around an enemy army, and swears by the LORD to protect a woman doing what the LORD forbade. She screams when it works.

Samuel's word is the old word with a date attached: the kingdom is David's, the reason is still Amalek, and tomorrow you and your sons shall be with me. The last meal Saul eats is cooked in the dark by the woman he had outlawed. Then he walks back to Gilboa and takes his place at the head of the army.
28.theology:
The consequence in the shape of the sin (v. 6). Saul does pray, and three channels answer nothing. Part of that is God's own withdrawal, announced at Gilgal and final. Part of it is Saul reaping what he sowed, since he destroyed the priests who kept the Urim (see the note on v. 6).

Meaning it is not obeying (v. 10). He invokes the living God as guarantor of a woman's safety while she does what God calls an abomination. He is not confused; he enforced that law himself. And the oath is sincere: he does mean to protect her. Saul never could tell the difference between meaning something and obeying.

Was it Samuel? Godly readers have answered both ways, and the question is set out under verse 12. This commentary leans, with the narrator's plain wording, to its being Samuel, brought by God and not by the woman's craft. An early Jewish reader took it the same way: Samuel prophesied after his death (Sirach 46:20, a book outside the Protestant canon). Either way the lesson stands: Saul went where he was forbidden, got what he asked for, and it destroyed him.

Become your enemy (v. 16). The God who anointed him through this same prophet is on the other side of the field. Saul wants God's help and has God's enmity, and cannot see that they are one relationship seen from two ends. And Jonathan is in the sentence (v. 19): the righteous are caught in the wreckage other people's sin makes, and this chapter does not explain it.

A word from the dead, and a better one (vv. 11-15). Saul wanted someone brought back from the grave to tell him what to do, and what came back was only judgment. The New Testament answers that longing twice. Jesus said that people who will not hear Moses and the prophets will not be persuaded even if someone rises from the dead (Luke 16:31). And then he rose himself, not summoned by anyone’s craft but raised by the Father, holding the keys of Death and Hades (Revelation 1:18). God, who would not answer Saul, has spoken to us by his Son (Hebrews 1:2). No Christian needs a medium: the one who came back from the dead has already said what we most need to hear, and it is not a sentence but a pardon.

Courage without repentance (v. 25). The one voice Saul obeys in this chapter belongs to a medium, and she is the only one who does him a kindness. Then he walks back to a battle he has been told he will lose. He could face an army he knew would kill him, and could not face God and say he had been wrong.
28.examples:
Then: The king of Israel put on another man's clothes, walked at night around an enemy army, swore by the living God to protect a woman from a law he had himself enforced, and asked her to fetch up the prophet who had already told him everything he was about to hear again. Then he lay full length on her floor while she killed her calf to feed him.

Now: Saul is the warning for the season when the ordinary means seem to give nothing back: prayer flat, Scripture closed, no counsel available. The temptation is always to reach for something else, and something else is always findable. Two things hold in that season. God's silence toward a believer is not God's silence toward Saul, and the difference is a mediator: Christ has already been heard for us, and his Spirit keeps us asking when we feel nothing. And the illegitimate answer is still an answer, which is what makes it dangerous. Saul got exactly what he went for, and it put him on the floor.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — Neither by Dreams, nor by Urim, nor by Prophets
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Achish tells David he will march with the Philistines against Israel; David's ambiguous answer earns him a post as bodyguard for life (vv. 1-2). Samuel is dead, and Saul has expelled the mediums (v. 3). The armies face each other at Shunem and Gilboa, Saul is terrified, and when he inquires of the LORD there is no answer (vv. 4-6).
verseByVerse.theology: The three channels named in verse 6 were the lawful ways God spoke to Israel, and the man complaining that none of them answers had destroyed one of them himself.
verseByVerse.examples: David is now under orders to fight against Israel. Clever words can buy time, but they cannot undo the step that put him there.

verseByVerse.quote: In those days the Philistines gathered their forces for war, to fight against Israel. And Achish said to David, "Understand that you and your men are to go out with me in the army." David said to Achish, "Very well, you shall know what your servant can do." And Achish said to David, "Very well, I will make you my bodyguard for life." Now Samuel had died, and all Israel had mourned for him and buried him in Ramah, his own city. And Saul had put the mediums and the necromancers out of the land. The Philistines assembled and came and encamped at Shunem. And Saul gathered all Israel, and they encamped at Gilboa. When Saul saw the army of the Philistines, he was afraid, and his heart trembled greatly. And when Saul inquired of the LORD, the LORD did not answer him, either by dreams, or by Urim, or by prophets.
verseByVerse.commentary:
To fight against Israel (v. 1). There is the bill for chapter 27, and it arrives as such bills do, all at once and with no room to bargain. David went to Philistia because he decided in his own heart that he would die by Saul's hand. Sixteen months of successful deception later, his host requires what a host of that kind always eventually requires: come and fight my war. It is against his own nation, alongside the people he made his name killing, in the battle where Saul and Jonathan are going to die.

You shall know (v. 2). It is not a promise, not a refusal, and not a lie in any form that could be pinned on him. It is a sentence with two meanings, both of them true, and Achish hears the one he wants. It is also a man out of room. He cannot say no without ending the arrangement that keeps six hundred families alive, and he cannot say yes and mean it. So he says something clever and is promoted to the king's personal bodyguard with a battle coming. Somebody else will have to get him out, and in the next chapter somebody does.

Samuel had died (v. 3). The narrator puts two facts side by side, and the chapter lives in the gap between them. Samuel is dead: the door Saul would have used, closed by ordinary mortality. And the mediums are gone, because Saul removed them. That was obedience: the law is explicit and severe about consulting the dead (Lev. 19:31; Deut. 18:10-12). The writer mentions it now so that we know exactly what Saul is about to do, and that he knows it too.

His heart trembled (vv. 4-5). This is a soldier who has beaten the Philistines before, at Michmash and elsewhere. What he is looking at is not worse than what he has faced. But the man looking at it is not the man who faced it.

The LORD did not answer (v. 6). He asks. Saul does pray, and goes to God before he goes anywhere else. And nothing comes back. The three channels named are the three legitimate means by which God spoke to Israel. Dreams, as to Jacob, Joseph and Solomon. Urim, the sacred lot carried in the high priest's breastpiece, the means of asking a direct question and getting a direct answer. Prophets, the living voice, which is how Samuel had come to him for years.

Now hold that against something Saul appears not to have thought about. The Urim was carried in the ephod, and Saul had every priest at Nob killed by an Edomite because one of them gave David bread (22:18-19). The single survivor ran to David carrying the ephod, and it has been in the fugitive's camp ever since (23:6). God is silent through the Urim because there is no Urim to be silent through. That is not all of it: the dreams and the prophets are God's own withdrawal, and Samuel had told him at Gilgal that the rejection was final. But it is the pattern of the whole reign: the consequence arriving in the shape of the sin.

The silence itself is one of the terrors of Scripture, and it is not only Saul's. Amos names it as a judgment worse than famine: not a famine of bread, nor a thirst for water, but of hearing the words of the LORD (Amos 8:11). Micah says of the false prophets that there is no answer from God (Mic. 3:7). And the Lord Jesus describes men on the last day who will list their credentials and hear I never knew you (Matt. 7:23).

What must be said alongside that, because it matters enormously to anyone reading in the dark: this is not what is happening to a Christian who feels God has gone quiet. Saul's silence is the end of a long refusal, announced in advance. The believer in a dry season has a mediator whose blood speaks, and a standing promise never to be left or forsaken (Hebrews 13:5). Feeling unheard and being unheard are different things, and Saul is the second.

Saul inquired of the LORD and got no answer, yet 1 Chronicles 10:13–14 says he did not seek the LORD. The two fit together: his asking was not true seeking, and when God was silent he turned to a medium, which is what Chronicles condemns.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–14 — Seek Out for Me a Woman Who Is a Medium
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Saul asks his servants for a medium, and they know of one at Endor (v. 7). He disguises himself and goes by night (v. 8). She fears a trap (v. 9), so he swears by the LORD that she will not be punished (v. 10). He asks for Samuel (v. 11), and when she sees him she cries out, and knows who her visitor is (v. 12).
verseByVerse.theology: His servants produce a medium at once, which tells us what the purge was worth: he expelled them as royal policy, and nobody in his own household has any difficulty finding one at short notice.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 10 is the chapter in one line: an oath in God's name to protect a woman doing what God forbade, because God will not talk to him.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Saul said to his servants, "Seek out for me a woman who is a medium, that I may go to her and inquire of her." And his servants said to him, "Behold, there is a medium at En-dor." So Saul disguised himself and put on other garments and went, he and two men with him. And they came to the woman by night. And he said, "Divine for me by a spirit and bring up for me whomever I shall name to you." The woman said to him, "Surely you know what Saul has done, how he has cut off the mediums and the necromancers from the land. Why then are you laying a trap for my life to bring about my death?" But Saul swore to her by the LORD, "As the LORD lives, no punishment shall come upon you for this thing." Then the woman said, "Whom shall I bring up for you?" He said, "Bring up Samuel for me." When the woman saw Samuel, she cried out with a loud voice. And the woman said to Saul, "Why have you deceived me? You are Saul." The king said to her, "Do not be afraid. What do you see?" And the woman said to Saul, "I see a god coming up out of the earth." He said to her, "What is his appearance?" And she said, "An old man is coming up, and he is wrapped in a robe." And Saul knew that it was Samuel, and he bowed with his face to the ground and paid homage.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Seek out for me a woman (v. 7). They answer immediately: they know one. And note the verb: inquire. He has asked God and heard nothing, so he will go on inquiring, now of someone else. Endor is also on the far side of the Philistine lines. To get there he has to travel by night around an enemy army, on the eve of a battle, with his kingdom at stake. That is the measure of what he wants.

Saul disguised himself (v. 8). The disguise gives everything away. He puts on other clothes so that a woman practising a craft he made illegal will not know she is talking to the king who made it illegal. He is hiding from his own law, in order to break it, in the dark, wearing somebody else's coat. Look back at what he was. In chapters 9 and 10 he was a head taller than everybody in Israel, and on the day he was presented he was found hiding among the baggage. In chapter 10 the Spirit rushed on him and he prophesied among prophets, and people asked whether Saul was one of them. This is the same man, on a track in the dark, going to a witch.

A trap for my life (v. 9). She thinks this is entrapment: a stranger at night asking her to do the one thing that carries a death sentence. She has survived by being careful, and this is not careful.

As the LORD lives (v. 10). He invokes the living God as guarantor, to reassure a woman that she may safely do the thing God's law calls an abomination and commands Israel to punish with death. He is not being blasphemous by accident; he enforced that law. He is using the name of the God who will not speak to him as collateral in a transaction God forbade. And it is, in a terrible way, sincere. The oath is honest and the use of it is monstrous.

Bring up Samuel (v. 11). Of course it is Samuel: the man who anointed him, whose robe tore in his hand, who told him the kingdom was gone and did not see him again until the day he died. He has been told what Samuel will say, and he wants him anyway.

She cried out (v. 12). Hold on to that, because it is the hinge of the question this chapter raises. Whatever she normally did in her sessions, what happened terrified her.

Now the question that has occupied serious readers for two thousand years, and it must be put honestly: is this really Samuel? Godly men have taken it different ways, and both deserve to be heard.

Some, including several of the Reformers, have held that what appeared was not Samuel at all: that God does not put his prophets at the disposal of a witch's summons, that the dead are at rest and not subject to being fetched, and that what came up was a spirit permitted to impersonate him, or a vision God caused her to see. The strength of this view is its instinct about God's holiness: it will not have the Lord's servant on call to necromancy.

Others, and this is where the weight of the passage seems to fall, hold that it was Samuel, brought up by God's own act and not by the woman's craft. The narrator simply calls him Samuel, repeatedly, without qualification. Her terror suggests she got something she had not arranged and could not control. What is said is true, specific, and in Samuel's own manner, a rebuke quoting his own earlier words and a prophecy fulfilled in detail within a day. And it is very hard to see God permitting a lying spirit to deliver an accurate final verdict in his own name.

There is a fair reply: God once permitted a lying spirit to speak to a king (1 Kings 22:22), and demons sometimes spoke the truth about Jesus (Mark 1:24), so accuracy alone does not prove the speaker. But the narrator’s plain naming of Samuel, and her terror, still weigh heavily.

On that reading, God broke into her performance. The God who had refused to answer Saul answered him after all, not because she compelled anything, but because he had one more thing to say, and it was a sentence. The silence was judgment, and so was the breaking of it.

Certainty is not available and does not need to be. What both views agree on is what matters: Saul went where he was forbidden to go, got what he asked for, and it destroyed him.

Wrapped in a robe (vv. 13-14). That is how Saul knows him, and the robe has a history. Saul grabbed at it as the prophet turned to leave Gilgal and it tore in his hand, and Samuel said the LORD has torn the kingdom of Israel from you this day (15:27-28). The last thing Saul saw of Samuel alive was a piece of that robe in his fist. The first thing he sees of him now is the robe again.

Can the dead be contacted, and may Christians consult mediums? The law forbids it absolutely (Lev 19:31; Deut 18:10–12), and Saul died for it (1 Chr 10:13). Whatever happened at Endor was God’s exception, not the medium’s power. Séances, psychics, Ouija boards and horoscopes are forbidden to God’s people; should not a people inquire of their God? (Isa 8:19).

When the woman says she sees a god coming up (v. 13), the Hebrew word (elohim) here means a spirit or mighty being, not a deity: she saw a figure of power.
verseByVerse.note: Endor lay north of the hill of Moreh. Saul had expelled the mediums, as the law commanded.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–19 — Tomorrow You and Your Sons Shall Be with Me
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Samuel asks why he has been disturbed, and Saul explains that God answers him no more (v. 15). The answer is merciless: the LORD has become his enemy (v. 16), the kingdom is given to David because of Amalek (vv. 17-18), and tomorrow Saul and his sons will be with Samuel (v. 19).
verseByVerse.theology: Nothing here is new. Every word of it was said at Gilgal (15:26-28). The last word Saul ever receives from God is the first word repeated, with a date attached.
verseByVerse.examples: The date is exact: by the next evening three of his sons are dead on Gilboa and Saul has fallen on his own sword. God's warnings are not empty, and neither are his promises.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Samuel said to Saul, "Why have you disturbed me by bringing me up?" Saul answered, "I am in great distress, for the Philistines are warring against me, and God has turned away from me and answers me no more, either by prophets or by dreams. Therefore I have summoned you to tell me what I shall do." And Samuel said, "Why then do you ask me, since the LORD has turned from you and become your enemy? The LORD has done to you as he spoke by me, for the LORD has torn the kingdom out of your hand and given it to your neighbor, David. Because you did not obey the voice of the LORD and did not carry out his fierce wrath against Amalek, therefore the LORD has done this thing to you this day. Moreover, the LORD will give Israel also with you into the hand of the Philistines, and tomorrow you and your sons shall be with me. The LORD will give the army of Israel also into the hand of the Philistines."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Samuel's first words in verse 15 are a reproach, and they are about rest.

Why have you disturbed me? He was somewhere, and it was somewhere he did not wish to be called out of. There is no eagerness here, no gladness at the reunion, and no interest in the occasion. He wants to know why he has been troubled.

God has turned away from me (v. 15). Saul's explanation is accurate and condemns him as he says it. He is not confused about his position; he states it in one sentence, without excuse. And then: therefore I have summoned you. God will not answer, therefore I will go round him. Not "therefore I have repented", or even "therefore tell me what I must do to be forgiven". And what he wants is tell me what I shall do: tactics, on the eve of a battle he expects to lose, from a man who told him years ago that the problem was never a shortage of advice.

Become your enemy (v. 16). Do not soften it. Not withdrawn, not disappointed, not standing back. The God who anointed him through this same prophet, who gave him the Spirit and a new heart and victory after victory, is now on the other side of the field. It is a sentence the Bible does not use lightly and does not withdraw when it uses it, addressed to a man who still, at some level, wants God's help.

As he spoke by me (v. 17). Not one syllable of this is information. Samuel is quoting himself at Gilgal: the LORD has torn the kingdom of Israel from you this day and has given it to a neighbor of yours, who is better than you (15:28). The only thing added in thirteen chapters is the name. Saul travelled through enemy lines in the dark and broke his own law for an answer he was given years ago and did not accept.

Against Amalek (v. 18). Thirteen chapters later, it is still Amalek. The kingdom slipped away on one day at Gilgal, when he was given a clear command, kept the best of the sheep and the king alive, and told Samuel it was for sacrifice. To obey is better than sacrifice, and to listen than the fat of rams (15:22). And at about the time Saul is on his knees at Endor, Amalekites are burning Ziklag and carrying off the families of the man who will replace him. The nation Saul spared is not finished with the story.

Tomorrow (v. 19). He came for a battle plan and he is given a date. The word is fulfilled exactly: on Gilboa Jonathan, Abinadab and Malchishua are killed, and Saul falls on his own sword (31:1-6).

Which means Jonathan is included in the sentence: Jonathan, who defended David to his father's face and was nearly speared for it, gave away his own robe, walked into a wilderness to strengthen a hunted man's hand in God, and said you shall be king over Israel, and I shall be next to you. He dies in his father's catastrophe, on his father's mountain, and the text offers no comfort about it at all.

This is one of the places where Scripture declines to tidy the world up. Job knew it, the psalms know it, and it is not explained here. What is said elsewhere is that men and women like Jonathan died in faith, not having received the things promised, and that God is not ashamed to be called their God, for he has prepared for them a city (Hebrews 11:13, 16). Jonathan is not lost. But nothing in this chapter says so, and pretending otherwise would be dishonest to the text.

With me means among the dead, not in the same blessed state as Samuel. It says that Saul would die, not where he would go.

Was Samuel in the earth, or in some dark place? The woman sees him coming up out of the earth because Israel spoke of the realm of the dead, Sheol, as below; it describes how death looked from this side, not Samuel’s condition. Nor does the chapter teach that the dead hover near us or can be called. A believer who dies is away from the body and at home with the Lord (2 Corinthians 5:8), and no one fetches him from there.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 20–25 — She Killed the Fattened Calf
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Saul collapses, terrified and faint with hunger (v. 20). The woman comes to him and asks him, as she obeyed him, now to obey her and eat (vv. 21-22). He refuses until his servants and the woman together urge him up (v. 23). She kills her fattened calf, bakes bread, and they eat and go out into the night (vv. 24-25).
verseByVerse.theology: After he has been told he dies tomorrow, Saul's last meal is cooked for him in the dark by a woman he had outlawed on pain of death.
verseByVerse.examples: Kindness can come from unexpected people, and the writer is honest enough to record it without approving her trade.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Saul fell at once full length on the ground, filled with fear because of the words of Samuel. And there was no strength in him, for he had eaten nothing all day and all night. And the woman came to Saul, and when she saw that he was terrified, she said to him, "Behold, your servant has obeyed you. I have taken my life in my hand and have listened to what you have said to me. Now therefore, you also obey your servant. Let me set a morsel of bread before you; and eat, that you may have strength when you go on your way." He refused and said, "I will not eat." But his servants, together with the woman, urged him, and he listened to their words. So he arose from the earth and sat on the bed. Now the woman had a fattened calf in the house, and she quickly killed it, and she took flour and kneaded it and baked unleavened bread of it, and she put it before Saul and his servants, and they ate. Then they rose and went away that night.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Full length on the ground (v. 20). He goes down like a felled tree. The narrator gives both causes and does not rank them: terror at what he has heard, and a frightened man who has not eaten for twenty-four hours. The tallest man in Israel is lying on the floor of a hut at Endor.

Your servant has obeyed you (v. 21). She comes to him, which nobody else in this chapter does. And she uses the vocabulary of this whole book, obeying a voice, put in the mouth of a woman breaking the law of God, speaking to a king destroyed for not obeying. I have taken my life in my hand is simply true.

He listened to their words (vv. 22-23). They have to argue him up off the floor. Two soldiers and a witch stand over a collapsed king in the dark, persuading him to sit on a bed and take some food, and the narrator notes, in what may be the driest line in the chapter, that he listened to their words. The one voice Saul obeys in this chapter belongs to a medium at Endor.

A fattened calf (v. 24). It is the animal kept for a feast, not a casual dinner. She kills it for a man who will be dead by tomorrow evening, bakes bread with her own hands, and sets a table in the middle of the night. It is the best thing she owned, in a village behind enemy lines. Nothing in this excuses what she did, and the chapter does not offer it as a defence; the law against her trade was God's law and Saul was right to enforce it. But she is the only person in this chapter who shows Saul the slightest kindness. Not his servants until she prompted them. Not Samuel. A woman he had criminalised took a risk nobody had repaid her for, and fed him.

The writer records both things and reconciles neither, which is how he handles most people. He told us Ahimelech gave holy bread to a man who lied to him, and the Lord Jesus later cited the episode without a word against it (Matt. 12:3-4). He told us David killed villages to protect a story. He is not in the business of sorting characters into piles.

Away that night (v. 25). Out he goes into the dark, back around the Philistine lines, to Gilboa. He has been given the day and the outcome and the names, and he goes back and takes his place at the head of the army anyway. He could have run: he is in disguise, behind the lines, with a night's start, and the throne is gone regardless. It is courage, the courage of a man who has nothing left, and it saves nothing and no one. Saul was never short of the raw material of a great king. He was short of one thing from the day at Gilgal onward, and that is the whole tragedy: he would not come to God and say he had been wrong, which is the one thing God never refuses to hear: a broken and contrite heart, O God, you will not despise (Psalm 51:17).

29.title: David Sent Away from the Battle
29.text: <sup>1</sup>Now the Philistines had gathered all their forces at Aphek. And the Israelites were encamped by the spring that is in Jezreel.<sup>2</sup>As the lords of the Philistines were passing on by hundreds and by thousands, and David and his men were passing on in the rear with Achish,<sup>3</sup>the commanders of the Philistines said, "What are these Hebrews doing here?" And Achish said to the commanders of the Philistines, "Is this not David, the servant of Saul, king of Israel, who has been with me now for days and years, and since he deserted to me I have found no fault in him to this day."<sup>4</sup>But the commanders of the Philistines were angry with him. And the commanders of the Philistines said to him, "Send the man back, that he may return to the place to which you have assigned him. He shall not go down with us to battle, lest in the battle he become an adversary to us. For how could this fellow reconcile himself to his lord? Would it not be with the heads of the men here?<sup>5</sup>Is not this David, of whom they sing to one another in dances, 'Saul has struck down his thousands, and David his ten thousands'?"<sup>6</sup>Then Achish called David and said to him, "As the LORD lives, you have been honest, and to me it seems right that you should march out and in with me in the campaign. For I have found nothing wrong in you from the day of your coming to me to this day. Nevertheless, the lords do not approve of you.<sup>7</sup>So go back now; and go peaceably, that you may not displease the lords of the Philistines."<sup>8</sup>And David said to Achish, "But what have I done? What have you found in your servant from the day I entered your service until now, that I may not go and fight against the enemies of my lord the king?"<sup>9</sup>And Achish answered David and said, "I know that you are as blameless in my sight as an angel of God. Nevertheless, the commanders of the Philistines have said, 'He shall not go up with us to the battle.'<sup>10</sup>Now then rise early in the morning with the servants of your lord who came with you, and start early in the morning, and depart as soon as you have light."<sup>11</sup>So David set out with his men early in the morning to return to the land of the Philistines. But the Philistines went up to Jezreel.
29.overview:
The armies muster, and the man God anointed to be king of Israel is marching at the back of the Philistine column with the king of Gath, toward the battle in which Saul and Jonathan will die. Every part of the position is his own doing: the arrangement that kept six hundred families fed has presented its bill, and he can neither refuse to march nor march and fight.

What gets him out is not David. The Philistine commanders refuse to have the Hebrews in the line, and their suspicion is exactly right; they have thought it through better than Achish, and better than David appears to have. They quote the old song of David's ten thousands, which once nearly cost him his life and now rescues him. Achish, the most decent man in the chapter and wrong about everything, sends him home, and God has extracted his anointed from a trap he built himself, using enemy generals who did not care whether he lived.
29.theology:
Rescue through people with no interest in rescuing (vv. 4-5). The Philistine commanders are protecting a flank, not saving anybody, and they are professionally correct about the risk. The song that once made Saul throw a spear and drove David to feign madness at Gath now keeps him out of the battle line. Nothing about the fact changed; his circumstances changed, and God used the same fact both ways.

Blameless as an angel of God (vv. 6, 9). A Philistine king swears by the covenant name to certify the honesty of a man who has deceived him for sixteen months. Achish is generous, loyal, and completely wrong, and he deserved better than he got. The narrator lets the irony stand, and leaves David's reply in verse 8 open too (see the note there): it is a fitting close to a chapter of his life that began with him settling matters privately in his own heart.

What Romans 8:28 does and does not promise. David built this trap himself, and God got him out using a committee of enemy generals and an old song. But all things work together for good does not mean all things are good, or that the foolish decision was secretly wise. Chapter 27 was a failure and the bill is still unpaid. The promise is that God is not stopped by his people's stupidity, and that he works with material which has no intention of serving him.

The line God guarded at Aphek. The promise to David’s house survives this chapter only because God kept it, not because David did. Had he marched into the battle where Saul died, he would have come to the throne with the anointed king’s blood on his side of the field. The line God protected here runs to Bethlehem and to the one Son of David who never needed rescuing from a trap of his own making. He walked on purpose into the trap other men set for him, and Peter says even that was the definite plan and foreknowledge of God (Acts 2:23), so that people like David might be got out of far worse.
29.examples:
Then: A committee of Philistine generals, annoyed with their own king and quoting an Israelite folk song, refused to let David into the battle line, and so kept the future king of Israel out of the fight in which his predecessor and his best friend were killed.

Now: For anyone who has walked themselves into a corner: the exit here did not come from David, and it did not look like rescue while it was happening. It looked like being dismissed, in front of everybody, from a job he had argued to keep. Deliverance often arrives disguised as a closed door, administered by people who are not thinking about you at all. That is not a reason to make the chapter-27 decision; the cost of that is still coming. It is a reason not to conclude that a mess of your own making has put you beyond the reach of a God who keeps his promises when we do not.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The armies muster at Aphek, and David and his men march in the rear with Achish (vv. 1-2). The Philistine commanders ask what these Hebrews are doing there; Achish vouches for him as a deserter from Saul who has given no cause for complaint in over a year (v. 3). The commanders will not have it: he could buy his way back to Saul with their heads (v. 4), and they quote the song of his ten thousands (v. 5).
verseByVerse.theology: God rescues his anointed here by means of accurate suspicion from men protecting their own flank.
verseByVerse.examples: The reputation that made David a fugitive is the very thing that gets him out of the worst position of his life.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the Philistines had gathered all their forces at Aphek. And the Israelites were encamped by the spring that is in Jezreel. As the lords of the Philistines were passing on by hundreds and by thousands, and David and his men were passing on in the rear with Achish, the commanders of the Philistines said, "What are these Hebrews doing here?" And Achish said to the commanders of the Philistines, "Is this not David, the servant of Saul, king of Israel, who has been with me now for days and years, and since he deserted to me I have found no fault in him to this day." But the commanders of the Philistines were angry with him. And the commanders of the Philistines said to him, "Send the man back, that he may return to the place to which you have assigned him. He shall not go down with us to battle, lest in the battle he become an adversary to us. For how could this fellow reconcile himself to his lord? Would it not be with the heads of the men here? Is not this David, of whom they sing to one another in dances, 'Saul has struck down his thousands, and David his ten thousands'?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
At Aphek (v. 1). The writer has stepped back in time: this muster at Aphek, some forty miles south, comes before the armies face each other at Shunem and Gilboa (28:4). Hebrew narrative often groups events by subject rather than by date.

In the rear with Achish (v. 2). It is the worst position David has ever been in. The Philistine army is marching to the battle in which Saul and Jonathan will die, and the man God anointed to be king of Israel is at the back of the column with the king of Gath. He went to Philistia on his own private reasoning, without asking God, and the arrangement that kept six hundred families fed has now presented its bill. He cannot refuse to march. He cannot march and fight. And he appears to have no plan for what happens when the lines close. He does not get himself out.

What are these Hebrews doing here (v. 3). Achish defends him warmly, and every word of the defence is built on a lie. Since he deserted to me I have found no fault in him covers sixteen months of raids David reported as attacks on his own tribe, and villages emptied of every living person so that nobody could correct the story (27:8-12). The trust is total and it is manufactured.

The commanders were angry (v. 4). They are not fooled, and they are right. You do not put a foreign contingent with divided loyalties in your own line, and this foreigner is the most famous Israelite soldier alive. If he turns mid-battle your formation collapses from the inside. How could this fellow reconcile himself to his lord? is precisely the question: by turning in the battle and arriving home with Philistine heads. They have thought it through better than Achish, and better than David appears to have.

That song again (v. 5). The women sang it when he came home from killing Goliath, and from that day Saul eyed David and threw a spear at him (18:7-9). The courtiers of Achish quoted it the first time he came to Gath, alone and terrified, and he saved his life by drooling into his beard (21:11-13). Here it is a third time, in the mouths of enemy commanders, and it is the thing that gets him out. The reputation that made him a fugitive will not let a Philistine army have him in its ranks.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–11 — As the LORD Lives, You Have Been Honest
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Achish swears by the LORD that David has been honest, but the lords do not approve of him, so he must go back (vv. 6-7). David protests (v. 8). Achish calls him blameless as an angel of God but will not overrule his commanders (v. 9). David leaves at first light, and the Philistines go up to Jezreel (vv. 10-11).
verseByVerse.theology: The deception of chapter 27 has been so complete that a Philistine king calls the deceiver blameless, and swears it by the God of Israel.
verseByVerse.examples: Sometimes a door shut in our face is God's mercy, though it feels at the time like rejection.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Achish called David and said to him, "As the LORD lives, you have been honest, and to me it seems right that you should march out and in with me in the campaign. For I have found nothing wrong in you from the day of your coming to me to this day. Nevertheless, the lords do not approve of you. So go back now; and go peaceably, that you may not displease the lords of the Philistines." And David said to Achish, "But what have I done? What have you found in your servant from the day I entered your service until now, that I may not go and fight against the enemies of my lord the king?" And Achish answered David and said, "I know that you are as blameless in my sight as an angel of God. Nevertheless, the commanders of the Philistines have said, 'He shall not go up with us to the battle.' Now then rise early in the morning with the servants of your lord who came with you, and start early in the morning, and depart as soon as you have light." So David set out with his men early in the morning to return to the land of the Philistines. But the Philistines went up to Jezreel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As the LORD lives (v. 6). A Philistine king uses the covenant name, presumably as a courtesy to the Israelite he is addressing, to certify that David has been honest with him. David has not been honest with him about anything for sixteen months. The narrator sets it down and moves on. He does not tell us what to feel about it. It is simply there: the God whose name is being sworn by knows exactly what has been going on, and the man being called honest is standing in front of him.

What have I done (v. 8). Here is the hardest verse in the chapter, and the honest thing is to leave it open. He is being handed the way out of an impossible position and he pushes back, using the words the enemies of my lord the king. Which lord? Which king?

Read it one way and it is a lie sustained to the last possible inch: he means Achish, and he is protesting his loyalty to a Philistine because that is the character he has been playing for a year and a third.

Read it the other and it is exactly true in a sense only he can hear: his lord is the LORD, and the enemies of that king are the men standing round him, so that every syllable is honest and Achish hears the opposite.

It may well be that the protest is theatre, required by the part, and that David is enormously relieved; that is the reading most people take, and it may be correct. It may also be that he had genuinely lost his bearings; a man who has been lying for sixteen months is not always able to find the edge of it any more. What can be said is this: it is the last thing he says in Philistia, and it is ambiguous, and that is a fitting end to the chapter of his life that began with him deciding matters privately in his own heart.

As an angel of God (v. 9). It is about as high a thing as a man can say about another man, said by a deceived king about the man deceiving him, in the language of that man's own religion. Achish is the most consistently decent character in these chapters and he is completely wrong about everything. He has been generous, given David a town, defended him to his own officers, sworn by his guest's God, and gone on believing him against professional advice. He deserved better.

Early in the morning (vv. 10-11). The two parties separate on the road, and the chapter ends. Now stand back and look at what has just happened, because it is the point of having this chapter at all.

David built this trap himself. He lived in enemy country for sixteen months, secured his position by deception, and ended up marching toward the battle where his own king and his closest friend would die. There was no honourable way out that he could see, and by the evidence of verse 8 he was not looking very hard. God got him out, and look at the instruments: Philistine generals who would cheerfully have killed him, and an old song that had already ruined his life twice.

Anyone who has walked themselves into a corner and cannot see the exit should read this chapter slowly. The way out did not come from David, and it did not look like rescue while it was happening: it looked like being sacked. And the terms of the promise in Romans 8 matter here: for those who love God all things work together for good. The cost of chapter 27 is still to be paid, for he comes home in the next chapter to a burnt town and his wives in Amalekite hands.

30.title: David Strengthened Himself in the LORD His God
30.text: <sup>1</sup>Now when David and his men came to Ziklag on the third day, the Amalekites had made a raid against the Negeb and against Ziklag. They had overcome Ziklag and burned it with fire<sup>2</sup>and taken captive the women and all who were in it, both small and great. They killed no one, but carried them off and went their way.<sup>3</sup>And when David and his men came to the city, they found it burned with fire, and their wives and sons and daughters taken captive.<sup>4</sup>Then David and the people who were with him raised their voices and wept until they had no more strength to weep.<sup>5</sup>David's two wives also had been taken captive, Ahinoam of Jezreel and Abigail the widow of Nabal of Carmel.<sup>6</sup>And David was greatly distressed, for the people spoke of stoning him, because all the people were bitter in soul, each for his sons and daughters. But David strengthened himself in the LORD his God.<sup>7</sup>And David said to Abiathar the priest, the son of Ahimelech, "Bring me the ephod." So Abiathar brought the ephod to David.<sup>8</sup>And David inquired of the LORD, "Shall I pursue after this band? Shall I overtake them?" He answered him, "Pursue, for you shall surely overtake and shall surely rescue."<sup>9</sup>So David set out, and the six hundred men who were with him, and they came to the brook Besor, where those who were left behind stayed.<sup>10</sup>But David pursued, he and four hundred men. Two hundred stayed behind, who were too exhausted to cross the brook Besor.<sup>11</sup>They found an Egyptian in the open country and brought him to David. And they gave him bread and he ate. They gave him water to drink,<sup>12</sup>and they gave him a piece of a cake of figs and two clusters of raisins. And when he had eaten, his spirit revived, for he had not eaten bread or drunk water for three days and three nights.<sup>13</sup>And David said to him, "To whom do you belong? And where are you from?" He said, "I am a young man of Egypt, servant to an Amalekite, and my master left me behind because I fell sick three days ago.<sup>14</sup>We had made a raid against the Negeb of the Cherethites and against that which belongs to Judah and against the Negeb of Caleb, and we burned Ziklag with fire."<sup>15</sup>And David said to him, "Will you take me down to this band?" And he said, "Swear to me by God that you will not kill me or deliver me into the hands of my master, and I will take you down to this band."<sup>16</sup>And when he had taken him down, behold, they were spread abroad over all the land, eating and drinking and dancing, because of all the great spoil they had taken from the land of the Philistines and from the land of Judah.<sup>17</sup>And David struck them down from twilight until the evening of the next day, and not a man of them escaped, except four hundred young men, who mounted camels and fled.<sup>18</sup>David recovered all that the Amalekites had taken, and David rescued his two wives.<sup>19</sup>Nothing was missing, whether small or great, sons or daughters, spoil or anything that had been taken. David brought back all.<sup>20</sup>David also captured all the flocks and herds, and the people drove the livestock before him, and said, "This is David's spoil."<sup>21</sup>Then David came to the two hundred men who had been too exhausted to follow David, and who had been left at the brook Besor. And they went out to meet David and to meet the people who were with him. And when David came near to the people he greeted them.<sup>22</sup>Then all the wicked and worthless fellows among the men who had gone with David said, "Because they did not go with us, we will not give them any of the spoil that we have recovered, except that each man may lead away his wife and children, and depart."<sup>23</sup>But David said, "You shall not do so, my brothers, with what the LORD has given us. He has preserved us and given into our hand the band that came against us.<sup>24</sup>Who would listen to you in this matter? For as his share is who goes down into the battle, so shall his share be who stays by the baggage. They shall share alike."<sup>25</sup>And he made it a statute and a rule for Israel from that day forward to this day.<sup>26</sup>When David came to Ziklag, he sent part of the spoil to his friends, the elders of Judah, saying, "Here is a present for you from the spoil of the enemies of the LORD."<sup>27</sup>It was for those in Bethel, in Ramoth of the Negeb, in Jattir,<sup>28</sup>in Aroer, in Siphmoth, in Eshtemoa,<sup>29</sup>in Racal, in the cities of the Jerahmeelites, in the cities of the Kenites,<sup>30</sup>in Hormah, in Bor-ashan, in Athach,<sup>31</sup>in Hebron, for all the places where David and his men had roamed.
30.overview:
David comes home on the third day to a burnt town and no families. The Amalekites did it, the nation Saul spared, and David's own men, weeping until they physically cannot, start picking up stones. But David strengthened himself in the LORD his God. That sentence is the hinge of the chapter.

Then bring me the ephod, his first recorded question to God since Keilah, and an answer that promises more than he asked. Two hundred are too exhausted to cross the brook. In a field the rest find a dying Egyptian slave, feed him before asking him anything, and he turns out to be the one person who can lead them to the raiders. David brought back all. Then comes a quarrel over the spoil, which David settles in one sentence, and the equal share for the men at the baggage becomes a statute for Israel. Finally he sends gifts to the towns of Judah, ending with Hebron, without knowing that he is being made king.
30.theology:
