He strengthened himself in the LORD his God (v. 6). The word is the one used of Jonathan at 23:16; here there is nobody, and David goes himself to the place his friend once took him. The verse does not say his circumstances improved or that he felt better; it names a place he went. Three chapters earlier the same man talked himself out of the land by speaking to his own heart; here the same practice runs the opposite way, because of what, and whom, he tells himself about. It is not positive thinking, which has nothing outside itself to hold. And for the Christian the one he goes to is not far off: the Spirit of Christ lives in his people, and it is he who takes what we know of God and makes it hold in the ashes.

Bring me the ephod (v. 7). Nothing before Philistia, nothing at Gath, nothing on the march to Aphek, and the ephod was in the camp the whole time. It took a burnt town and a mutiny to get the question asked. And the God he had ignored for sixteen months answered at once, with more than was asked for. That is the way back for anyone who has gone quiet on God: he is not waiting to be won round.

The man his master threw away (vv. 11-15). God's you shall surely overtake arrives in the form of a discarded slave, found because four hundred men in desperate haste stopped to feed a stranger. God's promises often come through ordinary kindness done for its own sake.

Nobody earned anything (vv. 23-25). The objectors speak of the spoil that we have recovered; David speaks of what the LORD has given us, and grace settles the argument. The equal share for the exhausted becomes law in Israel, and the same principle answers the grumblers in Jesus' vineyard (see v. 25).

The shepherd who brought back all (vv. 18-24). David goes after his stolen flock, loses none of them, and then shares the spoil with men who could not fight. The New Testament draws that same shape around the Son of David. The good shepherd says it is his Father’s will that I should lose nothing of all that he has given me (John 6:39). And the victory over our enemies is won by him alone, yet the spoil is shared: Isaiah’s Servant shall divide the spoil (Isaiah 53:12), and the ascended Christ gave gifts to men (Ephesians 4:8). Every believer stands among the two hundred at the brook, worn out and given a full share.

Made king while sharing out spoil (vv. 26-31). The towns he named to Achish as his victims now receive a share of the plunder, and the list ends at Hebron, where the men of Judah will shortly anoint him king (2 Sam. 2:1-4).
30.examples:
Then: A commander stood in the ashes of his own town with his wives taken, his men discussing whether to stone him, and every human support gone, and the next thing recorded about him is where he went: he strengthened himself in the LORD his God. Then he asked God a question for the first time in sixteen months, and was answered at once.

Now: There will be a day when the people who normally hold you up are unavailable, unaware, or part of the problem, and the only thing left in the room is what you actually know about God. That day is not the time to start learning it. What David did is repeatable and unglamorous: he spoke to himself about God, in the ruins, ahead of his feelings, and then he asked God what to do, and did it. Even when the ruin is your own doing, as Ziklag partly was, the LORD is still his God, and the way back starts there. And verse 24 adds the other half: the people who could not cross the brook were not lazy, they were spent, and they got the same share. That is a rule worth having in any church, in any family, and in your own head on the days you are one of the two hundred.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — David Strengthened Himself in the LORD His God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: David comes home to Ziklag on the third day and finds it burned, the women and children carried off, nobody killed (vv. 1-3). The men weep until they can weep no more, and his own two wives are among the captives (vv. 4-5). The people speak of stoning him, but David strengthens himself in the LORD his God (v. 6).
verseByVerse.theology: Everything has gone at once: the town, the families, and the loyalty of the men. And he is genuinely responsible for leaving the town undefended.
verseByVerse.examples: When the people who would normally strengthen us are gone, the question is whether we know enough of God to say it to ourselves.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when David and his men came to Ziklag on the third day, the Amalekites had made a raid against the Negeb and against Ziklag. They had overcome Ziklag and burned it with fire and taken captive the women and all who were in it, both small and great. They killed no one, but carried them off and went their way. And when David and his men came to the city, they found it burned with fire, and their wives and sons and daughters taken captive. Then David and the people who were with him raised their voices and wept until they had no more strength to weep. David's two wives also had been taken captive, Ahinoam of Jezreel and Abigail the widow of Nabal of Carmel. And David was greatly distressed, for the people spoke of stoning him, because all the people were bitter in soul, each for his sons and daughters. But David strengthened himself in the LORD his God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Amalekites (v. 1). Of all the peoples in the region, it is that one: the nation whose survival cost Saul the kingdom at Gilgal (15:1-23). Two chapters ago Samuel named them as the reason, and at about that time they were putting a torch to Ziklag. David has been raiding them himself from this very town (27:8), so it may well be a reprisal. The unfinished business of chapter 15 comes back and takes David's own family.

Killing no one (v. 2). Nobody is dead. That is the one mercy in the verse, and it is not mercy: live captives are worth money and dead ones are not.

Until they had no more strength (vv. 3-4). Six hundred soldiers stand in a burnt town crying until they physically cannot. The phrase is not decorative: they wept to the point of exhaustion. These are hard men, most of them the distressed and indebted and bitter who gathered at Adullam, and they are on the ground in the ashes of their houses.

Abigail (v. 5). The woman who came down the mountain track with two hundred loaves and stopped him committing a massacre is now in an Amalekite column somewhere south with a rope on her.

The people spoke of stoning him (v. 6). Now everything is gone. His men, the six hundred who followed him out of caves and wildernesses for years, are picking up stones. And they are not being irrational. He chose Ziklag. He chose to march north with Achish and take every fighting man with him, leaving a town of women and children on the southern frontier with no garrison, in country he had spent sixteen months raiding. The Amalekites came for it while he was away, and he is the reason it was empty. Every father standing in that ruin has worked this out. Samuel is dead. Jonathan is about to die on Gilboa. Abigail is in the hands of the enemy. And the men are bitter in soul.

But David strengthened himself (v. 6). The whole chapter turns on it. Take the word first, because it has a history in this book. At Horesh, Jonathan, Saul's son, rose and went to David at Horesh, and strengthened his hand in God (23:16). Somebody came, took hold of a grip that was going slack, and put it back where it belonged. Here there is no Jonathan on the road, no Samuel to send for, no Abigail to argue with him; the six hundred are the threat. He is alone in the middle of a crowd that wants him dead. So he does for himself what his friend once did for him.

Notice what the sentence does not say. It does not say his circumstances improved, or that he felt better, or that he received a vision, or that he pulled himself together. It says he strengthened himself in the LORD his God, which is a location, not a mood. He took hold of something outside the situation, and the God he took hold of was still, after Philistia and the burnt villages, his God.

What that looks like in practice is written all over the psalms. Why are you cast down, O my soul, and why are you in turmoil within me? Hope in God; for I shall again praise him, my salvation and my God (Ps. 42:5-6). That is a man asking his own soul a question and then answering it with what he knows about God, out loud, whether he feels it or not. It is the deliberate act of taking what you already know to be true about God and applying it, by force if necessary, to the place you are standing in.

And for the Christian it is not a lonely discipline: the Spirit of Christ is the one who brings what we know of God home to us.

He was not always able to do it. Three chapters ago he talked himself out of the land. The same man, the same practice of speaking to himself, and everything turns on what he is telling himself, and whom he is telling it about.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: David calls for the ephod and asks whether to pursue; he is told he will surely overtake and surely rescue (vv. 7-8). Two hundred are too exhausted to cross the brook Besor (vv. 9-10). In a field they find an abandoned Egyptian and feed him (vv. 11-13), and he guides them to the raiders on condition that they neither kill him nor hand him back (vv. 14-15).
verseByVerse.theology: Sixteen months of deciding in his own heart end with a question asked standing in ashes.
verseByVerse.examples: The whole rescue turns on a man somebody threw away, cared for before anyone knew he could help.

verseByVerse.quote: And David said to Abiathar the priest, the son of Ahimelech, "Bring me the ephod." So Abiathar brought the ephod to David. And David inquired of the LORD, "Shall I pursue after this band? Shall I overtake them?" He answered him, "Pursue, for you shall surely overtake and shall surely rescue." So David set out, and the six hundred men who were with him, and they came to the brook Besor, where those who were left behind stayed. But David pursued, he and four hundred men. Two hundred stayed behind, who were too exhausted to cross the brook Besor. They found an Egyptian in the open country and brought him to David. And they gave him bread and he ate. They gave him water to drink, and they gave him a piece of a cake of figs and two clusters of raisins. And when he had eaten, his spirit revived, for he had not eaten bread or drunk water for three days and three nights. And David said to him, "To whom do you belong? And where are you from?" He said, "I am a young man of Egypt, servant to an Amalekite, and my master left me behind because I fell sick three days ago. We had made a raid against the Negeb of the Cherethites and against that which belongs to Judah and against the Negeb of Caleb, and we burned Ziklag with fire." And David said to him, "Will you take me down to this band?" And he said, "Swear to me by God that you will not kill me or deliver me into the hands of my master, and I will take you down to this band."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Bring me the ephod (v. 7). Four words, and they are the sound of a man coming home. The last recorded enquiry was at Keilah in chapter 23, where he asked four times about one operation and was answered four times. Since then: the decision to leave Israel in his heart, sixteen months in Philistia without a question put to God, the march to Aphek, the argument with Achish. Abiathar and the ephod have been in the camp the whole time. The first thing David does after strengthening himself in the LORD is to ask the LORD something, and it takes a burnt town and a mutiny to get him there.

Surely rescue (v. 8). He asked whether to go and whether he would catch them. He is told to go, that he will surely overtake, and, which he did not ask, that he will surely rescue. Not it may be that: a guarantee, in the emphatic form. That word is what the next twenty verses run on, and it is what makes the difference between six hundred exhausted men marching south and six hundred exhausted men marching south with something.

The brook Besor (vv. 9-10). A third of the force cannot go on. They have marched north with the Philistines, been dismissed, marched three days back, found their homes burnt, wept themselves to a standstill, and are now expected to chase mounted raiders across the Negeb. Two hundred reach a stream and cannot get over it. Remember them, because there is going to be an argument about them.

They gave him bread (vv. 11-12). Read the order of operations. They feed him, and then they ask him questions. Four hundred men chasing an enemy with a three-day start and their own children in his hands stop for a half-dead stranger in a field, give him bread and water, figs and raisins, and wait while he comes round. Nobody yet knows that he is useful. They do not stop because it is efficient. They stop because he is dying in a field.

My master left me (v. 13). An Egyptian slave, sick, dumped in open country three days ago and left to die. That is the whole character of the Amalekites in one line: they took the women and children alive because captives are worth money, and they threw away a slave who had stopped being worth anything, and the two decisions are the same decision.

We burned Ziklag (v. 14). He knows exactly where they went. The promise said nothing about how it would be done, and this is how: the only man alive who can find the raiders is a slave his master threw away.

Swear to me (v. 15). His two conditions tell you what his life has been. Do not kill me, which is what he expects from armed men. And do not give me back to my master, which he fears more: he has just been left to die by that master, and he would still rather face four hundred armed men than be returned. David swears it. The writer does not tell us what became of him, which is a pity, because he is one of the more moving people in the book.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–25 — So Shall His Share Be Who Stays by the Baggage
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: They find the Amalekites feasting on the spoil, and David strikes them from twilight to the next evening; only four hundred escape on camels (vv. 16-17). David recovers everything (vv. 18-20). Then the quarrel: wicked and worthless fellows say the two hundred who stayed behind should get only their families back (vv. 21-22). David refuses, and they shall share alike (vv. 23-24). It becomes a statute for Israel (v. 25).
verseByVerse.theology: The promise is met exactly. God's word, acted on, does precisely what it said.
verseByVerse.examples: A church that counts who did the most will always find some it thinks deserve less; grace counts differently.

verseByVerse.quote: And when he had taken him down, behold, they were spread abroad over all the land, eating and drinking and dancing, because of all the great spoil they had taken from the land of the Philistines and from the land of Judah. And David struck them down from twilight until the evening of the next day, and not a man of them escaped, except four hundred young men, who mounted camels and fled. David recovered all that the Amalekites had taken, and David rescued his two wives. Nothing was missing, whether small or great, sons or daughters, spoil or anything that had been taken. David brought back all. David also captured all the flocks and herds, and the people drove the livestock before him, and said, "This is David's spoil." Then David came to the two hundred men who had been too exhausted to follow David, and who had been left at the brook Besor. And they went out to meet David and to meet the people who were with him. And when David came near to the people he greeted them. Then all the wicked and worthless fellows among the men who had gone with David said, "Because they did not go with us, we will not give them any of the spoil that we have recovered, except that each man may lead away his wife and children, and depart." But David said, "You shall not do so, my brothers, with what the LORD has given us. He has preserved us and given into our hand the band that came against us. Who would listen to you in this matter? For as his share is who goes down into the battle, so shall his share be who stays by the baggage. They shall share alike." And he made it a statute and a rule for Israel from that day forward to this day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Eating and drinking and dancing (v. 16). They are having a party: spread over the ground, no watch set, the women and children of Ziklag somewhere in the middle of it. They think there is nobody left to come after them.

From twilight (v. 17). Four hundred exhausted men who could not persuade two hundred comrades to cross a brook fight from dusk to the following evening, and hold. And four hundred Amalekites get away on camels, which matters. Saul was told to destroy Amalek and did not; centuries later Haman the Agagite, whom Jewish tradition and most readers take to be of the line of Agag, the Amalekite king Saul spared, will try to have every Jew in the Persian empire killed (Esth. 3:1-6). Sin that is not dealt with when it is commanded does not stay where it was left.

Nothing was missing (vv. 18-19). The writer will not let this go by quickly, and he is not padding. Small or great, sons or daughters: he lists the categories and then says it again in three words, David brought back all. The account is being reconciled against God's sentence line by line. The promise said surely twice; the outcome is all. Every family in Ziklag got back every person they had lost. It is almost the only unmixed good news in the last ten chapters of this book.

He greeted them (v. 21). That is the first thing he does with the two hundred, and in a sense it settles the argument before it starts.

Wicked and worthless fellows (v. 22). The narrator does not wait for us to form an opinion; the phrase is the one used of Eli's sons and of Nabal. And the proposal is more calculated than simple greed. The two hundred may have their own wives and children back, and nothing else. It has the form of fairness: you did not fight, so you get no plunder, but we are not monsters. It is the reasoning of men who have decided that what they hold, they earned.

What the LORD has given us (v. 23). They said, in effect, the spoil that we have recovered. He says what the LORD has given us. That is the entire argument. If the four hundred won this, they may distribute it as they please. If God gave it, it is not theirs to ration. And he has the facts on his side: they were half dead when they started, they found the camp because a discarded slave was lying where they happened to pass, and they were told in advance that they would surely rescue. Nobody in that company earned anything. Note also my brothers, said to men who were talking about stoning him a few days ago.

They shall share alike (v. 24). The men at the front and the men at the stores get the same. Not a token for the stragglers: the same share, because the two hundred were not skiving. They were finished. They had marched to Aphek and back and could not cross a stream, and they stayed and guarded the baggage, which had to be guarded by somebody.

A statute (v. 25). A decision made by an exhausted commander in a wadi becomes permanent Israelite practice, still applied when the writer wrote. The principle turns up again in a vineyard, where men hired at five in the afternoon are paid the same as men who worked from dawn, and the owner asks: do you begrudge my generosity? (Matt. 20:1-16). The complaint in both places is identical, and so is the answer: it was never yours to allocate. There will be Christians in heaven who came in at the eleventh hour, and Christians who have carried the work for fifty years, and they will be given the same Christ. Anyone who finds that uncomfortable should read verse 23 slowly.

How can there be Amalekites left? Saul had struck them (15:7–8), yet many remain here: his campaign defeated those in his path, and others lived elsewhere in the wilderness. The language of total destruction describes a victory, not the end of every Amalekite.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 26–31 — To the Elders of Judah
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: David sends part of the spoil to the elders of Judah, a present for you from the spoil of the enemies of the LORD (v. 26), to a list of towns ending at Hebron, all the places where he and his men had roamed (vv. 27-31).
verseByVerse.theology: He calls it a present, and it is also politics of the best kind, sent while Saul is dying on a mountain far to the north.
verseByVerse.examples: Faithfulness in small and generous acts is often how God prepares what he has promised.

verseByVerse.quote: When David came to Ziklag, he sent part of the spoil to his friends, the elders of Judah, saying, "Here is a present for you from the spoil of the enemies of the LORD." It was for those in Bethel, in Ramoth of the Negeb, in Jattir, in Aroer, in Siphmoth, in Eshtemoa, in Racal, in the cities of the Jerahmeelites, in the cities of the Kenites, in Hormah, in Bor-ashan, in Athach, in Hebron, for all the places where David and his men had roamed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A present (v. 26). Having just argued that the plunder was not his to withhold from his own men, he now sends a large part of it out of his camp altogether. And the phrase he sends with it is the enemies of the LORD, not my enemies: this is God's plunder, which is exactly what he told the four hundred.

Jerahmeelites and Kenites (vv. 27-29). Two of those names should stop a careful reader. They are on the list of places David told Achish he had been raiding (27:10): his cover story, the towns he named as his victims. He now sends them a share of Amalekite spoil. The writer does not comment, as usual. But the man who lied about attacking these people is putting plunder into their hands, and whatever else it is, it is the beginning of undoing sixteen months of damage.

In Hebron (vv. 30-31). The list ends at Hebron, and 1 Samuel ends one chapter later. The last town on this list to receive a gift is the town where, very shortly, the men of Judah will give him a crown.

All the places where David and his men had roamed covers the whole story: the towns of Judah that sheltered him, informed on him, fed him, refused him, and watched him hunted. Keilah is that country. Ziph is that country. He sends every one of them a present. It is generosity and it is also politics, and there is no reason to think less of him for it. He is putting himself in the memory of every elder in the south as the man who fights their enemies and shares the proceeds, at the very hour (the reader knows it and David does not) when Saul is dying on Mount Gilboa. By the time the news reaches Ziklag, thirteen towns in Judah will have had a gift from David in their hands. He thinks he is being generous to his friends. He is being made king.

31.title: The Death of Saul
31.text: <sup>1</sup>Now the Philistines were fighting against Israel, and the men of Israel fled before the Philistines and fell slain on Mount Gilboa.<sup>2</sup>And the Philistines overtook Saul and his sons, and the Philistines struck down Jonathan and Abinadab and Malchi-shua, the sons of Saul.<sup>3</sup>The battle pressed hard against Saul, and the archers found him, and he was badly wounded by the archers.<sup>4</sup>Then Saul said to his armor-bearer, "Draw your sword, and thrust me through with it, lest these uncircumcised come and thrust me through, and mistreat me." But his armor-bearer would not, for he feared greatly. Therefore Saul took his own sword and fell upon it.<sup>5</sup>And when his armor-bearer saw that Saul was dead, he also fell upon his sword and died with him.<sup>6</sup>Thus Saul died, and his three sons, and his armor-bearer, and all his men, on the same day together.<sup>7</sup>And when the men of Israel who were on the other side of the valley and those beyond the Jordan saw that the men of Israel had fled and that Saul and his sons were dead, they abandoned their cities and fled. And the Philistines came and lived in them.<sup>8</sup>The next day, when the Philistines came to strip the slain, they found Saul and his three sons fallen on Mount Gilboa.<sup>9</sup>So they cut off his head and stripped off his armor and sent messengers throughout the land of the Philistines, to carry the good news to the house of their idols and to the people.<sup>10</sup>They put his armor in the temple of Ashtaroth, and they fastened his body to the wall of Beth-shan.<sup>11</sup>But when the inhabitants of Jabesh-gilead heard what the Philistines had done to Saul,<sup>12</sup>all the valiant men arose and went all night and took the body of Saul and the bodies of his sons from the wall of Beth-shan, and they came to Jabesh and burned them there.<sup>13</sup>And they took their bones and buried them under the tamarisk tree in Jabesh and fasted seven days.
31.overview:
Thirteen verses for the end of a long reign (Acts 13:21 gives forty years; the Hebrew numbers in 1 Samuel 13:1 appear to have been lost in copying), and no preamble at all: the Philistines fight, Israel runs, and the men of Israel fall on Mount Gilboa. Jonathan dies in half a clause. Saul, wounded by the archers, falls on his own sword, exactly as Samuel had said the night before.

The Philistines celebrate in their temples, and his body hangs on the wall of Beth-shan. Then the men of Jabesh-gilead, the town Saul rescued in his first act as king, go all night into occupied territory to bring him home. The book ends in a gap, with no coronation and David not yet knowing, but not one word God spoke has fallen to the ground.
31.theology:
Jonathan, in one clause (v. 2). The best man in the book dies in his father's lost battle, and the text records it in a list and moves on. Consequences do not stop at the edge of the person who caused them. What answers it has to be brought from elsewhere: the God who let Jonathan die on Gilboa came and took that kind of death himself, and the last enemy to be destroyed is death (1 Cor. 15:26). Death remains an enemy, not a friend, even for those it cannot finally hold.

His last fear (v. 4). Not death, but being made sport of: the same man who at Gilgal asked only honor me now before the elders of my people (15:30). It should be said without contempt. Most people know that fear better than they would like to.

Like all the nations (v. 10). Israel had demanded a king to be like all the nations (8:5), and now the nations are celebrating that their gods have won. A king was never going to be enough.

Covenant love at Jabesh-gilead (vv. 11-13). The men of Jabesh repay a night march forty years old, with no reward possible and the dynasty finished. David's word for it is hesed (2 Sam. 2:5): covenant love that keeps going after the reason for it has gone.

Not one word fell to the ground. Eli's house cut off (2:31-34); the kingdom torn from Saul and given to a better neighbour (15:28); tomorrow you and your sons; the eighth son anointed and every spear, ambush and army sent after him failing. The writer never once stops to point at a fulfilment. He trusts the reader.

Hannah's frame. He will give strength to his king and exalt the horn of his anointed (2:10), sung when there was no king in Israel. And the horn is not lifted yet: David is not the answer either (see the closing note on vv. 8-13). The horn is raised a thousand years later, when a young woman of David's line sings almost Hannah's song (Luke 1:52), and an old priest blesses God for a horn of salvation for us in the house of his servant David (Luke 1:69).
31.examples:
Then: A king's body was nailed to the wall of an occupied city and his armour hung in a foreign temple, and men from a town a night's march away walked all night through enemy country to take him down, buried the bones under a tree and fasted for a week, for a king who had been failing them for years and could never repay them.

Now: The men of Jabesh-gilead are the last picture in the book and the one to keep. They remembered one night forty years earlier when a young man came for them and the Spirit of God was on him, and they held on to that after the man himself had gone wrong in almost every way a man can. Loyalty like that, to a person who has disappointed everybody, at cost, with no prospect of return, is the nearest thing in this chapter to the love God has for people who have gone wrong. We can show it only because we have first been shown it: the Son of David came for us when we had nothing to repay.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Israel flees and falls on Mount Gilboa (v. 1). Jonathan and two brothers are killed (v. 2). Saul, badly wounded by the archers, asks his armour-bearer to finish him, and when he will not, Saul falls on his own sword and the armour-bearer with him (vv. 3-5). All die on the same day, and the towns of the valley are abandoned to the Philistines (vv. 6-7).
verseByVerse.theology: Samuel had said it the night before at Endor (28:19), and every clause of it happens, in order.
verseByVerse.examples: Grief is not always given words in Scripture at the moment of loss; David will supply them in the next chapter.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the Philistines were fighting against Israel, and the men of Israel fled before the Philistines and fell slain on Mount Gilboa. And the Philistines overtook Saul and his sons, and the Philistines struck down Jonathan and Abinadab and Malchi-shua, the sons of Saul. The battle pressed hard against Saul, and the archers found him, and he was badly wounded by the archers. Then Saul said to his armor-bearer, "Draw your sword, and thrust me through with it, lest these uncircumcised come and thrust me through, and mistreat me." But his armor-bearer would not, for he feared greatly. Therefore Saul took his own sword and fell upon it. And when his armor-bearer saw that Saul was dead, he also fell upon his sword and died with him. Thus Saul died, and his three sons, and his armor-bearer, and all his men, on the same day together. And when the men of Israel who were on the other side of the valley and those beyond the Jordan saw that the men of Israel had fled and that Saul and his sons were dead, they abandoned their cities and fled. And the Philistines came and lived in them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The men of Israel fled (v. 1). No preamble and no speeches. The writer has spent more than twenty chapters on this reign and gives the end of it thirteen verses, and the first thing he says is that the army ran.

Jonathan (v. 2). One name in a list of three, and then the narrator goes straight on to Saul's wound. This is the man who went up a cliff with one armour-bearer and said nothing can hinder the LORD from saving by many or by few. Who gave his own robe and armour and sword to a shepherd boy. Who told his father the truth about David and was nearly speared for it. Who walked into the Wilderness of Ziph while his father's army was searching it, and strengthened his hand in God. Who said you shall be king over Israel, and I shall be next to you and then went home to his father's house. He goes home to it one last time, and dies in it.

The best man in the book dies in his father's lost battle, on his father's mountain, for his father's sin. Scripture keeps declining to tidy this up. Job knew it, the psalms know it: the consequences of one man's choices do not stop at the edge of the man who made them, and the righteous are caught in the wreckage.

What answers it is not here and has to be brought from elsewhere: the God who let Jonathan die on Gilboa did not stay at a distance from that kind of death. He came and took one, on a hill, at the hands of an occupying army, and death itself will be destroyed. Jonathan is not lost. But saying it too quickly cheats the reader out of what the chapter does say. David will say the true thing about him soon afterwards: I am distressed for you, my brother Jonathan; very pleasant have you been to me; your love to me was extraordinary, surpassing the love of women (2 Sam. 1:26).

The archers found him (v. 3). Whatever else is true of Saul, he went back. He could have run in the dark with a night's start, and he stood in the line and fought until archers brought him down, with his sons dying around him.

Lest these uncircumcised (v. 4). His last recorded words are about being humiliated. The verb means to abuse, to make sport of. He is bleeding to death already; he is afraid of being laughed at. That has been the shape of him the whole way through: he hid among the baggage on the day he was made king, raged when the women sang a better number about somebody else, and at Gilgal asked to be honoured before the elders. It is a small and human thing to be frightened of, and it ruined a man who had everything else.

The armour-bearer will not do it. He refuses out of fear rather than principle, but Saul's guards refused to kill the priests of Nob too, and one of the quiet threads of this book is ordinary men declining to do what a king tells them.

Fell upon it (vv. 4-5). His armour-bearer follows him. The man had already refused an order, the king was dead, and he could have gone. At the very end there was still somebody who would not leave Saul, and we do not know his name.

On the same day together (v. 6). The sentence is deliberately flat, and it counts them. The night before, an old prophet said tomorrow you and your sons shall be with me, and here is the accounting.

The Philistines came and lived in them (v. 7). The whole valley empties. Set it beside the book's beginning: the Philistines beating Israel at Aphek, capturing the ark, and a dying mother naming her son Ichabod, the glory has departed from Israel (4:21). Israel demanded a king to fix precisely this, one who would go out before us and fight our battles (8:20). Forty years later the Philistines are living in Israelite towns and the king is dead on a mountain. A king was never going to be enough. That is one of the two things this book was written to say.

Is suicide a sin, and is it unforgivable? Taking one’s own life breaks the sixth commandment, a grave sin against the God who gives life (Exod 20:13). But it is not the unforgivable sin; that is the settled rejection of Christ (Mark 3:28–29). A true believer who dies this way, in despair or illness of mind, is not cut off from the grace that saves sinners, for salvation rests on Christ’s work, not on the state of our last moment (Rom 8:38–39). Anyone thinking of it should speak to someone today: a pastor, a friend, a doctor, or a crisis line. Your life is not worthless to God or to those around you.

For those who have lost someone this way. Grief after a suicide is often tangled with guilt, anger and questions that will never be answered. You are not the cause of another person’s choice, and you were not given the power to see into their mind. See how Scripture itself treats Saul’s death: the men of Jabesh bury him with honour and fast for him, and David’s lament in the next chapter praises him without a word about the manner of his death. The judgment of anyone’s soul belongs to the Judge of all the earth, who knows the whole of a person’s suffering and will do right (Genesis 18:25). And the Lord who wept at a friend’s grave (John 11:35) does not ask the bereaved to stop grieving, only to bring their grief to him.

Why does 1 Chronicles 10:6 say all his house died together, when a son, Ish-bosheth, survives to reign? Chronicles probably means the household on the field and the end of the dynasty; the surviving son was a figurehead who soon fell. Chronicles also says the head was fastened in the temple of Dagon (1 Chronicles 10:10); the armour went to Ashtaroth and the head to Dagon, and the two accounts complete each other.

Second Samuel 1 has an Amalekite claim he killed Saul at his request. The likeliest answer is that he lied, hoping for a reward from David, and found Saul already dead.
verseByVerse.note: Mount Gilboa overlooks the Jezreel valley.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Philistines find the bodies, cut off Saul's head, strip his armour, and send the news round their temples (vv. 8-9). His armour goes to the temple of Ashtaroth and his body to the wall of Beth-shan (v. 10). The men of Jabesh-gilead go all night and take the bodies down (vv. 11-12), burn them, bury the bones under the tamarisk at Jabesh, and fast seven days (vv. 12-13).
verseByVerse.theology: The war gear of the LORD's anointed is now a dedication in a foreign goddess's temple.
verseByVerse.examples: A kindness received long ago can still be repaid long after the giver has stopped deserving it.

verseByVerse.quote: The next day, when the Philistines came to strip the slain, they found Saul and his three sons fallen on Mount Gilboa. So they cut off his head and stripped off his armor and sent messengers throughout the land of the Philistines, to carry the good news to the house of their idols and to the people. They put his armor in the temple of Ashtaroth, and they fastened his body to the wall of Beth-shan. But when the inhabitants of Jabesh-gilead heard what the Philistines had done to Saul, all the valiant men arose and went all night and took the body of Saul and the bodies of his sons from the wall of Beth-shan, and they came to Jabesh and burned them there. And they took their bones and buried them under the tamarisk tree in Jabesh and fasted seven days.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The good news (vv. 8-9). That is what the word is, and the Philistines are the ones using it. They send runners to every town and every temple. This is a religious event to them: their gods have beaten Israel's God, and the proof is on a stretcher.

Ashtaroth and Beth-shan (v. 10). Two things, and both are the end of an argument that began in chapter 8. The war gear of the LORD's anointed is laid up in a shrine as evidence that a Canaanite goddess is stronger than the God of Israel, and his body is nailed to a city wall for people to walk past. Samuel told the nation what a king would cost, and they said no! But there shall be a king over us, that we also may be like all the nations. The nations are at this moment celebrating in their temples because that king is a trophy on a wall.

The reader has been set up for this since chapter 5. When the Philistines put the captured ark in the temple of Dagon, in the morning Dagon was face down before it, and the next morning his head and hands were broken off on the threshold (5:1-5). They tried to make the LORD a trophy once. It did not go well for them. Saul's armour stays where they put it.

Jabesh-gilead (v. 11). Of every town in Israel, that one, and it closes a circle forty years wide. Nahash the Ammonite besieged it and offered a treaty on condition that he gouge out every man's right eye, and thus bring disgrace on all Israel (11:2). The messengers came to Gibeah as Saul was coming in behind the oxen, and the Spirit of God rushed upon Saul when he heard these words (11:6). He raised the nation, marched all night, and cut the Ammonites to pieces in the morning watch. That was his first act as king, and it was magnificent, and he did it because the Spirit came on him.

Went all night (v. 12). Saul marched through the night to reach Jabesh (11:9-11), and forty years later the men of Jabesh go all night for Saul. Beth-shan is a Philistine-held city in the valley Israel has just abandoned. These men cross enemy country in the dark, take four bodies off a public wall, and carry them home, and there is nothing in it for them. The king is dead, the dynasty is finished, and no reward is coming. He had not been a good king for a long time. They came anyway.

Under the tamarisk (v. 13). The kind of tree he once sat beneath at Gibeah with a spear in his hand (22:6). And seven days of fasting, the full mourning of a household for its own. The last recorded act in 1 Samuel is a kindness done for a failed king by a town that remembered when he was good. The writer could have ended on the Philistines celebrating, or on David at Ziklag. He ends with a burial and a fast. David will send them a message: may you be blessed by the LORD, because you showed this loyalty to Saul your lord and buried him (2 Sam. 2:5). He calls it hesed, covenant kindness, the word for love that keeps going when the reason for it has gone.

Now stand at the end of the book and look back down it. There is no coronation here, no triumph and no resolution. David is at Ziklag and does not yet know that Saul is dead. The book ends in a gap.

But every single thing God said has happened, and the writer has trusted his reader to see it. Eli's sons died on one day, and the priests of Nob died at Nob. The kingdom was torn from Saul and given to a better neighbour. He died tomorrow with his sons, as Samuel said. David was anointed in front of seven passed-over brothers, and every attempt to kill him failed: the spears, the ambushes, the three thousand chosen men, twice.

The frame around the whole of it was set at the start by a woman nobody was listening to. Hannah sang at Shiloh: the LORD kills and brings to life; he brings down to Sheol and raises up. The LORD makes poor and makes rich; he brings low and he exalts. He raises up the poor from the dust... he will guard the feet of his faithful ones, but the wicked shall be cut off in darkness (2:6-9). She sang about the LORD's anointed while handing a weaned child to an old priest whose own sons were stealing the sacrifices.

Everything between her song and this grave is God bringing it about, through a barren woman, a corrupt priesthood, a captured ark, a demanded king, a rejected king, a hunted shepherd, and a mountain covered in the dead. The horn is not exalted yet, which is why the book stops where it does. There is a man at Ziklag who has been anointed and is not yet crowned, and even when he is crowned he will be a king who takes another man's wife and murders her husband, and his sons will tear his kingdom apart. David is not the answer either. The horn Hannah sang about is lifted only when David's promised son comes.

1 Samuel ends with a king dead on a mountain, his armour in an idol's temple, and a good man buried under a tree. It was always pointing somewhere else.

Why burn the bodies? They had been mutilated and exposed; burning them, then burying the bones (v. 13), may have been to spare them further desecration.
verseByVerse.note: Beth-shan was a fortress city where the Jezreel valley meets the Jordan.
